Learn SRE and platform engineering well enough to teach them

This course walks you through four books, one lesson per chapter: all 23 chapters of Site Reliability Engineering, 2nd Edition, the 10 chapters published so far of Platform Engineering at Google, and the two newest observability books on O’Reilly, Mastering Prometheus (2024) and Observability with Grafana (2024), 15 chapters each. Part I · SRE in contextChapter 1 · 6 min read

What SRE is, and the model behind it

You will learn
  • what each word in “Site Reliability Engineering” commits you to
  • the hierarchy of production health and why it replaced the old pyramid
  • a crisp answer to “how is SRE different from DevOps?”

The big picture

The name breaks into three parts. Site is the reason SRE exists: users must be able to use the product, so the work ties back to business impact. Reliability is the single thing SREs own, and that narrow focus lets them build expertise generalists can't.

1 · Sociotechnical foundationsCulture, people, how teams work
→
2 · Situational awarenessSLOs and observability
→
3 · Continuous preparednessIncidents, learning, safety analysis
→
4 · Infrastructure designAutomation, testing, capacity, data
→
5 · Resilient productsReliability designed in
→
6 · Emergent reliabilityReliable by default

The hierarchy of production health, base first. Grow it wider and taller together: don’t build the top before the base can hold it.

Engineering is the method: you solve operational problems with software and repeatable processes rather than heroics. A quick test for any project is whether it helps the business, improves reliability, and uses an engineering approach.

The book replaces the old Dickerson pyramid (monitoring, incident response, postmortems, testing, capacity, development, product) with a hierarchy of production health: sociotechnical foundations, then situational awareness, continuous preparedness, infrastructure design, resilient products and finally emergent reliability, where the platform makes systems reliable by default.

The old pyramid was mostly reactive and left culture and data integrity implicit. You grow the new one wider and taller at the same time; don't build the top before the base can hold it.

Why the old pyramid was replaced

The first edition used a pyramid drawn by Mikey Dickerson in 2013, modelled on Maslow. Interviewers who read that edition may still have it in mind, so know both and know what changed.

Dickerson’s hierarchy (2013)Hierarchy of production health (2nd edition)
BaseMonitoringSociotechnical foundations: culture and people
ThenIncident response, postmortemsSituational awareness: SLOs, observability, toil tracking, goals
ThenTesting and release, capacity planningContinuous preparedness: incidents, learning, training
ThenDevelopmentInfrastructure design: delivery, testing, data, capacity
TopProductResilient products, then emergent reliability

The book gives four reasons for the redesign. The lower layers were all reactive. Capacity planning had a layer of its own while data integrity was hidden inside “development”. Culture was assumed, not named. And nothing described the end state, where a platform makes services reliable by default.

The inverted pyramidYou don’t have to finish one layer before starting the next. Grow the pyramid wider and taller at the same time. What you must avoid is a wide top on a narrow base: clever self-healing platforms run by a team with no blameless culture and no SLOs.
Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the platform book also covers, from the knowledge map:
  • Toil: Manual, repetitive, automatable, no lasting value; keep engineering above half. See platform ch 16.
Going deeper what a full re-read of the chapter adds

Details from the full chapter

SRE is a role, not only a skill set

Any team can borrow SRE methods, and DevOps shows that works. The book still argues for a dedicated role, for three reasons.

  • It’s hard to do part-time. Feature deadlines always win the week.
  • It needs depth and breadth. An SRE sees across service boundaries, where most large outages live.
  • Reliability needs its own voice. It is a long-term investment, and the next launch will override it unless someone is accountable for it.

The stance matters as much as the role: SREs are enablers, not gatekeepers.

Three advantages of the software mindset

Objective understandingHealth is measured through SLOs and observability, and processes are derived from first principles: postmortems, STPA, CAST.
AutomationEfficiency and consistency together. It also gives you a reason to simplify, because simple systems are easier to automate.
Dev and ops integratedOne shared language and a feedback loop from production back into design.

That is why every SRE is expected to write code, even if on a given day the code is only a monitoring configuration.

Three ways to shrink an incident

LengthDetect fast, mitigate fast
→
FrequencyFollow through on postmortem actions
→
ScopeFailure domains and graceful degradation

Preparedness cuts impact along these three dimensions. On-call is a means to that, not the purpose of the team.

What each upper layer contains

LayerWhat the chapter puts in it
Situational awarenessSLOs and observability, plus two things people forget: toil tracking (no exact number exists, so use outages, ticket throughput and a rough maintenance estimate) and business alignment through OKRs and feature velocity. Without the last one SRE gets sidelined.
Infrastructure designSix areas: release management (changes are the top cause of outages, so use incremental rollouts, trunk-based development and many small releases), configuration management (GitOps, feature flags), data, capacity (load balancing, throttling, DoS protection), production testing (probers, fault injection, load tests) and observability.
Resilient productsShrink the blast radius with failure domains, horizontal scaling with failover, and graceful degradation (a page that loads without profile pictures still works). Then simplify, above all by removing circular and unnecessary dependencies.
Emergent reliabilityThe platform makes whole classes of failure impossible. Where it can’t enforce, it monitors, for example by spotting a global push in the logs. Teams rarely break rules on purpose, so teach as well as block.

AI is missing from the pyramid on purpose. The authors treat it as something that cuts across every layer, which is why it gets its own part at the end of the book.

Say it in an interview

"SRE treats operations as a software problem. That gives you three things: you measure production health objectively with SLOs and observability, you automate for efficiency and for consistency, and you share a language with developers so feedback from production flows back into design. Toil has a ceiling of 50% of an SRE's time. That's a limit, not a goal, and good teams sit far below it."

On AWSThe hierarchy maps neatly onto the Well-Architected Reliability pillar and its operational-excellence practices. Situational awareness means CloudWatch and X-Ray; preparedness means Incident Manager and game days; infrastructure design means multi-AZ, CodeDeploy, AWS Backup and FIS; emergent reliability means golden paths through Service Catalog or Control Tower guardrails.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

How is SRE different from DevOps?

Show a model answer

DevOps is a culture: developers and operations share responsibility for running software, instead of developers “throwing code over the wall”. It tells you what to value but not exactly how to do it.

SRE is one concrete way to do it. It turns the culture into mechanisms you can point at. SLOs and error budgets decide, with numbers, when to ship faster and when to slow down for reliability. A cap on toil (at least half of the team’s time goes on engineering) stops operations work from swallowing the team. Blameless postmortems turn failures into fixes. And SREs write software to automate operations away.

The book adds one more difference: SRE is a role. A small company can use these mechanisms without hiring SREs. At scale, a dedicated team gives reliability a voice that the next feature deadline can’t drown out.

A one-line version: DevOps says “share responsibility”; SRE says “here is the budget, the policy and the team that make shared responsibility work”.

Quick check: In the hierarchy of production health, what sits at the base?
Culture and people come first. Emergent reliability, where the platform makes systems reliable by default, is the top.
Your turnPick a project you finished recently and run the three-part test on it. Did it help the business? Did it improve reliability? Did it use an engineering approach rather than heroics? Write one sentence for each.
Key takeaways
  • SRE treats operations as a software problem, with reliability as the one thing it owns.
  • The hierarchy of production health starts with culture and ends with platforms that make systems reliable by default.
  • The 50% toil ceiling is a limit, not a target. Good teams sit far below it.
Part I · SRE in contextChapter 2 · 6 min read

The value of reliability

You will learn
  • how to present SRE as an investment with a return
  • what each stakeholder gets from it
  • the full cost of unreliability, beyond lost sales

The big picture

Present SRE as an investment with a return, not as a cost centre. The headline mechanism is sublinear scaling: by automating and standardising, operating costs grow more slowly than the service does. Traditional ops teams are rewarded for stability and so resist change. SRE uses the error budget so that stability and velocity are traded deliberately and both sides share the goal.

CustomersReliability is the feature every other feature depends on. Not 100%, though: that is always the wrong target.
The CFOSoftware leverage. Code runs again and again at almost no extra cost, and shared platforms spread the gain.
Product teamsObjective targets and less cognitive load.
The SRE teamProtection from burnout, including the right to hand a pager back.

Different stakeholders get different value. Customers get reliability as the feature everything else depends on (but not 100%, which is always the wrong target). The CFO gets software leverage: code runs again and again at almost no extra cost, and shared platforms like one global load balancer spread the gains.

Product teams get objective targets and less cognitive load. The SRE team gets protection from burnout; at Google, SRE can hand the pager back to a team whose service keeps missing its SLO.

The cost of unreliability is more than lost sales. There's churn, the opportunity cost of engineers firefighting, rising toil, slower velocity, expensive retrofits, SLA penalties, and a management fan-out of roughly 100 to 1000 engineer-hours per hour of major downtime once you count reviews, comms and remediation.

Systems also atrophy without investment: small fixes turn into projects, engineers grow afraid to change anything, and the spiral feeds itself.

One hour of downtime, counted properly

The chapter’s most quotable table argues that a major outage costs 100 to 1,000 times its length in engineering time. Roughly, for one hour of serious downtime:

Where the hours goEngineer-hours
Operations team managing the outage5–10
Post-incident review, timeline and bug tracking10–20
Internal communication and presentations20–50
Remediation: working through the repair itemsabout 100
Customer communicationabout 100

On top of that, rollouts slow down for weeks afterwards because everyone is cautious. The same chapter has a simple worked example for an internal system: a finance outage that idles 400 people for two days at $325 a day is $260,000 before anyone counts the knock-on effects.

A number worth rememberingGoogle’s research found that 53% of visitors give up on a task when a page takes more than three seconds to load. Slow counts as down.
Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the platform book and Mastering Prometheus also cover, from the knowledge map:
  • Error budget: One minus the SLO: the failure you are allowed, to be spent on change. See Prometheus ch 13.
  • The nines: Each extra nine cuts allowed downtime tenfold and costs far more than the last. See platform ch 16.
Going deeper what a full re-read of the chapter adds

Details from the full chapter

The startup that deferred everything

A sidebar describes a SaaS company growing revenue 200% a year while putting off basic production hygiene. The bill arrived as twelve months of all-hands catch-up work. Uptime went from 99.84% to 99.999%, which is the difference between about an hour of downtime a month and a few seconds. The operations lead joked that the recovery plan had so many phases it ran out of letters.

The lesson for an interview: reliability debt compounds, and paying it later costs a year of feature work.

What to adopt, by stage

Early stage: the cheap fiveAutomated tests, CI/CD (changes are the largest outage trigger at Google), basic observability, a simple incident process, and design reviews.
Mature organisationSLOs as a tool for strategic decisions, managing accumulated complexity, formal incident response with defined roles, and centrally maintained tools.

Six questions before you adopt SRE

  1. What are your biggest operational challenges?
  2. What resources do you have? That includes skills, and whether the culture will fall back to quick fixes.
  3. Can you start small?
  4. What is at stake if you’re unreliable?
  5. How do users interact with you? If they retry, short outages hurt less than long ones. A flash sale may still sell out during a blip and damage your reputation anyway.
  6. Is timing a factor, such as a peak season?

Smaller points that come up

  • Not every Google system has SRE support. The mission-critical ones do, and SRE can hand a pager back.
  • Traditional operations is rewarded for stability, so it resists change. SRE shares an error budget with developers, so both sides own the trade.
  • The CFO’s argument: machines are fast and cheap, people are slower and far more valuable. One global load-balancing platform serves Search, Maps and YouTube.
  • Reliability is a company-wide habit. Sales and marketing should warn engineering before a campaign. Google Meet’s growth during COVID is the example of business growth arriving without warning.
Say it in an interview

"For a startup I'd start with the cheap, high-return practices: automated tests, a CI/CD pipeline, symptom-based alerting, a simple incident process with clear roles and blameless reviews, and lightweight design reviews that look at failure domains, rate limits, rollbacks and data recovery. In a mature organisation, SLOs turn into the tool for deciding where reliability investment goes, and centralised platforms give everyone the same reliable building blocks."

On AWSBack the business case with SLA credits from your own customer contracts, AWS Cost Explorer for spend, and the time-to-mitigate trend from Incident Manager. A worked example from the book: 400 finance staff idle for two days at $325 a day is $260,000 in productivity alone.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Your CTO asks why she should fund an SRE team. What do you say?

Show a model answer

I wouldn’t start with the team. I’d start with what unreliability costs her today, in her terms.

First, what is at stake. How much revenue does a minute of checkout downtime lose? Do users retry, or leave for a competitor? When are the peak periods, and what would an outage then cost?

Second, the hidden cost. The book’s point is that one hour of major downtime costs 100 to 1,000 engineer-hours once you count the response, the review, internal communication, customer communication and the fixes. Many companies spend a large share of engineering time on incidents and repetitive operations without measuring it. Google reports production work under 15% of engineering time, with SRE under 4% of headcount.

Third, a small proposal with a measurable result. One or two SREs on the most critical service for a quarter: define SLOs, make alerts actionable, cut the top sources of toil, and add safe rollouts with rollback. Then report the change in incidents, time to mitigate, and how much developer time came back to features.

That turns “fund a team” into “fund an experiment with a clear success test”, which is much easier to approve.

Quick check: What does “sublinear scaling” mean for an SRE team?
Automation and shared platforms let the same team run far more, which is the core of the business case.
Your turnEstimate what one hour of downtime costs for a service you know: lost revenue, engineer-hours for the response and the reviews afterwards, SLA credits, and churn. Which number surprised you?
Key takeaways
  • The headline benefit is sublinear scaling: cost grows more slowly than the service.
  • The error budget turns stability versus velocity into a deliberate, shared trade.
  • Unreliability costs far more than lost sales, and systems atrophy without investment.
Part I · SRE in contextChapter 3 · 7 min read

Trends in production: what the cloud changed

You will learn
  • why capacity planning became financial engineering
  • the three decouplings behind modern architecture
  • why RTO and RPO alone can’t describe reliability

The big picture

The cloud swapped physical constraints for financial and logical ones. Capacity planning becomes financial engineering (FinOps): pay for just-in-time elasticity around Black Friday instead of holding idle hardware all year, and trade the stability of long-term commitments against cheap but interruptible Spot.

Compute from locationOrchestrators place workloads; VMs stop being pets
→
Storage from computeWarehouses and query engines over object storage
→
Network from hardwareDefined by software and identity

Three decouplings. Platforms followed the same path: from tickets, to self-service golden paths, towards intent-based systems where you declare a target and the platform reconciles it.

Managed services push the abstraction boundary up, so you stop patching hypervisors and focus on failure modes unique to your business. Open standards (Kubernetes, OpenTelemetry) reduce lock-in.

Troubleshooting now involves shared state: the first question is "is it us or the provider?", so treat providers as partners, use account-specific health dashboards and integrated telemetry, and see their SLA as a floor.

Architecture moved from long-lived VM "pets" to workloads, with three decouplings: compute from location (orchestrators), storage from compute (warehouses over object storage), and networking defined by software and identity (eBPF-style kernel hooks).

Platforms moved from tickets to self-service golden paths and are heading towards intent-based systems: you declare a latency target or a budget and the platform reconciles it. The SRE role shifts accordingly towards setting policy.

The book also argues that RTO and RPO are disaster-recovery metrics that see the world as up or down. They can't express gray failures like "30% slower for 10% of users", and they only start counting after a disaster. User-centric SLOs and error budgets move the work earlier.

How platforms evolved

About 2010 · TicketsA service desk, days or weeks of waiting, and a “wall of confusion” between dev and ops
→
2016–2026 · Self-serviceInternal developer platforms and golden paths. A “vending machine”: pick a template and get an instance with monitoring, security logging and backups already on
→
Next · Intent-basedYou declare a latency target or a budget. The platform picks tiers, isolates, migrates and throttles to meet it

Governance moved with it: from auditing what humans did, to guardrails built into the system.

The book names three things an intent-based platform has to get good at: filtering signals adaptively, carrying regulatory logic inside the platform, and treating energy and sustainability as constraints alongside cost.

Google’s production stack, with AWS equivalents

The chapter walks through Google’s environment. You won’t be asked to recite it, but being able to translate it shows you understand what each piece is for.

GoogleWhat it doesClosest on AWS
BorgCluster operating system: runs jobs made of tasksEKS or ECS
ColossusCluster file system under everything elseS3 and EBS
SpannerGlobally consistent relational databaseAurora (global database), DynamoDB global tables
BigtableSorted key-value map at petabyte scaleDynamoDB, Keyspaces
BlobstoreLarge immutable objectsS3
gRPC and Protocol BuffersTyped RPC between servicesgRPC on ALB or VPC Lattice
GSLBLoad balancing at three levels: DNS by geography, service, and RPCRoute 53, Global Accelerator, ALB, VPC Lattice
PiperOne repository for code and configurationA monorepo with infrastructure as code (CDK, Terraform)
Push-on-green CITests run on production clusters; green builds shipCodePipeline with automated gates
MonarchPlanet-scale time-series monitoringCloudWatch, Managed Service for Prometheus
BoqInternal developer platform with conformance rules and built-in overload, retry and caching hooksA platform team’s golden path: Backstage, Service Catalog, shared CDK constructs
BeyondCorpZero trust: access by identity and device, not networkVerified Access, IAM Identity Center

How the storage layers stack

Spanner · Bigtable · BlobstoreThree services with different data models
→
ColossusOne cluster file system under all of them
→
Byte storageDisks and flash

After Figure 3-1. Blobstore even splits its own work: small objects go into Bigtable, large ones straight to Colossus.

The design lesson is layering. Each service solves one problem and builds on the one below, so an improvement in Colossus reaches everything above it. The risk is the mirror image: a Colossus problem is everybody’s problem, which is why the lower a layer sits, the stricter its SLO has to be.

Details from the full chapter

Capacity became a finance problem

On-premises, you bought for the peak and the hardware sat idle 51 weeks a year. In the cloud you rent elasticity for Black Friday. The catch is that capital expense turns into operating expense that can swing wildly if nobody watches it. That is the job FinOps does: commitments for the steady base, spot for work that can be interrupted, and tags so every team sees its own bill.

From the 2016 “fortress” to now

Ten years ago the unit was a hand-tended VM on a SAN, with configuration drift and a specialist team per layer. Three decouplings changed that. Separating storage from compute removed what the book calls the preallocation tax: you no longer pay for disks sized for a peak that may never come. Networking became software-defined and driven by identity.

Two forces shape the next decade. One is digital sovereignty: a single service may need to run under ten sets of national rules. The other is autonomous optimisation, where control loops trade performance against energy and cost on their own. Both push SRE away from allocating resources and towards governing policy.

Observability: components to context

  • The single pane of glass is a myth. Use open standards so context flows between tools.
  • Distributed tracing is now a basic primitive, not an advanced extra.
  • Quality over quantity: SLOs are the primary signal, and cardinality needs discipline.
  • Access should be open across teams. Telemetry silos are an antipattern.

Why RTO and RPO fall short

They are binary and reactive, like a stopwatch that only starts after a disaster, and their values often come from history or politics. They can’t describe a gray failure such as “30% slower for 10% of users”. An SLO can.

How Google’s own environment changed

  • Platformisation. The P2020 programme set standards for CI/CD and observability. Boq gave Borg applications a paved road with conformance requirements.
  • Compliance shifted left. Rules such as GDPR, the DSA and the DMA are written as policy-as-code and checked before deployment.
  • AI at scale. More than 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month by mid-2026, accelerator use up fifteen-fold in two years, and machine learning used to predict hardware failures and tune cooling.
Data ingestionand processing
→
Trainingand experimentation
→
Deploymentand serving
→
ObservabilityDrift, decay, retraining

The four stages of an AI pipeline. Each one needs its own reliability thinking, which chapter 20 picks up.

On AWSThe AWS Health Dashboard is the shared-state tool; Savings Plans, Spot and on-demand are the FinOps levers; EKS/ECS/Lambda are the workload-centric compute; S3 + Athena/Redshift are storage-compute separation; Control Tower and Service Catalog are the self-service platform; ADOT is the open standard for telemetry.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Why aren’t RTO and RPO enough as reliability metrics?

Show a model answer

Because they only describe disasters. RTO (recovery time objective) says how fast you’ll be back after a catastrophe; RPO (recovery point objective) says how much data you can lose. Both assume the service is either up or down.

Most real failures aren’t like that. Checkout is slow for 10% of users. One feature is broken in one region. Searches succeed but return nothing. RTO and RPO have nothing to say about any of these, and they only start counting after things have gone badly wrong.

SLOs on critical user journeys fill that gap. They measure continuously, from the user’s side, so a partial degradation shows up as error budget being spent. You can act before it becomes an outage.

So I’d keep RTO and RPO for what they’re good at, which is disaster recovery and data protection planning, and use SLOs for everyday reliability.

Quick check: A cloud-hosted service starts failing. What does the book say is the first question?
You share state with your provider, so you first work out whose side the fault is on, using account-specific health dashboards and integrated telemetry.
Your turnList the managed services one of your systems depends on. For each, where would you look to answer “is it us or the provider?” within two minutes?
Key takeaways
  • The cloud swapped physical limits for financial and logical ones (FinOps).
  • Treat providers as partners and their SLA as a floor, not a promise about your service.
  • RTO and RPO see the world as up or down. SLOs capture the partial failures that are far more common.
Part II · Sociotechnical foundationsChapter 4 · 9 min read

The cultural context of SRE

You will learn
  • the two foundations and seven elements of a reliability culture
  • blame awareness, just culture and Westrum’s three culture types
  • how to change culture through behaviour, in brownfield and greenfield

The big picture

Culture is the foundation layer: practices fail when the environment punishes the behaviour they need. Two fundamentals, focus on the user and reliability as a core value, are supported by seven elements: a data-driven mindset, collaboration and shared responsibility, continuous learning, blamelessness, psychological safety, trust and empowerment.

LearningTraining builds skill
→
ConfidencePeople believe they can do it
→
BehaviourThey do it, repeatedly
→
CultureIt becomes how things are done

You change culture by changing what people do. Their thinking follows.

Being data-driven applies to ops health as well as services: track the share of unactionable pages (noisy monitoring), the share of incidents first noticed by humans (wrong SLIs or gaps in coverage), pages per incident, and on-call hours.

Avoid heroics. They hide systemic problems, set unrealistic expectations, burn people out and create knowledge silos. Blamelessness moves the focus from people to systems; blame awareness goes further and asks why the action made sense at the time.

Neither means zero accountability: a "just culture" separates honest mistakes and at-risk behaviour from reckless or criminal conduct.

DORA research ties culture to delivery performance. Westrum's typology sorts organisations into pathological (messengers punished, failure leads to scapegoating), bureaucratic (messengers neglected, failure leads to "justice") and generative (messengers trained, failure leads to inquiry), and generative cultures predict better outcomes.

You change culture by changing behaviour: learning builds confidence, confidence changes behaviour, and repeated behaviour becomes culture. Measure it with surveys on a grounded confidence scale before training, after it, and at one and six months.

Adopting SRE in practice

Brownfield: educate stakeholders together, pick a service that matters with an engaged team and code access, gather baseline SLIs over a few business cycles, have the crucial conversation ("is our current reliability good enough, and what does slow or down cost us?"), set two or three simple, realistic, agreed SLOs, introduce blameless postmortems, then publicise the wins.

Greenfield: treat SLOs as a design input that shapes architecture, build instrumentation in as a feature, and have CI/CD with rollback and runbooks from day one. Then let error budgets gate deployments instead of a fixed release calendar.

Three lines worth quoting from the chapter
  • “The fifth nine is people”, from Google SRE manager Trisha Weir. Reaching 99.999% depends on culture as much as on technology.
  • John Shook’s point that you change culture by changing what people do, not first what they think. It is easier to act your way into a new way of thinking than to think your way into a new way of acting. That is why the chapter’s chain runs learning, confidence, behaviour, culture.
  • DORA’s findings echo Google’s Project Aristotle, which found psychological safety to be the most important factor in high-performing teams.
Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the platform book and Observability with Grafana also cover, from the knowledge map:
  • Blameless postmortem: Why the action made sense at the time; several contributing factors. See Grafana ch 9.
  • Psychological safety: Safe to be wrong, to not know, to make an honest novel mistake. See platform ch 24.
Going deeper the case studies, numbers and named models from the full chapter

Seven elements, two foundations

The chapter rests everything on two foundations: put the user first (which is not the same as reliability at any cost) and treat reliability as a core value that's rewarded like a feature. On top sit seven cultural elements: a data-driven mindset, collaboration and shared responsibility, continuous learning, blamelessness, psychological safety, trust and empowerment.

If you're asked "what does a good SRE culture look like?", list the two foundations first and then give one concrete practice per element.

Data-driven means measuring the process too

Google noticed postmortems were being written late and their action items left open, so it put SLOs on the postmortem process itself: a maximum time to the first draft and to publication, with dashboards and reports to management.

Publication got faster, more action items closed, and repeat incidents with the same root cause dropped. Three incident-health metrics come up repeatedly: the share of incidents that weren't actionable (noisy monitoring), the share detected manually by users or other teams (weak SLIs or coverage) and pages per incident (an on-caller drowning in alerts).

On the people side they track on-call time and how often on-callers make manual production changes, aiming for nearly zero.

Blame awareness and just culture

Blamelessness is the default, but the book goes further with blame awareness: admit that blaming is a natural reflex, then ask why the action made sense to the person given what they knew and the pressure they were under. Watch for the fundamental attribution error (others' mistakes are character flaws, ours are circumstances) and hindsight bias.

Blameless doesn't mean nobody is accountable. Postmortems still check whether engineering standards were met. For regulated industries that worry about malice, the just culture model separates honest mistakes, at-risk behaviour, reckless conduct and criminal acts.

Only the last two justify discipline, and even then you still ask what least-privilege, auditing or approval control should have made the act impossible.

Trust, safety, empowerment

Psychological safety (Amy Edmondson's definition) is what makes people escalate early and ask awkward questions like "have we ever tested a restore?". Managers build it by admitting what they don't understand and by not reacting with feigned surprise to questions.

Repairing trust after one tense exchange takes roughly five to seven positive ones, which is why distributed teams invest in meeting in person. Empowerment at Google means any engineer can propose a code change anywhere, any team can request a postmortem (near misses included) and assign action items to other teams, and SRE can push back on launches or, in extreme cases, hand the pager back.

DORA and Westrum

Westrum's three cultures differ in how information flows. In pathological cultures messengers are punished, failure leads to scapegoating and new ideas get crushed. In bureaucratic ones messengers are neglected, failure leads to "justice" and new ideas cause problems.

PathologicalBureaucraticGenerative
Messengers arepunishedneglectedtrained
Failure leads toscapegoatingjusticeinquiry
New ideas arecrusheda source of problemsimplemented
Responsibilities areshirkednarrowshared risks
Bridging between teams isdiscouragedtoleratedencouraged

In generative ones messengers are trained, risks are shared, failure leads to inquiry and new ideas get implemented. DORA found that teams strong in modern operations practices are 1.4× more likely to report better delivery and operational performance and 1.8× more likely to report better business outcomes. Teams with good documentation are 3.5× more likely to adopt SRE practices.

Learning → confidence → behaviour → culture

You change culture by changing what people do; their thinking follows. Training builds confidence, and you can measure culture cheaply by asking people to rate their confidence in action-oriented tasks on a grounded scale: no idea, could do it with help, could work it out from docs, could do it from memory, could teach it.

Survey before training, straight after, at one month and at six. People who went through SRE onboarding scored 15 to 49 percentage points higher on top-box confidence than those who did general onboarding. When you design training, think about three groups: the change-curious, the change resisters ("what's in it for me?") and change champions (experienced hires who can tell success stories).

Brownfield and greenfield

For an existing service, the sequence is: train all stakeholders together, pick one service that matters and has an engaged team and code access, assess its maturity, collect a baseline SLI on a critical user journey, then hold the crucial conversation with the business: is today's reliability good enough, and what does slow, broken or down cost us?

Engineers tend to underestimate what's needed and business stakeholders tend to overestimate it. Set two or three realistic SLOs (if you're at 99.5% today, don't promise 99.999%), start blameless postmortems, then publicise the wins.

For a new service, the SLO is a design input: 99.99% pushes you away from single-homed designs and towards redundancy, idempotent operations for retries, instrumentation built in as a feature, and load and chaos testing. Swap fixed-cadence releases ("every other Tuesday") for SLO-gated ones.

On AWSCulture has no service, but you can make it visible: publish SLO dashboards widely, use Incident Manager's post-incident analysis templates, and track action-item closure. DORA metrics can be computed from CodePipeline/CodeDeploy events.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

An engineer ran a command that took down production. How do you handle the postmortem?

Show a model answer

I’d run it blameless, which means the goal is to understand why the action made sense to them at the time, not to find someone to punish.

I’d reconstruct their view: what did they believe about the system? What did the tool show them, and what did it not show? Were they under time pressure? Why did nothing stop a command with that much blast radius?

The answers usually point at the system, so the fixes go there: a dry-run mode, a confirmation step when a command affects many hosts, least-privilege access so one person can’t take everything down, and applying changes progressively instead of everywhere at once.

Accountability still exists. It means the people closest to the incident help design and own the fixes. Discipline is only for reckless or malicious behaviour, which is rare. If people fear punishment, they hide mistakes, and you lose the information you need.

Our new SRE team keeps getting blamed after outages. What would you change?

Show a model answer

That is a culture problem, and it will kill the SRE team if nothing changes.

First I’d name it. The book uses Westrum’s three culture types: pathological (power-oriented), bureaucratic (rule-oriented) and generative (performance-oriented). Blaming whoever was holding the pager is a sign of the first two.

Then I’d change how postmortems are run: blameless, written by someone not involved, focused on contributing factors, with actions owned by the teams who can fix them. I’d get one senior leader to model it visibly, because people copy what leaders do.

I’d also check one thing: did the organisation just rename an operations team to “SRE” without giving it the power to say no, such as an error budget policy? If so, fix that too. Otherwise the label takes the blame and the idea gets discredited for years.

Quick check: In Westrum’s generative culture, failure leads to…
Generative organisations treat failure as a chance to inquire into the system.
Your turnRate yourself on the grounded scale (no idea, with help, from docs, from memory, could teach it) for “explain the benefits of a blameless postmortem culture”. Then rewrite this question without judgement: “Why did you think it was OK to deploy on a Friday?”
Key takeaways
  • Two foundations: focus on the user, and reliability as a core value. Seven elements sit on top.
  • Blameless is not accountability-free. Just culture reserves discipline for reckless or criminal acts.
  • Learning builds confidence, confidence changes behaviour, and repeated behaviour becomes culture.
Part II · Sociotechnical foundationsChapter 5 · 10 min read

Hiring, training and career management

You will learn
  • what Google looks for when hiring SREs, and the two hiring profiles
  • how to design onboarding that gets people on call with confidence
  • the three keys to an SRE career, and why retention matters so much

The big picture

SRE works only as well as its people, and good SREs are hard to find because the role needs software skill and systems depth together, the T shape. Google values helpfulness highly (thank the person who found the hard bug), along with the ability to challenge the status quo respectfully, and it expects managers to be technically strong.

Checklist and starter projectLearn the systems with a mentor
→
Breakage labsFix simulated outages in a private stack
→
ShadowWatch a real on-call shift
→
Reverse shadowHold the pager with a mentor watching
→
On-callWith confidence

An onboarding ramp built from the chapter’s methods.

Hiring follows role profiles and structured interviews that cover set topics, and a separate committee makes the decision so the bar stays consistent. A common antipattern is interviewers hunting for reasons to reject.

Training pays for itself: new hires become productive sooner and fewer leave in their first year (Appendix A works through the ROI). How much to invest depends on size and growth.

Small and slow-growing teams can rely on mentoring, shadowing and starter projects; small and fast-growing ones need an onboarding programme; large and slow ones benefit from continuing education as a retention tool; large and fast ones need a full-lifecycle programme.

Professionals learn by doing, so Google's SRE orientation is built around hands-on breakage scenarios on real but isolated stacks, followed by a self-paced on-call curriculum. Use ADDIE (analyse, design, develop, implement, evaluate) and write objectives as "a student should be able to…" with action verbs.

Skills deepen in stages from reactive (troubleshoot, run changes) to proactive, comprehensive, long-term and finally directional (set technical strategy and build consensus). The core keys to an SRE career are breadth, initiative and teamwork. The heaviest driver of attrition is on-call load, so design teams to survive the loss of any one person.

The Treynor curve

Ben Treynor Sloss drew Google’s hiring bar as a curve, not a line. A candidate who clears the software bar is a fit, and so is one who clears the systems bar. The interesting part is the middle.

This is why the interview loops differ but the job doesn’t. It also explains a line you can use about yourself: “I’m stronger on the systems side, and here is the software I’ve written to automate it.”

How scope grows with seniority

ReactiveHandles what arrives
→
ProactivePrevents the next one
→
ComprehensiveOwns a whole system
→
Long-termPlans across years
→
DirectionalSets where the organisation goes

After Figure 5-3. The move is from tactical to strategic. Promotion cases are easier to write when you can say which step you are working at.

Growing your own hiring pipeline

Figure 5-2 charts a university outreach programme Google ran in Ireland over seven years. Internships and placements grow first, and full-time hires follow a few years later as interns return. Two points to take from it: get students in early, in their first or second year, because the bar for an internship is lower and it lets both sides try the job. And report short-term wins, such as applicant numbers and interns hired, because a seven-year payoff needs sponsors who stay interested. Much of the benefit showed up in under three years.

What to do when someone breaks somethingEvery new Google SRE is given a short passage from Tanya Reilly. Paraphrased: when someone breaks something or finds it hard to debug, you say thank you. Thank them for the edge case, the overcomplicated part, the gap in the docs. Then make sure nobody can break it the same way again. It is the hiring chapter’s emphasis on helpfulness in one practice, and a good answer to “how do you respond when a junior engineer causes an outage?”
Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the platform book also covers, from the knowledge map:
  • Education: Belongs to the platform team; next task to the most junior who can do it with guidance. See platform ch 24.
Going deeper the case studies, numbers and named models from the full chapter

What predicts a good SRE

Breadth predicts success better than depth, so Google hiring committees are told to look for strengths rather than gaps, and to remember that one bad interview may say more about the interviewer. Most Google SRE hires have no previous SRE experience.

Backgrounds range from computer science to physics and music theory. The non-technical traits are curiosity, a low tolerance for toil, helpfulness (the incident response team helps whoever escalates, even if the escalation turns out to be unnecessary) and the confidence to challenge the status quo respectfully.

New SRE managers and directors spend their first six months as individual contributors, qualifying for on-call.

Two hiring profiles

SRE-SWE candidates go through the standard software engineering loop with data structures, algorithms and API design. SRE-SE candidates have a systems focus and a dedicated non-abstract large system design (NALSD) interview, where they must give realistic numerical estimates and reason about trade-offs down to the hardware.

SRE-SWESRE-SE
BackgroundSoftware developmentSystems engineering
Interview focusData structures, algorithms, API designNon-abstract large system design with real numbers
Day jobThe same dutiesThe same duties

The "Treynor curve" plots the acceptable mix of the two skill sets. Every senior candidate gets a leadership interview. Process lessons: dropout rises sharply once time from application to offer passes about 40 calendar days, so optimise latency for each candidate rather than throughput; avoid brainteasers; and let a committee, not the hiring manager, decide.

The new-graduate programme (Ireland)

Students didn't know Google hired engineers in Dublin, didn't know what SRE was, had little practical coding and struggled to think aloud in interviews. Volunteers fixed this with open days, campus talks, CV workshops, algorithm workshops, code retreats, public NALSD material and early internships.

Recent graduates proved especially relatable as speakers. Over seven years, hiring grew more than tenfold, with much of the gain within two years. The "circle of life" means former students now run the programme. Each volunteer gave one to eight hours a quarter.

Training design

The ROI comparison (Appendix A) puts sink-or-swim against structured onboarding: faster ramp-up and lower first-year attrition pay back the instructor hours. Match investment to the organisation: small and slow-growing, rely on mentoring; small and fast, build an onboarding programme; large and slow, invest in continuing education for retention; large and fast, build the full lifecycle.

Informal methods include N+1 mentoring (a mentor from another team), shadowing and reverse shadowing, the Wheel of Misfortune, reverse-engineering systems and reading postmortems.

Team-specific methods include an on-call learning checklist, whiteboard talks where the newcomer draws the architecture (as a forcing function, not a test) and starter projects that are useful, self-contained, achievable, not time-critical and off the critical path.

SRE EDU

The week-long orientation focuses on building confidence rather than overwhelming people with information. Its test for adding material: does a two-week-old hire need it, and is it more important than something already in the course?

The centrepiece is breakage scenarios on real production infrastructure, with a private stack per group of three. The instructor triggers a page, and their role shifts from driving the response, to coaching, to standing aside as a guide.

A self-paced Going On-Call series follows one to two months in: On-Call Basics, IMAG and declaring an incident, and escalations. The Annual Week of Education runs near round the clock and gets recorded. Write learning objectives with ADDIE and "a student should be able to…" plus an action verb ("identify memory usage in our monitoring tool", never "understand").

Running training like a production service

To teach production safety to tens of thousands of developers (more than ten times orientation's capacity of about 1,000 a year), the team built a self-paced course with automated reminders that escalate up the management chain. They canaried it to 1% of the audience, then rolled it out progressively.

Net Promoter Score rose 30 points for what was essentially a compliance module, and over 95% completed it. "On-Call Ready" turned the breakage labs into a self-service reservation system with automated reset and a volunteer teaching assistant in each group of three, reaching five times the old maximum.

Careers and retention

Three keys: breadth, initiative and teamwork, each scaling from team scope to organisation scope. (For example, a junior SRE tunes one service's alert thresholds; a senior SRE designs alerting principles and libraries for a whole product area.)

Managers aren't expected to be the team's best engineer, which leaves room for IC technical leaders. Teams are typically 7–10 people per site across two sites. Onboarding to on-call can take up to a year, which makes attrition expensive, so managers keep N+1 coverage for on-call and for expertise.

They also offer flexible on-call (shorter or split shifts, swaps, exemptions), since on-call is the most common reason people leave, and they encourage moves within SRE: Mission Control, a one-week SRE exchange, and mobility made easier by standardisation.

On AWSBuild breakage labs in a sandbox account or with AWS FIS so trainees practise real failures safely; AWS Skill Builder and Well-Architected labs cover the platform knowledge; game days are the AWS term for Wheel of Misfortune exercises.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

How would you onboard a new SRE onto your team’s on-call rotation?

Show a model answer

I’d build confidence step by step, so their first real page isn’t their first time seeing the system break.

Week one: a checklist of systems, dashboards and playbooks to work through, plus a small starter project that isn’t urgent, so they learn the code and tools by doing.

Then practice: “Wheel of Misfortune” sessions, where we replay a past incident and they play the on-caller while a teammate plays the system. They also give short whiteboard talks explaining a system back to the team. Teaching it is the best test of understanding it.

Then real on-call in two steps: shadowing, where they watch the primary on-caller, then reverse shadowing, where they lead and the experienced person watches and steps in if needed.

They go primary once they can handle the top five failure modes from the playbooks. I’d measure their confidence with a short survey before, after and a few months later, because the book uses confidence as the evidence that training worked.

Quick check: In Google’s hiring experience, which predicts SRE success better?
Breadth beats depth, which is why committees look for strengths rather than gaps. Most Google SRE hires have no previous SRE experience.
Your turnGive a whiteboard talk to yourself: draw one system you support from memory, name each component’s purpose and trace one critical request through it. Where did you get stuck? That is your on-call learning checklist.
Key takeaways
  • Breadth predicts SRE success better than depth, so hire for strengths.
  • Training should build confidence through practice, and can be run like a production service.
  • Careers grow along breadth, initiative and teamwork. On-call is the top reason people leave, so make it flexible.
Part II · Sociotechnical foundationsChapter 6 · 9 min read

Organisational structures for SRE

You will learn
  • the trade-offs between centralised, decentralised and hybrid SRE
  • the team-size and on-call numbers Google uses
  • the five maturity phases, and how to use scorecards without harm

The big picture

SRE is an organisational construct, and Conway's law means reporting lines shape the systems you build. Centralised teams concentrate expertise and give consistency, economies of scale and clear career paths, but risk a transactional "IT services" mindset.

CentralisedDecentralised
StrengthConcentrated expertise, consistent practiceDeep product context, fast feedback, real ownership
RiskA transactional “IT services” mindset, slow onboardingUs-versus-them, or the role being quietly dropped
FitsLow-trust, high-control organisations starting outHigh-trust organisations with strong product teams

Decentralised teams gain context, ownership and fast feedback, but drift and can fall back into us-versus-them.

Most organisations use a hybrid: a central group runs time-limited engagements (reliability reviews, SLO construction, postmortem facilitation), sets production-readiness standards and builds tooling, while the largest and most critical products get dedicated SRE teams, all held together by a community of practice and strong SRE TPMs. Roll out reorgs gradually; they come with a J-curve dip in performance.

Spotify shows a different balance. There's no central SRE organisation: teams own their services' reliability and the platform group provides standards and golden paths. A small Incident Manager On-Call (IMOC) rotation steps in only when coordination is the bottleneck. It owns no services and doesn't take over mitigation.

An SRE team needs a charter (mission, scope, partners, offerings, what success looks like; Appendices B and C), a manager, a tech lead and a TPM, and enough people that the on-caller absorbs ops work (around 15% of capacity) while the team stays under 50% ops overall.

The weekly production meeting reviews pages and outages, postmortems, SLOs and service health, tickets and non-paging alerts, and upcoming changes, then follows up on actions. Maturity runs absent → reactive → proactive (the target for critical services) → strategic → visionary.

Scorecards help, but KPIs are proxies and Goodhart's law applies, so pair the data with a conversation, as Google's ProdEx reviews do.

When scorecards go wrongThe chapter names two failure modes. Leaders who manage by numbers without understanding a team’s situation spread fear and undermine psychological safety; it quotes Jeff Bezos’s view that when data and anecdotes disagree, the anecdotes are usually right. And teams not committed to the spirit of a metric game it: measure deployment frequency and someone deploys the same binary every hour. Hence the rule in this lesson: scorecards are for coaching, never ranking.
Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that Observability with Grafana also covers, from the knowledge map:
  • Sustainable on-call: Limits on on-call share, rotation size and incidents per shift. See Grafana ch 9.
Going deeper the case studies, numbers and named models from the full chapter

Centralised, decentralised or hybrid

A centralised model concentrates expertise and keeps practice consistent. It's the natural start in low-trust, high-control organisations, but it risks a transactional "IT services" mindset and slow onboarding. A decentralised model gives deep context, fast feedback and real ownership, but it risks an us-versus-them split and the role being quietly redefined or dropped.

Trust has to run both ways. Google is centralised but uses hybrid mechanisms: a community of practice, written engagement models, and a dedicated SRE technical programme manager role. Let practice drift too far and you get "shadow SRE".

Reorganisations cost trust and context, and the organisation dips before it improves (a J-curve), so roll changes out gradually with first-mover teams and metrics.

Spotify: ownership without a central SRE org

Teams operate what they build ("Ops in Squads", now "Ops in Areas"). A platform group supplies standard stacks, observability defaults (dashboards and alerts come bundled with the service framework) and automation. A small IMOC (Incident Manager On-Call) rotation of senior engineers follows the sun.

It owns no services, doesn't debug and doesn't take over mitigation. It's engaged only when coordination is the bottleneck: unclear ownership, incidents spanning teams, or cross-cutting decisions such as rerouting traffic or contacting external parties.

Two lessons: distributed ownership only scales once operational variance is reduced through standardisation, and IMOC must not become a quiet way to hand off accountability.

Team design numbers

A lone SRE is a single point of failure; without the headcount for a team, prefer a DevOps model. Every Google SRE team has a leadership-approved charter (Appendix B): mission, scope as a connected whole, services, and success criteria as time-bound outcomes.

Limits: at least 50% engineering time, at most 50% operational work, at most 25% on-call. Two sites 6–9 hours apart allow follow-the-sun, with at least six engineers per site (two to three on-call weeks a quarter each). A single site needs at least eight.

Split a team once it reaches twice its minimum size. Ideally the current on-caller absorbs all the ops work, about 15% of team capacity. Meet key partners in person at least once a year to pay down "relationship debt".

Working with developers

Every Google SRE team has at least one active development partner, often more than ten. Share on-call: developers cover business hours with SRE as escalation, and SRE covers nights with developers as escalation. If SRE alone is primary, developers keep a 24×7 secondary rotation.

Keep a shared backlog and give work to whichever team can do it best. Internally, "look left and right" before building something custom. Managers can't block transfers.

The weekly production meeting

It's about services, not people's status updates. The agenda: outages and pages (did monitoring work, is the fix durable?), postmortems (written, reviewed, actions done?), SLOs and trends, non-paging alerts and tickets (delete the unactionable ones, promote the critical ones to pages, automate anything found manually) and upcoming changes (raise awareness, don't block).

With many partners, hold separate syncs with delegates. Track action items between meetings (Appendix D shows example minutes).

Maturity matrix

The dimensions are operational process, risk management, productivity, velocity, system complexity, product lifecycle, teams and leadership. The phases:

AbsentOnly features count
→
ReactiveFixing the latest outage
→
ProactiveJoint risk reviews. The floor for critical services
→
StrategicClasses of risk designed out. 4+ years
→
VisionarySelf-healing. Rare
  • Absent: only features count, and users find the bugs. Fine for incubation or a fully automated sunset.
  • Reactive: fixing the latest outage, heroics, brief freezes.
  • Proactive: joint risk reviews, dependency management, graceful degradation required (except for policy-enforcing systems that can't fail open). This should be the minimum for anything critical.
  • Strategic: whole classes of risk removed through architecture, and reliability and velocity both sustained. Expect four or more years to get here.
  • Visionary: self-healing systems, production knowledge spread everywhere, publishing for the industry. Rare.

It isn't a score, organisations can regress, and the right level depends on context.

Scorecards: useful proxies, dangerous targets

KPIs reduce subjective arguments (if the SLOs are green, there's nothing to debate). But they're proxies, and they fail in four ways: leaders weaponise them, teams game them (deploying the same binary every hour to inflate DORA deployment frequency), Goodhart's law kicks in, and you get tunnel vision.

Google's ProdEx, running since 2015 with more than 1,900 reviews, shows how to do it well. A central scorecard covers on-call load, alert quality, outages, postmortems, SLOs, data integrity, efficiency, bug hygiene and OKR discipline.

Reviews happen every few quarters, run by two very senior SREs from outside the team's management chain, who coach rather than judge and set scores by hand with context. Alternatives seen at customers include a capabilities model (a baseline set plus per-product maps) for a siloed bank, and tiered "model services" with a shared dev and SRE backlog for a retailer.

On AWSThe Cloud Center of Excellence model is the AWS equivalent of a central SRE group; AWS Resilience Hub scores give you a scorecard, but treat them as conversation starters, not targets.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Centralised or embedded SRE? Defend a choice.

Show a model answer

For an organisation starting out, I’d centralise first.

Expertise is scarce at the start. A central team can set the common standards everyone needs: how SLOs are defined, the alerting approach, the deployment pipeline, the incident process. If you scatter the first few SREs across product teams, each one reinvents those alone.

Once one or two products are critical enough to justify dedicated people, I’d embed SREs with them. Embedded SREs learn the product deeply and are close to the developers.

Two safeguards make that work. Embedded SREs keep reporting through the SRE line, so they keep their reliability voice and a career path, and don’t become the product team’s operations staff. And a community of practice across all SREs, so a fix one of them makes becomes a standard for everyone.

I’d revisit the balance every year or so. The book is clear that any model drifts as the organisation grows.

Leadership wants a reliability scorecard that ranks teams. What do you think?

Show a model answer

Measuring is good: things nobody measures tend to get worse. Ranking is the problem.

Two things go wrong, and the book names both. When numbers are used to judge without understanding a team’s situation, people become afraid, and psychological safety suffers. And when a number becomes a target, people game it. The book’s example: if you score deployment frequency, a team can redeploy the same binary every hour.

So I’d offer a version that coaches instead of ranks. Score several areas of health, not one number. Have reviewers outside the team’s management chain, who understand the context. Use the result to agree each team’s next improvement, not to name winners and losers.

And I’d keep listening to the stories behind the numbers. When the data and the anecdotes disagree, the anecdotes are often right.

Quick check: Who reviews a team in Google’s ProdEx program?
Organisational distance reduces the pressure to show good numbers, so the review can coach rather than judge.
Quick check: In Spotify’s model, when is IMOC engaged?
Owning teams keep diagnosis and mitigation; IMOC clarifies ownership and enables cross-cutting decisions.
Your turnWrite this week’s production-meeting agenda for your team using the five headings: outages and pages, postmortems, SLOs and trends, non-paging alerts and tickets, upcoming changes. What had no owner?
Key takeaways
  • Most organisations end up hybrid: central standards and community, with dedicated teams for critical products.
  • Limits to remember: at least 50% engineering, at most 25% on-call, six engineers per site across two sites or eight at one.
  • Scorecards are proxies. Use them to coach, never to rank.
Part II · Sociotechnical foundationsChapter 7 · 10 min read

SRE engagement models

You will learn
  • the difference between an org structure and an engagement model
  • the scoping archetypes, and how consumer and enterprise SRE differ
  • why Google moved from launch reviews, to tiers, to outcomes

The big picture

An engagement model is the written contract between SRE and product teams: how they work together, what SRE offers and how SRE chooses its work. Org structure answers "who reports to whom"; the engagement model answers "what work do we do together".

1 · PRR gateSupported or not. Thorough, but sticky and late
→
2 · TiersBaseline, assisted, full. Still about who holds the pager
→
3 · Outcomes (2025)Foundational offerings for all, plus time-boxed engineering efforts

How Google’s engagement model evolved.

Archetypes: kitchen sink (often a renamed ops team, reactive), embedded, product/application (easy to show value), infrastructure (effectively platform engineering), tools, consulting, and blended.

Google moved through three models. First, a binary "SRE-supported or not" gated by production readiness reviews: SLOs, less paging, docs, progressive rollouts, backups, capacity plans, failure domains. That was thorough but slow and "sticky".

Next came baseline / assisted / full tiers, which were still centred on who held the pager. Since 2025 it has been outcome-focused: every service in a partnership gets foundational offerings, and SRE and dev agree concrete outcomes with rough timelines, such as faster detection and mitigation, an exercised DR plan, lower operational cost, or faster releases and rollbacks. Then they split the work.

Consumer and enterprise products differ. Consumer SLOs work well because volume smooths the signal; enterprise customers rely on implicit guarantees, one large customer's complaint can matter as much as an outage, and mitigations have to respect each customer's risk tolerance.

Case studies: Azure grew from about 40 to about 200 SREs on a six-phase playbook (fundamentals; CUJs and SLOs with safe rollout; operational metrics; dev loop; risk modelling; capacity). Disney embeds central SREs long-term and pivots engagements rather than ending them, learning the hard way that leadership support must be continuous.

A second worked example: the Azure playbook

The chapter includes Microsoft’s engagement playbook, which is useful because it attaches a measurable KPI to each phase. A service in phases 1 to 3 is “nascent”; 4 to 6 is “mature”.

PhaseWhat is measured
1Compliance with security and quality baselines; security posture score
2Share of critical user journeys covered by an SLO; share of outages detected automatically
375th-percentile time to mitigate; incident volume and repeat rate; alert noise ratio and routing accuracy
4Lead time, change failure rate, deployment frequency
5Number of critical risks; age of the last threat model
6Capacity plans kept up to date

Notice the order. It follows the hierarchy of production health: see the service first, respond well next, then deliver safely, then manage risk. If an interviewer asks how you would measure an SRE engagement, this table is a ready answer.

Where security fits in the Azure playbookThe first phase of Microsoft’s engagement playbook, service fundamentals, is defined by two company programmes: the Secure Future Initiative and the Quality Excellence Initiative. Security posture is checked before SLOs and safe deployment, not after. Useful if you are asked how SRE and security engagement fit together.
Going deeper the case studies, numbers and named models from the full chapter

Organisation structure vs engagement model

Org structure answers who pays and who manages. The engagement model is the contract of work: does SRE consult, build, or carry the pager? You can judge an engagement's maturity on three axes: intent (reactive, then specialised, then integrated), impact (depth-first or breadth-first) and value (tactical, then optimised, then strategic, the last asking "how do we make launches succeed?").

Scoping archetypes

  • Kitchen sink: everything SRE. The most common archetype, often an ops team that has just been renamed.
  • Embedded: depth-first, but risks isolation.
  • Product or application: business-aligned, but infrastructure gets duplicated without a platform.
  • Infrastructure: in its modern form, essentially a platform engineering team.
  • Tools: risks solving the wrong problems.
  • Consulting: office hours and PRRs, but advisers can lack context.
  • Blended: a central function, embedded SREs for young products, product SRE for critical ones, infrastructure SRE publishing infrastructure SLOs, shared onboarding and a chief reliability officer.

Monoliths pull you towards product teams; uniform microservices pull you towards infrastructure teams. Re-scope regularly.

Consumer vs enterprise

Consumer products have millions of users, so you lean on metrics, SLOs, error budgets and even sentiment from search trends, and incident response is mitigate first, ask questions later. Enterprise products have concentrated revenue and contracts, so one big customer's broken workload can matter even within SLO.

ConsumerEnterprise
BuyerThe userA CTO or committee, under contract
What you lean onMetrics, SLOs, error budgetsRelationships and customer-specific context
Extra detection signalSentiment from search and socialSupport cases
Incident stanceMitigate firstCommunicate first, mitigate second
DesignSharding and graceful degradation, hidden from usersCustomer-facing failure domains, isolation of large customers

Implicit guarantees (Hyrum's law) mean you have to watch business logic on critical journeys. Synthetic probers can drown out real signal, so support cases become a detection channel. Response becomes communicate first, mitigate second, with dedicated comms responders.

Rolling back a change that customers already depend on may be unsafe, which calls for surgical fixes and architectural isolation of large customers. Expose customer-facing failure domains so customers can build their own fallbacks.

Freeze changes around customers' big days (Black Friday, New Year's Eve), and organise teams around customer experience (say, all authentication services together) rather than frontend versus backend.

Google's three engagement models

1. PRR gate (the original). A service was either SRE-supported or "you build it, you run it". The SRE mission: meet availability targets; subject to that, maximise long-term feature velocity; use software instead of toil; and engage only where SRE is more efficient than developers.

Funding came through headcount transfers, which pushed developers to build simpler services. A PRR took quarters and typically produced SLOs, lower pager load, documentation, progressive rollouts, backup plans, capacity plans and failure domains. The problems: engagements became sticky, knowledge stayed with SRE, and SRE arrived late in the lifecycle.

2. Tiers. Baseline (consulting and office hours, no funding), assisted (projects, embedded SREs, maybe shared on-call) and full. It failed because moving between tiers was as painful as onboarding, nobody wanted to give up a tier they'd "earned", and everything still revolved around who holds the pager.

3. Outcomes (2025). Funding is negotiated once per product-area partnership. Foundational offerings go to every service: postmortem reviews, office hours, an incident response team. Everything else is an outcome delivered through a few time-boxed engineering efforts, ranked by business priority and staffed until capacity runs out.

Examples: cut operational load by x%, define and defend user-centric SLOs, build a multi-failure-domain architecture, a data integrity and restore plan. On-call exists to gather information for that engineering work. If the same outcome keeps recurring across partnerships, it becomes an infrastructure team or platform feature.

Case studies

Persistent Disk had SREs semi-embedded in feature teams, overloaded tech leads, unclear ownership (developers assumed SRE owned "all monitoring") and low morale.

Leadership agreed foundational offerings (incident response, product SLO alerts, ownership of expanding into new regions) and four outcomes (faster detect-to-mitigate, an exercised disaster recovery plan, lower ops cost, faster releases and rollbacks).

They regrouped into four teams, decoupled on-call rotations from team structure and wrote OKRs as progress on outcomes. SRE also built self-service alerting so developers no longer depended on them.

Microsoft Azure grew from about 40 SREs in 2015 to about 200.

It uses a written playbook with six sequential phases, each with KPIs: service fundamentals; service health and safe deployment practices (critical user journeys, SLOs, phased rollout of code, config and data); operational efficiency (time-to-x metrics measured at P75); release management (three of the four DORA metrics); risk reduction through threat modelling; and scalability.

Proven solutions become reusable "SRE patterns". The team scales through platforms, horizontal teams (Service Health, Change) and shift-left standards. Its strongest evidence wasn't dollar ROI but the fact that SRE-supported services improved faster on division quality KPIs.

Disney runs a central team embedded long-term: engagements pivot rather than end, with lightweight agreements (what outcome, what risk, what's reliable enough, how it's measured). Proximity builds empathy, empathy builds trust, and trust speeds things up.

On-call is treated as a signal of system health, and models vary by domain (theme-park systems hand over to park engineering after launch). Their hard lesson: when new business leadership no longer wanted modern practices, staying on burned people out. Their rule: don't go where you aren't invited, and leave when the invitation lapses.

Beyond PRRs

Building the engagement around on-call is an antipattern, and so is SRE "holding the pager" after developers move on; hand services back with a plan. PRRs gatekeep, cost effort that grows linearly with launches, and arrive too late.

Replace them with opinionated platforms, standard rollouts, horizontal regression monitoring and automatic rollback, keeping deep reviews for the riskiest launches. Scale influence by guiding (office hours), sharing knowledge (don't be the "human abstraction layer for production") and reducing the need for SRE (standard frameworks, automated policy).

Bring product managers in: they should own the definition of SLOs and hear about user impact regularly. An SLO of 99.99% under 10 ms needs a very different design from 99% under 250 ms.

On AWSEnterprise Support's Well-Architected and Countdown (launch readiness) engagements resemble PRRs; AWS's own Operational Readiness Reviews are a public example of the checklist style.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

A product team wants you to “just take the pager”. How do you respond?

Show a model answer

I’d say no to that version, and offer something better.

If SRE simply takes over on-call, the developers stop feeling the pain of their own failures. Nothing in the code improves, SRE becomes a human buffer, and the pager gets worse over time. The book treats this as an antipattern.

What I’d offer is a partnership with agreed outcomes. Together we set SLOs for the service. We fix the top sources of pages first. We add progressive rollouts and playbooks. Then we share on-call: either one combined rotation, or SRE takes infrastructure problems while developers take application problems.

And one rule up front: if the page load stays above an agreed level, some of it goes back to the developers until the causes are fixed. That keeps the feedback loop alive.

SRE is drowning in services it inherited. How do you fix the engagement model?

Show a model answer

Stop treating every service the same, and choose deliberately.

Split the work in two. Foundational offerings are things every service gets with little SRE time: the platform, templates, documentation, office hours. Outcome-based engagements are where SREs work directly on one service towards a specific result, such as “cut pages by half” or “add multi-region failover”.

Rank the possible outcomes with development leadership, staff only the top few, and time-box each one. When an engagement finishes, the SREs move on.

For low-priority services the team inherited, plan a handback: train the developers, give them playbooks and alerts that make sense, and return the pager. Decouple on-call from team structure so one team doesn’t carry rotations for dozens of services it can’t improve.

Quick check: In Google’s outcome-focused engagement model, why do SREs go on-call?
On-call is a means to an end: it reveals the failures that shape the outcome-focused engineering efforts.
Quick check: An enterprise customer’s workload broke but the service is well within SLO. What does an enterprise SRE do?
With concentrated revenue and implicit guarantees (Hyrum’s law), one key customer’s trust can matter as much as any SLO.
Your turnDescribe your current team as one of the archetypes (kitchen sink, embedded, product, infrastructure, tools, consulting, blended). Then write two foundational offerings and two time-boxed outcomes you would propose instead of “SRE holds the pager”.
Key takeaways
  • The engagement model is the contract of work, separate from who reports to whom.
  • Building an engagement around on-call is an antipattern. On-call exists to inform engineering.
  • Consumer SRE mitigates first. Enterprise SRE communicates first.
Part III · Awareness and preparednessChapter 8 · 9 min read · POC 01

SLOs, error budgets and burn rate

You will learn
  • the vocabulary: SLI, SLO, SLA, error budget, burn rate, CUJ
  • the numbers to know cold, and how to derive them on a whiteboard
  • how to alert on burn rate, including for low-traffic services
  • what the second edition adds, and where SLOs fall short

Four terms, each built on the last

SLIAn indicator: good events ÷ valid events
→
SLOAn objective: a target for that ratio over a window
→
Error budget1 − SLO: the failure you are allowed
→
Burn rateHow fast you spend it. At 1× it lasts exactly the window

An SLA is different. It is the agreement about what happens, usually money, when a target is missed, and it is normally looser than the internal SLO.

A critical user journey (CUJ) is a task the user cares about, such as logging in or checking out. It usually spans several services, which is why SLOs written only by backend teams miss things.

The numbers to know cold

SLOError budgetFull downtime allowed in 30 days
99%1%7.2 hours
99.5%0.5%3.6 hours
99.9%0.1%43.2 minutes
99.95%0.05%21.6 minutes
99.99%0.01%4.32 minutes

The sum for 99.9% is 0.001 × 30 days × 1,440 minutes a day = 43.2 minutes. Be ready to do it on a whiteboard.

Choosing your first SLO

  • Measure the happy path at the load balancer. It is the simplest place to see what users see.
  • Pick an availability target. 99% is relaxed, 99.9% is the common choice and 99.99% is demanding.
  • Pick a goodness threshold, usually latency. Around 100 ms feels instant; over a second feels clunky. A latency SLO is the percentage of requests faster than the threshold.
  • Set the target as a group. Business, product, engineering and operations decide together, because the target is a business decision about user experience.
  • Keep it small. Fewer than five high-level SLOs usually describe a service.
Don’t just codify today’s performanceIt skips the conversation that matters: what should it be?
Kind of systemSLIs to choose from
Request and response servicesAvailability, latency, quality
Data pipelinesCoverage, correctness, freshness, throughput
StorageThroughput, latency, durability

Alerting on burn rate

Alert on how fast the budget is burning, not on a raw error threshold. A long window proves the burn is significant. A short window proves it is still happening, so the page clears soon after you recover.

Budget spentOverConfirmed byBurn rateAction
2%1 hour5 minutes14.4×Page
5%6 hours30 minutes6×Page
10%3 days6 hours1×Ticket

Where 14.4 comes from: 2% of a 30-day budget in one hour is 0.02 × 720 hours ÷ 1 hour = 14.4 times the sustainable rate. At that pace the whole budget is gone in about 50 hours.

Low traffic needs statisticsWith 200 requests in an hour, a handful of errors proves nothing. Page only when the lower bound of a confidence interval (a Wilson score) is above the error rate you care about. For a 14.4% threshold at 99% confidence, that takes 173 failures in 1,000 requests, 42 in 200, or 24 in 100. Try it in the Labs station.

What the second edition adds

  • Adoption pitfalls. Tie the programme to a business reason, iterate, share credit, and give teams templates and SRE help instead of bare mandates. “Eat from both ends”: start with end-user SLOs and core components.
  • Critical user journeys. A synthetic probe must exercise the whole journey. In one case a single 99.99% probe stayed green while small combinations of protocol and destination were completely broken.
  • Per-customer SLOs for B2B, where revenue follows a Pareto curve. An aggregate burn of 10× could be one customer at 100× and nine at zero.
