  • Implicit SLOs. Users depend on whatever you have actually delivered (Hyrum’s law). Raising the level wastes the workarounds they built and invites more load; lowering it pushes your costs onto them. Be explicit and over-communicate.
  • Client-side SLOs have a high noise floor. Use bad minutes: a minute is bad if its error rate is above, say, 6% when the noise is 5%. Use sessionised SLIs where there is no denominator.
  • Tooling. Pick one SLO tool and generate the alerts from it automatically.
  • Labels record ownership and lifecycle: experimental, aspirational, committed, deprecated.
  • Failure concentration. Use entropy or decision trees to find the cohort that a single number hides.

Where SLOs fall short

  • They assume countable success and failure events.
  • Nines aren’t intuitive to people.
  • The response is binary: in budget or out.
  • A budget blown in January still needs a monthly refresh, plus a longer programme to fix the cause.

The error budget policy is a ramp, not a cliff

People often describe the policy as a switch: budget gone, features stop. The book’s figure shows something gentler and more useful.

Write your policy with all three zones. In the middle one, name the trade-offs explicitly: slower rollouts, a reliability item in every sprint, a second approver for risky changes. A freeze should be the last step of a ramp everyone saw coming.

Hyrum’s law and Hidalgo’s corollaryHyrum’s law says every observable behaviour of a system will be depended on by somebody. Alex Hidalgo’s corollary applies it to reliability: the level you actually deliver is an observable behaviour too. Run at 99.99% for a year against a 99.9% SLO and your users will build on 99.99%. That is the argument for controlled budget burn, and for checking in with consumers every quarter or two.
Code Yellow and Code RedGoogle’s names for an organised emergency. A Code Red is already causing major damage, or will within a day or two. A Code Yellow could cause outages or business problems over the coming quarter: feature work stops and a temporary team forms. An exhausted error budget on a critical journey is a common trigger for a Code Yellow.
Implementing this in Prometheus

This chapter explains multiwindow burn-rate alerting as a concept. Mastering Prometheus chapter 13 turns it into rules: recording rules for the error ratio over 5 minutes, 30 minutes, 1, 2 and 6 hours, 1 and 3 days, and alert expressions that join a long and a short window with and, so a page needs a sustained burn that is still happening. Tools such as Sloth and Pyrra generate the whole set from a short spec, which is safer than writing them by hand.

For low-traffic services the Prometheus book offers a window-based SLO: count good and bad time windows instead of requests, so one failed request in a quiet hour doesn’t swamp the ratio. It is a practical alternative to the confidence-interval approach described here. One trap the book itself falls into: burn rate must be computed from the error ratio, not the success ratio. POC 24 generates and simulates these rules.

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the platform book, Mastering Prometheus and Observability with Grafana also cover, from the knowledge map:
  • SLI, SLO, SLA: Indicator (good events over valid events), objective (the target), agreement (what happens if it is missed). See Prometheus ch 13, Grafana ch 9.
  • Error budget: One minus the SLO: the failure you are allowed, to be spent on change. See Prometheus ch 13.
  • Burn rate: How fast the budget is being spent. Page on a fast burn confirmed by a short window. See Prometheus ch 13.
  • Low-traffic alerting: Page only when a confidence interval’s lower bound exceeds the threshold. See Prometheus ch 13.
  • Risk profile: A service’s tier and remaining budget set its rollout policy automatically. See platform ch 16.
  • The nines: Each extra nine cuts allowed downtime tenfold and costs far more than the last. See platform ch 16.
  • Hyrum’s law: With enough users, every observable behaviour is depended on by someone. See platform ch 9, platform ch 14.
  • Window-based SLO: Count good and bad time windows instead of requests; suits low traffic. See Prometheus ch 13.
On AWSCloudWatch metric math gives you the SLI, composite alarms (long AND short window) give you burn-rate paging, and CloudWatch Application Signals offers native SLO objects. Use Synthetics canaries for CUJ probes and CloudWatch RUM for client-side SLIs. See POC 01 and 02.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Walk me through setting an SLO and alerting for a new checkout API.

Show a model answer

I’d start from the user, not from the server.

1. The journey. What does the user do? Add to cart, then pay. Checkout working means the payment request succeeds and is fast enough.

2. The target, agreed with product. For example: 99.9% of valid checkout requests succeed, and 99% finish in under 300 ms, measured over a rolling 30 days. “Valid” excludes things like malformed requests from a buggy client.

3. The budget. 99.9% over 30 days allows 0.1% failures, which is about 43 minutes of full downtime. That budget is what the team can spend on risk.

4. Where to measure. At the load balancer or frontend, so it includes everything behind it, plus a synthetic probe that runs the whole flow every minute.

5. Alerts on burn rate, meaning how fast the budget is being used. Page someone if 2% of the monthly budget is gone in an hour (a burn rate of 14.4), confirmed by the last 5 minutes so it stops paging once fixed. Open a ticket for slower burns. If traffic is low, require statistical confidence before paging, or one failed request will wake someone up.

6. A policy. Write down what happens when the budget runs out: releases limited to fixes, and the next sprint goes to reliability. Agree it before you need it.

On AWS: CloudWatch Application Signals for the SLO, CloudWatch Synthetics for the probe, and burn-rate alarms. POC 01 builds this.

Quick check: A team has run at 99.99% for a year against a 99.9% SLO. What does Hidalgo’s corollary predict?
The level you deliver is an observable behaviour, and people build on what they observe. Check in with consumers, or burn budget on purpose.
Quick check: Your 30-day SLO is 99.9%. How much full downtime does the budget allow?
0.001 × 30 × 1440 = 43.2 minutes. Know this cold.
Quick check: A fast-burn page fires when 2% of a 30-day budget is consumed in 1 hour. What burn rate is that?
Burn = 0.02 × 720 h / 1 h = 14.4.
Your turnOpen poc-01-slo-error-budget in the repo. Before running the tests, work out by hand the burn-rate thresholds for a 99.95% SLO, then check them against slo/alerting.py. Finish in the Labs station: slide the 5-minute error rate to zero and explain why the page clears.
Key takeaways
  • An SLI is good events over valid events. The SLO is the target, and the error budget is what’s left over.
  • 99.9% over 30 days is 43.2 minutes. Page at 14.4× burn, confirmed by a short window.
  • The target is a business decision made by a cross-functional group, written down with an error budget policy.
Part III · Awareness and preparednessChapter 9 · 14 min read · POC 02

Observability and monitoring

You will learn
  • the difference between monitoring and observability
  • Google’s three strategies for observability at microservice scale
  • why alerting telemetry and analytics telemetry are separate systems
  • how OpenTelemetry correlates signals

Monitoring versus observability

Traditional monitoring depended on tribal knowledge and on engineers correlating dashboards by hand. It answers questions you already knew to ask.

Observability combines time series, logs (including wide structured events), traces and continuous profiles so that someone without deep prior knowledge can test and reject hypotheses quickly, without shipping new code.

LatencyHow long requests take
TrafficHow much demand there is
ErrorsHow many requests fail
SaturationHow full the system is

The four golden signals are the starting point. RED (rate, errors, duration) suits services; USE (utilisation, saturation, errors) suits resources.

The metric that matters most is time to mitigate, from customer-centric detection to containment, followed by time to detect. The trend is towards knowledge graphs of assets and dependencies, AI-assisted investigation and views centred on customers instead of services.

Google’s three strategies at microservice scale

Out-of-the-box dashboardsShared libraries export the same metrics everywhere
→
Intelligent alertingStatistical or ML baselines instead of one static threshold
→
Automatic mitigationPre-checked symptoms, then rollback, scale-up or drain
  • Universal, horizontal alerts now make up nearly a fifth of all SRE alerts.
  • When an alert fires, a dashboard is generated with the common symptoms already checked.
  • Generic mitigations then run automatically: roll back on a statistically significant regression, scale up, or drain a failing cluster.

Two kinds of telemetry

High-availability telemetryAnalytics telemetry
Used forAlerting, control loops, probersTrends, capacity, investigations
SpeedSub-second, freshest data firstMinutes are fine
DependenciesAs few as possibleCan be many
CompletenessCan be sacrificedMust be complete
Cardinality and storageLow, short-livedHigh, cheap and long-lived

Give users one SDK, one config and one query endpoint across both. Keep the alerting path independent of the systems it watches.

OpenTelemetry

OpenTelemetry grew out of Google’s Census. Its principles are open, extensible, correlatable, universal and loosely coupled. Its parts are the OTLP protocol, the Collector, the APIs and zero-code instrumentation. It joins signals together in three ways:

ResourceWhere it ran: service, zone, instance.
Context propagationWhich request: trace IDs and baggage passed along each call.
Instrumentation scopeWhich code: the library, plus stack traces.
A ten-year decisionTreat the choice of an observability product as something you will live with for a decade; the chapter’s Waze migration story shows why. eBPF lets you observe without changing the application at all.

What only clients can see

Client telemetry reveals what backends can’t: DNS and load-balancer problems, expired certificates, failures hidden by retries, and crashes. It has to respect battery, network and privacy, and it must count the data it loses.

Customer-centric monitoring builds critical user journeys out of critical user interactions, and passes the journey ID through the RPC side channel so every hop can label its metrics.

Change, retention and privacy

  • Change supervision covers binaries, config, mobile releases, feature ramps and data pushes, not just code deploys.
  • Retention follows value. Google keeps minute-level data in memory for hours, on disk for weeks, and as 30-minute rollups for years.
  • Privacy needs data classification, minimisation, regional locality, deletion, fine-grained access control and customer-managed keys. Keep user IDs out of metric labels.

The statistics worth knowing

  • Paging on low traffic: page when the lower confidence bound is above the SLO’s error rate.
  • Composing dependencies: in series, success multiplies (80% × 90% = 72%). With hedging, failure multiplies (1 − 0.2 × 0.1 = 98%). Both assume the failures are independent.
  • Latency regressions: build per-cohort baselines, compute z-scores and watch the share of requests above 2. A jump means a regression.

From user goal to SLO

Server SLOs can be green while users can’t finish what they came to do. The book’s example is an email client whose send button is disabled: every API is healthy and nobody can send mail. The fix is to define SLOs from the user’s journey downward.

Goal“Stay in touch with my friends.” Why the user came. You can’t instrument this
→
Tasks“Send an email.” Steps towards the goal
→
InteractionsClick compose, type, click send. The critical ones are very common or essential
→
InstrumentationServer SLI, client SLI, end-to-end SLI
→
SLOsAvailability, latency, client-side success, quality

After Figure 9-4. A critical user journey (CUJ) is a goal plus its tasks; tasks are built from critical user interactions (CUIs).

  • Bad minute. To roll several SLIs up into one journey SLO, call a minute bad if any SLI in the journey was bad in that minute.
  • The journey is a dimension. A CUJ or CUI identifier travels with the request in trace context, so every metric can be sliced by journey.
  • Change supervision per journey. Watch each journey across five kinds of change: server binary, server configuration, mobile app release (which can’t be rolled back), feature ramps and data updates.
  • A central registry of journeys and an SDK give teams a well-lit path.

Case study: Maps and the “successful” failure

Maps has more than two billion monthly users. A server once returned well-formed responses built from malformed data, so searches “succeeded” with zero results. Server metrics saw nothing. The team wrote an invariant from the user’s side: the customer sees a non-zero number of valid results.

Two things followed that are worth telling in an interview. First, better detection looked like more outages for a while, because problems that had always been there became visible. Second, once the signal existed, canary rollouts that raised the zero-results rate paused themselves. The team then sold customer-centric monitoring to product leads as delivery speed: the supervision built during the emergency could now protect every new feature.

Client-side telemetry

InstrumentationIn the app or browser
→
UploaderBatches and sends
→
Public endpoint
→
Collector serviceSamples, validates
→
Storage

Server metrics can’t see failed DNS, an expired certificate, a crash, or retries hiding an error. The client can.

Trade-offWhat to do about it
Batched uploads arrive late, with device clocks that driftRecord both device and server time, and expect late events in pipelines
On-device storage fills up and events are droppedDropping the oldest hides the trigger; dropping the newest hides the present. Report counts ingested, uploaded and dropped, with reasons, so you have error bars
A crash-looping app turns telemetry into a DDoS on yourselfSample at the collector and push sampling down to clients
The collector shares fate with the main serviceIsolate it, or you lose telemetry exactly when you need it
Old builds never updateTag everything with build, release channel and OS or browser

YouTube uploads are the book’s example: server-side API availability looked high, and client-side instrumentation showed a noticeably worse experience.

Alerting on evidence, not on a single ratio

One error in twenty requests is a 5% error rate, and it is almost certainly noise. The book’s method treats each request as a trial, computes a confidence interval for the true error rate, and pages only when the lower bound is above the SLO threshold. The observed rate can cross the line many times without the alert firing (Figure 9-7 shows exactly this). The Labs station has a calculator for it.

For latency, compare against the service’s own past: group requests into cohorts by method, customer and workload shape, keep a 30-day mean and standard deviation, and alert on z-scores. “Slower than usual” is an implicit SLO that works across products.

What telemetry costs, and what you keep

Data loses value as it ages, so retention is a design decision. Google’s Horizontal Monitoring Data (HMD) collects a common set of series centrally, so a new service gets them without asking.

DataKept in memoryKept on disk
Raw, minute-levelHoursWeeks
Precomputed aggregatesHoursFull resolution for weeks, then 30-minute resolution for years

Aggregation saves at least ten-fold, series nobody has read for months are phased out, and owners can extend retention if they have quota. On AWS the same thinking gives you CloudWatch metric resolution tiers, log retention per log group, S3 lifecycle rules for traces and logs, and cost allocation tags for chargeback.

Four questions before adopting an observability product

  1. How well supported is it?
  2. Does it conform to open standards such as those from the CNCF?
  3. Does it work on every platform you have: backend, mobile, web?
  4. What happens if you don’t adopt it?

Waze is the cautionary tale. It moved from an in-house library to OpenCensus to OpenTelemetry, the last migration took over a year, and overlapping systems confused developers. The team calls instrumentation a ten-year decision. Open standards let you keep the agent and swap the backend, but dashboards and alerts still have to be migrated.

Also in the chapter

  • Universal and horizontal alerts. About a fifth of all SRE alerts at Google are universal ones every service inherits. Component owners also publish alerts for everything that uses their component, such as an auth library.
  • High-availability telemetry must come back fresh. After a monitoring outage, serve the newest data first and relax completeness before availability. Monitoring must not depend on the services it watches.
  • eBPF gives logs, profiles, network metrics and traces without code changes, in exchange for kernel-level permissions and less depth than hand instrumentation.
  • Privacy. “Anonymous” per-region data is not anonymous when one customer is alone in a region. Classify data, minimise and redact, keep it in its locale, set wipe-out periods by type, and use one vetted SDK so teams can’t overshare.
  • Agents. A trace shows what an agent was asked and what it answered, and says nothing about whether the answer was good. Quality needs its own signal.

The knowledge graph, drawn

Product AWhere users notice
→
Service
→
Service
→
Shared dependencyWhere it started

After Figures 9-1 and 9-5, simplified. The book’s versions show whole product areas as nodes, with normal call paths in one colour and the path of a performance problem in another.

This is what “product-focused observability” looks like in practice. An investigator sees which products are affected and where the degradation entered, without needing to be an expert in every service in between. It is also the structure an AI assistant needs: a graph it can walk is far more useful to it than a wall of dashboards.

On AWS you can get part of the way with X-Ray or Application Signals service maps, and resource tags that name the product each service belongs to. The tags are the part teams skip, and the part that makes the graph answer product questions.

What the Maps failure looked likeFigure 9-6 is a screenshot worth picturing: a search for “coffee” in the middle of San Francisco, and Maps replying that it can’t find any. Every server returned success. That one image is the argument for measuring from the user’s side.
Instrumenting agentsOpenTelemetry has semantic conventions for generative AI, covering model calls, agents, and agent-to-tool and agent-to-agent protocols such as MCP and A2A. Using them means agent traces look the same in every backend. The chapter’s caveat still holds: a trace shows what the agent did, not whether the answer was good.
Doing it with the Prometheus and Grafana stack

Testing hypotheses quickly depends on moving between signals. The Grafana book’s answer is correlation by design: exemplars attach a trace ID to a metric sample, Loki derived fields turn a trace ID in a log line into a link, and span metrics give RED metrics for every operation from the traces themselves (Grafana ch 5, ch 6).

Each signal stores what it is good at: numbers in metrics with few labels, events in logs indexed only by a handful of labels, and high-cardinality context such as customer IDs in spans. The customer-centric invariant in this chapter is a black-box probe (the blackbox exporter, or CloudWatch Synthetics) plus real user monitoring (Grafana ch 12), and the universal alerts every service inherits are what monitoring mixins package (Prometheus ch 11).

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the platform book, Mastering Prometheus and Observability with Grafana also cover, from the knowledge map:
  • Low-traffic alerting: Page only when a confidence interval’s lower bound exceeds the threshold. See Prometheus ch 13.
  • Observability: Someone without tribal knowledge can test and reject hypotheses quickly. See Prometheus ch 1, Grafana ch 1.
  • Four golden signals: Latency, traffic, errors, saturation, with the same names everywhere. See platform ch 16, Grafana ch 8, Grafana ch 9.
  • Client-side telemetry: What servers can’t see: DNS, certificates, crashes, retries hiding errors. See Grafana ch 12.
  • RED and USE: Rate, errors, duration for requests; utilisation, saturation, errors for resources. See Grafana ch 9.
On AWSADOT collector → CloudWatch EMF metrics and X-Ray traces; CloudWatch Logs Insights and Athena for analytics; Anomaly Detection alarms; Synthetics and RUM; Managed Prometheus/Grafana; KMS CMKs for telemetry encryption. See POC 02.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

What’s the difference between monitoring and observability, and how would you roll out observability on AWS?

Show a model answer

Monitoring answers questions you thought of in advance. You decided beforehand that error rate matters, so you built a graph and an alert: “is the error rate above 1%?”. It tells you that something is wrong.

Observability lets you answer questions you didn’t think of in advance, during an incident, without shipping new code. For example: “Are the failing requests all from the new mobile app version, in one region, for customers with large baskets?” If your telemetry carries enough context, you can slice it that way on the spot. It helps you find why.

The book’s test is practical: can someone without tribal knowledge form a hypothesis, check it and rule it out quickly? If only the person who built the service can debug it, you have monitoring but not observability.

How I’d roll it out on AWS:

1. One standard way to emit telemetry. OpenTelemetry, an open standard for metrics, logs and traces, deployed through ADOT (the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry). One SDK in every service means one format everywhere and you can change backends later.

2. Make signals joinable. Every metric, log line and trace carries the same identity tags (service name, version, environment, region) and the trace ID. Then you can jump from an alert to the logs of the exact failing request. These shared tags are what the lesson calls resource identity and trace context.

3. Put high-detail data in the right place. Don’t put user IDs or request IDs on metrics: every unique value creates a new time series, and cost explodes. Keep them in logs and traces, which are built for that detail.

4. Alerts first, on what users feel. SLO-based alerts on critical journeys, plus automatic first checks (recent deploys, error breakdown by region) attached to each page.

5. Keep alerting independent. Alerts must not depend on the system they watch. If the service and its monitoring share fate, both go dark together.

In AWS services: ADOT collectors, CloudWatch metrics and Application Signals for SLOs, X-Ray for traces, CloudWatch Logs Insights for questions you didn’t plan, and CloudWatch RUM and Synthetics for the user’s view. POC 02 sets this up.

Quick check: Every server metric is green, but users searching for “coffee” get zero results. Which practice catches this?
The Maps case. The server “successfully” returned empty answers, so only a customer-centric signal could see it.
Quick check: Service A calls B (99.9%) then C (99.9%), and both are required. What is A’s best-case availability?
0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 0.998. Serial dependencies multiply.
Quick check: Low-traffic service: 200 requests in an hour. How do you page soundly?
With N = 200 and a 14.4% target at 99% confidence, you need 42 failures.
Your turnRun poc-02-observability-otel locally with Docker Compose. Send a few requests, then find one request’s trace ID in the JSON logs and follow it. Which three things let you join the log line, the metric and the trace?
Show the answer

1. The trace ID (and span ID), written into the log line, so a log entry points at exactly one request’s trace. 2. The same resource attributes on all three signals: service name, version, environment, region. They tell you which service and deployment produced each one. 3. The time: a metric is an aggregate with no trace ID, so you join it to traces and logs through the same service tags and the same time window. Metrics can also carry exemplars, sample trace IDs attached to a data point, which link a spike straight to example requests.

Key takeaways
  • Observability lets someone without tribal knowledge test and reject hypotheses quickly.
  • The metric that matters most is time to mitigate.
  • Keep the alerting path fast and simple, the analytics path complete and cheap, and one SDK in front of both.
Part III · Awareness and preparednessChapter 10 · 9 min read · POC 03

Incident management and on-call

You will learn
  • the IMAG roles and how an incident moves through its lifecycle
  • why you mitigate before you understand, and the five generic mitigations
  • how to design on-call that people can sustain
  • what to measure instead of MTTR

The big picture

Define your terms. An incident means users are having a bad time, important properties are degraded, or an outage is happening or imminent; an outage means a service or critical feature can't do its job. Anyone may declare an incident or escalate it, and false positives get relabelled later, which keeps politics out. On-call is a mechanism for coordinating urgent work; paging a whole team triggers the bystander effect.

Incident CommanderHolds every role until they delegate it. Directs, and in big incidents takes no hands-on tasks.
Communications LeadKeeps stakeholders and customers informed on a fixed cadence. May split into internal and external.
Operations LeadRuns the hands-on response: investigating and applying mitigations.

Rotation design has six inputs:

  • Load: roughly two incidents per shift at most. Overload and underload both degrade response.
  • Coverage that matches users: business hours is “on duty”, daylight across two sites gives about 21 hours, and follow-the-sun gives 24×7.
  • Response time: three minutes or less needs two people; 30 minutes allows normal life.
  • System properties that buy slack, such as graceful degradation.
  • Customer constraints, like where responders must be located.
  • Labour law.

Incident response teams coordinate incidents that span many teams. Large organisations run a global IRT plus product-area IRTs with clear escalation triggers and one common command framework; small ones keep a volunteer pool with "inversion of authority" and avoid incident theatre (as large as necessary, as small as possible). Watch for coordination overhead, handoffs, late engagement and skill atrophy.

The incident lifecycle has six stages:

  1. Detect.
  2. Triage. How many users, global or local, which journeys? Declare early. Success means fast, accurate classification and escalation.
  3. Investigate. Root cause analysis is slow and political, and OODA is still linear, so Google prefers multiple hypotheses tested in parallel by trying to disprove them.
  4. Mitigate. Generic, safe mitigations come first: rollback, more capacity, restart, drain. A mitigation is also a diagnostic experiment, and whether you can mitigate is an architectural property.
  5. Resolve. Causes understood, or the change rolled back and blocked, followed by a “wait and see” period.
  6. Learn.

AI in incident response: start with detection and triage (the worst case is over-escalation), summaries, dynamic dashboards and hypotheses. Allow production changes only with guardrails, where each change is reversible and atomic (action, validation and automatic rollback in one audited transaction).

Two additions from the Grafana book

The Grafana book adds a gold–silver–bronze structure above the incident roles here: responders work at bronze, managers own the tactical plan at silver, and senior leaders own strategy, legal and media at gold. Agreeing those levels in advance is what lets a serious incident escalate cleanly (Grafana ch 9).

Tooling matters for the communications role too. Alertmanager grouping and inhibition stop one failure from producing a hundred pages (Prometheus ch 5), and incident tools such as Grafana Incident or AWS Systems Manager Incident Manager record the timeline automatically, so the postmortem starts from facts.

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that Observability with Grafana also covers, from the knowledge map:
  • Incident roles: Commander directs, operations acts, communications informs. See Grafana ch 9.
  • Sustainable on-call: Limits on on-call share, rotation size and incidents per shift. See Grafana ch 9.
  • Gold, silver, bronze: Strategic, tactical and operational levels of incident command. See Grafana ch 9.
Going deeper the case studies, numbers and named models from the full chapter

Classify before you respond

Bugs, incidents and outages need different behaviour (immediate engagement versus a ticket). Watch the politics in both directions: if leadership counts outages, people under-label; if declaring an outage lets you bypass policy, people over-escalate. Notifying a whole team invites the bystander effect, while relying on one person creates a single point of failure.

On-call design

Aim for no more than two incidents per shift, assuming each takes four to six hours end to end. A service that almost never pages may not justify SRE at all. Schedule options include business hours, daytime (6am–8pm), a daylight span across sites of about 21 hours, and 24-hour coverage via follow-the-sun or compensatory time.

Required response time drives staffing: about three minutes needs at least two engineers ready to act; thirty minutes or more may not need a laptop at all. Constraints such as data residency, citizenship or security clearance matter, and Google uses a constraint solver for fair rotations. Relax requirements before you burn people out.

IMAG and IRTs

The incident commander holds every role until they delegate one, and comms may split into internal and external leads. Incidents can move between states in any order, and big ones become a tree of child incidents under a parent that waits until all the children are resolved.

Incident response teams are paged directly by criteria. Large organisations run federated IRTs (Google has Tech IRT plus Cloud, Search and YouTube IRTs, all on the same framework). Small organisations use a swarm of senior volunteers per incident.

Google found consensus-driven and executive-as-IC models slower and more stressful. Make business context queryable ahead of time: which customers are critical, which racks hold whose workloads.

Triage and mitigation

Favour data about user experience over whatever errors are easiest to see. Don't penalise false-positive declarations, but remember investigation isn't free, so curate dashboards. Risk tolerance scales with impact: a widely visible outage justifies a riskier mitigation, while a minor one calls for caution, and standing down quickly after triage counts as a win.

DrainMove traffic away
→
Roll backUndo the last change
→
UpsizeAdd capacity
→
DegradeShed features or quality
→
BlockStop the bad input

The five generic mitigations. None of them needs a root cause.

Mitigate first, and never blame a reasonable mitigation that didn't work; that's outcome bias ("resulting"). Weigh any action against the risk of doing nothing. OODA has a weakness here: it's hard to tell whether your action caused the change or it was coincidence.

Coordination costs

Humans are poor at passive monitoring beyond about 30 minutes. Assume a responder who has had no question, input or task for an hour has disengaged. Tens or hundreds of responders means you need better observability or training. MTTR averages mislead, because a rollback takes minutes and a physical repair takes days.

Track coordination instead: ramp-up time for new joiners, how often status interrupts work, and the number of channels and tools. In big incidents the IC directs and shouldn't pick up tasks. Assignments should be specific ("check whether the latest rollout's timing and locations match the latency rise").

AI in incidents and Etsy's model

Use AI as a rubber duck, and for agents that log their full reasoning with signals and confidence, each with its own identity and authorisation. Treat human approvals as training feedback towards autonomy, not as clutter.

Etsy reports monthly incident metrics to leadership, runs an incident-announce channel with about 1,000 members, gives every incident its own Slack channel created automatically from alerts, sets safe defaults (severity can change later) and runs a weekly 24×7 LSE coordinator rotation of senior leaders.

That coordinator separates business decisions from technical restoration. Postmortems are mandatory for SEV1/2 and open with a standard blameless statement that avoids "root cause" and names. The motto: slow is smooth, smooth is fast.

On AWSIncident Manager (response plans, contacts, escalation plans, chat channels, timelines, post-incident analysis), AWS Chatbot, SSM Automation runbooks, AWS Health for provider-side events. See POC 03.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

You’re paged at 3am: checkout errors are spiking. What do you do in the first 15 minutes?

Show a model answer

Priority one is stopping the damage, not understanding it. Diagnosis can wait until users are safe.

Minutes 0–2. Acknowledge the page so nobody else is woken for the same thing, and take the incident commander role until someone else does.

Minutes 2–5. Size it. Check the SLO dashboard and probes: which journeys are failing, what share of users, which region or availability zone?

Minutes 5–10. Ask what changed. Deploys, config pushes, feature flags, dependency incidents. If a change lines up with the start of the errors, roll it back now, without proving it was the cause first. Rollback is cheap and safe; debugging at 3am is slow. If the problem is confined to one zone, move traffic away from it (on AWS, a zonal shift).

Minutes 10–15. If it isn’t contained, get help explicitly: page the service owner and a second responder, hand communications to someone, and split the work into named hypotheses with one owner each. Post a first update to stakeholders: what we know, what we’re doing, when the next update comes.

Throughout, say each mitigation out loud in the incident channel and watch the SLO graph to see whether it worked.

Your incident has 60 people on the bridge and no progress. What do you do?

Show a model answer

Sixty people is a coordination failure, not a staffing success. The book cites research showing the cost of coordination is often what slows incidents down.

I’d restructure: one incident commander who stops doing hands-on work, an operations lead who directs the fixing, and a communications lead who handles all updates.

Split the problem into child incidents, each with its own lead and small team, for example “database latency” and “payment provider errors”.

Give everyone else a specific task or release them. People who are only watching add noise and ask for updates.

Set a fixed update rhythm, such as every 20 minutes, so people stop interrupting the responders. If the decisions span several organisations, escalate to a senior incident coordinator.

Quick check: During an incident you don’t yet know the cause, but a deploy went out 10 minutes before impact. What first?
Mitigate first. Rollback is the safest generic mitigation when the timing lines up with a change.
Quick check: Which investigation approach does Google prefer?
Parallel hypotheses that you try to disprove reduce confirmation bias and usually mitigate faster.
Your turnOpen poc-03-incident-management/playbooks/slo-burn.md and role-play it aloud as Incident Commander for a checkout outage: declare, assign roles, pick the first mitigation and give two status updates. Time yourself.
Key takeaways
  • Clear roles first. The Incident Commander directs and delegates.
  • Mitigate before you understand: drain, roll back, upsize, degrade or block.
  • Risk tolerance for a mitigation scales with impact, and a reasonable mitigation that fails is never blameworthy.
Part III · Awareness and preparednessChapter 11 · 8 min read · POC 03

Learning from incidents

You will learn
  • what a good postmortem contains and who should write it
  • the safety-science models interviewers expect you to know
  • the Paris data centre outage, start to finish, and what it changed

The big picture

An outage is an unplanned investment, and the postmortem collects the return. Foundations: put learning first (timeline, impact, contributing causes, lessons), stay blameless, collaborate across teams, and have executives model the behaviour and give it visibility.

In practice: study the incident thoroughly to find the earliest point it could have been detected, ask open questions without judgment, don't let temporary fixes become permanent, give every action item an owner and close it out, and share widely (weekly outage digests, a company-wide newsletter).

What has changed in a decade: safety science and systems thinking (STPA and CAST), storytelling, analysis of communication logs and responders' mental models, an independent postmortem lead who wasn't in the response, accountability that keeps the people closest to the decisions involved in fixing them, customer-centric impact analysis, and layered reviews at peer, team, organisation and executive level.

The chapter also leans on safety science: Swiss cheese, Rasmussen, Safety-II, Cook, Woods and STAMP. Each gets a line in the section on safety-science models below.

Rasmussen’s boundaries, drawn

Of the safety-science models in this chapter, Rasmussen’s is the one that needs a picture. A team works inside a space with three edges. Go past the first and the business fails. Go past the second and people burn out. Go past the third and you have an accident.

This explains “drift into failure”. Nobody chose to be unsafe. Each shortcut was a sensible answer to cost or workload pressure, and each one that didn’t cause an outage looked like proof it was fine. The counter-force has to be deliberate and continuous: error budgets, game days, postmortem follow-through. A poster campaign after an outage pushes back for a week.

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that Observability with Grafana also covers, from the knowledge map:
  • Blameless postmortem: Why the action made sense at the time; several contributing factors. See Grafana ch 9.
Going deeper the case studies, numbers and named models from the full chapter

What a postmortem must contain

Key facts (timeline, activities, people), impact (which customers and systems), contributing causes (deviations, actions, data) and lessons learned. Ask non-judgemental questions: not "why did you think it was OK to deploy?" but "what about the situation made deploying look like the best option?". Socialise widely: Google sends curated weekly outage reports and a twice-yearly "Greatest Hits" newsletter.

How the practice evolved

Postmortems now look at the sociotechnical system through STPA and CAST, incident storytelling, communication logs and interviews about responders' mental models. An independent postmortem lead, someone who wasn't in the incident, interviews participants, guards against outcome bias and hindsight bias, and also records what went right.

Restorative accountability means the people closest to the decisions help design and own the fixes. Reviews happen in layers: peer, team, organisation and executive. AI helps too: load a notebook with past postmortems and ask whether a proposed design change would have prevented them.

Safety-science models to name-drop correctly

  • Swiss cheese (Reason): active and latent holes line up, the slices are both technical and human, and near misses are the cases where only one slice held, so ask where you got lucky.
  • Rasmussen: economic and workload pressures push operations towards the edge of acceptable performance, so you need continuous "fire prevention".
  • Hollnagel's Safety-I vs Safety-II: Safety-I prevents bad outcomes; Safety-II makes good outcomes more likely by studying normal work and human adaptation.
  • Cook: complex systems always run degraded (some disks in Colossus are always failing), change constantly, and need several failures lined up to collapse.
  • Woods: graceful extensibility and sustained adaptability. The danger is decompensation: points of presence fail one by one and get absorbed, until one more failure takes the whole network down.
  • Leveson's STAMP, with CAST for analysis after the fact and STPA for analysis before it.

Case study: Paris, April 2023

A cooling-pipe water leak in europe-west9 led to a battery-room fire, and the fire brigade ordered power off for one of the region's three buildings. Regional Spanner lost quorum, and a design flaw turned that into a global outage for some API methods that fan out across regions.

  1. 16:46A cooling pipe starts leaking above one zone.
  2. 17:25First automated alert. Engineers respond within minutes.
  3. 18:30VMs in the affected cluster are brought down in a controlled way.
  4. 19:17A product communications lead is paged in. Updates get specific.
  5. 20:00The fire brigade takes command of a battery-room fire.
  6. 23:04Power is cut to one building. A regional database loses quorum, and a design flaw spreads that to some global APIs.
  7. 23:46A known mitigation has failed. Three new ones are built in parallel.
  8. 03:38The first new mitigation works. Impact is regional again.
  9. 19:00Next day: control plane restored across the region.

A known generic mitigation failed. The IC had the team brainstorm, picked the three options that could be built and tested in hours, and ran them in parallel; the first fixed the global impact about four hours later. Customers' complaints were nearly 12 hours of recovery after power returned, and slow, vague updates; one awkward phrase in an update became a media joke.

The analysis found that nobody was making decisions for Compute Engine as a whole, even though it has separate control plane, data plane and hardware on-call rotations.

It also found that fact-checking slowed updates yet still let errors through (a wrong region was named as impacted), that no process existed for large-scale customer outreach, and that generic mitigations took hours when they needed minutes. Paging in a product communications lead was what went right. The actions:

  • A rotation of product-level incident commanders.
  • Faster cluster shutdown and restore.
  • "Hide the region" made into a safe, repeatable tool.
  • Broken generic mitigations fixed and added to disaster recovery exercises.
  • The comms lead paged automatically for significant outages, with templates and a formal outreach process.

In March 2025, a power loss in us-east5-c stayed local and took about 6 hours instead of more than 11.

On AWSIncident Manager's post-incident analysis with custom templates (use the CAST template in POC 03), action items tracked through OpsCenter or Jira, and Correction of Error (CoE), Amazon's own postmortem format with its "5 whys", which is worth comparing with CAST in an interview.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

How do you make sure postmortem action items actually prevent recurrence?

Show a model answer

Most postmortems fail after they are written: the action items quietly expire. So I’d manage them like real work.

Every item traces back to a specific contributing factor in the analysis, so nobody adds generic “be more careful” items.

Sort them into four kinds: prevent (stop it happening), detect (notice it faster), mitigate (shorten it) and process. Many teams write only prevention items; the detection and mitigation ones often pay off more.

Each item has one owner and a due date, and completion is reviewed every week in the production meeting and in leadership reliability reviews. Overdue items are visible.

Finally, look across incidents, not only within one. Google’s line is that there are rarely new outages, only new instances of old ones. A regular digest of postmortems helps spot the same pattern in other services and fix it there too.

What makes a postmortem good?

Show a model answer

Five things.

An author who wasn’t directly involved, so the account isn’t defensive.

A complete timeline, including when people were told, not only what the system did.

Several contributing factors, across people, process and technology. A single “root cause” usually means the analysis stopped too early.

An honest section on what went well and where we got lucky. Luck is a risk you haven’t fixed.

Action items sorted into prevent, detect and mitigate, each with an owner. The real proof is the follow-up: the next similar incident was shorter or smaller. The book has an example of exactly that, comparing how two similar regional incidents went.

Quick check: In Rasmussen’s model, why does a system drift towards the accident boundary?
Each shortcut is a rational response to pressure, and each one that doesn’t fail looks like proof it was safe.
Quick check: What turned a regional Spanner quorum loss in Paris into a global outage?
A regional dependency had global blast radius through a fan-out design flaw.
Quick check: Which Paris action item addressed the missing decision maker for Compute Engine?
GCE has control plane, data plane and hardware rotations; nobody owned product-wide decisions until this rotation existed.
Your turnTake an incident you were part of and add the two sections most postmortems lack: what went right, and where you got lucky. Then use poc-03-incident-management/templates/postmortem-cast.md to restate one “human error” as a question about the system.
Key takeaways
  • An independent lead, several contributing factors, and what went right as well as what went wrong.
  • Know one line each on Swiss cheese, Rasmussen, Safety-II, Cook, Woods and STAMP.
  • Paris led to product-level incident commanders and auto-paged comms leads, and the next similar outage took about half the time.
Part III · Awareness and preparednessChapter 12 · 11 min read · POC 03

Safety engineering with STPA and CAST

You will learn
  • why “no component failed” outages need a different model
  • the four steps of STPA and the parts of a control loop
  • how CAST analyses an incident without blame
  • how to get a team to try it

The big picture

Some major outages happen without any single component failing, as when a large Maps data update for Japan broke search. The chain-of-events model ("the root cause was the bug") assumes that sequence means causation and stops at a simple story.

1 · Losses and hazardsWhat must never happen, and the states that lead there
→
2 · Control structureWho controls what, and what feedback they get
→
3 · Unsafe control actionsMissing, wrong, mistimed, or too long or short
→
4 · Causal scenariosWhy a controller would do that

STPA looks forward at a design. CAST uses the same model to look back at an incident.

STAMP says accidents happen when the system's design fails to constrain its components' behaviour: missing tests, code too complex to review, global rollouts and aggressive deadlines are why a risky release looked reasonable.

STPA looks forward, and you can run it on a design doc. It has four steps:

  1. Define losses and hazards: detectable states that lead to a loss in the worst case.
  2. Model the control structure: controllers, control actions going down, feedback coming up, and each controller’s process or mental model.
  3. List unsafe control actions: not taken when needed, taken when unsafe, taken too early, too late or in the wrong order, or stopped too soon or applied too long.
  4. Build causal scenarios for each.

CAST looks backward at an incident. It has five steps:

  1. Basic information: losses, hazards, timeline, questions.
  2. The control structure as it was.
  3. Each controller’s contribution, described neutrally (no “should have”), with its mental-model gaps and context.
  4. Flaws in the control structure through systemic factors: safety culture, communication and coordination, management of change, safety information, and changes in the environment.
  5. An improvement plan that traces back to those factors.

The control loop, drawn

Read the picture as four places to look for trouble: the control action can be wrong or late, the feedback can be missing or misleading, the controller’s mental model can be out of date, and the process can behave in a way nobody modelled.

Two ways to explain the same outage

A change with a bug is submittedFix: add a test
→
The release includes itFix: run tests on every build
→
It rolls out to productionFix: progressive rollout
→
Services crashFix: crash alerts

After Figure 12-1. The chain-of-events view. Each link gets a patch, and each patch is reasonable.

The trouble is that the chain only describes this bug. The systems view in Figure 12-2 asks a different question at each step: what influenced the decision?

ControllerFactors that shaped its decisionsWhat followed
EngineersMissing tests, time pressure, tool limits, code complexity, skillsThe change was submitted, rolled out, and not rolled back
Build systemMissing tests, flaky or skipped tests, no QA acceptance stepThe bug was included in the release
Deployment systemGlobal rollouts, limited telemetry, complex production configurationProduction crashed

Notice that software systems are treated as decision-makers too. Fixing “time pressure” or “global rollouts” prevents many future outages, including ones with entirely different bugs.

A worked unsafe control action

In the Maps example a geospatial data specialist asks for approval, and a review team’s approver consults subject-matter experts before answering. One unsafe control action falls straight out of the diagram: the approver approves when the experts have not approved. Nothing failed. The structure allowed it. The hazard that analysis is protecting against is stated plainly: the published map disagrees with the real world.

How CAST layers an incident

Adverse eventsBug introduced, buggy release deployed, not rolled back, service crashed
→
Controllers’ behaviourWhat each person or system did, and why it made sense to them
→
Causal factorsGlobal rollouts, missing tests, limited telemetry, time pressure, tool limits
→
Systemic factorsManagement of change, safety culture, safety information, communication, environment

After Figure 12-9. A postmortem that stops at the first box fixes one bug. Recommendations aimed at the last box fix a class of them.

Why bother before launchThe book’s Figure 12-11 makes the economic case in one picture: most design flaws are introduced during design, most are found in testing or production, and fixing them is most expensive by far in production. Ben Treynor Sloss’s summary of STPA is that it is like being told about your outages before they happen, so you can choose which to fix and which to live with.

The misnamed cities, in one picture

Census dataset arrives
→
EvaluatedBy sampling
→
Published to Maps
→
Users report wrong names
→
Data rolled back
→
Fixed

The data was too large to review by hand, so the specialists checked four states where they had local knowledge: Washington, California, Texas and New York. The six states with wrong city names were Montana, Kansas, Indiana, Kentucky, Tennessee and Georgia. Figure 12-7 puts both sets on a map and they don’t overlap at all.

A classic postmortem calls that imperfect sampling and stops. CAST asks why sampling four states seemed sufficient, who knew the sample wasn’t representative, and what feedback would have shown it. That is how the same incident produced 22 recommendations where the postmortem had 8.

The final figure in the chapter repeats the design-flaw grid with one arrow added, labelled STPA, pointing from production back to design. The whole method is that arrow: find the flaw where fixing it is cheap.

Going deeper the case studies, numbers and named models from the full chapter

Why safety engineering

A 2019 Google Maps postmortem was well written, yet leaders felt it was insufficient, because no component had failed. Chain-of-events models are about a century old, and picking a "root cause" is arbitrary, since you can always go further back.

A better question is whether the fix would prevent similar incidents, not just this one. Safety is an emergent property: you can't read it from one component's spec.

Doing STPA well

Losses include "loss of mission" (a user can't navigate) as well as revenue and trust. A hazard is a state, for example a published map that doesn't match the real world. Build a functional control structure, not a structural one: five teams that can deploy become one "deploys updates" controller.

Google's diagrams usually have 5–10 boxes, roughly a tenth the size of a dataflow diagram, and drawing one together gives teams a shared language. Every controller has responsibilities, a control algorithm and a process model (for software) or mental model (for humans), and those models are only as good as the feedback is correct, complete and timely.

To find causal scenarios, ask: was feedback missing or wrong, was the model inaccurate, was a safe action overridden or lost in communication, or did the system react unexpectedly?

Maps in Japan

A team deliberately dropped connections between nested administrative polygons, expecting the daily repair pipeline to restore them. The update was split into smaller serialised changes, so dashboards declined gradually. Nobody had ever validated the design assumption that inconsistencies would be local in time and space; in reality many features stayed broken for weeks.

PostmortemSystems analysis
Maps in Japan (STPA)7 recommendations56 causal scenarios, 34 recommendations
Misnamed cities (CAST)3 people, 16 hours, 8 recommendations5 people, 81 hours, 22 recommendations

The approval was rushed under data-freshness pressure, across a Japanese public holiday. The STPA took 2 engineers part-time for 5 weeks and covered more than 30 subsystems and over a dozen teams. It found 56 causal scenarios: almost every defect in the original postmortem plus gaps that could cause at least four other major incidents. It made 34 recommendations against the postmortem's 7.

CAST and misnamed cities

Authority increases as you go up the control structure, and confusion about responsibilities points to causes. Blame is the enemy of safety: replace the person and the same system leads the next one to the same choice. The incident unfolds in layers: events, then controller behaviour, then causal factors, then systemic factors.

Validation sampled four large states while the bug hit six others. As datasets grew over the years, the system drifted into a riskier state (Rasmussen's drift again), and splitting the data by state let each piece pass a "small change" check.

CAST took 5 people and 81 hours and produced 22 recommendations; the postmortem took 3 people and 16 hours and produced 8. Its recommendations reach the top of the control structure: processes, hiring rubrics, ownership after reorganisations, and measuring whether postmortem fixes worked.

Getting adoption

A design flaw costs one engineer an afternoon in a design doc, or a whole team a month once it's in production. Senior engineers' design intuition can't be taught directly, but STPA can. Lead with a surprising finding and reveal the method afterwards.

Start small: a limited STPA with one or two subject experts in under a week. Pick systems with past surprises, high consequences, people working alongside automation, or that are still in early design. STPA also feeds DiRT: it suggests multi-step, multi-controller scenarios that go beyond what people can imagine on their own.

On AWSDraw the control structure from your pipeline (CodePipeline → CodeDeploy → Lambda/ECS, with CloudWatch alarms as feedback). UCAs translate into requirements such as "rollback must work with only the on-call role" or "a canary with no data must not promote". See POC 03's worksheet.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

What would STPA find that a traditional design review would miss?

Show a model answer

A design review checks each component against good practice: is the database replicated, does the service have timeouts. STPA (system-theoretic process analysis) looks at how components control each other, and what each one believes about the others.

That finds a different kind of problem: failures where nothing is broken. For example, an automated deployer promotes a release because a health signal is missing, and it treats “no data” as “healthy”. Or two teams each assume the other one is approving a change, so nobody does.

It has three advantages. It doesn’t rely on someone happening to imagine the failure, because the method walks every control action systematically. It works before any code exists. And fixing a design flaw at the design stage is far cheaper than fixing it in production.

The book’s example: STPA on one Maps system produced 34 recommendations, against 7 from the earlier postmortem.

Nothing broke, but users got wrong data. How do you analyse that?

Show a model answer

I’d use CAST, which is STPA applied backwards to an incident that already happened.

Map the control structure: who and what decided the data was ready to publish, and what information did each of them have?

Then find where someone’s mental model was wrong and why feedback didn’t correct it. The book’s example is a dataset of US city names: reviewers checked a sample of four states, the errors were in six other states, and nothing told them the sample wasn’t representative.

Then go up to systemic factors: time pressure, incentives, how the review process drifted over time.

The recommendations should remove the whole class of problem, for example continuously checking whether the assumptions behind a design still hold, not just fixing the one bad dataset.

Quick check: Reviewers sampled four states and the errors were in six other states. What would CAST ask that a classic postmortem might not?
CAST looks for why the decision made sense at the time and how the control structure allowed it.
Quick check: In STPA, a hazard is…
Hazards are states, not events; losses are the unacceptable outcomes.
Quick check: In STPA, what should a control structure model?
Five teams that can deploy collapse into one “deploys updates” controller. Function, not structure.
Your turnFill in poc-03-incident-management/templates/stpa-worksheet.md for a deploy pipeline you know. Name one controller, its control actions and its feedback, then write one unsafe control action of each of the four types.
Key takeaways
  • Safety is an emergent property of the whole system. You can’t read it from one component.
  • Model functional controllers, their process models and their feedback.
  • Blame is the enemy of safety. Ask why the action made sense, then fix the system.
Part IV · Infrastructure designChapter 13 · 9 min read · POC 09

Automation, tooling and toil

You will learn
  • the four reasons to automate and the levels of automation
  • the ironies and pitfalls of automation
  • how to decide what to automate, and how to do it incrementally
  • what toil is, when it is acceptable, and what doesn’t fix it

The big picture

You automate to save time in normal operations and in emergencies, and for consistency and scale. Automation moves through levels: none, then partial (where teams can get stuck), then full, which can be local, platform-wide, or best of all inherent system behaviour that removes the task altogether.

Detect and alertThe automation only tells humans
→
SuggestIt proposes an action; a human does it
→
Act and notifyIt acts and reports what it did

The safety ladder for new automation. Move up one rung at a time, and the whole team can follow along.

Capacity provisioning shows the progression: hardcoded replicas → autoscaling across locations → sizing by customer usage → continuously optimised placement, run by two layers of platform automation (minutes to hours, and days to months).

Bainbridge's ironies of automation: it creates new work (monitoring and fixing the automation), erodes operators' skills, and leaves humans the hardest cases. The pitfalls are dangerous automation without safety checks, deskilling, automation surprise, automating over a broken foundation (auto-restarting a memory leak), automating a moving target, and automating ambiguous decisions.

To decide, combine quantifiable costs and benefits (engineers underestimate maintenance) with strategic value, hidden risk costs, ambiguity and the human annoyance of the toil. Build up incrementally (the automation snowball of quick wins first earns trust), add extra safety to early versions, and don't stop at 90%. The Traffic Director and Pod story shows configuration sprawl turning into cascading failures.

Toil is manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, without lasting value, and grows linearly with the service. It isn't just "work I dislike".

Measure it, keep it below 50% (a ceiling), reward fixing whole classes of problems, spot procedural causes (a team that just forwards tickets), and avoid the false fixes: declaring an emergency, more spreadsheets, ignoring it, appointing a "toil expert", outsourcing it, or handing it to the newest person.

Toil is acceptable during mitigation, while learning a process, or where human judgment is needed. It isn't acceptable when it plugs a product gap, grows with the system, or exists only because access is restricted; build narrow, least-privilege tools for that instead.

Where automation fits in the incident loop

Detect
→
Triage
→
Mitigate
→
Resolve
→
Learn
→
RemediateFix the class, which feeds detection

After Figure 13-2. Automation can help at every stage. Start where humans are slowest and the action is safest, which is usually detection and generic mitigation.

Two footnotes from the chapter are worth carrying into an interview. Static thresholds force a trade between false alarms and missed problems, so the more ambiguous the signal, the more hand-tuning it needs: that is toil with a mathematical cause. And automation has limits of its own. Google’s automatic capacity tool never worked for one large traffic system because the configuration grew big enough to break the solver.

Is it worth the time?

For the pure time-saving case, the chapter points to the well-known xkcd chart (number 1205) that tells you how long you can spend automating a task before you lose more time than you save, counted over five years. The sum behind it is simple enough to do in an interview: time saved per run × runs per day × 1,825 days.

You saveHow oftenBreak-even over five years
30 seconds50 times a dayabout 760 hours
5 minutesonce a dayabout 150 hours
1 houronce a month60 hours
5 minutesonce a year25 minutes

Then say why the chart is not the whole answer, because the book does. Time is only one of four reasons to automate. A task you run once a year in an emergency fails the chart and may still be the most valuable thing to automate, because consistency under stress and scale matter more than minutes.

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the platform book also covers, from the knowledge map:
  • Toil: Manual, repetitive, automatable, no lasting value; keep engineering above half. See platform ch 16.
Going deeper the case studies, numbers and named models from the full chapter

Why and how far to automate

There are four reasons to automate: saving time in normal operations, saving time in emergencies (cutting a Cyber Monday outage from 15 minutes to 5 beats shaving an hour off weekly qualification), consistency (especially for emergency actions that need elevated privileges) and scale.

The levels run from none, to partial (where teams can get stuck), to full, which can be local, platform-wide or, best of all, inherent behaviour (for example, a sync job disappears once there's one source of truth).

Capacity provisioning shows the path: a hard-coded prototype becomes platform defaults until GA, then automated planning with two independent layers (minutes-to-hours autoscaling and days-to-months forecasting). Pick the abstraction carefully, letting users choose mean, P90 or peak load rather than tuning forecasts themselves.

Pitfalls and the ironies

Bainbridge's ironies of automation: automation creates new and harder work (watching it and repairing it), erodes operators' skills, and so demands more skilled people.

The other traps are dangerous automation without rate limits, scope limits, do-no-harm checks and circuit breakers; deskilling (the 99% case); automation surprise; automating over a broken foundation; automating a moving target; and automating ambiguity.

Deciding

Run the cost-benefit numbers (and assume you've underestimated the costs), then weigh the things you can't quantify: strategic value (patching a fleet fast), the cost of the safety mechanisms themselves, the ambiguity factor, and the annoyance factor (a five-minute task that wakes someone at night).

In Google's network fault mitigation case, speed dominated, but a bad signal could drain healthy infrastructure, so it needed a safety system ("never drain more than X% of a region"). Over time those overlapping checks became hard to reason about and started blocking legitimate repairs.

Standardising deployment on Pod changed the economics: once regionalisation came built in, hundreds of low- and medium-risk services adopted it. Restarting a process with a memory leak is fine if the leak is rare and expensive to fix, but it becomes debt if the restarts outpace your release cadence.

Incremental automation

"See one, do one, automate one." Use the production meeting to pick candidates, then go from manual, to scripts a human triggers, to fully integrated. An early safety ladder: the automation first only detects and alerts, then suggests an action, then acts and notifies, so the whole team can follow along.

Prioritise the fastest wins first to start an automation snowball. Don't stop at 90%, because half-automated processes confuse people and add cognitive load; give the automation readable logs and dashboards with linkable events. Make sure defaults never act on everything: outages have happened when a missing variable such as the region was treated as "all".

Traffic Director

Google chose multi-single-tenant (one instance per tenant) for velocity and to limit each tenant's blast radius, and Pod's single config made complexity grow sublinearly for a while. Eventually it became the largest config at Google.

Per-tenant flags diverged, rollouts got stuck and production ran a two-month-old binary. The postmortem's "Blood and Toil" section described hundreds of manual operations per release. After an 18-month joint stabilisation effort with the platform team, the service moved to multi-tenancy. The lesson: revisiting an architecture that served well for five years is a sign of maturity, not of failure.

Toil

Toil is manual, repetitive, scales linearly and leaves nothing lasting behind. Hard engineering work, like a new security policy or tests after an outage, isn't toil. Measure toil, and track the ratio of actionable to noisy alerts.

Keep engineering above 50% (for example, reduce toil from 50% to 30%). Catch toil at launch with a checklist, and notice the pages you should have received. Reward fixing whole classes of problems, through peer bonuses and promotion criteria.

Watch for process toil, like reports nobody acts on, and for relay on-call, where the page should go straight to the team that can act. What doesn't work: declaring toil an emergency, making everyone fill in spreadsheets (toil on top of toil), declaring bug bankruptcy, naming a "toil expert", outsourcing toil to a team that isn't on-call, and handing toil to new hires.

Toil is acceptable for mitigation (a few days of manual restarts while you investigate a deadlock), for learning (log every command in a recovery drill, then turn them into reusable logical operations) and for human judgement (a human kept the trigger on database recovery, which paid off when a monitoring glitch fired every alert at once).

It isn't acceptable to cover product gaps, to absorb work that grows with the system, or to stand in for safe tools when access is restricted.

On AWSSSM Automation with aws:approve steps and rate controls; EventBridge to trigger it; Step Functions for multi-step workflows; Config auto-remediation. See POC 09.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Your team restarts a stuck worker 60 times a month. Do you automate the restart?

Show a model answer

Not as the first move. Automating the restart hides the defect, and you end up building more automation on top of something broken.

First measure the toil, then find the cause with the developers: a memory leak, a deadlock, a dependency that hangs. Fix that.

If the real fix will take weeks, an automatic restart is fine as a temporary measure, with conditions. It is rate-limited, so it can’t restart in a loop. It raises an alert and logs every restart, so the problem stays visible. And it has an expiry date and a ticket for the real fix.

Then count the restarts and track them down to zero.

Should we auto-restart the service when memory goes above 90%?

Show a model answer

It depends on how often it happens and which way it’s heading.

Yes, as a tactical measure, if the leak is rare and expensive to fix: rate-limit the restarts, alert on each one, and keep a ticket open for the real fix.

No, if restarts are becoming more frequent than releases. Then the automation is hiding growing technical debt, and one day it will restart everything at once.

Quick check: Toil is best described as…
Toil is defined by its properties, not by how people feel about it.
Quick check: An automation receives a request with the region variable missing. What should it do?
Several major outages came from defaults that acted on everything when an input was missing.
Your turnRun poc-09-toil-automation/toil_report.py against the sample tickets. Which class of toil would you automate first if you prioritised the fastest win instead of the biggest return? Why might that be the better choice?
Key takeaways
  • Automate for emergencies, consistency and scale, not only to save time.
  • Automation creates new work and erodes skills, so keep it observable, limited and reversible.
  • Toil is defined by its properties. Fix whole classes of it, and keep engineering above 50%.
Part IV · Infrastructure designChapter 14 · 9 min read · POC 05, 06

Testing for reliability

You will learn
  • why configuration needs the same testing discipline as code
  • the VOIS properties and the layers of config tests
  • what canaries, DiRT and fault injection each prove
  • where formal methods and agent testing fit

The big picture

Testing stands in for a perfect model of the world, and production is the only fully accurate environment, which is why testing in production keeps growing. Know the types: unit, integration, system, smoke, performance, regression, resilience, production tests (canaries above all), fuzzing, property-based, mutation, static analysis and agentic. Infrastructure for testing means version control, reproducible central runs and hermetic environments.

VersionedThere is always a known version to roll back to.
ObservableYou can tell whether a change is live.
IndependentConfig can change, and soft-launch, separately from code.
SafeThere is an explicit safe default for emergencies.

Configuration is as dangerous as code. The VOIS invariants: Versioned, Observable, Independent of code deploys, Safe with explicit safe defaults. Test config at three levels: syntax (cheap, and invaluable in an emergency), semantic and dynamic.

Watch for drift. Canaries send production traffic to a subset during an incubation period and run continuous statistical analysis; they are especially valuable for config. Even emergency rollouts need a fast tested path.

DiRT began as a yearly week-long exercise and became a continuous programme. It works top-down and bottom-up, it's framed as making systems better rather than compliance, and it's marketed internally. It found entangled systems, recovery plans that couldn't be carried out, and workflows that lived on one person's workstation.

Service-level test dimensions: capacity and stability, data, infrastructure, dependencies (including running a dependency at its SLO to see if clients still meet theirs), failure handling, operations, change, business continuity, observability (the most fruitful) and security.

Client-focused change supervision adds the backend version to RPC responses so callers' metrics reveal a bad canary. Fault injection follows "workflow X is resilient to fault Y as measured by Z". Formal methods: TLA+ model checking against Rocq theorem proving, with real uses such as P4-BAR for switches, TPU design and Fiat Cryptography in BoringSSL.

Agentic testing tiers: classic, then agents generating content (version-control prompts and models, golden evals for drift, cost budgets, PII checks), then agents using tools (trajectory budgets, termination policies, the lethal trifecta).

The hierarchy of tests

A rollout rule of thumb

0.1%Start here
→
1%Ramp fast at the low end
→
10%A day per step
→
50% → 100%Slow down at the high end

From a footnote in the chapter: begin at 0.1% of traffic and grow roughly ten-fold every 24 hours, moving across server locations as you go.

The reasoning is about exposure. At 0.1% a bad release hurts almost nobody, so move quickly. At 50% a bad release is a major outage, so bake longer. On AWS this is a CodeDeploy or AppConfig deployment strategy with a bake time and a CloudWatch alarm that triggers rollback.

Client-focused supervisionThe book’s Figure 14-3 shows why you watch a rollout from the caller’s side. A frontend calls two backend tasks. The one on the new version returns bad data with a success code, and the user sees an error. The backend’s own dashboards look healthy, and only the client-side view shows the failure.

One more honest detail: the old claim that a bug costs 100 times more to fix in production is more nuanced than the slogan. The chapter notes it is closer to 100 to 1 for severe defects and about 2 to 1 for minor ones. Use the nuanced version and you will sound like you’ve read the source.

Testing monitoring itself

Alert and recording rules are configuration and deserve the same tests. promtool test rules runs unit tests with synthetic series and checks exactly when an alert fires and with which labels; Pint lints rules against a live Prometheus and comments on pull requests (Prometheus ch 12). Load tests belong in the release pipeline with thresholds taken from SLOs (Grafana ch 13), and after deploy, verification queries can trigger the automatic rollback this chapter calls for (Grafana ch 14).

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the platform book, Mastering Prometheus and Observability with Grafana also cover, from the knowledge map:
  • Progressive rollout: Small exposure first, growing in stages with bake time. See platform ch 16, Grafana ch 14.
  • Canary analysis: Compare the new version with a control serving the same traffic at the same time. See platform ch 16.
  • Configuration as code: Versioned, reviewed, tested and rolled out like a binary. See platform ch 15, Prometheus ch 12, Grafana ch 10.
  • Deployment verification: Query telemetry after a deploy and roll back automatically. See platform ch 16, Grafana ch 14.
Going deeper the case studies, numbers and named models from the full chapter

Philosophy

Testing measures how wrong your mental model of the system is. The pyramid shows which tests depend on which, not their value; the "testing trophy" puts more weight on integration and testing in production. Watch for performance creep: a run of small regressions took one service from 50 to 250 ms in a year.

Other techniques: property tests (the output is sorted and a permutation of the input), mutation tests, fuzzing (never on production PII), and making illegal states unrepresentable. Hermetic tests have no network calls and use controlled dependencies.

Configuration is the sharpest edge

Several big Google outages came from config. VOIS gives you a version to roll back to, a way to see whether a change is live, the ability to soft-launch separately from code, and a safe default for emergencies. Test in three layers:

SyntaxDoes it parse? Kept even for emergency pushes
→
SemanticZeroed values, 300× jumps, new ports
→
DynamicDry runs and hermetic launches with probes
→
CanaryCompare new against old in production
  • Syntax checks, kept even in the emergency push tool.
  • Semantic checks: did something drop to zero, jump 300×, or open new ports? Write these as policy (OPA).
  • Dynamic checks: dry runs, hermetic launches with probes, going beyond terraform plan.

Config drift (production differing from what's committed) breaks the safe-default guarantee. Your options are bundling config with code (not recommended), alerting on drift, or auto-reconciling, as Google and ArgoCD do.

Canaries and emergencies

Canary analysis is an A/B comparison between versions, not monitoring. It's also the first time production config and new code meet, so it's really an integration test. Emergency pushes may bypass the gate, but tests keep running and their failures get annotated back onto the push.

DiRT

The test week isn't announced in advance. Tests range from tabletop to live ("tear down this datacentre and rebuild it elsewhere with no downtime"), and teams proctor each other across time zones. Google once ran itself for a week from Dublin without Mountain View.

Taking the incident management system offline went fine; taking document rendering offline lasted only hours. Fault injection needs a back-out plan anyone can run, peer review including downstream owners, broadcast results even when they're bad, and tests at enough traffic to give a signal.

Google tools inject RPC errors and delays (Catzilla) or drop packets per datacentre. Example: a nightly soft-dependency test makes spellcheck fail and checks the product still works.

Client-focused change supervision

A low overall error rate during a rollout can hide failing clients. Propagate version metadata through RPC side channels using interceptors or Envoy. Track hops with outbound bookkeeping, TTLs and logical groupings, and build the server-to-client map daily from monitoring. The cost is cardinality: more than 5,000 label values per metric.

Formal methods and agents

TLA+ catches non-atomic check-and-set races. Model checking is push-button and produces counterexamples, but the state space explodes. Theorem proving (Isabelle, PVS, TLAPS, Rocq) handles infinite state. A formal spec also solves the oracle problem for model-based testing. Google applies formal methods selectively: P4 verification has found more than 300 forwarding bugs since 2020. For agents:

  • Treat evals as tests.
  • Use several LLM judges and check their agreement (Cohen's kappa).
  • Follow OTel GenAI conventions.
