  • Set budgets with explicit fail-open or fail-closed behaviour, and test failover to a local model.
  • Watch for sycophancy drift and tool-name collisions.
  • Test how agents handle 429s and malformed tool responses, and replay trajectories.

Failures at one level of agent complexity are hard to see with the tools built for the level below.

On AWSCodeDeploy canaries, AppConfig validators and deployment strategies, FIS, Synthetics, Distributed Load Testing on AWS, and CodeGuru Reviewer / Inspector for static analysis. See POC 05 and 06.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

How do you decide whether a canary is healthy?

Show a model answer

A canary is a new version serving a small share of real traffic. The question is whether it is worse than the current version, so you need a fair comparison.

Compare it with a control: a few instances of the current version, started at the same time and given the same share of traffic. Comparing with the whole fleet is unfair, because fresh instances behave differently from long-running ones.

Use statistics, not eyeballing: a test on error rate, a comparison of the whole latency distribution (not only the average), and the business metrics of the journeys that matter.

Require a minimum number of requests. A canary that got almost no traffic is inconclusive, not healthy.

Look at it from the callers’ side as well, because a new version can return “success” with bad data. Bake long enough to see the normal traffic mix and a peak. If it fails, roll back automatically.

On AWS: CodeDeploy canary deployments with CloudWatch alarms for automatic rollback. POC 05 implements the comparison.

How do you stop configuration pushes from causing outages?

Show a model answer

Treat configuration exactly like code, because config changes cause as many outages.

Check it in layers before it ships: syntax (does it parse?), semantics (is a limit set to zero, did a value change by 300 times, is a new port exposed?) using policy-as-code, and a dynamic test that actually starts something with the new config.

Roll it out progressively with a canary comparison, like a binary. Detect drift between what’s running and what’s committed.

Keep an emergency path for urgent changes that still validates them and records them afterwards. And keep the last good config ready so you can switch back instantly.

Quick check: What does VOIS stand for in configuration safety?
Config must be versioned, observable, changeable independently of code, and have safe defaults.
Quick check: A canary received only 20 requests during its bake time. What is the right verdict?
Without enough data you can’t tell, and a silent canary must never be promoted automatically.
Your turnRead poc-05-progressive-delivery/canary_analysis.py and predict its verdict for a canary that saw 20 requests and no errors. Then open poc-06-chaos-fis and write one test as “X is resilient to Y, measured by Z”.
Key takeaways
  • Testing measures how wrong your mental model is.
  • Config must be versioned, observable, independent and safe, and checked in layers.
  • A canary is an A/B comparison and the first integration test of production config with new code.
Part IV · Infrastructure designChapter 15 · 12 min read · POC 07

Capacity planning

You will learn
  • when capacity planning is worth doing at all
  • the three kinds of demand and how to forecast each
  • how traffic tags, failure domains and pooling change the sums
  • the Google Meet and AI-era case studies

The big picture

Capacity planning means forecasting demand and providing supply, and it is really a risk-versus-cost trade-off much like an error budget. Ask first whether you need it at all: if autoscaling and a fault-tolerant design absorb a shortfall, spend the effort elsewhere.

OrganicSteady growth. Forecast it from trends.
Planned inorganicLaunches, Black Friday, the Olympics. Plan it with the launch.
Unplanned inorganicGoing viral. Handle it with buffers, autoscaling and demand shaping.

Otherwise, forecast demand as organic growth plus inorganic events (planned launches, unplanned shocks); express it through a driver metric such as DAU or QPS; quantify the uncertainty with scenarios and backtesting; and include capacity in postmortems. Track the ratio of infrastructure to product demand as a living model and alert when it drifts.

Supply depends on fungibility (location, latency, regulation), lead time and elasticity, and your cloud provider's trade-offs become your risks, which means reservations for peaks you can't miss and scarce accelerators.

Latency and availability needs belong to traffic, not to the service, so tag traffic with criticality (shed the least important first), mark latency-tolerant work, and provision so you can drain a failure domain. Build capacity isolation and failure domains, and remember transitive dependencies.

In overload, use crumple zones: shaping demand is cheaper than adding supply; move supply away from low-value work and hold central inventory.

Efficiency means utilisation, the cost of capacity and business value per dollar. Look first at high-cost and low-utilisation services. Pooling works because the peak of sums is below the sum of peaks: Google's Flex oversubscribes logical quota against physical capacity, scales composite services within limits, and reclaims stranded capacity with latency-tolerant work, though never all of it.

Case: Google Meet in 2020 saw regional growth of up to 400×, handled with adaptive long-running incident response, separate workstreams, pooled resources, control knobs (load shedding, lower video quality) and attention to burnout.

The iron triangle of capacity

Spare capacity buys reliability and costs money. Running hot saves money and costs latency under load. There is no free corner, which is why the chapter keeps repeating that the target is a business choice.

Making capacity fungible

Stranded capacity is capacity you own in a place or shape you can’t use. The chapter’s figures show two ways out. Work that tolerates delay can fill the troughs of local demand, which lowers the global total. And you can make workloads easier to move:

Architect for constraintsBreak a rigid application into services that scale on their own and don’t care which region they run in.
Shift work in timeBatch, training and backfills run when interactive demand is low.
Improve connectivityA better network lets demand in one place use supply in another.

On AWS: Spot and Batch for time-shifted work, Auto Scaling groups with several instance types so you aren’t tied to one, and multi-Region designs so demand can follow supply.

Case study: the Google Meet loop

When COVID lockdowns began, demand for Meet grew faster than any forecast. Figure 15-7 shows the process the team ran every day. It is the best single diagram in the chapter for an interview, because it turns “we scaled” into a method.

Review the inputsCustomer onboarding and promotions, lockdown trends, forecast models, usage trends
→
One questionDo we have enough for the load we expect a week from now?
→
YesWait a day and ask again
→
NoStart the four workstreams
CapacityAre there more raw resources we can turn into capacity? If not, find some.
DependenciesCan every system we depend on take the extra load? If not, find workarounds.
BottlenecksCan we remove artificial limits to use what we have better? Then find the next limit.
Control knobsCan we change the system quickly to head off a large outage? If not, build more escape hatches.

Everything the four workstreams produce goes through a fifth, production changes, whose only job is to deploy safely. Then the loop starts again. The one-week horizon is the detail to remember: short enough to forecast, long enough to act.

Why pooling works

Figure 15-4 plots resource use for four regions over three days. Each has a daily peak, and the peaks fall at different hours. That is the whole reason a shared pool needs less than the sum of its parts. Figure 15-3 shows how Google layers it: physical CPU, memory and drives feed foundational pooled services (compute and memory in Borg, disk in Colossus), and those feed composite services built on top, such as Bigtable.

Capacity tests and the capacity of monitoring

The Grafana book’s load test types map onto capacity questions: stress for a sustained peak, spike for a surge, breakpoint for where the service breaks, soak for slow leaks (Grafana ch 13). And monitoring has its own capacity limit: every new label value is a new series, so scrape limits and cardinality reviews are capacity planning for Prometheus (Prometheus ch 7).

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the platform book and Observability with Grafana also cover, from the knowledge map:
  • Failure domains and N+1: Survive the loss of a zone or region; say which domain you mean. See platform ch 16.
  • Load shedding by criticality: Drop the least important work first; tag requests. See platform ch 14.
  • Pooling: Peaks rarely coincide, so a shared pool needs less than the sum of its parts. See platform ch 14.
  • Load test types: Smoke, average, stress, spike, breakpoint, soak; thresholds from SLOs. See Grafana ch 13.
Going deeper the case studies, numbers and named models from the full chapter

First decide if you need it

Provisioning for every edge case is like aiming for 100% availability. Small workloads should just overprovision, because compute is cheap compared with engineering time. Simple autoscaling rules (add two instances above 70% CPU for five minutes, remove one below 40% with a floor of five) cover most services.

Demand

Organic demand you forecast from trends (regression, Holt–Winters, ARIMA). Planned inorganic demand comes from launches, the Olympics and Black Friday. Unplanned inorganic demand (going viral, an unannounced celebrity livestream) you handle with buffers, autoscaling and demand shaping.

Also budget for performance regressions and DDoS. Forecast in percentiles (P50, P95, P99) across scenarios, backtest old forecasts, and check postmortems for capacity contributions. Track the ratio of infrastructure to business metrics (cores per 1,000 active users) and alert when it shifts, which catches regressions. Shorter provisioning lead times shrink how far ahead you must forecast.

Supply and the plan of record

Constraints turn the unconstrained forecast into a plan of record, and layering business metrics on top tells you what a shortfall costs. Supply varies in fungibility, lead time and elasticity. Shared cloud supply carries contention risk, because the same event that spikes your traffic can strain the provider, so pre-buy dedicated capacity for big events. Don't do that permanently, except in regulated, trading or large ML-training settings.

Requirements belong to traffic, not services

Provision redundantly for the strict subset of traffic and serve relaxed traffic from spare capacity. Tag requests through OTel context with criticality (cheap to discard under overload) and latency tolerance (route it to idle datacentres on the other side of the world).

Shedding assumes you have enough global capacity for critical and batch traffic combined, sized for the single global peak rather than the sum of regional peaks, so batch work rejected in one region retries in another. Physical partitioning (reserved instances for users, spot for batch) is simple but costly; sharing with criticality is efficient but brings noisy neighbours. Clients you don't control can cause a thundering herd as you recover.

Failure domains through a capacity lens

Typical cloud SLAs are 99.5% for a zone and 99.99% for multi-region services. Avoid single-zone deployments. Pre-provisioned spare capacity beats autoscaling when the whole internet is scaling at once. Know where your provider's control plane lives, because the failover API may sit in the zone you're fleeing.

With two zones, losing one doubles the load on the other. Run evictable work in reserved resilience capacity. Multicloud cuts correlated failure, but only if your cross-cloud orchestration doesn't become the weak link.

Crumple zones and efficiency

Define the degradation profile: how much slower, when users notice, and whether failure means throttling or days of manual restore. A cat-photo app and a grid controller are different universes. Shaping demand is cheaper than adding supply; measure shedding so the business can see what it gave up.

Utilisation is usage over capacity. Prioritise costly services, don't assume low utilisation means waste (DDoS defences sit idle until needed), question high-frequency low-value work (a query every minute versus once a day) and skip cheap services.

Peak of sums and Flex

In the book’s example, provisioning each service separately at its own peak needs 60 units; pooled at the combined peak they need 48. Google's Flex pools quota and saves about 5–20%. It gives each account a ceiling and an optional committed floor, oversubscribes, and keeps unused capacity committed for a while to avoid cold starts.

Sum of peaks: 60 unitsEach service provisioned separately for its own peak.
Peak of sums: 48 unitsOne pool sized for the combined peak. Same demand, 20% less capacity.

When oversubscription fails you get a stockout, so services need to survive stockouts. Flex Autoscaling halts at scaling limits to protect the underlying services and alerts SREs; responders can disable it for one service rather than globally.

Reclaiming stranded capacity (Maps reroutes background navigation requests across the globe) must still provision for the combined peak, or low-priority work fails at peak.

Google Meet during COVID

Meet was stable enough that nobody had invested in deployment automation. Then it grew up to 30× (and up to 400× in some regions by mid-May 2020), with first pages on 17 February in Asia. The team ran it as an incident with workstreams:

  • Capacity estimation: spreadsheets grew into models, and machines were borrowed from other teams.
  • Dependency mapping: a 10× target against the pre-COVID peak, tracked in one sheet.
  • Bottlenecks: fewer log writes, and doubling per-instance size halved the instance count by cutting per-instance overhead.
  • Degradation knobs: lower video and audio quality, or drop video entirely.
  • Manual production changes: a month of toil before there was time to automate.

The lessons: adapt incident management for month-long events, use pooling, prepare for unplanned inorganic demand, build control knobs ahead of time, and watch for burnout.

The AI era

Supply and demand curves converge, and because you can reshape both the bins and their contents, it stops being simple bin packing. "Minimum viable capacity" brings riskier early capacity online, and tolerant workloads get routed to it.

Spatial flexibility moves and resizes workloads automatically to prevent stockouts. AI agents triage capacity crises, reclaim expired ML quota and propose and implement optimisations.

Principles: think like FinOps, weighing resource, engineering, inflexibility and unreliability costs; scale planning effort to the service tier; automate by default; keep services mobile; size buffers from SLOs; collaborate with finance.

On AWSPredictive Scaling, target tracking on requests per target, scheduled actions, On-Demand Capacity Reservations and Capacity Blocks, Savings Plans versus Spot, service quotas (raise them early), Compute Optimizer. See POC 07.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

How many instances do you need for 9,000 requests a second at peak, if one instance handles 100 within the SLO, across three availability zones?

Show a model answer

Work it out in three steps, out loud.

1. Headroom. Don’t plan to run instances at 100%: latency rises sharply near the limit. Target about 70%, so each instance carries 70 requests a second. 9,000 ÷ 70 ≈ 129 instances.

2. Survive losing a zone. If one of three zones fails, the other two must carry everything without waiting for autoscaling. So two zones need 129 between them: 65 each. Three zones of 65 is 195 instances.

3. Check it. At peak, with all zones up, the fleet runs at 9,000 ÷ (195 × 100) ≈ 46%. That looks wasteful, but it is the price of surviving a zone loss.

Then the insight that impresses interviewers: the extra capacity for losing one of N zones is 1 ÷ (N − 1). With three zones that’s 50%. Spread across six cells, it drops to 20%. More, smaller failure domains are cheaper.

We expect 10 times normal traffic for a one-off event in six weeks. What do you do?

Show a model answer

Treat it as a planned incident with six weeks of preparation.

Map every dependency, including third parties, and ask each one whether it can take 10 times the load.

Load-test until throughput stops rising, to find the real bottleneck before the event does.

Buy the capacity in advance. Don’t rely on autoscaling during the spike, because it reacts too late and the capacity may not be available.

Build and test ways to degrade gracefully: switch off expensive features, and shed low-priority traffic first so checkout survives. Then staff the event like an incident, with roles and a war room.

Quick check: Peak demand 9,000 QPS, 100 QPS per instance, 3 AZs, 70% target utilisation, N+1. How many instances in total?
129 needed; two AZs must carry it, so 65 per AZ and 195 in total.
Your turnRun poc-07-capacity-planning/capacity.py. Then work this by hand: peak 9,000 QPS, 100 QPS per instance, 70% target utilisation, three zones, survive the loss of one. How many instances in total? (The quiz has the answer.)
Key takeaways
  • Planning for every edge case is like targeting 100%. Choose your risk.
  • Latency and availability needs belong to traffic, not to services. Tag requests and shed by criticality.
  • Pooling works because peaks rarely coincide, but pooled services must survive a stockout.
Part IV · Infrastructure designChapter 16 · 12 min read · POC 08

Data management

You will learn
  • the legal and ethical constraints that come before any design
  • the hierarchy of data needs
  • RPO, RTO and RWO, and what each mechanism does and doesn’t protect
  • how to plan, test and govern backups and recovery

The big picture

Users rarely forgive data failures. Start with the law and ethics: children's data, retention and deletion (soft and hard deletes, TTLs; Bigtable has a "fast" deletion SLO and a guaranteed "eventual" one), residency, purpose restrictions and cross-division sharing limits.

1 · IntegrityWhat you read is what you wrote
→
2 · SecurityYou, and only you
→
3 · AvailabilityThere when you need it
→
4 · EfficiencyAt a cost you can sustain

The hierarchy of data needs. Each layer rests on the one before.

Classify data as original or derived (derived data that's expensive to rebuild counts as original), identifiable or not, and flag high-value personal data, which you should avoid collecting if you can. The hierarchy of data needs: integrity, then security, then availability, then efficiency.

Integrity comes from redundancy, checksums at every layer including RPCs (the case where a bad network cable corrupted replicas), append-only logs and MVCC, and application-level reconciliation.

Map failure scenarios to defences. Operator error or malice: backups, and no single person with unilateral access. Bad application writes: PITR or snapshots, transaction logs, reconciliation. Replication does not help with either, because the corruption or the delete replicates too.

A storage-system bug: back up into a different system. Hardware loss: erasure coding or replication. Region loss: cross-region copies. Objectives: RPO (how stale restored data may be, which sets backup frequency), RTO (Restore Time Objective; snapshots are fast but share fate with the source) and RWO (how far back you can restore, limited by deletion law and cost).

Replication involves single or multi-leader, sync or async with a lag bound, guaranteed or best-effort delivery, and planning for losing a leader. Snapshots are logical and share fate; backups are physical copies. Follow 3-2-1. Writers to live data get no admin rights over backups.

Weigh full, incremental and differential backups, and prefer simple over clever when restore reliability matters. Test restores of every type. Plan backups in five stages (discover and classify, set SLOs, choose architecture, design validation, get sign-off), cover new data sources automatically, and write a data recovery policy before you need it.

RPO, RTO and RWO on one timeline

The figure also marks a point of no return. If the corruption is older than your oldest retained backup, no restore can help, which is why RWO has to be longer than your worst realistic time to notice a problem. Silent corruption found after 40 days with 30 days of backups is unrecoverable.

Incremental or differential?

IncrementalDifferential
Each backup holdsChanges since the last backup of any kindChanges since the last full backup
To restore Wednesday you needThe full backup plus Monday, Tuesday and WednesdayThe full backup plus Wednesday
Backup sizeSmallestGrows through the week
RestoreMore steps, more that can go wrongFaster and simpler

This is an RPO-against-RTO trade in miniature: incrementals are cheap to take often, differentials are quick to restore. AWS Backup takes incremental backups for most services and handles the chain for you, but the trade still shows up in restore time, so measure it with a restore test.

Integrity outranks recoveryThe chapter describes Bigtable’s stance: recover as much as possible before declaring data lost, but never at the price of integrity. The team must be able to say that no person compromised user data on the way, and exceptions need senior engineering, customer and legal approval.

Legal is not the same as right

Lawful goodLawful neutralLawful evil
With users’ dataFollows the law and puts the user’s interest first, even at a costFollows the law, makes no sacrifices for usersFollows the law and uses every permitted advantage for itself

The chapter borrows the alignment grid from Dungeons & Dragons (Figure 16-1) to make one point: all three columns obey the law. Aim for the first. Its test is practical: if you use data in a way the user didn’t ask for and only you benefit, think about how they would react on finding out.

Going deeper the case studies, numbers and named models from the full chapter

Why data failures are different

Lost data stays lost without a working backup, and exfiltrated data can't be pulled back. On 9/11, Aon's planning had it operating again within hours with no data lost. The chapter's authors run Bigtable: 10 exabytes and 7 billion queries per second.

Legal and ethical first

Check the law in every place where data originates, is stored and is processed.

  • Minors: COPPA needs verifiable adult consent under 13, and no behavioural profiles.
  • Retention and deletion: backups expiring counts as part of deletion, which caps backup retention. Support soft and hard deletes, and TTLs you can clear or disable. GDPR fines reach €20M or 4% of global revenue.
  • Bigtable offers a fast deletion SLO and an eventual one that it honours even when underprovisioned, by putting deletion ahead of user traffic.
  • Residency: Google Cloud's "hurricane policy" means regionally restricted data is never moved, even to save it, because those customers prefer data loss to breaking the law.
  • Purpose limits: under the DMA, music preferences aren't used for ads without consent, and HIPAA restricts patient data.
  • Ethics: aim to be "lawful good", not merely lawful.

Classification

Original data needs more care than derived data, but derived data that's expensive to rebuild (like the Search index) gets treated as original. Hashing or stripping identifiers doesn't anonymise data; it has to be generalised across many subjects. Avoid collecting high-value personal data (keys, government IDs, sensitive attributes) unless you truly need it.

Hierarchy of data needs

Integrity, then security, then availability, then efficiency, captured in the storage team's motto that you, and only you, can always read your data.

  • Integrity ("what you read is what you wrote") needs redundancy across disks, servers, racks and regions; DB constraints; checksums at the application, every storage layer and the RPC layer; append-only logs and MVCC.
  • The GFS case: one read in three failed application checksums. Swapping RAM, CPUs and switches didn't help; a faulty Cat5 cable was corrupting data in a way that passed the TCP, RPC and GFS checksums. Bigtable now sees about one minor silent-corruption event a year.
  • Reconciliation versus repair: reconciliation handles expected inconsistency by design; repair fixes unexpected inconsistency and signals a bug. Log repairs with debugging info and alert on a threshold, which may be one.
  • Security: exceptional access should be narrow (one account, limited time) and logged to a system the accessor doesn't control. Use least privilege, customer-managed keys and multi-party approval. Never test on production data; Google's "crash" instances are wiped regularly, and sandboxes are named nothing like production.
  • Availability: how often data is read is a poor proxy for how much its unavailability hurts.
  • Efficiency: cross-region "RAID" (half the data in A, half in B, parity in C) has 50% overhead instead of 100%, cutting cost by 25%.

Failure scenarios and defences

  • Operator error or malice (agents included): snapshots, backups, and no unilateral human access.
  • Bad application writes: snapshots, transaction logs for replay, invariant checks and reconciliation. Replication doesn't help.
  • Storage-system bugs: RocksDB research found roughly one corruption per 3 months per 100 PB, with 40% already copied to replicas. Use backups or dual writes to separate systems.
  • Hardware: change the encoding (RAID5 to RAID6), replicate, back up. Snapshots won't help.
  • Region loss: off-region backups and replication.

RPO, RTO, RWO

Set the objectives first and let them drive the design, not the other way round. RPO sets backup frequency, which limits how long each backup can take, which can force sharding and application changes. RTO is cumulative: detection, plus action, plus restore.

RPORecovery point: how much recent data you can afford to lose.
RTORestore time: how long until it’s back. The clock starts at the incident, so it includes time to detect, time to act and time to restore.
RWORestore window: how far back in time you can go.

It also tells you how much spare bandwidth a full restore needs. Partial restores can be slow: tape is sequential, a SQL backup restores whole tables, and tar archives must be read in full. RWO example: daily backups kept for two days can't recover corruption from three days ago, and with 14 days you can still lose up to 24 hours if the corruption landed at 23:50.

Replication

Replication alone isn't recovery: corruption propagates, and so do deletes. If async replication is five minutes behind, failing over means losing those five minutes. Three replicas in separate regions is the norm. Single-leader setups give ordering; multi-leader setups need conflict resolution, and last-write-wins may be wrong.

Async needs an upper bound and per-shard lag telemetry, and best-effort replication leads to divergent replicas. On losing a follower, wait or replace it; on losing a leader, promote one and bound the lost writes. Watch for split-brain.

Backups

  • Snapshots are copy-on-write metadata: cheap and quick, ideal before a risky change, but they share fate with live data.
  • Backups are separate physical copies. Follow 3-2-1, and anything that can write live data must have no admin rights over backups.
  • PITR is a backup plus a write log.
  • Full, incremental or differential: full backups are simple and independent but slow. Incrementals are cheapest, but one bad link breaks the chain. Differentials need only the full plus one diff, though each grows until the next full.
  • Smart vs simple: a raw file copy is smart but version-locked and fragile; a SQL export is simple and portable but spikes load.
MechanismGood forBlind spot
ReplicationHardware, zone and region lossCopies corruption and deletes everywhere
SnapshotA fast rollback before a risky changeShares fate with the live data
BackupAlmost everything, including storage bugsSlow and costly; loses changes since the last run
Point-in-time recoveryBad writes, with a tiny RPOStoring every write; slow replay

Restore testing, plans and recovery policy

If you can't afford a test restore, you can't afford a real one, so make manual restore just the automated test run with different flags. Cover routine restores, user-requested partial restores, bad-data restores and hardware loss.

The YouTube backup race: listing videos, copying files, then copying all metadata leaves metadata without video. Catch bugs like this with STPA and with application-level validation of restored data. Plan in five stages: discover and classify, define SLOs, design the architecture, design validation, then governance with CTO, CFO and COO sign-off.

Build a catalogue with labels and group it into buckets, then give each bucket objectives (24 h RPO with 12 h RTO works manually; 5 min RPO with 3 min RTO must be software-driven). Give data without backups an explicit SLO. Stagger backups so they don't all run at midnight, and make backup setup automatic for new data sources.

A restore is the routine path; recovery is extraordinary. Bigtable's policy forbids manual data edits even if data is lost, unless an authorised person signs off, to preserve provenance. Decide in advance: repair or restore, partial restore, salvaging records around a bit flip, who decides what to lose, whether engineers may inspect data, who can override and who approves after hours.

On AWSAWS Backup plans selected by tag, Vault Lock in compliance mode, cross-Region and cross-account copies, restore testing, DynamoDB PITR and deletion protection, S3 versioning and Object Lock, Aurora backtrack. See POC 08.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

We use DynamoDB global tables across two Regions, so we don’t need backups. Right?

Show a model answer

No. Replication and backups protect against different things.

Global tables protect you if a whole Region fails: the other Region has a copy.

But replication copies everything, including mistakes. If a bad deploy corrupts items, or someone deletes data by accident, that change reaches the other Region within seconds. Now both copies are wrong.

You still need three things. Point-in-time recovery, to rewind the table to just before the corruption. Separate backups in a different account with a locked vault (AWS Backup with Vault Lock), so an operator mistake or an attacker can’t delete them. And regular restore tests, because a backup you have never restored is only a hope.

Design backups for a new orders database.

Show a model answer

Start with the business, then the tooling.

Classify the data and get the business to set three numbers: RPO, how much data we can lose; RTO, how long until we’re back (counted from when the problem starts, so detection time is included); and how far back we must be able to go, which the book calls RWO and which deletion laws may limit.

Then cover each kind of failure. Point-in-time recovery for bad writes. Locked, cross-account backups for operator mistakes and ransomware. Cross-Region copies for losing a Region.

Automate restore tests that also check the restored data makes sense, for example that order totals add up. Write the recovery policy down and get leadership to sign it. POC 08 covers this.

Quick check: Detection took 3 hours, the decision took 1 hour, and the restore took 4. What was the achieved recovery time?
RTO is cumulative: detect, act and restore. Slow detection spends recovery time before the restore begins.
Quick check: Which of these is NOT protected by cross-Region replication?
Corrupt writes replicate everywhere. You need PITR or backups.
Quick check: Your daily backups are kept for 2 days. Corruption from 3 days ago is discovered. What fails?
The restore window objective (how far back you can go) is too short.
Your turnRun poc-08-data-resilience/backup_slo.py on the sample recovery points. Then pick one datastore you own and write its RPO, RTO and RWO in one line each. Who in the business agreed to those numbers?
Key takeaways
  • Law and ethics first, then integrity, security, availability, efficiency.
  • Replication is not a backup. Set RPO, RTO and RWO first and let them drive the design.
  • A backup you haven’t restored is a hope. Test restores automatically and validate the data.
Part V · Resilient productsChapter 17 · 11 min read · POC 04

Designing for resilience

You will learn
  • how reliability and resilience differ, and how to prioritise rare risks
  • the rules for safe change, dependencies and failure domains
  • how to survive overload and bad input
  • incident modes and the response journeys to practise

The big picture

Resilience is keeping adequate service quality during failures, including ones nobody anticipated, or degrading clearly when you can't. Handle high-probability failures cheaply, prioritise by severity, and decide deliberately about rare but high-impact ones (some aren't worth the cost).

NormalRich tools, many dependencies, used by everyone.
EmergencyLow-dependency fallbacks with the same interfaces. Most responders, little training. Invest here first.
DisasterZero-dependency command-line tools and direct access, for small trained teams.

Responses can be manual, automated or architectural, and architectural is best because it removes the need to react at all.

Google's principles cover risk management, change management, dependency management, failure domains, overload management, input validation, data resilience, qualification and emergency mode, and they're enforced through common platforms, with exceptions sought explicitly and remaining risks escalated.

Change management: small, progressive changes across failure domains, including data and config; one change at a time; supervision; and safe mitigations: drain, roll back, upsize, degrade, block (a query of death). Mitigations obey the same rules and must be tested.

Set risk-tolerance levels from normal to medium, high and highest (only break-fixes and critical security). Use defence in depth: feature flags, emergency stops and independent health monitors that halt rollouts.

Dependencies: never depend on something less reliable than you need; document mechanism, criticality (optional or required) and when it's needed (build, startup, runtime); prove optional dependencies are optional; protect your dependents; plan fallbacks.

Failure domains: geographic, functional (partitioning or user sharding), infrastructure (racks, networks) and operational (the scope of operators' and automation's credentials). Align deployments to them, look for hidden shared dependencies, and keep a pristine known-good copy of global state in at least one domain.

To recover: isolate, repair, reassemble, and reach into other domains only with checks and balances. Overload: cascades come from long queues, missed deadlines that trigger retries, restarts and cold caches. On the server side, shed load early, by criticality, with an explicit retry signal, and degrade gracefully.

On the client side, use exponential backoff with jitter, adaptive throttling, retry budgets per request and per service, and per-user quotas. In an emergency, block excess sources, add capacity, stop the automation that restarts "unhealthy" servers, restart in a controlled way, and plan for a cold start.

Input validation: reject empty, partial or corrupt updates and huge diffs, keep serving the last good state, allowlist what "good" looks like, and alert. Data resilience: deglobalise risky operations, delete in stages with grace periods, keep independent fallback backups of metadata and keys, and plan fast recovery.

Qualification: keep tests fresh, realistic and mandatory, shift them left, and prove resilience in realistic environments. Emergency mode: incident tooling must keep working when core services are down.

Two pictures from the chapter

Region A · zone 125% of capacity
Region A · zone 225% of capacity
Region B · zone 125% of capacity
Region B · zone 225% of capacity

After Figure 17-1: two regions with two zones each. Lose a zone and you lose a quarter; lose a region and you lose half. So “N+1” is not a number you can state without saying which failure domain you mean. Sized to survive a zone, each remaining zone must take a third more. Sized to survive a region, each region must carry everything.

Figure 17-2 shows incident severity growing from normal, to emergency, to disaster, which is the same three-step scale as the incident modes above. The practical point is that the tooling for each step must depend on less than the step before it.

Risk registerFor rare, severe risks the chapter suggests a simple register: for each risk, its probability, its impact, an owner and a mitigation. It turns “what if a region disappears?” from a debate into a list someone is accountable for.
The overload error has to say whether to retryWhen a server sheds load, its error must tell the client two things: that it is overloaded, and whether retrying is appropriate (“overloaded” or “overloaded, don’t retry”). Without that, well-behaved clients retry into the overload. On AWS, think of a throttling error carrying a retry hint (HTTP 429 or 503 with Retry-After), which the SDK’s adaptive retry mode respects. Pair it with criticality labels on requests so the server knows what to drop first.
Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the platform book and Observability with Grafana also cover, from the knowledge map:
  • Progressive rollout: Small exposure first, growing in stages with bake time. See platform ch 16, Grafana ch 14.
  • Automatic rollback: A regression halts and reverts the rollout without a human. See platform ch 16, Grafana ch 14.
  • Failure domains and N+1: Survive the loss of a zone or region; say which domain you mean. See platform ch 16.
  • Load shedding by criticality: Drop the least important work first; tag requests. See platform ch 14.
  • Retry budgets and adaptive throttling: Bound retries in the client library so one service can’t start a cascade. See platform ch 16.
Going deeper the case studies, numbers and named models from the full chapter

Reliability vs resilience

Reliability means staying within designed norms. Resilience means detecting and handling active failures, novel ones included, with prepared responses. Five nines is a practical ceiling for many systems, but the remaining tail can still burn years of budget, so look for cheap partial mitigations.

Likelihood times impact breaks down for rare catastrophes. For likely failures, use cheap default-on mitigations and test with all optional dependencies disabled. For rare ones, first write down how you'd handle it today, then fully address a few rather than half-addressing many.

Prioritise what has happened to you, then what has happened to others, then realistic risks, then known unknowns.

Enforce through technology

A written policy alone overloads people; platform defaults and programmatic checks compound over time. A complex plan might work, but resilience has to work every time. Teams see risk vertically, through their own stack; leadership sees it horizontally, asking every team the same risk questions.

Change management details

  • Avoid both too many components in one update and several updates to one component.
  • Global data needs versioning, and its clients must fail safe on bad data.
  • Roll binaries and data separately: one zone, then two, then more. Never change interacting components (a server and its clients or schema) in parallel.
  • Google's Canary Analysis Service checks each replica's health; for the most critical systems, include the health of dependents too.
  • Rollback isn't guaranteed, so be ready to roll forward.
  • Feature flags have fewer dependencies than a binary rollback.
  • Give people an inherently safe emergency stop, and the psychological safety to press it.
  • Alert when more outages than usual are being declared, because the cause may be outside your system.

Dependencies

Lock down which dependencies are allowed, at build, config, startup and runtime. Production must never depend on non-production. Optional dependencies fail open; if you can't prove a dependency is optional, treat it as required. When defending dependents, restore critical ones first, start risky changes where dependents matter least, and protect your fallbacks.

A fallback can be an earlier version (cheap, but shares fate) or a distinct low-dependency implementation (expensive, but shares little).

Failure domains and alignment

A failure domain is only real if everything it needs is local. Alignment matters: two regions with two zones each lose 25% of capacity per zone, while one zone per region without anti-affinity loses 50%. Scale by adding zones rather than growing them, or a zone becomes too large to fail, since draining it would cause a thundering herd.

Recovery means isolating, repairing, reassembling and reaching the domain, keeping security patches current while parts are in repair, and keeping global recovery powers in safe places. Protect global state with a pristine domain: rollouts delayed by weeks, no emergency pushes, used only to recover others (it's not a warm standby).

Overload and input

The goal: a system sized for X that receives 10X should still serve about X and recover on its own. Degrade to roughly 80% quality for 20% of the compute. Load-test until goodput plateaus. Retry at one layer only, using standard client libraries.

Reuse per-user quotas for shedding and retry budgets: servers keep a per-request budget, and clients a per-service one. Treat config and code as control inputs. Reject empty updates (an empty ACL locks everyone out), use expected-size fields, keep the previous version in memory to swap back, and alert on bad input.

Data resilience and qualification

Risks include losing metadata, losing encryption keys (restores need them) and lower storage layers dropping replicas without understanding the data. Deglobalise storage rollouts, pause mutating operations when redundancy is short, block accidental TTLs on critical data, keep independent metadata backups in a different DBMS, and preserve keys.

Qualify through pretend disaster role-play (D&D meets IMAG), then run safer variants for real. Isolating a test environment from DNS and load balancers exposed local cyclic dependencies. One drill revealed too little quota to restore all user data.

Incident modes and response journeys

  • Normal: rich tools for everyone.
  • Emergency: low-dependency fallbacks with the same interfaces, usable by most responders with minimal training. Invest here first, because it's more likely than disaster.
  • Disaster: zero-dependency CLIs and direct network access, for small trained teams.

Tools need to keep their security posture in every mode, and errors should point people to the fallback. Response user journeys are comms, IMAG, dashboards, reaching people, docs, privileged access (including multi-party approval), debugging and fixing.

Train people to know these exist, then practise them in order: core (reach, comms, privileged access, docs, IMAG), then common (dashboards, debugging, fixing), then bespoke. A common regression is a fallback quietly acquiring a dependency on the system it's meant to replace.

On AWSMulti-AZ and cells; Route 53 ARC zonal shift and zonal autoshift; static stability; SDK adaptive retries; API Gateway and WAF throttles; SQS buffering; AppConfig flags; Incident Manager replicated across Regions; break-glass IAM roles. See POC 04.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Explain how a retry storm becomes an outage, and how you’d prevent it.

Show a model answer

It is a feedback loop that keeps going after the original cause is gone.

How it happens. A traffic spike makes the server slow. Requests wait in queues until their callers give up, but the server still processes them: wasted work. Each caller retries, and often every layer of the stack retries too, so one user click becomes many requests. Load climbs further, health checks fail, instances restart and caches go cold. Now the system can’t recover even when the spike ends. The book calls this a metastable failure.

How to prevent it, on the server. Keep queues short and reject early with a clear “overloaded, retry later” or “overloaded, don’t retry”. Pass deadlines along with requests so nobody works on something the caller has abandoned.

On the client. Exponential backoff with random jitter, so retries spread out. A retry budget, for example retries may add at most 10% to normal traffic. Adaptive throttling, so a client backs off when it sees many errors. Retry at one layer only.

Priorities. Label requests by importance so checkout survives while batch jobs are dropped.

In an emergency. Turn off automatic restarts and bring capacity back gradually, so the system isn’t knocked over again as it starts up.

Your chat and video tools are down during an outage. Now what?

Show a model answer

Switch to the emergency plan you agreed beforehand, which is the point: this has to be prepared before the day.

Use the fallback channel: a phone bridge or a separate chat system that doesn’t depend on your own infrastructure. Use offline copies of playbooks and a contact list.

Use break-glass access if normal access is down, with more than one person approving and everything logged.

In the interview, add that you’d prove all of this in drills, starting with the most important journeys, because an emergency path nobody has used tends not to work.

Quick check: Clients retry immediately on every failure during an overload. What is the most likely result?
Retries plus work on already-expired requests keep the system saturated.
Quick check: Which incident mode should you invest in first?
Emergency mode is more likely than disaster and usable by most responders with minimal training.
Your turnRun poc-04-resilience-patterns/simulate_cascade.py. The naive client never recovers after the spike; the protected one does. Remove one protection at a time (jittered backoff, retry budget, shedding) and see which one matters most.
Key takeaways
  • A complex plan might work. Resilience has to work every time, so enforce it through the platform.
  • Sized for X and receiving 10X, serve about X and recover without humans.
  • Practise the emergency mode: fallbacks for comms, access, docs and reaching people.
Part V · Resilient productsChapter 18 · 9 min read · POC 10

Platform engineering in SRE

You will learn
  • what a platform is, and why curated solutions beat requirements alone
  • golden paths, guardrails, exceptions and incentives
  • shifting down, legibility, and handling brownfield systems

The big picture

A production platform is the organisation's abstraction layer over infrastructure (RPC, CI/CD, observability, orchestration, capacity, load balancing, storage). Designed well, it's a self-service product; left undesigned, it's a mess.

Golden pathThe easy, supported route
→
HintA nudge in the editor
→
WarningFlagged, but allowed
→
ErrorBlocked, with a break-glass path

Guardrails from gentle to firm. Use the gentlest one that achieves the goal.

Building one involves policy decisions: who gets access, how many instances and where, whether you need permission to depend on something, chargeback, standards, control-plane access, reuse versus rebuild, and whether it should be hard to get things wrong or easy to experiment.

Google shifted from "bring me requirements" to requirements plus curated solutions, encoding reliability principles into the tools (for example, the approved deployment system has canary analysis, progressive rollout and SLO monitoring built in). Policies are like style guides, enforced by compliance checkers at different levels.

Useful lenses: the garden metaphor (direct versus indirect control); Cynefin (move production problems from chaotic and complex towards complicated and clear); cybernetics (Meadows's leverage points, Ashby's requisite variety, Bainbridge again).

Use abstraction and coupling deliberately. Strong defaults reduce cognitive load. Incentives beat mandates: make the good outcome the rational choice. Provide golden paths and guardrails (IDE hints, warnings, errors that block unsafe actions), learn from desire paths, and offer escape hatches while keeping a list of every exception.

Treat the platform as a product for developers, operators and the business. Shift down as well as shift left: push capabilities into shared frameworks so every team doesn't need expertise in everything. Ecosystems range from "YOLO" to "assured" depending on the consequence of failure.

Make risk legible by introspecting config-as-code against policies (at least two locations, alerts routed to an active team, SLOs defined, on-call load below a threshold), then remediate automatically where you're confident. Block non-compliance in greenfield systems; give brownfield systems time-boxed exemptions.

The effectiveness zone

A hard block on a typo-level risk teaches people to route around the platform. A gentle hint on an action that can delete production data relies on nobody ever having a bad day. When a team complains that a guardrail is annoying, place it on this chart before arguing.

How far has a practice been built into the platform?

0 · YOLONothing in place
→
1 · Ad hocEach team does it its own way
→
2 · GuidedDocumented best practice
→
3 · EngineeredBuilt into the paved path
→
4 · AssuredEnforced and verified by the platform

After Figure 18-3. A typology for any one quality attribute, such as “safe rollouts” or “backups”.

“Shift down” means moving a practice from type 2, where every feature team has to know and do it, to type 3 or 4, where the platform does it. The chapter’s first figure draws this as a line: assurance moves from above the line (feature teams) to below it (the platform).

Build horizonOne of Google’s quieter guardrails: binaries older than roughly six months are not allowed to run. Nobody has to chase teams to pick up security fixes, because standing still stops being an option. It is a good example of changing the game so the safe choice is the easy one.
Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the platform book and Observability with Grafana also cover, from the knowledge map:
  • Shift down: Move responsibility into the platform so teams inherit the result. See platform ch 15, platform ch 16.
  • Ecosystem types 0 to 4: YOLO, ad hoc, guided, engineered, assured. See platform ch 12.
  • Golden path: The supported, documented, easiest way to do a common task. See platform ch 18, platform ch 19, Grafana ch 10.
Going deeper the case studies, numbers and named models from the full chapter

What a platform is

A platform is the abstraction over your infrastructure plus the culture around it. A good one makes the reliable way the default. A horizontal SRE team (advisory, shared tools, standards) does mostly platform engineering.

Google moved from "bring me requirements, not solutions" to requirements plus curated solutions: a vetted set of tools, not one monolith, because the old approach led to duplication and made it hard for SREs to move between teams. Curation done well makes the right way the easy way.

Policy as a style guide for production

Enforce it with compliance checkers, the way a linter enforces a style guide: in the editor, at commit or at runtime, minding how much noise each adds. Ask what goal a rule serves before adding it. Use warnings unless you're certain no exceptions exist, and even errors need a break-glass path.

Models to cite

  • Cynefin: the domains are clear, complicated, complex, chaotic and, in the middle, confusion. A platform moves accidental complexity towards clear, making the routine 90% easy so experts can focus on the hard 10%.
  • Systems thinking: system dynamics, Meadows' leverage points, and Ashby's law of requisite variety (a controller needs at least as many states as the system it controls).
  • Direct versus indirect control: pulling a weed versus improving the soil.
  • Legibility (James C. Scott): make systems readable by imposing order.
  • Techne versus metis: shift down the universal knowledge so teams can focus on their system-specific knowledge.

Choices, incentives and paths

Use strong defaults (JVM tuning), small menus (regional, continental or global databases) and remove options whose downsides dominate. Stop bikeshedding about the monitoring tool and talk about SLOs instead. Punishment invites gaming; make the good practice the easy one, or as Daria Barteneva puts it, change the game so the good outcome is the rational one.

Desire paths are informal, shared tacit knowledge; golden paths are self-service, opinionated templates built on transparent abstractions. Guardrails range from landscape design and antipaths, to IDE hints, to warnings, to hard errors.

Exceptions and feedback

Too many exceptions builds complexity debt; too few builds workaround debt. Make reversible exceptions self-service, and send risky ones to review by whoever would have to staff the risk. Enumerate every exception.

Get feedback from three personas: developers (adoption, onboarding time, boilerplate, why desire paths appear), operators (training needed, how many services one team can run, toil, CSAT) and the business (SLOs, incident time, DORA metrics, efficiency).

Shift down, effectiveness zones, frameworks

Shift left puts quality work earlier in the lifecycle, but it doesn't scale if every team needs every kind of expertise. Shift down embeds those capabilities in the platform, and the two complement each other. The ecosystem effectiveness zone runs from YOLO through ad hoc, guided and engineered to assured.

Shift leftDeal with reliability earlier in the lifecycle. Every team needs the expertise.
Shift downBuild it into the platform once. Every team gets it by default.

It isn't a maturity ladder: match the constraints to the consequences of failure. Frameworks own the binary's lifecycle, RPC, auth, logging, backoff with jitter and hedging. In a monorepo (one version, live at head), fixing a framework module, such as moving ACL storage, rolls out everywhere at the next build, and introspection tells you when the old version is gone.

Legible risk and brownfield exemptions

Write SRE knowledge down as opinionated checks, for example:

  • Customer-facing services run in at least two points of presence.
  • Alerts route to an active team.
  • SLOs exist.
  • Incident load stays under a threshold.

Introspect production for these signals, show owners their gaps and give leadership rollups; uncertainty about technical debt is a bigger problem than its cost. Remediate with bugs, proposed changes (AI can draft them) or automatic fixes when you're confident (enabling overload protection everywhere).

Block greenfield violations at commit. Exempt brownfield by default with a structured exemption: policy, services, bug, expiry date, reason. Then choose a convergence rate: allow indefinitely, require periodic risk acceptance, require compliance on the next substantive change, or set a deadline. Think of it as eventual consistency for best practices. Building a platform is product management.

On AWSService Catalog, Proton or Backstage for golden paths; Control Tower controls, SCPs and RCPs for guardrails; Config conformance packs and Resilience Hub for legibility; CDK constructs for shifting down; cfn-guard in CI. See POC 10.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Teams keep bypassing your platform. What do you do?

Show a model answer

Treat it as product feedback, not disobedience.

Find out what they’re doing instead and why. The book calls these “desire paths”, like the trodden path across a lawn. Is a feature missing? Is the platform slower or harder than the workaround? Is there a use case nobody planned for?

Make the paved road cheaper than the workaround: templates, good defaults, faster provisioning.

Offer an official escape hatch for genuine special cases, recorded with an owner and an expiry date, so exceptions stay visible.

Use hard blocks only for actions that are genuinely unsafe. Then measure adoption, developer satisfaction and incidents for teams on the platform against teams off it.

How do you roll out a new reliability policy to 500 services?

Show a model answer

Make compliance automatic for most services and visible for the rest.

Encode the policy as an automated check. Make the platform’s defaults compliant, so new services pass without effort. Block new violations from the day it starts.

For existing services, grant automatic exemptions with a reason and an expiry date, so nothing breaks on day one but nothing is exempt forever.

Publish a clear rollup of who complies, fix things automatically where that’s safe, and choose how hard to push based on risk. POC 10 does exactly this.

Quick check: A hard block is placed on a mistake whose worst outcome is a cosmetic glitch. Where does this sit on the effectiveness chart?
Strength of control should match severity. Heavy controls on minor risks teach people to work around the platform.
Quick check: Brownfield services that don’t meet a new platform policy should…
Make the risk legible and owned; block only greenfield systems or substantive changes.
Your turnRun poc-10-platform-policy/policy_check.py against the example catalogue. Add an exemption with an expiry date and a reason for one failing service, then decide which of the four convergence options you would apply to it.
Key takeaways
  • A good platform makes the reliable way the easy way.
  • Golden paths over mandates: change the game so the good outcome is the rational one.
  • Block new violations, exempt old ones explicitly with an expiry, and make the remaining risk visible.
Part VI · OutlookChapter 19 · 4 min read

SRE at the tipping point

You will learn
  • what changes when writing code becomes nearly free
  • the chapter’s predictions for rollouts, debugging and incidents
  • what “strategic incoherence” means and how to counter it

The big picture

AI-driven development is pushing the cost of writing plausible code towards zero and the rate of change beyond human timescales. The SDLC still holds (work is roughly serial, and it loops), but non-functional properties such as reliability can be destroyed by a single line, and the SDLC is social as well as technical (Conway's law).

Plan
→
Analyse
→
Design
→
Build
→
Test
→
DeployThe hard boundary stays
→
Maintain

The phases stay, but AI compresses and blends the ones before deployment. Production doesn’t care how the code was written.

If you ship ten times faster and change nothing else, expect roughly ten times the incidents, odd interactions and resource exhaustion. Cherry-picking fixes gets harder, versioning stops partitioning risk well, staging environments drift further from production, and manual production debugging won't keep up.

Humans stay essential until AGI, because models hallucinate and outages need accountability. Expect longer causal chains, skill erosion and the risk that prevention gets under-funded because response becomes so good. The bright spots: observability gets cheaper and formal methods become more practical.

Going deeper the case studies, numbers and named models from the full chapter

More from the chapter

If generating code becomes nearly free, what becomes expensive? The development lifecycle phases stay the same but shrink, and a two-hour build phase leaves no time for the small refinements a two-week one allowed. Fast feedback helps functional requirements, not reliability or security.

AI-written code is about as reliable as before (there's evidence it may be less), and models learned from far more code that merely works than code that's reliable in production. Conway's law weakens when one person with one agent can take a spec to production.

Non-functional trade-offs, like whether to prioritise paid over free traffic, are social, and AI may recommend, decide or design them away.

The predictions:

  • The rate of change will outrun human timescales, cherry-picking fixes stops working, and roll-forward may become primary, the reverse of the usual SRE preference.
  • Ten times the delivery likely means about ten times the incidents. Automation will take the easy cases, so humans see the hard ones at the rate they used to see easy ones (and how do you learn on those?).
  • Strategic incoherence: agents handle low-context tasks well, but coherence degrades as features pile up, duplication bloats the context window, and agents become tireless generators of technical debt. Specification-driven development counters this.
  • Versioning may need to work per request; "what's actually running?" becomes hard to answer; staging may become impossible.
  • Debugging context has to be built on the fly with lossy tools; there may be disposable production environments, replaced when recovery is exhausted; causal chains get longer (more suspects in the murder mystery).
  • Cheap response could starve prevention of funding, and skills erode while tools are weakest in the tail where SREs work.

The bright spots are cheaper observability (with more duplicated metrics) and tractable formal methods. Humans remain the understanders of last resort, with comprehension shifting from when code is written to when it fails, and the SRE role starts to look like a staff engineer's.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

How should SRE adapt to the volume of AI-generated code?

Show a model answer

Assume much more change is coming, and strengthen the safeguards that don’t care who wrote the code.

Reviewers can’t read everything, so production-side protection matters more: progressive rollouts with automatic statistical canaries, monitoring of critical user journeys during every change, feature flags, and rollback that is fast and tested.

Use stronger checks where they pay off: specifications, tests generated from them, and formal methods for the most critical parts.

Use AI on the defensive side too, for review and incident investigation, inside guardrails.

And keep humans in practice with drills, so people can still take over when the automation is wrong. The book also warns about “roll-forward pressure”: with so many changes, people prefer fixing forward to rolling back, so make every change easy to reverse.

Quick check: Which is a sign of “strategic incoherence” in AI-generated code?
Coherence degrades as features are repeatedly extended, with duplication growing until it overloads the context window.
Your turnTake a feature you shipped with AI help. Write the three-line specification you wish had existed first: the invariant it must keep, how you would know in production that it broke, and how you would undo it.
Key takeaways
  • Faster delivery without other changes means proportionally more incidents.
  • Agents generate technical debt tirelessly unless specifications keep the design coherent.
  • Humans stay the understanders of last resort, so keep skills sharp.
Part VI · OutlookChapter 20 · 10 min read

How SRE supports AI

You will learn
  • the four SLO pillars for AI systems, with quality as the new one
  • how models and accelerators are qualified for production
  • the six losses that explain idle accelerators
  • power as a first-class constraint, and the new security risks

The big picture

AI systems are layered (accelerators, a shared inference layer, models, applications and agents) and need clear control and data planes, careful accelerator management, observability and a clean artifact lifecycle (versions, deployment, rollback).

AvailabilityHardware, the training control plane, attestation.
ThroughputML goodput: the share of allocated time doing useful work.
LatencyTime to first token, scheduling delay, data staleness.
QualityIs the answer right? The defining pillar for AI.

Agents are usually supported by the existing product SRE team. SLOs rest on four pillars: availability, throughput (training), latency (including time to first token) and quality, which is the defining one. Evaluation scores act as SLIs, alongside model-as-judge checks, data lineage and statistical drift detection.

Responses run on a spectrum from server error through "gave up" and low quality to high quality, so HTTP status codes aren't enough. Launch AI features with phased experiments, monitoring of both system and model quality, capacity plans, fast rollback to the previous model, and feedback loops.

Qualification covers new hardware generations (a continuous test matrix of workload, architecture and topology; accelerators become "SLO-eligible" only once proven) and every model submission (compatibility, performance and quality regressions across its lifecycle).

Accelerator utilisation losses come from headroom needed for latency, unrealised demand (fill it with preemptible work, pool it, grow in steps), N+1 redundancy (smaller domains, scope by criticality), prefill/decode imbalance, load balancing (least-loaded, peak EWMA, cost-aware routing) and fragmentation (consolidate models, prefer prompting over fine-tuning, share serving across tenants).

Other tools: central fleet management, hardware fungibility across TPU and GPU, cost per query, topology-aware, gang and goodput-aware scheduling, and bin packing. Power is now the bottleneck: oversubscribe it and shed safely before breakers trip, by throttling accelerators first, then killing tasks by priority, then shutting machines down.

On security, model weights are a theft target, the supply chain (pretrained models, datasets) is a risk, and agents introduce new trust boundaries (MCP) and dynamic code execution.

Three pictures from the chapter

The model release pipeline

Develop and versionModel, prompt and config together
→
Qualify automaticallyPlatform checks, then model evals, then simulated user journeys
→
Readiness gateFail and it goes back
→
Progressive rolloutCanary
→
Serve and monitorFeedback returns to development

After Figure 20-2. The same shape as a software release, with one extra kind of test: does the model still give good answers?

The qualification step has three layers on purpose. Infrastructure checks ask whether the model runs at all on this hardware. Evals ask whether its answers are good. Journey simulation asks whether the product built on it still works. A model can pass the first two and fail the third.

Why idle accelerators are expensive twice

So a half-idle fleet wastes the hardware and still pays most of the power bill. Run fewer machines hotter, and turn the rest off, since shutting down is the only way to remove idle draw.

Securing agents: two layers and a test loop

Runtime policy enforcementHard limits on what the agent is allowed to do, checked outside the model. Dependable, because it doesn’t rely on the model behaving.
Reasoning-based defencesA hardened base model, classifiers and safety fine-tuning. Flexible, but probabilistic.
Continuous assuranceRegression tests, variant analysis, red teams and human reviewers keep both layers honest.

After Figure 20-5. The interview line: never let the model be its own only guardrail. On AWS that means IAM policies and service control policies as the hard layer, Bedrock Guardrails as the reasoning layer, and evaluation jobs as the test loop.

Isolation is more than memoryA footnote warns that sharing accelerators between models needs isolation of high-bandwidth memory, interconnect bandwidth and duty cycle. Otherwise one model’s prefill phase can starve another model’s decoding, and a noisy neighbour shows up as someone else’s latency.

Planning accelerator capacity

DemandOrganic growth plus inorganic: launches, model changes, new hardware generations
→
Forecast
→
Order or rebalancePeriodic orders, or move supply across the fleet
→
AllocateA footprint and sizing matrix, with redundancy and location rules
→
DeployMoves and resizes
→
Monitor7-day 95th-percentile occupancy against targets

After Figure 20-3. Monitoring feeds the next forecast. The loop is the ordinary capacity loop from chapter 15; what changes is that supply takes months to arrive and can’t be bought on demand.

Security for AI systemsThe chapter frames AI security with Google’s Secure AI Framework (SAIF). The risks it lists for SREs: model weights as a theft target, supply-chain risk in pretrained models and datasets, trust boundaries around agent tools such as MCP servers, and dynamic code execution. Its advice is to converge on one common AI platform so these controls are built once. On AWS: Bedrock Guardrails, model access through IAM, signed artifacts, and confidential compute for weights.
Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the platform book also covers, from the knowledge map:
  • Model signals: Freshness, drift, confidence; for agents, tokens, latency, tool calls. See platform ch 16, platform ch 22.
  • Quality as a reliability signal: A fast success with a wrong answer is a failure. See platform ch 22.
Going deeper the case studies, numbers and named models from the full chapter

The stack and engagement

Google's first ML SRE team started in 2009 for ad click prediction. The stack runs from accelerators, to cluster management (topology-aware and gang scheduling), to frameworks (JAX or PyTorch compiled through XLA to Pathways), to shared inference, to data lineage (often underbuilt), to agents and applications.

Teams supporting researchers mix enterprise-style partnership with consumer-style "mitigate first". Agents are supported by the existing product SRE team, because the expertise is domain-specific. The serving layer routes between model sizes and can fall back to a smaller model, trading quality for availability.

SRE engages deeply once a model enters a continuous training pipeline. In Ads, failing to produce a fresh model on time counts as an outage.

Four SLO pillars

Availability covers hardware, the training control plane and attestation. Throughput is measured as ML goodput, the share of allocated time doing useful work. Latency covers time to first token, scheduling latency and data staleness.

Quality covers golden datasets, prediction bias and tool-call success rates. For online learning, put SLOs on upstream data producers, and have degraded inputs pause training before the model is corrupted. Evaluate in tiers: lineage checks (halt on freshness or volume drops), cheap statistical drift checks, then sampled model-as-judge scoring.

An eval score is an SLI, and its pass threshold is the SLO. For agents, track tool-use success, valid JSON and divergence from the task, since an early hallucination cascades. Security SLOs cover evidence freshness and attestation availability, because for Private AI Compute an attestation failure is an outage.

Reliability is a spectrum

Responses range from server errors, to the model giving up or answering poorly, to good answers. Instrument intentional degradation (smaller-model fallbacks) and safety-filter hits. Capture explicit feedback (downvotes) and implicit feedback (prompt rewrites, abandonment). Load tests need quality thresholds. Request costs vary wildly, so uniform-cost assumptions and simple thresholds break.

Qualification

Hyrum's law hits harder because researchers depend on undocumented behaviour. Qualify accelerators continuously from late engineering validation onwards, testing performance, correctness and relative quality across a workload × architecture × topology matrix prioritised by production usage.

Hardware only becomes SLO-eligible after a steady stream of qualification data (pre-release and obsolete hardware aren't eligible). Gate new models on structure, op compatibility and resource estimates. Weights, preambles and prompt templates are all change surfaces to canary.

Performance gates watch duty cycle and HBM; quality gates use golden sets, human ratings and A/B comparison. Agent workflows need scenario tests for task success, robustness and the absence of destructive actions.

The loss framework

Utilisation is measured as duty cycle (for example, P95 occupancy over seven days). Starting from 100%, six losses explain the gap:

  1. Max utilisation: real-time serving may queue at around 50%, batch at around 90%. Find the real limit with a redline canary.
  2. Unrealised demand: fill launch buffers with preemptible work, pool capacity, grow in steps.
  3. N+1 redundancy: use smaller failure domains, and scope redundancy to the critical classes.
  4. Disaggregation imbalance: tune the prefill-to-decode server ratio.
  5. Load balancing: request costs are uneven and KV-cache locality pulls against even spread. Use least-loaded or peak-EWMA routing, plus cost-aware routing by input tokens.
  6. Fragmentation: a large model has a minimum footprint (say 100 chips), so consolidate models, prefer prompting over fine-tuning, and serve multiple tenants.

Also: central fleet pools, hardware fungibility, cost per query reported by the inference engine to drive automated planning, topology-aware, gang and goodput-aware scheduling, defragmentation, bin-packing models, and checkpointing to survive preemption.

Power

An ML machine draws roughly 3× a CPU machine, and a 1,000-machine job needs one grid, so its smallest useful footprint is about 3,000× larger. Training load is a square wave of tens of megawatts. Oversubscribe like an airline selling 105 seats for 100.

Throttle acceleratorsTakes milliseconds, easy to undo
→
Terminate tasksBy priority band, if it lasts past about 5 s
→
Shut machines downThe only way to remove idle draw

Shedding power before a breaker trips.

When everyone shows up, shed load before a breaker trips, since breakers tolerate an overload for only seconds. Throttle accelerators first (milliseconds), then after about 5 seconds terminate tasks by priority band (seconds), or shut machines down. Spread sensitive services across power domains.

Security

The model and its training data are crown-jewel IP. The system prompt shares a channel with user input, which is the root of prompt injection. Other risks are poisoned weights in the supply chain, MCP and agent-to-agent trust boundaries, and generated code that's effectively remote code execution as a feature, so sandbox it.

Centralise controls in the platform (audit logging, trusted execution environments), but don't platformise too early for frontier teams. Log prompts and responses (redacted), tool inputs and outputs, and reasoning traces. Detect quickly with embedding drift checks and regexes, and deeply with a model as judge.

On AWSBedrock (provisioned throughput, guardrails, model evaluation, cross-Region inference), SageMaker endpoints and inference components, EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML, CloudWatch metrics for TTFT and tokens per second.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Define SLOs for an LLM-powered support chatbot.

Show a model answer

Four kinds, because a chatbot can fail in four different ways.

Availability. 99.9% of conversations get a response without a server error.

Latency. 95% of responses start within 1.5 seconds (time to first token), and text streams faster than a minimum number of tokens per second. Users feel both.

Quality. This is the one people forget: a fast, successful answer can be wrong. Sample real conversations, score them weekly with an evaluation suite (a judge model plus human spot checks), and keep the score at or above an agreed baseline. If the system falls back to a smaller model, count that as degraded.

Safety. Zero personal-data leaks in a sampled audit.

Then act on them: alert when the distribution of answers drifts, and roll back the model version automatically if quality drops. POC 19 implements the quality and drift checks.

Quick check: Which is the defining SLO pillar for AI systems?
A 200 response with a wrong or harmful answer is still a failure.
Quick check: A datacentre power event is detected. What is the first shedding action?
Throttling takes effect in milliseconds and is easy to reverse; termination or shutdown follows only if the event lasts beyond about 5 seconds.
Your turnWrite SLOs for an LLM chat feature: one per pillar. What is your quality SLI, how is it sampled, and does a fallback to a smaller model count as good, degraded or bad?
Key takeaways
  • A successful response with a wrong answer is still a failure, so quality needs an SLO.
  • Qualify hardware, models and prompts continuously, and canary all three.
  • Accelerators are scarce. Explain idle capacity with the six losses before buying more.
Part VI · OutlookChapter 21 · 9 min read · POC 11

How AI supports SRE

You will learn
  • the safety architecture for agents with production access
  • how AI finds outages that metrics miss
  • the five levels of autonomy, with a real example at each
  • where the real value lies beyond toil reduction

The big picture

Scripts are brittle and AI is probabilistic, so adoption is organised around the production-health hierarchy. Foundations first: blamelessness becomes a prerequisite once automation is probabilistic. Humans aren't replaced; the Jevons paradox suggests demand for production expertise will grow.

LevelMonitorInvestigateApproveActuateSelf-direct
L0 ManualAutoHumanHumanHumanHuman
L1 AssistedAutoAutoHumanHumanHuman
L2 PartialAutoAutoHumanAutoHuman
L3 HighAutoAutoAutoAutoHuman
L4 FullAutoAutoAutoAutoAuto

The safety architecture rests on transparency, contextual awareness and progressive authorization, starting with least privilege and dry runs, keeping absolute human control, and following the reversible operations rule: no action unless the agent knows how to undo it.

In practice: Detectr clusters user feedback from social media, support and forums into outage reports; agents summarise incident chatter and build dashboards from similar past incidents, playbooks and the alert's intent. Mitigation is selection among known safe actions, which AI handles well; root-cause analysis is deep investigation.

AI also drafts postmortems, mines past incidents, clusters toil, tunes itself, verifies resilience tests (did traffic in the drained cluster really drop to zero?), and supports design and launch reviews. Autonomy levels, across monitor, investigate, approve, actuate and self-direct: L0 manual, L1 assisted, L2 partial (a human approves), L3 high (well-defined scenarios), L4 full.

Not every system should reach L4. Google's AI Operator acts as a first responder that moves up the levels as evaluations justify it.

The safety loop for an agent with production access

  • The agent sends its reason with the action, so a reviewer or an audit can check the thinking, not only the command.
  • Progressive authorisation: as a class of action proves safe, it moves from the approval queue to automatic execution.
  • The executor treats each action as a transaction: do it, validate the result, roll back if validation fails. Destructive migrations need extra design work to be reversible at all.
  • Below a confidence threshold, the system should not show the suggested mitigation to the on-caller. A weak suggestion during an incident is worse than none.
