What an investigation agent actually does

Plan
→
Read server errors
→
Fetch job details
→
Check for anomaliesIs this transient?
→
Is an incident open?
→
Find the owner
→
EscalateTo the right developer

After Figure 21-4, shortened. Each step is a tool call a human on-caller would also make. The value is doing all of them in seconds, in the same order every time.

Why anomaly detection is harder than the slide suggests

The idealA flat, predictable baseline and one clean spike. Any threshold finds it.
The realityA noisy line shaped by a feature launch, a viral search topic, a local ISP outage and a regional traffic migration, all in the same window.

After Figure 21-2. This is why the chapter argues for models that take context as input. A threshold can’t tell a launch from an outage. A system that knows a launch was scheduled can.

Grading the agent: LLM as judge

Figure 21-5 shows how Google evaluates its investigation agent. A second model scores each run against labelled incidents on two questions, was the diagnosis right and was the mitigation right, and writes a critique. A failed run also records the failure mode, the step where it went wrong, and why.

The example failure is instructive: the agent had a tool for correlating failures with recent rollouts, didn’t call it, and followed a log line about an old bug instead. It missed the chance to roll back. That is exactly the mistake a tired human makes, and having it written down per step is what lets you fix the prompt or the tool order.

On AWS the equivalent is a Bedrock evaluation job with a judge model, run against a set of past incidents every time you change the agent’s prompt, tools or model.

Playbooks that tune themselvesOne worked example in the chapter: agents learn playbooks from the actions humans took to resolve tickets, then execute them within guardrails and hand back to a person when the situation is novel. If a human reopens a ticket the agent resolved, the case goes to evaluation and the playbook is retuned. Where toil can’t be automated, the agent enriches the ticket first, for example by asking the submitter for missing information, because much resolution time is spent searching for it.
Going deeper the case studies, numbers and named models from the full chapter

Framing

Probabilistic tools at production scale bring probabilistic failure at scale: a 1% error rate spread across all of production is a catastrophe. Organise around three capabilities. Experimentation treats results as provisional, because what fails today may work in months.

Productionisation adds guardrails and evals and keeps validating, because a more capable model may take more action than you expect. Enablement: the hardest part is rebuilding senior engineers' intuition. The strategy follows the hierarchy of production health. The book expects more SRE work rather than less (the Jevons paradox).

Safety architecture

Production has no safe sandbox: a coding agent's worst case is a failed build, while a production agent's is draining a healthy cluster. The three pillars:

  • Transparency: the agent shows its reasoning, signals and confidence.
  • Contextual awareness: freezes, error budgets and active incidents all count.
  • Progressive authorisation: read-only, then proposing, then autonomous for low-risk actions.

Start with least privilege and dry-run audits. If the error budget is exhausted, downgrade the agent to advisory. Give agents SLOs too: proposal latency, a helpfulness SLO (say 95% of suggestions accepted) and a safety budget that pauses autonomy when spent.

Keep a break-glass block on agent access. Reversible operations: act only if you know the undo, and validate over a context-aware window that includes warm-up. Treat act, validate and roll back as one transaction. Agents force the strict reversibility the industry usually skips by fixing forward.

The foundations are real-time retrieval over topology and incident history, MCP tools, agent-to-agent protocols and agent orchestration.

Situational awareness: Detectr

Aggregate SLOs hide pain. At a 0.1% error rate, a customer making 1,000 calls per operation sees nearly every operation fail, and a 0.1% average might really be 1% of customers failing 10% of the time. Classic anomaly detection never caught on because launches and load shedding look like anomalies.

AugmentAttach system state
→
FilterLLM drops irrelevant posts
→
ClusterEmbeddings, then an LLM
→
ReportA structured outage report
→
NotifyEmail, ticket or page

Written feedback carries intent ("I tried X in Y and got Z"). Detectr pulls in social media, support and forum posts, attaches system state, filters with an LLM, clusters by embedding and then with an LLM, writes a structured report and notifies through normal channels.

Cluster volume works as a severity signal, and the effort it takes to write feedback filters out noise. It became core infrastructure in early 2026 and saved thousands of hours of customer impact. AI also maps incidents to impacted customers and matches incoming cases to live incidents.

Preparedness and infrastructure

Agents summarise incident channels for joiners and handoffs, and build incident-specific dashboards from similar past incidents, playbooks and intent. Mitigation is about selecting from a set (rollback, drain, upscale) with a confidence score; root cause analysis is detective work over topology.

Agents draft postmortems, mine the whole corpus, deduplicate bugs and generate a draft playbook when none existed. Rollout speed adapts to risk instead of a fixed wait between failure domains. AI reviews running config for drift.

For toil, it clusters tickets (avoiding recency bias), intercepts duplicates, generates playbooks from successful human fixes, retunes itself when a human reopens a ticket, and asks submitters for missing information up front.

For resilience tests, it tags each test with a property from a taxonomy, pre-reviews safety, compares the test window against steady state (checking that traffic in the drained datacentre really went to zero) and finds testing gaps by mapping incidents to the properties that would have prevented them.

Force multiplier and autonomy

Toil reduction has a ceiling: with toil at 25%, even processing it 5× faster barely moves overall productivity. The real value is new capability: design reviews trained on reliable designs and incident history, launch-review agents that examine the actual prototype, and codebase scans that find every other service sharing a lesson's vulnerability.

The autonomy table covers monitor, investigate, approve, actuate and self-direct, from L0 to L4. Not every system should reach L4. AI Operator works as the first responder:

  • L1: summarises and finds similar incidents.
  • L2: proposes a drain or rollback with the exact commands, for a human to approve.
  • L3: restarts one aberrant task or clears a known cache on its own, but only after a dedicated eval shows a very high L2 success rate.

It improves itself by comparing its actions with golden human responses and using LLM-judge critiques. Organisationally, Google accepted duplicated solutions and sponsored incubators, with paths to graduate the best ones, a reversal after a decade of standardisation.

On AWSAmazon Q Developer operational investigations, Bedrock Agents with read-only IAM to start, SSM Automation approvals for L2, ARC zonal shift as a reversible action. See POC 11.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Would you let an AI agent roll back production? Under what conditions?

Show a model answer

Yes, but it has to earn that permission, one kind of action at a time.

The book describes levels of autonomy. Start at L1: the agent investigates and suggests. Move to L2: it proposes a rollback with its evidence, and a human approves. Allow L3, acting without approval, only for one narrow situation, such as a clear statistical regression right after a deploy, and only after replayed past incidents show it gets that situation right almost every time.

Guardrails stay on at every level. The action must be reversible. The agent checks the result straight away and undoes it if things got worse. Everything is logged. Its permissions cover only what it needs. And there is a kill switch.

Promote it scenario by scenario, never in general. POC 11 implements these gates.

Quick check: An agent proposes a low-risk action. In the book’s safety loop, what happens next?
Risk assessment routes high-risk actions to people and low-risk ones to an executor that can undo them.
Quick check: At autonomy level L2, who approves an agent’s production action?
At L2 the agent investigates and acts, but each action needs human approval.
Your turnRun the tests in poc-11-ai-ops-guardrails and read agent_guardrails.py. Which checks stop an agent at L2 from acting alone? Add one action you would never allow above L2, and say why.
Key takeaways
  • Trust is earned: read-only, then proposing, then acting on narrow, reversible tasks.
  • An agent may only do what it knows how to undo, as one validated transaction.
  • Not every system should reach full autonomy. Match the level to the risk.
Part VI · OutlookChapter 22 · 6 min read

SRE in diverse environments

You will learn
  • what to do first as the only SRE at a company
  • how to apply SRE with legacy systems, silos and regulation
  • lessons from a startup, a bank, a lender and Waymo
  • how SRE skills carry over to security and privacy

The big picture

Most SRE doesn't look like Google. A solo SRE focuses on keeping the service running and making developers self-sufficient, and may start at around 80% toil. Priorities: P0 stop the bleeding; P1 visibility (metrics, symptom-based alerts, logs); P2 automate the scariest task; P3 developer self-service.

P0 · Stop the bleedingFix the outage that keeps repeating
→
P1 · VisibilityMetrics, symptom alerts, structured logs
→
P2 · Automate the scariest taskUsually deploys. Rollback first
→
P3 · Self-serviceTools and docs so developers don’t need you

The solo SRE’s priority stack.

In the first 90 days, answer four questions: is it down, is it slow, is it broken, is it driving users away? Use one lightweight toolset, write playbooks for the five most recent outages, share on-call with developers, and make sure every change gets reviewed by at least one other person.

In hybrid and legacy estates, sort out responders' access and authority before incidents (formal break-glass), protect the time to act on postmortems, and wrap closed third-party systems in an anticorruption layer.

Use generic mitigations, adopt in stages, limit scope, set goals that fit each context, run drills for rigid systems, standardise the tooling that manages what you can't change, and keep humans in the loop where regulation demands it.

Cases: a B2B startup (visibility standards, deployment automation, top-ten playbooks, all engineers on call); a multinational bank (a capabilities map per vertical, ratified baselines, meta-tools that plug into existing tooling); a mortgage lender (a workshop, 90-day engagements, an 8-week enablement programme, and less "weaponised blamelessness"); Waymo (SRE runs company-wide non-technical crisis response with a coordinator and a scribe).

Security and SRE share incident muscles, as the CrowdStrike (July 2024) and Log4j (November 2021) responses showed.

Going deeper the case studies, numbers and named models from the full chapter

Solo SRE

You're the firefighter, the builder and the evangelist, often starting at 80% toil. Priorities:

  • P0, stop the bleeding: fix the repeat outage first.
  • P1, visibility: business and system metrics, symptom alerts switched on at the start of the day (never at home time), and structured JSON logs.
  • P2, automate the scariest task, usually deploys. Rollback matters most, because it stops fix-forward chains.
  • P3, developer self-service.

Use one integrated toolset to answer four questions: is it down, slow, broken, or driving users away? Write playbooks for the last five outages, for non-SREs, and keep them available when everything's down (a repo, a local panic package). Probe critical user journeys, share on-call with developers, and insist on human code review even when AI reviews too.

Hybrid and legacy

Google on-callers can see their dependencies' telemetry and roll back or reroute without asking. Elsewhere, a NOC may have only surface access. Fix this by giving an IC explicit authority, with predefined time-bound emergency access the IC can grant, alongside least privilege, two-person rules and immutable audit logs.

If you can't walk away from a service, run a toil audit and turn it into a business case ("automating X frees Y hours"). In regulated industries, postmortems can serve as CAPA (corrective and preventive action) evidence for regulators, which raises the priority of fixes.

For closed COTS systems, stabilise what surrounds them: IaC, scripts for common mitigations, and an anticorruption layer, a wrapper you own that adds observability, rate limits and validated config. For silos, favour generic mitigations, incremental adoption, a limited scope, context-specific goals and drills for systems you can't change, with symptom-based alerts as the unifier.

Case studies

B2B SaaS: a 20-developer company stuck in "garage mode" set up visibility standards, one-click rollbacks, playbooks for its ten most common failures and basic SLOs, and put all of engineering on call. Six months later, downtime across critical journeys was down about 60% and a major feature shipped 60 days early.

It now has about a 7:1 developer-to-SRE ratio, and developers spend about 5% of their time on ops, down from nearly half.

Bank: independent silos meant taking a capabilities-based approach. Each vertical's map marked capabilities as existing, must-have, nice-to-have, unneeded or explicitly undesirable, with a ratified baseline. A "chief reliability officer" (a managing director) ran reliability as its own meta-vertical.

Third-party "meta tools" plugged into existing monitoring, then disaster role-plays and a standing postmortem review committee followed. Results: consistent SLO reporting, lower MTTR, and fewer layers than the old five-plus-level escalation stack.

Mortgage lender: a three-month SRE workshop seeded the practice. A central team offered issue-flow advice, 90-day engagements, one to three designated SREs at 50–75% for critical services, and a training rotation, then ran an eight-week enablement programme. It cut weaponised blamelessness, where "no blame" was used to dodge ownership.

Waymo: crises, not just outages

Waymo's IRT covers on-road incidents, physical security and local events, drawing on legal, safety, ops, comms and policy on-callers, while SRE coordinates without mitigating.

It runs two simultaneous primary roles: the incident coordinator (a conductor who manages breakouts and dissent and keeps safety first) and the incident scribe (record-keeper and presenter who flags contradictions between what the room and the field are saying).

SRE fits because it's continuously trained in incident management and owns the tooling. It works at a "Goldilocks" size, past the point where all senior people can jump on a call but before you have dedicated corporate responders, and in companies with diverse job functions.

Security and privacy

These share SRE's constructive pessimism; only the adversary differs. In the CrowdStrike incident (19 July 2024), Windows VMs crash-looped. The VM-infrastructure SRE team and the guest OS team each had the wrong scope, so support went straight to the vendor.

The lesson was about knowing roles across boundaries. For Log4j (CVSS 10), security and Tech IRT launched per-department response groups under a Code Red with exit criteria: upgrade everything, file exceptions, document status. That happened during a holiday code freeze.

What went well: defining the end-to-end process up front and tracking centrally. What to improve: instructions for verifying an upgrade.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

You’re the first SRE at a 40-engineer startup. What are your first 90 days?

Show a model answer

Earn trust by fixing real pain first, then build the foundations.

Weeks 1–2. Join every incident and fix the failure that happens most often. That shows value fast.

Weeks 3–6. Make the system visible: logs, metrics and traces in one place, and alerts on symptoms users feel. Make deploys automatic with one-click rollback, because changes are usually the biggest cause of outages. Write playbooks for the last few incidents.

Weeks 7–12. Agree two or three SLOs with the founders and product. Start a shared on-call rotation with the developers instead of taking the pager alone. Require review for every change.

Report progress with numbers: fewer incidents, faster mitigation, safer deploys. The book’s startup example cut downtime on critical journeys by about 60% in six months this way.

Quick check: A culture where blamelessness is used to avoid owning problems is called…
Seen at the mortgage lender, it raised MTTM and MTTR until clearer SRE norms spread.
Your turnYou join a 20-person startup tomorrow as its first SRE. Write your priority stack with one concrete target and date for each level, and the four questions your first dashboard will answer.
Key takeaways
  • Alone, prioritise ruthlessly: stop the bleeding, see, make deploys safe, enable developers.
  • With closed or legacy systems, stabilise what surrounds them and standardise the layer above.
  • Adapt the principles to your constraints. Don’t try to copy Google.
Part VI · OutlookChapter 23 · 5 min read

The future of SRE, and the appendices

You will learn
  • what the book expects to stay the same
  • the three shifts under way: shift down, risk as a leading indicator, agentic operations
  • what each appendix is for

The big picture

Two things won't change: reliability matters, and humans stay involved.

TrailingAvailability: tells you after it broke
→
LeadingCatalogued risk: tells you what could break

From measuring failure to measuring risk.

What's changing: shift left becomes shift down (managed services and opinionated frameworks with best practice built in); risk becomes a leading indicator of reliability, so you identify, catalogue and mitigate it before availability suffers, with AI speeding that up; agents bring far more code and far more services, and SREs move from specialists towards generalists. The book ends optimistic, expecting abundance.

Appendices worth knowing

A: the ROI of training, comparing "sink or swim" with structured onboarding. B/C: an SRE team charter template and an example. D: example production-meeting minutes. E: composing SLOs: in series, success probabilities multiply (0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72); with hedging, failure probabilities multiply (1 − 0.2 × 0.1 = 0.98); both assume independence.

F: latency alerting: build cohorts big enough to be meaningful (say 10,000 or more samples with low variance, covering at least 65% of workloads), baseline over 30–60 days, compute z-scores and watch the share above 2. In theory that's 2.28%, around 4% in practice, and a jump means a regression.

Use empirical distributions for log-normal latency, or hierarchical Bayes for small cohorts. G: modern observability with statistics and ML.

“What got us here won’t get us there”The authors borrow Marshall Goldsmith’s line for the shift from human-centric to human-supervised operations. If agents produce orders of magnitude more code, today’s release process would pack more changes into each release, making releases riskier and rollbacks harder. The answer is a heavily pipelined flow of many smaller changes, and SREs moving from specialists to generalists who direct agents. They close optimistically: SREs are not automating themselves out of jobs but “into jobs”, with less toil, less on-call and more autonomy.
Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the platform book also covers, from the knowledge map:
  • Shift down: Move responsibility into the platform so teams inherit the result. See platform ch 15, platform ch 16.
Going deeper the case studies, numbers and named models from the full chapter

More from the chapter

Two things won't change: reliability matters more as technology becomes societal infrastructure, and humans stay involved for novel problems. Three things are transforming. First, shift left is becoming shift down, with managed services and opinionated frameworks.

Second, risk is becoming a leading indicator, because availability only tells you after the fact. Every postmortem should catalogue the risks it uncovered, alongside proactive STPA and AI reviews of designs and code, all classified with a taxonomy based on the SEI's risk taxonomy.

Mapping incidents against it showed that many came from mishandled overload, which led to overload protection being built into the core RPC stack. Third, AI changes the practice itself: release pipelines for many more, smaller changes, more systems and tools to standardise, and SREs moving from specialists to generalists who direct agents. The closing idea is that SREs will automate themselves into new jobs rather than out of them.

Appendices

  • A, training ROI: sink-or-swim takes 550 weeks plus $220k; structured training takes 483 weeks plus $210k. That saves 67 weeks and $10k.
  • B, charter template: status, mission, scope, services, success measures, values.
  • C, example charter (gShoe): success looks like 100% SLO coverage, toil 50% below the 2022 level, launch prep cut from three months to one, at least 60% utilisation while absorbing a 5× spike for an hour.
  • D, production meeting minutes: announcements, action-item review, outages, paging and non-paging events, a toil check, monitoring changes, planned changes, key metrics, resources and new action items.
  • G, statistics and ML: a Wilson baseline from the last two weeks suits most metrics, and a forecasting model (TimesFM) helps for strongly cyclical ones. Weigh explainability and cost; ML is most cost-effective after an alert, for analysis, rather than for detection.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

How will SRE change over the next five years?

Show a model answer

The book’s answer is that the principles stay and the work changes.

There will be far more change, because AI will produce far more code. Releasing it the old way would pack more changes into each release and make every release riskier. So releases become many small, heavily automated steps.

The work shifts from doing to supervising. Agents investigate, detect and mitigate; humans handle novel problems and set the guardrails. The authors call this moving from human-centric to human-supervised operations, and say SREs will be “automating themselves into jobs, not out of them”.

The fundamentals that remain: user-focused SLOs, reliability built into platforms by default, and treating risk as a leading indicator instead of waiting for outages.

In an interview, finish with what you’d do now: make every change reversible, invest in the platform, and practise the skills you’d need if the automation fails.

Quick check: Why does the book call availability a trailing indicator?
Availability shows risk that has already turned into failure. Cataloguing risks from postmortems, STPA and design reviews gives you leading indicators.
Your turnTake your most recent postmortem and list the risks it revealed, not just the action items. Group them. Is there one class of risk a platform change could remove for everyone?
Key takeaways
  • Reliability matters more each year, and humans stay in the loop for novel problems.
  • Shift down: put reliability into platforms so it’s the default.
  • Treat risk as the leading indicator, and use AI to find and remove whole classes of it.
Platform Engineering at GoogleO’Reilly early release · 10 of a planned 31 chapters · 4 min read

Platform engineering: the second book on the map

You will learn
  • What this book argues, in one paragraph
  • Which chapters exist today and where they sit in the final book
  • How it connects to the SRE lessons you have already done

The argument in one paragraph

Every engineering organisation wants the same things from its software: secure, reliable, efficient, compliant. The usual way to get them is to ask every developer to remember every rule. That fails at scale, because developers are human and there are never enough experts to check their work.

Platform engineering takes the opposite route. It moves those responsibilities down into the things developers already build on: languages, libraries, frameworks, build systems, deployment pipelines, runtime infrastructure. Experts solve a problem once, inside the platform, and every team inherits the answer. The book calls this shifting down. It is different from shifting left, which moves the same work earlier but leaves it with the developer.

Shift leftFind the problem earlier. The developer still has to find it
→
Shift downMake the problem impossible, or handled by default, in the platform

Shift left reduces the cost of each mistake. Shift down reduces the number of mistakes that can be made.

If you finished the SRE lessons, you met this idea in chapter 18, with its 0-to-4 scale from YOLO to Assured. This book is the long version, written by the people who built Google’s internal platforms.

What is in the early release

The book is still being written. O’Reilly publishes chapters as they are drafted, so the numbering you see online is temporary. Ten chapters are available. I read all ten in full, and all five figures. The other twenty-one are listed in the table of contents and can’t be read yet, so they are not in this course.

Several of the available chapters refer to them. Where a lesson leans on one of those, I say so.

Five words the whole book uses

TermMeaning
Developer ecosystemEverything an organisation could build with: languages, libraries, frameworks, build tools, runtimes, practices. A marketplace of parts.
Developer platformAn opinionated selection from that marketplace, integrated and configured for one kind of application, so that quality comes by design and by default.
Quality attributesThe “ilities”: security, reliability, efficiency, compliance, maintainability. What a platform is meant to guarantee.
Golden path / well-lit path / paved roadThe supported, documented, easiest way to do a common task. Three names for one idea.
Ecosystem typeHow tightly integrated an ecosystem is. Type 2 is guided, type 3 engineered, type 4 assured. The more integrated, the more the platform can promise.

How to study this track

Architecture firstLessons 1 to 6: coupling, layers, shared fate, then the three deep dives. These are design questions.
Then executionLessons 7 to 10: developer experience, product management, AI, education. These are leadership questions.
Then the codePOCs 12 to 19 in the repo turn each idea into something you can run, mapped to AWS.
Key takeaways
  • Shift down means the platform takes the responsibility; shift left only moves it earlier.
  • A platform is an opinionated assembly from an ecosystem, built for one kind of application.
  • Ten chapters are published. The lessons cover those and nothing else.
Platform book · Architecture and ecosystem designChapter 9 in the final book · Michelle Brush · 11 min read · POC 12

Coupling: decide what depends on what

You will learn
  • Explicit and implicit coupling, tight and loose, and how cohesion relates
  • Four reasons to couple on purpose and four costs of doing it
  • Five patterns that loosen coupling and four antipatterns that tighten it by accident
  • Four ways to find coupling nobody intended

The big picture

Coupling is how much the parts of a system depend on each other. It is usually talked about as a defect. This chapter’s position is more useful: some coupling is unavoidable, some is valuable, and the real failure is coupling nobody chose.

Two distinctions set up everything else.

MeaningExample
ExplicitOne part calls another directlyA service makes an RPC to another service
ImplicitNo direct interaction, but one part assumes the other exists or behaves a certain wayA producer writes to a queue. It has never heard of the consumer, and a change to the message format still breaks it
TightParts know each other’s internalsA service reads another team’s database tables
LooseParts know only each other’s interfacesA service calls a versioned API

Cohesion is the mirror image: how closely related the things inside one module are. A module with low cohesion does many unrelated jobs, so either it depends on many things or many things depend on it. Low cohesion and high coupling tend to arrive together.

When coupling pays

EfficiencyOne safe path for everyone. Google’s tooling is coupled to its issue tracker, so every change has a tracked reason and bugs close themselves when the fix is fully rolled out.
PerformanceFewer layers and hops. Spanner can interleave child rows with their parent. Maths lives in libraries, not services, because an RPC would cost more than the sum.
AtomicityAll-or-nothing changes. Deleting a cloud project must also delete its VMs and disks, or resources leak.
TraceabilityFollow data end to end. Google’s tracing works everywhere because every service uses the same RPC layer, which gives one place to instrument.

Google has a name for what you give up: retargetability, the ability to reuse a part of the system for a different purpose. The trade is engineering efficiency against retargetability.

One warning on performance. Couple for speed only after other options are exhausted. Tight coupling can block later optimisation, because speeding up one module may break a timing assumption in another.

When coupling costs

ReuseCoupled parts can’t be used alone. And reuse itself creates coupling: when the tiny left-pad package was unpublished in 2016, thousands of builds broke.
ExtensibilityA change in one place has side effects elsewhere, and isolated tests are hard to write.
RobustnessHyrum’s law: with enough users, every observable behaviour is depended on by someone. Failures cascade.
Freedom of choiceLock-in. Teams can’t adopt something better without engineering work, and can’t self-serve.

Finding the balance

No platform can be the best on every axis. A tool that does one job will eventually beat the platform at that job, and users will want to leave for it. Leaving needs loose coupling. Meeting expectations across several axes needs tight coupling. The chapter’s answer is to look for the design that gets the most benefit from the least coupling, which is Pareto efficiency: a point where you can’t improve one dimension without giving up another.

How do you choose the point? Ask what your users value most. If they need raw performance, couple. If they need to extend and customise, don’t.

Google’s own tradeSource control, code review, build and deployment are tightly coupled at Google. That lets them mark one change as bad so it can never ship, even by accident. When Log4Shell appeared, a central profiler wired into the build and scheduling systems showed quickly that exposure was small. The price was that every team had to use the same tools, whatever they were missing.
Going deeper types, patterns, antipatterns and how to find hidden coupling

Five kinds of coupling

The chapter borrows Kruchten’s “4+1” architectural views and asks, for each one, how two components can be tied together.

ViewCoupled when…How restrictive
LogicalCode in one calls functions or classes in the otherMost
DevelopmentOne package needs the other to be deployed with it, like a shared libraryHigh
ProcessThey talk at runtime through RPCs or messagesLower: each can be updated on its own
PhysicalThey must share a machine, rack or data centre to workDeceptive: hidden assumptions about latency and failure domains
ScenarioNothing technical links them, and a real-world event doesInvisible until it happens

The scenario examples are memorable. A shark bit one of Google’s undersea cables. When many people left Twitter in 2022, they overwhelmed Mastodon’s servers. Neither pair of systems shared a line of code.

Patterns that loosen coupling

PatternHow it decouplesOn AWS
LayersEach layer knows only the one beneath itVPC, then EKS, then your services
Pipe and filterIndependent steps joined by a channel. Extend by adding a stepKinesis or MSK with Lambda or Flink stages; Step Functions for batch
Publish and subscribePublishers don’t know who is listeningSNS, EventBridge, MSK
FederationInterchangeable parts behind a strict contract. Each owns its data and behaviourIAM Identity Center with an external identity provider; a deletion workflow that asks each service to clean up its own resources
Fail openWhen a dependency fails, degrade, use a default or fall backCached responses, AppConfig defaults, circuit breakers

Fail open deserves care. It removes runtime coupling, since the caller survives, while logical coupling remains, since the call is still in the code. The opposite, fail closed, is correct when the dependency is a security or correctness check.

Antipatterns that tighten it by accident

Shared databaseSeveral services read and write the same tables. The schema becomes the interface, so every schema change needs a coordinated release. Fix: a store per service behind an API, and let the platform provide backup and replication.
Distributed monolithServices look separate and aren’t. Signs: releases must be orchestrated in order, they must sit in the same rack, or one failing takes all down. The costs of microservices with the constraints of a monolith.
Megamorphic artifactA config file or object that grew into a junk drawer. Nobody knows who reads which part, so every edit is risky.
Control couplingA flag lets the caller steer the callee’s internal behaviour. The caller now knows how the callee works. Fix: split into separate operations.

Data warehouses and lakes are not the shared-database antipattern. Their consumers expect schemas to change and use registries and ETL tools to cope.

The megamorphic file at Compute EngineOne large configuration file started as infrastructure as code. Because it was easy to extend, it collected per-customer preferences and behaviour flags. Almost every service read a piece of it and none needed all of it. Small edits began causing rollbacks and minor incidents. The team split it into smaller, cohesive files, audited every consumer, and removed access nobody needed. Dependencies became visible and the blast radius of a bad edit shrank.

The odd one: workflow engines

A workflow engine runs a process as a state machine and retries each step until the whole thing finishes. That decouples steps nicely, provided every step is idempotent and has no side effects beyond its output. Data pipelines usually qualify. Elsewhere, three problems appear.

  • Stuck flows. A step that can never succeed is retried forever. Someone must detect it and decide whether to roll back or leave things half done.
  • Orphaned state. Early steps wrote data that the failed workflow never used. You need compensating actions (the saga pattern) or a janitor job, and both are coupled to the business logic of the steps.
  • Version skew. A step is redeployed while workflows are in flight, and later steps depended on its old behaviour.

Finding coupling nobody intended

MethodFindsCostOn AWS
Static analysisLogical coupling: imports, shared data structures, global stateLowDependency graphs in CI; Amazon Q Developer or Inspector code scans
TracingRuntime calls, including through queues if messages carry trace contextLow once instrumentedX-Ray, Application Signals service map, OpenTelemetry
Log correlationTwo services touching the same state or the same requestMediumCloudWatch Logs Insights joined on request IDs; CloudTrail data events
Chaos engineeringPhysical and scenario coupling. Turn off a whole failure domain and see what else breaksHighestFault Injection Service, ARC zonal shift

When you find an accidental dependency, weigh it like a deliberate one. Does it buy efficiency, performance, atomicity or traceability? If not, migrate to one of the loose patterns.

Names to recognise

The lesson above describes these in plain words. An interviewer who has read the book may use the names, so know what each one refers to.

NameWhat it isClosest on AWS
BuganizerGoogle’s issue tracker, coupled to its tooling so every change has a tracked reasonJira or GitHub Issues linked to CodePipeline
DapperGoogle’s always-on distributed tracing, built into the RPC layerX-Ray, OpenTelemetry
Stubby / gRPCGoogle’s internal RPC framework, and its public descendantgRPC on ALB or VPC Lattice
Forge, BorgThe distributed build system and the cluster schedulerCodeBuild; EKS or ECS
Kruchten’s 4+1 viewsLogical, development, process, physical, plus scenarios
Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the SRE book also covers, from the knowledge map:
  • Hyrum’s law: With enough users, every observable behaviour is depended on by someone. See SRE ch 8.
Say it in an interview

I don’t treat coupling as good or bad. I ask what it buys and what it costs. It buys efficiency, performance, atomicity and traceability, and it costs reuse, extensibility, robustness and freedom of choice. So I decide which of those my users care about, couple deliberately for that, and then go looking for the coupling nobody chose, with dependency analysis, tracing and fault injection.

On AWSThe loose patterns map directly: SNS and EventBridge for publish-subscribe, Kinesis and Step Functions for pipelines, API Gateway and versioned APIs between services, IAM Identity Center for federation. For the shared-database antipattern, give each service its own DynamoDB table or Aurora cluster behind an API and let AWS Backup carry the common concerns. To discover hidden coupling, use the X-Ray or Application Signals service map for runtime calls, CloudTrail to see who touches which table or bucket, and Fault Injection Service to remove an Availability Zone and watch what fails.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Your team has thirty microservices and every release needs a spreadsheet to coordinate the deploy order. What is wrong, and what do you do?

Show a model answer

That is a distributed monolith. The services are separate in the code and coupled somewhere else, and the release spreadsheet is the evidence. I’d say so plainly, because the team is paying the operational cost of microservices and getting none of the independence.

First I’d find where the coupling lives. Shared database tables are the usual cause: I’d check which services read or write the same tables, using CloudTrail or database audit logs. Then implicit contracts: message formats on queues, and shared configuration that many services read. Tracing gives the runtime call graph, and the deploy history shows which services always ship together.

Then I’d fix the worst edge first, not everything. For a shared table, one service becomes the owner and exposes an API; the others migrate to it one at a time. For message formats, a schema registry with compatibility checks in CI. For a junk-drawer config file, split it by consumer.

I’d also ask whether some of those services should be merged. If two services always change together, they are one module with a network call in the middle, and merging them is a legitimate answer.

The measure of success is simple: the percentage of releases that ship one service alone, with no coordination.

Quick check: A producer writes events to a queue and has no knowledge of the consumer. The producer renames a field and the consumer breaks. What kind of coupling is this?
There is no direct interaction, yet one side assumes how the other behaves. That is implicit coupling, and it is why message schemas need contracts.
Quick check: Which method is best at finding physical and scenario coupling?
Only removing a real failure domain shows which components silently assumed it would be there. It is also the most expensive method.
Your turnRun POC 12. It builds a dependency graph from sample traces, table-access logs and deploy history, then reports shared databases, services that always deploy together, and config keys read by too many services. Add a service that reads another team’s table and watch the report change.
Key takeaways
  • Coupling should be a decision. The dangerous kind is the kind nobody chose.
  • It buys efficiency, performance, atomicity and traceability, and costs reuse, extensibility, robustness and choice.
  • Shared databases, distributed monoliths, junk-drawer configs and behaviour flags are how it sneaks in.
Platform book · Architecture and ecosystem designChapter 10 in the final book · Kaan Kivilcim · 7 min read

Layers: parts of a platform change at different speeds

You will learn
  • What the OSI model, shearing layers and pace layers each teach about platforms
  • The six-layer framework for platform engineering, from fastest to slowest
  • How the layers push on each other, told through one internal tool

The big picture

Abstractions give you reusable components. Coupling describes how they connect. Layers add time: which parts of a platform change quickly, which change slowly, and how they influence each other.

That matters because a platform team is always balancing two speeds. Product teams want to ship this week. Governance, security and compliance move on a scale of quarters and years. A layered view tells you which speed belongs where, so the fast parts can move without shaking the slow ones.

Three earlier ideas about layers

ModelFromWhat it gives platform engineers
OSI modelZimmermann, 1980Three benefits of strict layering: each layer adds value to those below, the problem is divided into manageable pieces, and a layer can change inside as long as it offers the same service upward. It is prescriptive, and real systems bend it.
Shearing layersFrank Duffy; Stewart Brand, 1994A building is six layers that age at different rates: site, structure, skin, services, space plan, stuff. The site is forever and the furniture moves weekly. It is descriptive, which suits platforms, since they mirror their organisation and resist forced standards.
Pace layersStewart Brand, 1999Civilisation as six layers by speed: fashion, commerce, infrastructure, governance, culture, nature. Health comes from the tension between them.

Brand’s summary of how fast and slow layers relate is the line to remember. The fast layers learn and propose. The slow layers remember and decide. Shocks are absorbed by the fast layers at the top, and stability comes from each layer respecting the pace of its neighbours.

Six layers of platform engineering

LayerWhat lives herePace
1 · Prototypes and experimentsBuilding to learn. Most of it is thrown away, and the lessons decide what moves down. Rust experiments at Google eventually shaped company-wide directives.Days to weeks
2 · ProductsThe marketplace. Proven ideas become features with requirements and stability. Product teams think about what, not how.Months
3 · InfrastructureThe paved road: runtimes, server frameworks, networking, CI/CD. Convergence here saves each team tens or hundreds of person-years, and every improvement reaches everyone.Quarters or longer
4 · Technical directivesThe law of the engineering organisation: binding cross-company decisions, such as safety expectations for AI agents or converging on a set of server frameworks.Quarters to years
5 · Business cultureWhy the company does what it does. Durable system health over short-term gain; protecting users by default.Years
6 · Regulatory and legalThe outside world. Everything above must eventually comply. A change here cascades upward through culture, directives and infrastructure.Slow, then sudden

One tool, six layers

The chapter follows an internal screenshot tool called SnipIt through every layer. It is a good story to retell because it shows the layers pushing on each other in both directions.

  1. PrototypeStarted in 2009 as a 20% project. Nobody would have funded a screenshot tool if asked.
  2. ProductFor more than 15 years a tiny team, often one person part-time, kept it running. By 2024 it was the third most used internal application at Google.
  3. InfrastructureIt reached 8 billion screenshots with no major rework, because it ran on App Engine. The leverage was so complete it was invisible.
  4. DirectiveSecurity standards moved on, and the tool needed finer-grained access controls. The first decision was to shut it down.
  5. CultureEmployees pushed back hard: testimonials, petitions, memes. Shutting down something this useful was called “ungoogley”.
  6. LegalThe obligation to protect internal data could not be argued with. So the only remaining answer was to invest and bring the tool up to standard.

Read it as two forces. A fast layer proposed something and it worked. A slow layer said no. A slower layer overruled that no, and the slowest layer set the terms of the yes.

Going deeper how to use the model

Using the layers in practice

  • Place every decision on a layer before arguing about it. A choice of library is layer 1 or 2 and should be cheap to reverse. A choice of deployment framework is layer 3. A mandate is layer 4 and needs an owner and a reason.
  • Let ideas move down only when proven. The top layers are where you learn cheaply. Promote what works; don’t standardise an experiment.
  • Don’t make slow layers move at the speed of fast ones. Rewriting your deployment platform every quarter to follow a trend is how platforms lose trust.
  • Expect shocks from the bottom. When regulation changes, plan the cascade: what the policy becomes, which directive it turns into, which platform component enforces it.

The AI chapter later uses the same picture: AI applications are the fast layer, and the platform is the slow layer that absorbs shocks and gradually takes on whatever has proven itself.

Connection to the SRE trackChapter 3 of the SRE book describes compliance being written as policy-as-code and checked before deployment. In this model that is a layer 6 requirement, turned into a layer 4 directive, implemented at layer 3.

Names to recognise

The lesson above describes these in plain words. An interviewer who has read the book may use the names, so know what each one refers to.

NameWhat it isClosest on AWS
SnipItThe internal screenshot tool followed through all six layers
App EngineThe managed platform that let it reach 8 billion screenshots without reworkApp Runner, Elastic Beanstalk
Pace layersStewart Brand’s six layers of civilisation by speed of change
Shearing layersFrank Duffy and Stewart Brand: a building’s layers age at different rates
Say it in an interview

I think about a platform as layers that change at different speeds. Experiments and products at the top change in days or months. Infrastructure, technical directives, culture and regulation below them change over quarters and years. The fast layers are where we learn; the slow layers are where we keep what we learned. Most platform arguments get easier once you agree which layer a decision belongs to.

On AWSA workable mapping: sandbox accounts for experiments (layer 1), product accounts and services (layer 2), the shared platform of landing zone, EKS or ECS base, pipelines and golden-path templates (layer 3), Service Control Policies, Config conformance packs and tagging standards as technical directives (layer 4), and compliance frameworks tracked in Audit Manager and Security Hub standards at the bottom (layer 6). Use AWS Organizations to give the layers different rates of change: sandbox OUs with loose guardrails, production OUs with strict ones.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

A team wants to use a new language that the platform doesn’t support. How do you decide?

Show a model answer

I’d start by asking which layer the request sits on. Trying a language in a prototype is a top-layer activity. It should be cheap and allowed, in a sandbox, without platform guarantees, and the team should know they own everything the platform would normally give them.

Putting it into a product that pages someone is a different request. Now it touches the infrastructure layer: build, dependency management, security scanning, observability and deployment all need to work for that language. That is a real cost, paid by the platform team for years.

So I’d set a path. Experiment freely. If the experiment shows a clear advantage for a class of workloads, write that up, and decide at the directive level whether to add the language to the paved road. Google’s Rust adoption followed that route: exploration first, then a company-wide direction, then investment in tooling.

What I’d avoid is the middle state, where a production service runs on a stack nobody supports. That gives the team the freedom of a low-integration ecosystem while they still expect the guarantees of a high-integration one.

Quick check: In the pace-layer view, what is the job of the slow layers?
Fast layers learn and propose; slow layers remember and decide. Stability comes from each respecting the other’s pace.
Your turnTake three decisions your team made this year (a library, a pipeline change, a policy) and place each on one of the six layers. For each, write how long it should take to reverse. If a top-layer decision would take a quarter to undo, you have found accidental coupling.
Key takeaways
  • Layers describe rates of change. Match each decision to the layer it belongs on.
  • Fast layers learn and propose; slow layers remember and decide.
  • Changes at the bottom cascade upward, so plan how a new rule becomes a directive and then a platform feature.
Platform book · Architecture and ecosystem designChapter 12 in the final book · Andy Qin · 9 min read · POC 14

Shared fate and shared responsibility

You will learn
  • What shared fate means and why it needs shared responsibility
  • The economic trade: architectural choice for platform liability
  • Resources, rights and responsibilities: the three Rs of the social contract
  • Why guardrails matter even more when AI agents write the code

The big picture

In a mature engineering ecosystem, components are connected on purpose. One team’s library update, security patch or shortcut reaches everyone who builds on it. The book calls this shared fate. It is what makes fleet-wide improvements possible, and it is also what makes fleet-wide failures possible.

Shared fate without shared responsibility ends in a tragedy of the commons. Each team does what is locally sensible, such as adding a risky dependency or ignoring a deprecation notice, and the common ground everyone depends on gets worse.

The economics: choice for liability

The whole chapter rests on one equation. The more an ecosystem limits a developer’s architectural choices, the more liability it can take on for that developer.

Type 4 · highly integratedType 2 or 3 · loosely integrated
You getLeverage. The platform owns security, reliability, efficiency and complianceFlexibility and a fast start. Any language, library or toolchain
You payConformity. Standard build system, languages and tools. The head of every library must always build and pass testsThe operational load comes back to you. You are your own security engineer and compliance officer
Good forMost production software at scaleAcquisitions, special projects, early experiments

Two of Google’s numbers show the dividend. A central improvement to the C++ memory allocator reached every team at once and saved a significant share of fleet CPU, with no team changing a line. And safe-by-design query APIs produced zero SQL injection in more than a decade in one ecosystem. Neither result came from training thousands of engineers.

One example across the types: third-party packages

EcosystemWhat the platform doesWhat is left to you
Type 2Stores packages in a registryReviewing updates, licences, freshness, patching. Everything
Type 3Handles ingestion and gives you scan dataChoosing versions and deciding how to mitigate each vulnerability
Type 4Ingests, scans for malware, enforces freshness and licences, blocks bad packagesAlmost nothing, and almost no choice

The chapter separates a resource from a guardrail with this example. A registry is a resource: it helps, and the easiest thing to do with it is ignore updates. A managed dependency system is a guardrail: the safe package is the only one you can get.

Governance: from policing to stewardship

Central enforcement works in a uniform ecosystem, where it can be automated until developers no longer notice it. It does not work across mixed environments, where a central team can’t enforce what it can’t see.

There the platform’s job changes to stewardship. It provides tools, data and guidance, including coverage metrics that let each team lead see how well they meet their own obligations. Accountability for accepting risk sits with the local team. The shift is from enforcement to enablement, and it keeps the central team from becoming a bottleneck.

Guardrails: the path of least resistance

You can’t run a large system on willpower. The safest action has to be the easiest one.

Type 2Find defects after the commit: static analysis, fuzzing. The developer must triage and fix
→
Type 4Assurance by design: safe-by-default frameworks, and raw risky APIs locked away from everyone except reviewed code

The chapter calls this the hierarchy of assurance. Enforcement is mechanical, through build visibility rules, and never by convention alone.

A useful phrase from the chapter: friction is a directive. People do what is easy. Remove friction from safe behaviour and add it to risky behaviour, and the system steers itself.

Uniformity also pays in maintenance. With one compiler and build chain, the platform team can make a large-scale change across thousands of projects quickly, for example to respond to a new security threat. In a mixed environment every team patches by hand.

Going deeper the social contract, its edges, and AI agents

The three Rs

ResourcesWhat the ecosystem gives the developer: compute, storage, safe APIs, managed dependencies.
RightsWhat the developer is allowed. In a loose ecosystem, unlimited choice. In an integrated one, that right is given up in exchange for the right to assured safety.
ResponsibilitiesWhat the developer puts in to keep the ecosystem healthy.

The contract is most often broken in one specific way: a team wants the rights of a loose ecosystem and the resources of an integrated one. Free choice of stack, and automatic security. Those two can’t be had together, and saying so explicitly is most of the work.

Walled garden (type 4)Frontier (types 2 and 3)
The dealConformity for leverageAutonomy for accountability
Platform’s obligationFull support for security, reliability and complianceResources, tools and visibility. No assurances
Team’s obligationSustainability: don’t add debt that blocks the automated machineryBe the primary guardian. You are the security team
The imageA passenger on a high-speed train. You don’t drive, and you don’t pull the emergency brakeA settler. Nobody is coming to save you
Typical failureA team quietly diverges and blocks a fleet-wide changeA team imports a malicious library, assuming central security would catch it

Where the contract strains

The friction shows at the edges. An acquired company arrives with a very different ecosystem. A team spinning out a special project tries to take the big machinery with it and finds it can’t run it alone. The chapter asks for permeability: moving between ecosystems is a renegotiation of the contract, and it goes better when framed as a trade the team is making, not a mandate imposed on them.

Why this matters more with AI agents

An agent writes code faster than people can review it. In a loose ecosystem, where safety depends on human vigilance and manual glue, that speed multiplies mistakes. In a tightly integrated one, the platform’s constraints act as a containment field: an agent can’t commit code that breaks a safety rule, because that code doesn’t build.

Agents also do better when there is less to get right. If the platform handles build flags, dependencies and safety properties, the agent only has to express the business intent. The human’s role moves to being a guardian of intent: define the goal and the success criteria precisely, trust the fast generation, and verify deliberately.

Not everything belongs in the walled gardenThe chapter ends on a menu of deliberate trade-offs. Start experiments where friction is low. Let acquisitions integrate gradually. What matters is that each team knows which contract it has signed.

Learning loops

Incidents, audit findings and red-team results are raw material for shared learning. To use them you need two kinds of metrics: team-level delivery metrics in the DORA style, and ecosystem-level ones such as toolchain effectiveness and governance coverage.

Names to recognise

The lesson above describes these in plain words. An interviewer who has read the book may use the names, so know what each one refers to.

NameWhat it isClosest on AWS
google3Google’s main monorepo ecosystem; the book’s example of a type 4 (assured) ecosystem
Green-at-headThe latest version of every library must always build and pass its testsTrunk-based development with required CI
Large-scale change (LSC)A change applied across thousands of projects at once by a central teamAutomated PRs (Renovate, Amazon Q Developer transformations)
TrustedSqlStringThe safe query type that kept SQL injection at zero for a decadeA typed wrapper over the RDS Data API (POC 13)
3RsResources, rights, responsibilitiesYour internal version of the AWS shared responsibility model
Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the SRE book also covers, from the knowledge map:
  • Ecosystem types 0 to 4: YOLO, ad hoc, guided, engineered, assured. See SRE ch 18.
Say it in an interview

Shared fate means one team’s choices land on everyone, so it has to come with shared responsibility. I frame it as a trade: the more a platform limits your choices, the more liability it can carry for you. I make that explicit with three Rs: what resources the platform gives, what rights the team has, and what responsibilities they keep. The failure I watch for is a team wanting free choice of stack and automatic guarantees at the same time.

On AWSAWS publishes its own shared responsibility model, and your internal platform needs one too. A type 2 account gets raw services and a registry (ECR, CodeArtifact) and owns everything else. A type 3 landing zone adds Control Tower guardrails, Config rules, Inspector scan results and Security Hub scores that teams must act on. A type 4 golden path makes the safe choice the only one: Service Control Policies block the risky APIs, CodeArtifact serves only vetted packages, pipelines are the sole route to production, and Lambda code signing or an EKS admission policy refuses unsigned artifacts. Publish a coverage dashboard so every team lead can see their own posture.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

A team asks for an exemption from the standard pipeline because it slows them down. How do you respond?

Show a model answer

I’d treat it as a conversation about which contract they want, not as a yes or no.

First I’d find out what is slow, because that may be a platform bug. If the pipeline takes forty minutes or blocks on a flaky check, that is our problem to fix, and their complaint is useful. Friction on the safe path pushes people off it.

If they need something the path really can’t do, I’d lay out the trade. On the standard path, the platform carries security scanning, signed artifacts, canary analysis, rollback and compliance evidence. Off it, they carry all of that, and they’re no longer eligible for fleet-wide fixes. I’d put that in writing: the resources they give up and the responsibilities they take on.

Then I’d make the exemption safe and visible: time-limited, with an owner, tracked as debt, and contained so a mistake can’t spread, for example in its own account with its own blast radius.

Finally I’d treat the request as product feedback. One exemption is a special case. Five for the same reason is a gap in the platform.

Quick check: What is the core economic equation of shared fate?
Conformity is the price of leverage. A platform can only guarantee what it controls.
Quick check: A package registry that stores dependencies and leaves updates to each team is best described as…
A resource helps and enforces nothing. A guardrail makes the safe choice the only available one.
Your turnWrite a one-page contract for your own platform using the three Rs. For each of security patching, dependency updates, backups and deployment safety, say what the platform provides, what teams may choose, and what teams must do. The repo has a template in docs/platform/shared-fate-contract.md.
Key takeaways
  • Limit choice and the platform can carry liability. That is the trade.
  • Make it explicit with resources, rights and responsibilities.
  • Guardrails must make the safe path the easy one, and that matters most when agents write the code.
Platform book · Architecture and ecosystem designChapter 14 in the final book · Chris Kennelly · 10 min read · POC 17

Efficiency: one optimisation, every team

You will learn
  • Why a common platform turns performance work into leverage
  • On by default, absorbed regressions and opt-outs
  • Application productivity metrics: telling “busier” from “slower”
  • Three lessons: take the long view, the platform is not fixed, build levers

The big picture

When every team runs on the same foundations, two things become possible. You can see where resources go across the whole fleet. And when you improve a shared component, everyone gets faster at once. Seeing leads to improving, and improving pays for more seeing. The chapter calls it a virtuous cycle.

Common infrastructureSame scheduler, RPC layer and libraries
→
Fleet-wide observabilityA profiler on every machine
→
Central optimisationFix the shared thing once
→
SavingsWhich fund more observability

Each new measurement rides on rails that already exist, so the next insight is cheaper than the last.

How Google got there

  • The scheduler hides placement. Borg decides which jobs share a machine. A CPU-heavy team and a memory-heavy team fit together, and spare capacity for failures is pooled across the data centre, not held by each team.
  • The same agents run on every machine. That made it possible to profile everything: Google-Wide Profiling gives each team a debugging tool and gives the company one aggregated picture.
  • The aggregate showed surprises. In 2015 the memory allocator accounted for about 8% of fleet usage, more than any single application. Nobody would have found that by looking at one service.
Profile-guided optimisation, made automaticCompilers can optimise better with a profile of real usage. Getting one used to mean each team building a load test, an instrumented binary and a second build step, so few did. Google used the fleet profiler to synthesise a profile for every team automatically, and adoption became a one-line change. In its first year this doubled the share of the fleet using the technique. The lesson: effort deters adoption more than doubt does.

Shifting optimisations down

On by default

The platform team prototypes an optimisation, canaries it on major workloads, evaluates it, and then turns it on for everyone. Teams pick it up at their next normal release and do nothing. This avoids the trap of building something and waiting for teams to discover it, and it keeps the decision with the people who understand the change.

Not every workload gets faster. The chapter is candid about how regressions are handled.

RegressionWhat they doWhy
Small, for a fewAbsorb itPer-application tuning adds options, and every option enlarges the set of states each future change must be tested against
Large, for a fewOffer an opt-out per application, and work to remove itAn opt-out is information: it shows which edge cases truly matter. One long-standing opt-out led to two further improvements
Large, for manyDon’t ship

The judgement behind this: an imperceptible slowdown or a little opt-out work for one team can be better than not shipping a major win for hundreds.

Spread the best local idea

A better hash table began as a collaboration between the core C++ library team and two engineers on the search index. The index team could have swapped their hottest tables and stopped. Instead the platform team rolled the new table out across the whole codebase with automated refactoring, and CPU and memory needs fell substantially.

A detail worth knowing: the designers made the table’s iteration order random on purpose. Earlier attempts to optimise hash tables had been blocked because code quietly relied on the order (Hyrum’s law again). Randomising it stopped that dependency from forming, which kept the door open for later improvements. Teams sometimes ask to switch it off. Saying yes would help them today and hurt everyone, including them, later.

Work further up the stack

A low-level copy routine can only be made so fast, because it must do the copy. Higher up, analysis of the code may show the copy was never needed. The fastest copy is the one you don’t make. Tools from linters to language models find these recurring patterns, and the central team sends ready-made changes to owners for review.

Shift left for performance too

  • Fleet telemetry raises alerts when a function, application or library regresses after a rollout.
  • Canaries pause for automated performance checks against the old version, not only reliability checks.
  • Benchmarks run periodically and on proposed changes.
  • Code-review tooling flags known slow patterns and proposes the fix.
  • Well-designed libraries make the efficient way the obvious way.
Going deeper measuring what matters

Connect efficiency to business value

Nobody buys servers in order to allocate memory. Low-level numbers are easy to measure and say little about value. What matters is how much useful work you get for what you buy.

The problem: a service’s CPU use went up 20%. Is that a regression, or is it handling more traffic? You can’t tell by looking.

Google’s answer is the application productivity metric (APM). Each service reports how much useful work it does, and the platform divides by resources used: videos processed per CPU-second, records per byte-second of memory, queries per accelerator-hour.

CPU usedUseful workWork per CPU-secondVerdict
+20%+20%FlatBusier. Nothing is wrong
+20%FlatDown 17%A regression. Find the change
Flat+15%Up 15%An optimisation landed
  • Defaults make it practical. RPC servers report requests; pipelines report records. Most services need no setup.
  • Outliers reveal bad metrics. A batch service should count items, not batches. A service whose work metric doesn’t track its resource use at all is probably misconfigured.
  • They catch what component metrics hide. Work on the allocator’s layout decisions made applications faster and made the allocator look more expensive in relative terms. Only a work-based metric showed the win. The team’s joke was that the allocator had become faster than light.

Not all work is equally valuable

Some resource use serves no user directly and is still necessary: monitoring probes, hedged requests, load tests, load balancing and shedding. Some serves nobody: a video still playing to an empty room, or a backend finishing a request whose caller has already given up. Deadline propagation stops the second kind. Knowing the criticality of each kind lets you shed the non-essential during a disruption and push background work off-peak, which means less idle capacity held in reserve.

Proxies and GoodhartMeasuring precisely costs something too. Use proxies that track the business goal closely, and remember Goodhart’s law: a measure that becomes a target stops being a good measure.

Three lessons

Take the long viewThe cost of an opinionated platform is visible. The cost of flexibility is not: every option must be discoverable, tested and carried forward, and it becomes a tax on every later change.
Don’t assume the platform is fixedApplication teams work around platform problems. If everyone works around the same one, it looks rare. Report it; the platform can change when the value is there.
Create leverage and use itImprove something already widely used. Or migrate ten implementations to one, so every later improvement lands on everybody.

Names to recognise

The lesson above describes these in plain words. An interviewer who has read the book may use the names, so know what each one refers to.

NameWhat it isClosest on AWS
Google-Wide Profiling (GWP)A profiler on every machine, aggregated into one fleet viewCodeGuru Profiler, an eBPF continuous profiler
AutoFDOProfile-guided optimisation with profiles synthesised from the fleet, adopted with a one-line changeCompiler PGO in the shared build image
TCMallocGoogle’s memory allocator; about 8% of fleet usage in 2015
TemeraireA TCMalloc improvement whose one long-standing opt-out led to two further gains
SwissMap (Abseil)The hash table rolled out across the monorepo, with randomised iteration order
Application productivity metric (APM)Useful work per unit of resourceCloudWatch metric math (POC 17)
Streetlamp effectOptimising the best-understood workloads instead of the biggest opportunities
Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the SRE book and Observability with Grafana also cover, from the knowledge map:
  • Load shedding by criticality: Drop the least important work first; tag requests. See SRE ch 15, SRE ch 17.
  • Pooling: Peaks rarely coincide, so a shared pool needs less than the sum of its parts. See SRE ch 15.
  • Fleet-wide profiling: One profiler everywhere shows which shared component costs the most. See Grafana ch 13.
  • Hyrum’s law: With enough users, every observable behaviour is depended on by someone. See SRE ch 8.
  • Continuous profiling: Self time and total time; flame graph width is share of samples. See Grafana ch 13.
Say it in an interview

Efficiency at scale comes from leverage. If every team shares the same libraries and runtime, I can profile the whole fleet, find that some shared component is the biggest consumer, fix it once, and ship it on by default. I’d measure with useful work per unit of resource, because raw CPU can’t tell me whether a service got slower or just busier.

On AWSStart with visibility: Cost and Usage Reports with cost allocation tags, Compute Optimizer, and a continuous profiler across the fleet (CodeGuru Profiler or an open-source eBPF profiler). Build an application productivity metric in CloudWatch with metric math: a business counter from your service divided by vCPU-seconds from Container Insights. Shift down with shared base images, a common runtime and Graviton as the default, delivered through the golden-path pipeline so teams get improvements at their next deploy. For criticality, use Spot and scheduled scaling for work that can wait.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Your cloud bill for a service rose 30% in a quarter. How do you find out whether that is a problem?

Show a model answer

I wouldn’t start from the bill. I’d start from what the service did for that money.

First I’d define useful work for this service: requests served, orders processed, records transformed. Then I’d plot work per vCPU-second and per gigabyte-hour over the quarter. If work also rose about 30%, the service is busier and the cost is growth. If work is flat, efficiency dropped and I have a regression to find.

For a regression I’d line the productivity curve up against deploys and config changes, and use profiles from before and after to see which functions grew. Common culprits are a new serialisation step, a logging change, a retry storm, or a dependency upgrade.

I’d also check criticality. Some growth is work nobody needs: retries against a failing dependency, requests that continue after the caller timed out, a batch job running at peak. Deadline propagation and moving batch off-peak fix those without touching the code path.

Finally I’d ask whether the fix belongs in the service or in the platform. If the cause is a shared library or base image, fixing it centrally helps every team that has the same problem and hasn’t noticed.

Quick check: A service uses 20% more CPU than last month and processes the same number of requests. What does its application productivity metric say?
Same work for more resources means work per CPU-second fell. That is a regression, not growth.
Quick check: Why did the hash-table designers make iteration order random?
Hyrum’s law: any observable behaviour gets depended on. Removing the stable order kept the implementation free to change.
Your turnRun POC 17. It computes work per CPU-second for a set of sample services, labels each change as growth, regression or optimisation, flags services whose work metric doesn’t track their usage, and decides whether an optimisation should ship on by default given who it helps and who it hurts.
Key takeaways
  • Shared foundations turn one optimisation into a fleet-wide saving.
  • Ship on by default, absorb small regressions, and treat opt-outs as information.
  • Measure useful work per unit of resource, or you can’t tell slower from busier.
Platform book · Architecture and ecosystem designChapter 15 in the final book · Christoph Kern · 22 min read · POC 13 · 14 · 15

Security: if it isn’t secure, it shouldn’t compile

You will learn
  • Why training and scanning can’t deliver assurance, however much you do
  • Security as an emergent property, application archetypes and invariants
  • Safe Coding: risky operations, safe abstractions and the two ways to build one
  • Supply chain (SLSA, attestations), safe deployment and security observability
  • What AI changes, and why prompt injection resists these techniques

The big picture

The same kinds of vulnerability top the incident reports year after year: memory corruption, injection, broken access control. The industry’s list of the most dangerous weaknesses has barely changed in a long time, despite decades of secure-coding training.

This chapter’s diagnosis is that the problem is structural. We ask every developer to avoid every known mistake at every call site, forever, and we check afterwards with tools that can only find some of what went wrong. People make mistakes because the systems they work in make mistakes easy. So do AI coding tools, which now write more code than humans can review.

The platform answer: move security out of each developer’s head and into the things all code is built from, so whole classes of bug can’t be written.

What “platform” means hereMore than the cluster your code runs on. It is the whole stack a developer touches: the language and its type system, libraries and frameworks, the build system, deployment and runtime, and the review and release process. Application bugs are born in the layers nearest the developer, so that is where they can be prevented.

Why the usual approaches fall short

Three facts frame the problem.

  • Experts are outnumbered several hundred to one. The ratio is about the same at Google as at a small company. Hiring can’t fix it.
  • Software is programming integrated over time. Code that was secure at launch may not be after next week’s commit, so a point-in-time review proves little.
  • Testing can’t show absence. Even a tiny program has more possible states than any test suite can visit. A two-by-two grid of 64-bit numbers has about as many states as there are atoms in the observable universe. For ordinary bugs this is tolerable, because a bug nobody hits hardly matters. For security it isn’t, because an attacker goes looking for the one input you never tried.

That last point defines the goal. Assurance is confidence that a requirement holds for every behaviour of the program. Continuous assurance is keeping that confidence for every version you ship.

ApproachWhat it isWhy it isn’t enough
Ship and patchFind vulnerabilities in productionReal exposure, an endless patch treadmill, lost trust. Hard to escape later
Find after commitStatic analysis, fuzzing, sanitizers, scanners, security review (increasingly by AI)Tools miss bugs or raise false alarms, usually both. Findings arrive after the author has moved on. Useful as defence in depth; can’t prove nothing remains
Shift leftTrain developers; analyse in the editorNobody can hold hundreds of vulnerability patterns in mind while solving a business problem. False alarms teach people to suppress warnings, real ones included
Initial and sustained velocitySecurity feels like it slows teams down when it is bolted on as reviews and gates. The chapter separates how fast you ship the first version from how fast you keep shipping. Shortcuts buy the first and cost the second. A platform pays the upfront cost once so applications inherit both. For a young product still finding its market, trading sustained speed for initial speed can be rational, if it is a conscious choice with a plan to pay it back.

Shift down: the platform as a security control

Security can’t be added afterwards. It emerges from how the system is designed, how the software is structured, and what the platform allows. That works in both directions.

If the platform enforces itApplications inherit the guarantee. In Rust, Java or Python, ordinary code can’t corrupt memory, and the exceptions are explicit and reviewable.
If the platform doesn’tApplications will have the defect. Any large C++ codebase contains memory-safety bugs, and decades of effort haven’t removed them after the fact.

Shifting down also compounds. Each class of bug the platform eliminates frees the security team from reviewing, advising and responding for that class. They spend the time eliminating the next one.

Three objectives

  1. Prevent common classes by construction. Design the platform so the bug can’t be introduced.
  2. Confine what is left. Keep security-critical code in a few well-reviewed platform components, not spread across every application.
  3. Keep the guarantee through change without an expert reviewing each commit.

Prevention never reaches zero defects, so containment stays essential: sandboxes, least-privilege identities and mediated access limit the damage of whatever slips through.

Application archetypes

Most applications are not architecturally unique. A stateless RPC service, a SQL-backed store, a browser frontend talking to an API, a mobile client: the same shapes recur, and the same threats come with each shape whether the app is a bank or a photo editor. The chapter calls a recurring whole-application shape an archetype.

ComponentThreat it bringsInvariant the platform can own
Relational storageSQL injectionEvery query’s structure comes only from the developer; untrusted values are bound as parameters
Web frontendXSS, CSRF, clickjackingUntrusted values reach the page only through types that guarantee correct escaping; state-changing requests are CSRF-checked; framing is restricted
RPC backendUnauthenticated or unauthorised callsEvery request is authenticated and authorised before any handler code runs
Mobile client and APITrusting the clientThe server treats all client input as untrusted and re-checks authorisation
