The infrastructure is healthy and the model is not. That is why freshness, data quality and confidence need to be monitored as reliability signals.
Quick check: What is the main purpose of a central feature store?
Skew arises when features are computed by different code paths. One source removes the difference.
Your turnRun POC 19. It computes a drift score between training and live feature distributions, checks a freshness objective, applies a confidence gate and reports how much availability it costs, and refuses to promote a model version that is unsigned or failed evaluation.
Key takeaways
  • Two mandates: build platforms for AI, and use AI to run platforms.
  • A model can be up and wrong. Monitor freshness, drift and confidence.
  • Abstract the hardware; give ML engineers pipelines, a feature store and a registry.
  • With agents operating, the platform’s job is the controls that always hold.
Platform book · Execution and product approachChapter 24 in the final book · Titus Winters · 10 min read

Education: why teaching belongs to the platform team

You will learn
  • Why a culture of learning is the root of engineering performance
  • What a computer science degree can’t cover
  • Why education fits the platform organisation, and how to staff it
  • What AI changes: documentation, specification and verification

The big picture

The chapter opens with a rule from its author that is worth memorising: if something is accidentally complex, simplify it; if it is inherently complex, educate.

Its argument has three steps. Engineering performance comes from culture. The root of good culture is learning and growth. And somebody has to be responsible for the learning that can’t be left to chance, which is most naturally the platform organisation.

A culture of learning

Management thinkers, academic researchers, Google’s own team studies and the DORA research all point the same way: culture is at the root of performance. The culture they describe is psychological safety, where it is safe to be wrong, safe not to know, and safe to make an honest mistake.

The chapter makes a sharper point than “people work better when they aren’t afraid”. Safety is what lets information move and makes learning valued.

What psychological safety does not excuseA sceptic once told the author that it just lets people off for failing. His answer: it excuses honest, novel mistakes. Repeating the same error, or doing something plainly careless, should still count against you. The aim is that an organisation learns each hard lesson once, not once per engineer because everyone hides their failures.

Who gets the next task?

An old model from the 1970s, the “surgical team”, gives the critical work to the best engineer and has everyone else support them. The chapter explains why that no longer fits, in game-theory terms. It was a strategy for a single game: assemble a team, build one system, disband. Modern engineering is an endless stream of projects with people moving between teams.

Single gameGive everything to your best person
→
Endless gameGive the next task to the most junior engineer who can do it with some guidance

The second rule values growth, and frees senior people for new problems and mentoring.

Brittle productivity

Research by Cat Hicks describes what happens without a learning culture. Only submitted code counts. Investigating, understanding and explaining look like waste. Teaching isn’t rewarded. Engineers come to define productivity as effort, hours and solitary work, which the chapter calls performative hustle. Her terms are learning debt and brittle productivity.

It suggests a reframing borrowed from her: stop saying “developer productivity” and say “developer problem solving”. That makes it obvious that skills and understanding are the thing to build.

Documentation is where this shows. It is the one factor in the DORA research that may matter even more than team culture, and it is the most visible, measurable sign of whether a team values the group’s output over individual output.

A thought experimentWhich team would you rather lead? One that is forbidden from using any IDE or AI assistant and keeps everything else. Or one with every modern tool that can never learn anything beyond what its members were taught at university. Tools help. Without learning, engineering stops.
Going deeper what degrees miss, how to organise education, and AI

Why universities can’t do it for us

  • The field is young. Certification works for disciplines that are centuries old. Software engineering is about fifty years old and still finding its best practices.
  • There aren’t enough hours. All the lectures, labs and homework in a computing degree add up to less than 18 months of full-time work, and less than a third of the popular “10,000 hours to mastery” figure.
  • The content is skewed. Students learn to implement a linked list more than they learn when to use one.
  • Software engineering is programming plus time plus people. Version control, testing and design patterns exist to cope with change over time and with other engineers. A course can’t make either of those real.
  • Student teams aren’t teams. Real teams mix experience levels, have authority structures and face a stream of work.
  • Nobody reads the code. Enrolment in the US grew about fivefold in 15 years and teaching staff didn’t, so early courses are graded automatically on whether the output is right. Some graduates have never had a person comment on their code.

At Google a new hire’s first code review is treated as a rite of passage. It teaches the difference between “it seems to work” and “it is done to a quality we can afford to maintain”.

Why education belongs with the platform

A company’s business strategy is to diversify into many products, each with its own specialists. Its infrastructure strategy should be to keep one platform. So the platform organisation is the one part of engineering that sees the whole enterprise and works on what all teams share.

  • Expertise accumulates there. Being the Java expert on a team of ten is one thing. Being the person 10,000 Java engineers bring their questions to is another. That depth is learned from answering the same questions and collecting the edge cases.
  • The platform chooses what is easy. If it has made one way standard, it owes people an explanation of that way. Managing the community actively beats hoping good practice spreads by itself.
  • The missions match. Education increases engineering capacity and reduces waste, misuse and misconfiguration of expensive systems. That is the platform’s purpose too.

How to staff it

OptionVerdict
Everyone teaches, with targetsNo. Good educators are rare, and the wrong person in that role does harm
A separate education departmentNo. It drifts away from current practice and real problems
MatrixedYes. On each component team, a few engineers who like to write or teach get part of their time for community support, writing up best practice, and building and delivering training. Reward it

The chapter compares this to how SRE treats toil. When you are tired of answering the same question, write the essay, record the talk or build the class. Done well, education reduces the support load the same way automation reduces operational load.

Keep the scope tied to what the platform supports. A company standardised on Go, Kubernetes and a managed Git service should teach those, and should not branch into unrelated topics. For general material, curate instead of producing. Popularity is a poor guide: studies in physics education found that students’ own rating of how much they learned tracks how much they liked the instructor, and has little to do with measured learning.

Education and AI

The chapter quotes the 2025 DORA finding that AI is an amplifier. It magnifies the strengths of organisations that work well and the dysfunction of those that don’t. The returns come from the underlying system: the quality of the internal platform, clear workflows, aligned teams.

Clean up your documentationYour tools are internal, so a general model doesn’t know them. You point it at your docs. If they are current, the assistant is useful. If they are stale, it repeats stale answers and invents the rest. AI can’t tell an outdated page from a current one.
Teach specificationWriting new code is no longer the bottleneck. Describing precisely what is needed is: requirements, contracts, constraints, architecture.
Teach verificationThe other bottleneck is checking that the result is fit for purpose: reading code, reviewing, testing, thinking critically.

Both onboarding and retraining need this. The chapter’s closing view is that software engineering can’t really be separated from education, and AI has made a long-postponed investment urgent.

Names to recognise

The lesson above describes these in plain words. An interviewer who has read the book may use the names, so know what each one refers to.

NameWhat it isClosest on AWS
Surgical Team, Pilot SystemTwo essays by Fred Brooks the chapter uses
Learning debt, brittle productivityCat Hicks’s terms for what happens without a learning culture
Generative cultureWestrum’s performance-oriented culture, where information flows
Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the SRE book also covers, from the knowledge map:
  • Psychological safety: Safe to be wrong, to not know, to make an honest novel mistake. See SRE ch 4.
  • Education: Belongs to the platform team; next task to the most junior who can do it with guidance. See SRE ch 5.
Say it in an interview

I think of education as part of the platform’s job. The platform team sees every team’s problems and decides what the standard way is, so it should also explain that way. I’d give a few engineers on each platform component real time for support, writing and teaching, and I’d treat repeated questions as toil to automate with documentation. With AI in the picture it matters more: assistants answer from our docs, and the scarce skills are now specifying what we want and verifying what we got.

On AWSMake documentation part of the golden path: every template ships a README, a runbook and architecture notes in the repository, rendered in the developer portal. Keep them current with ownership metadata and a staleness check in CI, because that corpus is what an internal assistant (Amazon Q Business or a Bedrock knowledge base) will answer from. Scope training to what the platform supports, and curate AWS Skill Builder paths instead of writing general cloud courses yourself. Use game days and Well-Architected reviews as teaching moments, not audits.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

We’re rolling out AI coding assistants to 500 engineers. What would you do to make that pay off?

Show a model answer

I’d start from the finding that AI amplifies whatever is already there. If our platform, workflows and documentation are in good shape, assistants will help a lot. If they aren’t, we’ll produce confusion faster. So part of the rollout is fixing the foundations.

First, documentation. Our internal tools aren’t in any public model’s training, so the assistant will answer from our docs. I’d audit the most-used pages, delete or fix the stale ones, give every page an owner and a review date, and make the content structured enough for a machine to use.

Second, guardrails in the platform, so generated code is safe by construction: safe APIs it must compile against, signed builds, policy checks at deploy. Then review doesn’t have to catch everything.

Third, training, aimed at the new bottlenecks. Writing code is cheap now. Specifying precisely what we want and verifying what comes back are the scarce skills, so I’d teach requirements and contracts, code reading, review and testing, to juniors and seniors alike.

Fourth, I’d protect how juniors learn. If the assistant does every task a junior would have learned from, we’ll have no seniors in five years. I’d keep giving juniors real tasks with guidance and make explaining the result part of review.

I’d measure delivery metrics and satisfaction before and after, by team, and expect the gain to be largest where the foundations were strongest.

Quick check: What does the chapter say psychological safety excuses?
The aim is to learn each hard lesson once as an organisation. Repeated or careless errors still count.
Quick check: According to the DORA finding quoted in the chapter, what is AI’s main effect on software organisations?
Returns depend on the underlying system: platform quality, clear workflows and aligned teams.
Your turnPick the five internal documentation pages your team is asked about most. For each, record when it was last updated, who owns it, and whether its first example still runs. Fix the worst one today. Then write down the last question you answered three times, and turn the answer into a page.
Key takeaways
  • If it is accidentally complex, simplify. If it is inherently complex, educate.
  • Give the next task to the most junior engineer who can do it with guidance.
  • Education fits the platform team: it sees everything and sets the standard way.
  • AI answers from your docs, and makes specification and verification the scarce skills.
Mastering PrometheusWilliam Hegedus · Packt, April 2024 · 15 chapters · 4 min read

Mastering Prometheus: the third book on the map

You will learn
  • Why this book follows the SRE and platform books
  • How its two halves are organised
  • Which POCs go with which lessons, and what is AWS-specific

Why Prometheus, and why now

The SRE book told you to measure reliability from the user’s side, to page on how fast an error budget burns, and to make telemetry consistent across services. It did not tell you how to build the system that does the measuring. In most companies that system is Prometheus, or something that speaks its protocols: Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, Grafana Mimir, Thanos or VictoriaMetrics.

This book is written by an SRE manager who runs Prometheus at scale, and it reads like one. It skips the beginner material and goes straight to how the storage engine works, how service discovery and relabeling really behave, why alerts flap, where Prometheus stops scaling, and what the ecosystem offers past that point. That is exactly the depth interviewers probe when a role says “observability”.

TermMeaning

Prometheus · FundamentalsChapters 1–2 · POC 22 · 6 min read

Observability, the Prometheus architecture, and deploying it

You will learn
  • Monitoring versus observability, and where metrics fit among the signals
  • What makes Prometheus different: pull, labels, PromQL, service discovery
  • The components inside one Prometheus server and how data moves between them
  • How kube-prometheus-stack and the Prometheus Operator deploy it on Kubernetes

The big picture

Monitoring means checking for conditions you decided in advance were bad. Observability means being able to ask a new question of a running system and get an answer without shipping new code. Metrics, logs and traces are the three classic signals; metrics are the cheapest to keep and the fastest to query, which is why they drive dashboards and alerts.

Prometheus is a metrics system with four ideas that set it apart. It pulls metrics over HTTP rather than waiting for them to be pushed. Every series is identified by labels, so you slice data by any dimension at query time. It has its own query language, PromQL. And it discovers what to scrape from Kubernetes, clouds and other sources, so targets come and go without config changes.

Why pull?

Pull gives youWhat it costs
An up series for every target: you know when collection fails, not just when data stopsPrometheus must be able to reach every target over the network
Targets need no knowledge of where metrics go; any number of servers can scrape themShort-lived jobs may finish before a scrape; they need the Pushgateway or the textfile collector
A target can be inspected by hand: open /metrics in a browserScrape interval sets the resolution; nothing between scrapes is seen

Inside one server

Two things in that picture matter later. First, Alertmanager is a separate program: Prometheus decides that an alert is firing, Alertmanager decides who hears about it. Second, everything leaves through the same storage, so a slow query and a heavy rule both compete with ingestion for memory and CPU.

Deploying it on Kubernetes

The book deploys everything with the kube-prometheus-stack Helm chart, which installs the Prometheus Operator, a Prometheus server, Alertmanager, Grafana, node exporter, kube-state-metrics and a large set of ready-made rules and dashboards (the kubernetes-mixin, which lesson 11 explains).

Operator resourceWhat it becomes
PrometheusA StatefulSet of Prometheus servers with replicas, shards, retention, external labels, remote write
ServiceMonitor / PodMonitorScrape jobs with kubernetes_sd_configs and the relabeling to select services or pods by label
ProbeBlackbox-exporter checks of URLs or ingresses
PrometheusRuleRecording and alerting rule files, loaded automatically
Alertmanager / AlertmanagerConfigAn Alertmanager cluster and per-namespace routing fragments
ScrapeConfigRaw scrape configs for non-Kubernetes discovery, such as EC2 or HTTP SD

The point of the Operator is that teams describe what to monitor in their own namespaces, as Kubernetes objects, and the Operator turns that into a valid Prometheus configuration and reloads it. Nobody edits a shared prometheus.yml by hand.

Going deeper what the chapters add on the details

Small things worth knowing

  • The book’s cluster is Linode Kubernetes Engine; nothing in it depends on Linode. On AWS the same chart runs on EKS.
  • Prometheus is a single Go binary; a server is not clustered. High availability means running copies (lesson 6).
  • Grafana is installed by the chart and pre-loaded with dashboards for the cluster, nodes and Prometheus itself.
  • The UI under Status has the pages you will use most when something is wrong: Targets, Service Discovery, TSDB Status, Configuration and Rules.
Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the SRE book and Observability with Grafana also cover, from the knowledge map:
  • Observability: Someone without tribal knowledge can test and reject hypotheses quickly. See SRE ch 9, Grafana ch 1.
Say it in an interview

Prometheus pulls metrics over HTTP from targets it discovers, stores each series by name and labels in a local time-series database, evaluates recording and alerting rules on a schedule, and hands firing alerts to a separate Alertmanager. On Kubernetes I deploy it with the Prometheus Operator so teams declare ServiceMonitors and PrometheusRules in their own namespaces instead of editing a central config.

On AWSOn EKS you have three options. Self-managed: kube-prometheus-stack on EKS with gp3 volumes for the TSDB. Hybrid: keep Prometheus (or Prometheus in agent mode, or the ADOT collector) as the scraper and remote-write to Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, which stores, replicates and serves PromQL. Fully managed: the AMP managed collector scrapes the cluster agentlessly from a Prometheus-format scrape config. Amazon Managed Grafana reads AMP with SigV4. For alerting, AMP has rule groups namespaces and a managed Alertmanager whose receivers are SNS topics.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Walk me through what happens between an application incrementing a counter and an engineer getting paged.

Show a model answer

The application exposes the counter on an HTTP /metrics endpoint in the Prometheus text format, usually through a client library. On Kubernetes, a ServiceMonitor tells the Prometheus Operator which services to scrape, and the Operator writes the matching scrape job.

Prometheus discovers the pod through the Kubernetes API, runs relabeling to decide whether to keep it and what labels it gets, then scrapes it every scrape interval. Each sample is appended to the head block in memory and to the write-ahead log on disk.

On every evaluation interval the rule manager runs the alerting rule’s PromQL. If the expression returns series, each becomes a pending alert; if it stays true for the rule’s for duration, it becomes firing and Prometheus sends it to every configured Alertmanager, and keeps re-sending while it fires.

Alertmanager matches the alert’s labels against its routing tree, groups it with similar alerts, waits group_wait to collect more, checks inhibitions and silences, and then notifies the receiver: PagerDuty, Slack, or on AWS an SNS topic that pages through Incident Manager.

The useful thing to add in an interview is where it can break: no up means the scrape failed, a missing sample can reset a pending alert, and the alert only reaches someone if every Prometheus can reach every Alertmanager.

Quick check: Which component decides who gets notified about a firing alert?
Prometheus evaluates rules and sends firing alerts; Alertmanager routes, groups, inhibits and notifies.
Quick check: What does the pull model give you that push does not?
Because Prometheus initiates every scrape, it knows when a target didn’t answer and records up = 0.
Your turnInstall kube-prometheus-stack on a local kind or k3d cluster (or EKS). Open Status → Targets and Status → Service Discovery, pick one ServiceMonitor and find the scrape job the Operator generated for it in Status → Configuration. Then read POC 22’s prometheus-ec2.yml to see the same ideas outside Kubernetes.
Key takeaways
  • Pull, labels, PromQL and service discovery are what make Prometheus different.
  • Prometheus decides alerts fire; Alertmanager decides who hears.
  • On Kubernetes, the Operator turns ServiceMonitors and PrometheusRules into config; on AWS, AMP can take over storage and rules.
Prometheus · FundamentalsChapter 3, first half · POC 21 · 7 min read

The data model and the TSDB: how samples are stored and found

You will learn
  • Metric, series, sample, and why labels decide cost
  • The four metric types and what each is for
  • The head block, the write-ahead log, checkpoints and memory-mapped chunks
  • Blocks, the index and postings, compaction and retention
  • Why delta-of-delta and XOR compression make samples cost about a byte

The big picture

A sample is a float64 value and a millisecond timestamp. A series is all the samples that share one metric name and one exact set of label values. A metric is the family of series with the same name. Change any label value and you have a new series, with its own memory, index entries and chunks.

http_requests_total{job="checkout", method="POST", code="500"}  1027  @1714052400000
└── metric name ──┘ └──────────── labels ───────────────┘ value  timestamp (ms)

Under the hood the metric name is just another label, __name__. So http_requests_total{code="500"} and {__name__="http_requests_total", code="500"} are the same selector.

Metric types

TypeBehaviourTypical query
CounterOnly goes up; resets to zero when the process restartsrate(), increase()
GaugeGoes up and down: temperature, queue depth, memorythe value itself, delta(), *_over_time()
HistogramCounts observations into cumulative buckets: _bucket{le=…}, _sum, _counthistogram_quantile() over rate() of buckets
SummaryQuantiles computed in the client, plus _sum and _countread the quantile; you can’t aggregate it across instances
Why histograms usually winA summary’s p99 from ten pods can’t be combined into a service p99: averaging percentiles is wrong. Histogram buckets are counters, so you sum them across pods first and compute the quantile once. The price is that the answer is interpolated inside a bucket, so bucket boundaries should sit near your SLO thresholds.

Where samples live

The head block and the WAL

Incoming samples are appended to an in-memory chunk per series. When a chunk fills (120 samples) it is written to disk and memory-mapped, so memory holds only the active chunk per series. To survive a crash, every sample is also written to the write-ahead log: 128 MB segment files that are replayed on startup. Periodically a checkpoint condenses old WAL segments so replay doesn’t have to read all of them.

That replay is why a Prometheus with millions of series can take many minutes to start, and why the book lists slow startup as one of the first signs of trouble.

Blocks

Every two hours the oldest two hours of the head are written out as a block: a directory named by a ULID containing chunks/, an index, meta.json and tombstones. Each block is a complete, immutable database for its time range. Deleting data writes a tombstone; the data disappears at the next compaction.

The compactor merges three adjacent blocks into one three times as long (2h, 6h, 18h, 54h…), up to 31 days or a tenth of the retention period. Fewer, larger blocks mean a smaller combined index and fewer files to open. Retention deletes whole blocks once they fall outside the retention time or size.

The index

The index is an inverted index. A symbol table stores every string once. For each label=value pair there is a postings list: the sorted IDs of every series that has it. A selector such as {job="api", code=~"5.."} fetches the postings for each matcher and intersects them, starting from the shortest list, then reads only the chunks of the surviving series.

That is why cardinality hurts. A label with a hundred thousand values adds a hundred thousand postings lists, symbols and series, and any query that touches it has to merge enormous lists.

Going deeper compression, and why scrape timing matters

Gorilla compression

Prometheus uses the encoding from Facebook’s Gorilla paper. Timestamps are stored as the difference between consecutive differences. If scrapes are exactly fifteen seconds apart, that delta-of-delta is zero and costs one bit. Values are XOR’d with the previous value; a value that didn’t change costs one bit, and a slowly growing counter costs a few bits more.

Together a sample averages one to two bytes instead of sixteen. POC 21 reproduces the arithmetic: a counter scraped on time costs about a byte per sample, and the same counter with ±30 ms of scrape jitter costs more than twice that. Lesson 7 shows how to find and fix jitter.

Delta-of-deltaBits spent
0 (perfectly regular)1
fits in 14 bits16
fits in 17 bits20
fits in 20 bits24
anything else68

Further reading the book recommends

Ganesh Vernekar’s blog series on the TSDB (head block, WAL, mmapping, compaction) and Fabian Reinartz’s original design write-up are the canonical deep dives if an interviewer goes further.

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that Observability with Grafana also covers, from the knowledge map:
  • Series and cardinality: A metric name plus one label set; every new value is a new series in memory and index. See Grafana ch 5.
  • Head block, WAL and blocks: Two hours in memory with a write-ahead log, then immutable blocks compacted up to 31 days. See Grafana ch 5.
  • rate, increase and irate: Reset-aware, extrapolated over the window; irate uses the last two samples. See Grafana ch 5.
Say it in an interview

A series is a metric name plus a unique label set; every new label value is a new series with its own memory, index entries and chunks, which is why cardinality is the cost driver. Samples land in an in-memory head block backed by a write-ahead log, get cut into immutable two-hour blocks, and the compactor merges those up to 31 days. Queries use an inverted index of postings lists, intersecting the lists for each label matcher.

On AWSAMP runs a Cortex-based storage engine that keeps the same data model in S3-backed blocks, so cardinality is still what you pay for: AMP bills per sample ingested and per GB stored, and has per-workspace quotas on active series. If you self-manage on EKS, give each Prometheus replica its own gp3 EBS volume in its own AZ, size memory for head-block series, and expect WAL replay after a restart to scale with series count.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Why does adding a user_id label to a request counter cause problems, and what would you do instead?

Show a model answer

Every distinct label value creates a new series. A counter with a user ID label goes from a handful of series per pod to one per active user, potentially millions. Each series costs memory in the head block, entries in the index, its own chunks on disk and WAL records, and any query over that metric has to merge postings across all of them.

The symptoms show up together: memory climbs, WAL replay after a restart gets slow, queries on that metric time out, and on a managed service the bill jumps because you pay per sample and per active series.

The fix is to keep metrics low-cardinality and push the per-user detail into the signals designed for it. The request counter keeps labels like method, route template and status class. Per-user information goes in logs or as span attributes in traces, which can hold high-cardinality fields cheaply, and exemplars can link a metric data point to a specific trace.

If the label is already being scraped, drop it at the edge with metric_relabel_configs or labeldrop, check that the series stay unique, and add sample_limit on the scrape job so the next mistake fails one scrape instead of the server.

Quick check: How often does Prometheus cut a new block from the head by default?
Blocks cover two hours; the compactor then merges them in steps of three.
Quick check: Why can’t you average summaries from ten pods to get a service-wide p99?
Histogram buckets are counters you can sum across pods; the quantile is computed once on the total.
Your turnRun POC 21. Change the jitter in test_jitter_costs_disk_and_tolerance_wins_it_back from ±30 ms to ±2 ms and watch the bytes per sample fall. Then feed cardinality_report() the /metrics output of any exporter you have and find the label with the most values.
Key takeaways
  • Every unique label set is a series, and series are what cost memory, disk and query time.
  • Head block plus WAL for recent data; immutable two-hour blocks compacted up to 31 days.
  • Regular scrapes and steady values compress to about a byte per sample.
Prometheus · FundamentalsChapter 3, second half · POC 20 · 7 min read

PromQL: selecting, combining and computing

You will learn
  • Instant vectors, range vectors, instant and range queries, staleness
  • Aggregation with by and without, and when to prefer without
  • Vector matching: on, ignoring, group_left, group_right, and info-metric joins
  • and, or, unless, and why unless is the alerting favourite
  • rate, irate, increase, changes and delta, including how rate extrapolates

The big picture

PromQL works on vectors of series, not on rows. A selector picks series by name and labels. An instant vector holds one sample per series at one moment. A range vector holds every sample in a window, like [5m], and only functions accept it. An instant query evaluates once; a range query (what Grafana graphs use) evaluates the same expression at every step across a time range.

Staleness and the five-minute lookback

At any evaluation time an instant selector returns the newest sample of each series that is at most five minutes old. When a target disappears, Prometheus writes a staleness marker so its series end immediately rather than lingering for five minutes. That lookback is also why a missing scrape doesn’t make a graph gap, and why an alert can reset when the series vanishes for longer.

SelectorMeans
up{job="api"}Exact label match
http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}Regex, always anchored: matches 500 to 599, never 1500
{__name__=~"node_.*", instance!=""}The name is a label too; every selector needs one matcher that doesn’t match empty
rate(x[5m] offset 1w)Same window one week earlier
max_over_time(rate(x[1m])[1h:1m])Subquery: evaluate the inner expression every minute for an hour

Aggregation: by versus without

sum by (namespace) (…) keeps only the listed labels. sum without (pod, instance) (…) drops the listed ones and keeps everything else. The book prefers without, because it preserves labels you didn’t think about, such as cluster or job, which later joins and alert routing often need.

count(kube_pod_info) by (namespace)                         # pods per namespace
count(kube_pod_container_status_running) without (uid, pod, container)

Vector matching

Arithmetic between two vectors pairs up elements with identical label sets (ignoring the name). Anything without a partner is dropped silently, which is the most common reason a ratio returns nothing.

ModifierUse
on (node)Match only on the listed labels
ignoring (code)Match on everything except the listed labels
group_left (os_image)Many on the left may match one on the right; copy os_image from the right
group_rightThe mirror image: many on the right
# copy node metadata onto every pod, using an info metric whose value is always 1
kube_pod_info * on (node) group_left (kubelet_version, os_image) kube_node_info

# one-to-one on node: memory used by containers over node capacity
sum by (node) (container_memory_rss) / on (node) machine_memory_bytes

An info metric has the value 1 and carries descriptive labels. Multiplying by it adds labels without changing values. The pattern keeps volatile metadata off every other series.

Set operators

OperatorKeeps
a and bElements of a that have a match in b
a or bAll of a, plus elements of b with no match in a
a unless bElements of a that have no match in b

unless is how you write “fire, except when…”. The NTP alert from chapter 5 ignores servers that rebooted in the last half hour: node_timex_offset_seconds > 0.05 unless on (instance) changes(node_boot_time_seconds[30m]) > 0. kube-prometheus’s InfoInhibitor uses it to show info alerts only when nothing worse is firing in the namespace.

Functions on counters and gauges

FunctionDoesUse for
rate(c[5m])Per-second average increase over the whole window, reset-aware, extrapolated to the edgesAlerts, dashboards, recording rules
irate(c[5m])Per-second rate from the last two samples onlyFast-moving graphs; never alerts
increase(c[1h])rate × range; can be fractional because of extrapolation“how many in the last hour”
changes(g[24h])How many times the value changedRestarts, via kube_pod_start_time
delta(g[24h])Last minus first for gauges; can be negativedelta(count(up)[24h:]) spots targets that quietly vanished
Two rules that prevent most mistakesrate, then sum: sum(rate(x[5m])), never rate(sum(x)[5m:]), because summing counters first hides each one’s reset. And make the window at least four scrape intervals long, so it always holds two samples; in Grafana, $__rate_interval does that for you.
Going deeper how rate really extrapolates

Extrapolation, exactly

Samples rarely fall on the window edges. rate() takes last minus first (plus any reset corrections) and stretches it to cover the whole window, but only by up to half an average scrape interval at each end when the gap is large, and never back past the point where a counter would have been zero. POC 20 ports the algorithm: a counter growing by 10 per 10 seconds with samples at 5…55 s in a 60 s window gives an increase of exactly 60, and one that starts at zero inside the window gives 55.

The book also counts about seventy functions and says a handful cover nine queries in ten. The ones above, plus histogram_quantile, label_replace, absent, predict_linear and the *_over_time family, are that handful.

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that Observability with Grafana also covers, from the knowledge map:
  • Series and cardinality: A metric name plus one label set; every new value is a new series in memory and index. See Grafana ch 5.
  • Head block, WAL and blocks: Two hours in memory with a write-ahead log, then immutable blocks compacted up to 31 days. See Grafana ch 5.
  • rate, increase and irate: Reset-aware, extrapolated over the window; irate uses the last two samples. See Grafana ch 5.
Say it in an interview

A selector returns an instant vector of the newest sample per series within five minutes; a range selector returns every sample in a window, and functions like rate turn that back into an instant vector. Binary operators match on all labels unless I narrow them with on or ignoring, group_left copies labels from an info metric, and unless is how I suppress an alert in a known condition. For counters I always rate first and aggregate second.

On AWSAMP and Amazon Managed Grafana speak standard PromQL, so everything here works unchanged: point the Grafana Prometheus data source at the AMP query endpoint with SigV4 enabled. CloudWatch has its own metric math and Metrics Insights for AWS service metrics; for application metrics PromQL is the more portable skill. AMP query limits (samples per query, query time) play the role of Prometheus’ --query.max-samples.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

A teammate writes sum(http_requests_total) / sum(http_requests_total offset 5m) to show request growth and the graph has strange negative spikes. What’s wrong and how do you fix it?

Show a model answer

The expression compares raw counter values. Counters reset to zero when a process restarts, so when any pod restarts the current sum drops, and comparing totals across a restart produces nonsense, including apparent negative growth.

Raw counter values are almost never what you want. The question “how fast are requests arriving” is answered by sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m])): rate per series first, which handles each reset correctly, then sum.

If the question really is growth compared with earlier, compare two rates: sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m] offset 1w)) for week-on-week. In Grafana use $__rate_interval rather than a fixed window so the window always contains at least two scrapes at any zoom level.

I’d also check the labels: if one side of a division has a label the other lacks, the match fails and returns nothing. Aggregating both sides the same way, or using on(), avoids that.

Quick check: What does group_left (os_image) do in kube_pod_info * on (node) group_left (os_image) kube_node_info?
Many-to-one matching on node, with the listed label copied from the one side.
Quick check: Which function should an alert on request rate use?
irate uses only the last two samples, so it is too jumpy for alerting.
Your turnRun POC 20 and read test_on_and_ignoring_narrow_the_match and test_many_to_one_needs_group_left: they are the Grafana book’s colour/smell vectors. Then write, in your own Prometheus, a query that copies os_image from kube_node_info onto container memory, and one that alerts on clock offset unless the node just rebooted.
Key takeaways
  • Instant vectors for values, range vectors for functions, five-minute lookback with staleness markers.
  • Matching is on all labels by default; on, ignoring and group_left are how you join.
  • Rate first, aggregate second; irate for graphs, rate for alerts.
Prometheus · FundamentalsChapter 4 · POC 22 · 6 min read

Service discovery and relabeling: deciding what to scrape and what to call it

You will learn
  • How discovery providers hand targets and metadata to Prometheus
  • How ServiceMonitors become kubernetes_sd_configs and relabel rules
  • Relabel actions, the three places relabeling runs, and how to debug it
  • How a provider works inside (the Linode example) and why HTTP SD replaced file_sd scripts

The big picture

In a cloud environment targets change by the minute, so a fixed list of hosts goes stale immediately. Prometheus ships more than two dozen service discovery providers, among them Kubernetes, AWS EC2 and Lightsail, Azure, GCP, Consul, Docker, file-based and HTTP. Each refreshes in the background and returns a list of candidate targets with an address and a set of hidden __meta_<provider>_* labels.

Discovery deliberately does almost nothing else. Deciding which candidates to keep and what labels they get is the job of relabeling. In the book’s words, relabeling is where the magic happens.

Discoverytargets + hidden __meta_* labels
→
relabel_configskeep or drop targets, build labels
→
Scrapepull /metrics
→
metric_relabel_configsdrop or fix series
→
TSDBstore
→
write_relabel_configschoose what to remote-write

Three relabeling hooks at three points in the pipeline. The first works on targets, the other two on series.

From ServiceMonitor to scrape job

With the Prometheus Operator you rarely write kubernetes_sd_configs yourself. A ServiceMonitor says “scrape services with these labels, on the port named http-metrics, and take the job name from the service’s jobLabel label”. The Operator expands that into a scrape job with a short discovery block and a long list of relabel rules.

- source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_endpoint_port_name]
  regex: http-metrics
  action: keep                       # endpoints on other ports are dropped
- source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_service_label_jobLabel]
  regex: (.+)
  target_label: job
  replacement: ${1}                  # job="node-exporter", not the generated job name

That last rule explains a confusing moment in the chapter: the scrape job is named serviceMonitor/prometheus/…-node-exporter/0, yet querying {job="serviceMonitor/…"} returns nothing, because relabeling overwrote job with node-exporter.

Relabel actions

ActionEffect
replace (default)Join source labels with ;, match the anchored regex, write the replacement to target_label; an empty result deletes the label
keep / dropKeep or drop the whole target (or series) if the joined value matches
hashmodmd5 of the joined value, modulo N, into a label: the basis of sharding
labelmapCopy every label whose name matches the regex to a new name, e.g. all __meta_ec2_tag_(.+) to $1
labeldrop / labelkeepRemove or keep labels by name

After target relabeling, any label still starting with __ is removed, and instance defaults to __address__ if you didn’t set it. Setting instance to a friendly host name while __address__ stays an IP is the book’s trick for readable labels without depending on DNS to scrape.

Debugging

Two pages under Status. Targets shows each target and, on hover, its labels before relabeling. Service Discovery is better: per job it lists every discovered target, whether it was dropped, and its labels before and after relabeling side by side.

Going deeper inside a provider, and writing your own

How a provider works: the Linode example

Every provider implements one Go interface with a single Run method that sends groups of targets on a channel. Most reuse a shared refresh helper that calls the provider’s refresh function on an interval. Linode’s refresh first asks the cheap events API whether anything changed since the last run and only lists every instance when it did, with a full refresh every tenth interval as a safety net.

A target group is just a set of target label sets plus labels common to the group. Providers may only set __address__ and __meta_* labels; everything visible is your relabeling’s doing.

HTTP SD

For years the project refused new providers; the moratorium ended in late 2019 and the count went from 11 to about 25. A provider must serve a widely used platform, so for your CMDB or inventory the answer is HTTP SD, added in 2021. It replaced cron jobs that wrote file_sd files nobody monitored.

RequirementDetail
StatusHTTP 200
HeaderContent-Type: application/json
EncodingUTF-8
BodyA JSON list of {"targets": [...], "labels": {...}}, the same shape as a static config

The chapter builds one in Go on SQLite. POC 22 builds one in Python from an EC2-style inventory, validates the contract, and shows how to label by name while connecting by IP.

Say it in an interview

Discovery returns candidate targets with hidden meta labels; relabel_configs decide which to scrape and what labels they get, metric_relabel_configs fix or drop series after the scrape, and write_relabel_configs choose what goes to remote storage. I debug with the Service Discovery page, which shows labels before and after relabeling. For anything without a built-in provider I serve HTTP SD.

On AWSOn EC2, ec2_sd_configs needs ec2:DescribeInstances; filter by tag server-side and turn tags into labels with labelmap on __meta_ec2_tag_(.+). On EKS, use ServiceMonitors with the Operator, or give the AMP managed collector a scrape config with kubernetes_sd_configs. For anything else (Cloud Map, a CMDB, an inventory in DynamoDB), serve HTTP SD from a small Lambda behind a function URL or internal ALB. POC 22 includes the IRSA role and a full EC2 scrape config.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

After a deploy, Prometheus stops scraping a service. The pods are healthy. How do you debug it?

Show a model answer

I’d start at Status → Service Discovery for the job. It answers the first question directly: was the target discovered at all, and if so, was it dropped by relabeling? The page shows the discovered labels next to the labels after relabeling.

If it was never discovered, the discovery side is wrong: the ServiceMonitor’s selector no longer matches the service’s labels, the service is in a namespace the Prometheus isn’t watching (serviceMonitorNamespaceSelector), or the Prometheus CR’s serviceMonitorSelector doesn’t match the ServiceMonitor’s own labels. A changed label in the deploy is the usual culprit.

If it was discovered but dropped, a keep rule no longer matches; most often the port was renamed and the rule keeps only http-metrics. The before-and-after view shows which meta label changed.

If it is kept and appears under Targets but is down, it is a scrape problem: wrong path, TLS, a network policy, or the scrape timing out. The error on the Targets page says which.

Afterwards I’d add an alert on absent(up{job="checkout"}) or on the target count dropping, because a target that silently disappears doesn’t fire any up == 0 alert.

Quick check: When does metric_relabel_configs run?
relabel_configs works on targets before scraping; metric_relabel_configs works on series after it.
Quick check: What are the three requirements of an HTTP SD endpoint?
HTTP 200, Content-Type application/json, UTF-8, with a static_config-shaped body.
Your turnRun POC 22 and change EC2_RELABEL so the job label comes from a Component tag and instances without it are dropped. Then start the HTTP SD server from http_sd_app() and point a local Prometheus at it with http_sd_configs.
Key takeaways
  • Discovery finds candidates; relabeling decides everything else.
  • Three hooks: targets before the scrape, series after it, and series before remote write.
  • Debug with the Service Discovery page; build custom discovery with HTTP SD.
Prometheus · FundamentalsChapter 5 · POC 23 · 7 min read

Alertmanager, and alerts that don’t wake people for nothing

You will learn
  • Routing trees, matchers, continue, and how to test routes
  • group_by, group_wait, group_interval and repeat_interval, on a timeline
  • Time intervals, receivers, send_resolved and inhibition
  • Alertmanager high availability: what it gossips and what it doesn’t
  • Robust rules: set operators, for durations, _over_time, unit tests

The big picture

A common misunderstanding is that Prometheus sends notifications. It doesn’t. Prometheus evaluates alerting rules, and when an expression has been true for the rule’s for duration it sends the alert to every Alertmanager it knows, re-sending while it fires. Alertmanager owns everything after that: routing, grouping, inhibition, silencing and delivery.

Routing

The only mandatory parts of an Alertmanager config are a top-level route and a receiver. The top route matches every alert and can’t have matchers; everything else is a tree of sub-routes underneath it. Matchers look like PromQL: =, !=, =~, !~. Quoting the value with double quotes is optional; single quotes become part of the value, a gotcha the book calls out.

Without continue, the first matching child wins and evaluation stops. With it, the alert also tries the following siblings, which is how you send the same alert to Slack and to PagerDuty.

A correction to the bookIn the chapter’s second routing table, {environment="production", team="sre"} is listed under fallthrough. With the configuration as printed it goes to default: every matcher on that route holds, because a missing namespace is not default and a missing service doesn’t match ^(api.+). POC 23 checks this, and amtool config routes test would show the same. In an interview, the lesson is that missing labels count as empty strings.

Grouping, on a timeline

SettingDefaultMeans
group_byper route, inheritedAlerts with the same values for these labels form one group and one notification
group_wait30sAfter the first alert of a new group, wait this long for more before sending
group_interval5mAfter a notification, wait at least this long before sending an update about changes to the group
repeat_interval4hRe-send an unchanged, still-firing group this often. The author sets 24h to fight fatigue
  1. 10:00:00First HighAPIErrorRate alert (api1) creates the group; group_wait starts
  2. 10:00:17api2 joins the group
  3. 10:00:30One notification with both alerts
  4. 10:00:35api3 joins; it has missed the first send
  5. 10:05:30Next flush, group_interval after the last one: api3 is announced

The book’s table puts the third notification at 10:05:00, five minutes after the first alert. In Alertmanager the group timer restarts when it fires, so the update goes out at 10:05:30. The difference is small, but explaining it shows you understand the mechanism.

Time intervals, receivers and inhibition

active_time_intervals and mute_time_intervals (added in 2022) reference named intervals built from weekdays, days of month (negative numbers count from the end), months, years, times and an IANA time zone. Routing still happens outside the interval; only the notification is held back. That catches people out: an incident fixed at 17:05 never gets its “resolved” message if warnings only notify in business hours.

A receiver has a name and one or more integrations (Slack, PagerDuty, email, webhooks, SNS and others). Every integration supports send_resolved; turn it off for event-like alerts such as an OOM kill, where “resolved” means nothing.

Inhibition mutes an incoming alert (the target) while another alert (the source) is firing with equal values for chosen labels. The standard rule mutes warnings and infos when a critical with the same namespace and alertname fires, which lets you keep a 90% disk warning and a 98% disk critical without double pages. An alert can’t inhibit itself, and inhibition is applied at notification time, so arrival order doesn’t matter.

High availability

Unlike Prometheus, Alertmanager clusters natively. Instances gossip silences and the notification log (which group was sent where), so only one of them notifies. They do not gossip alerts. Every Prometheus must therefore send to every Alertmanager, and you must never put a load balancer between them. There is no quorum, so two or three instances spread across availability zones is enough.

Going deeper writing rules that don’t flap, and testing them

Robust rules

  • Combine signals. High memory alone is noise; high memory and a high rate of major page faults is memory pressure. unless suppresses known conditions.
  • Choose for durations deliberately. The author’s rule of thumb: warnings wait at least 15 minutes, criticals fire within 15. Never make for shorter than the evaluation interval.
  • Wrap selectors in _over_time. One failed scrape makes probe_success != 1 return nothing, which resets a pending alert. last_over_time(probe_success[5m]) != 1 doesn’t.
  • Alert on symptoms. The chapter points to Rob Ewaschuk’s My Philosophy on Alerting; lesson 13 turns that into burn-rate alerts. For anomaly detection with z-scores and seasonality, see GitLab’s write-up.

Unit tests

promtool check rules checks syntax. promtool test rules runs real tests: input series written in expanding notation (1 1 1 1 0+0x12 means four ones then thirteen zeros; _ is a missing sample), evaluation times, and the exact labels and annotations you expect.

tests:
  - interval: 1m
    input_series:
      - series: 'probe_success{instance="server1", job="blackbox_ssh"}'
        values: '1 1 1 1 0+0x12'
    alert_rule_test:
      - alertname: SSHDown
        eval_time: 15m
        exp_alerts:
          - exp_labels: {severity: critical, instance: server1, job: blackbox_ssh}

The book expects the alert at 14 minutes. That is true in Prometheus 2.x; Prometheus 3 made range selectors left-open, so max_over_time(...[5m]) turns true a minute earlier. Testing at 15 minutes passes on both, which is the kind of robustness a test suite should have.

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that Observability with Grafana also covers, from the knowledge map:
  • Alertmanager routing: A tree of matchers with grouping, inhibition, silences and timers. See Grafana ch 9.
Say it in an interview

Prometheus decides that an alert is firing; Alertmanager routes it through a tree where the most specific match wins unless continue is set, groups alerts by labels with group_wait, group_interval and repeat_interval, mutes warnings while a related critical fires, and holds notifications outside active time intervals. In HA, Alertmanagers gossip silences and the notification log, so every Prometheus must send to every Alertmanager directly.

On AWSAMP’s managed Alertmanager accepts a standard Alertmanager config, but its receivers are SNS topics: fan out from SNS to email, chat through Amazon Q Developer in chat applications, PagerDuty, Lambda or AWS Systems Manager Incident Manager. Load rules into an AMP rule groups namespace unchanged. In Amazon Managed Grafana, Grafana alerting’s notification policies follow the same routing model. POC 23 has an Alertmanager config with SNS receivers and a CI workflow.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Your on-call engineers get forty pages when one availability zone fails. How would you fix that in Alertmanager and in the rules?

Show a model answer

Forty pages for one cause means the alerts are causes rather than symptoms and Alertmanager isn’t collapsing them. I’d work on both sides.

In Alertmanager, first look at group_by. If it includes instance or pod, every host gets its own page. Grouping by alertname, service and environment, or by zone, turns forty into a handful. Then add inhibition: an AvailabilityZoneDown or network alert as a source that mutes host-level alerts with the same zone label. Check group_wait is long enough for related alerts to arrive together.

In the rules, page on user-facing symptoms, such as error-budget burn for each service, and make host-level alerts warnings that go to a ticket queue. A zone failure that a service survives shouldn’t page at all; that is the point of running in three zones.

Finally I’d write regression tests: amtool config routes test for the routing, and a promtool test or a game day that kills a zone in staging, counting pages. The target is one page per incident with the context to act.

Quick check: Why must every Prometheus send alerts to every Alertmanager?
Each Alertmanager only knows about alerts sent to it directly; gossip stops duplicate notifications.
Quick check: Why wrap probe_success in last_over_time in an alert?
A missing result resets a pending alert; _over_time functions bridge single missing samples.
Your turnRun POC 23. Add a route for team="payments" that pages only in business hours, write the amtool config routes test command that proves it, and extend test_grouping_timeline with a fourth alert at 10:06:00. When does it go out?
Key takeaways
  • Most specific route wins; continue tries the siblings; missing labels are empty strings.
  • group_wait, group_interval, repeat_interval shape the noise; inhibition and time intervals cut it further.
  • Robust rules combine signals, use sensible for durations and _over_time, and are unit-tested.
Prometheus · ScalingChapter 6 · POC 22, 25 · 5 min read

When one Prometheus isn’t enough: sharding, federation and high availability

You will learn
  • The two limits that end single-server setups: cardinality and long-term storage
  • Sharding by service versus sharding with hashmod
  • What federation is for, and why it is usually the wrong answer
  • HA replicas, external labels, alert deduplication, and how to query a pair

The big picture

A single Prometheus eventually shows the same symptoms: memory creeps up, queries slow down, restarts take longer because of WAL replay. The book names two root causes. Cardinality: too many series, and the query engine is single-threaded, so more hardware only helps so far. Long-term storage: blocks max out at 31 days, so years of data means dozens of large independent databases on one disk.

LabelCardinality
method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE…)Good: a few fixed values
status_class (2xx…5xx)Good
ip, user_id, request_id, full URL pathUnbounded: never a metric label

The book’s rule of thumb: most labels should have fewer than ten values, and almost none more than a hundred.

Sharding

Prometheus servers don’t coordinate, so sharding means splitting scrape jobs, not data. There are two ways.

By serviceBy hashmod
HowEach server scrapes a set of teams, or a type of infrastructureEvery server sees all targets; relabeling keeps those where md5(address) mod N equals its shard number
GoodPredictable: people know where their metrics areEven-ish load, automatic, no ownership decisions
BadUneven load; reshuffles when teams changeNobody knows which shard holds a series; uneven with few targets (the book saw 8 vs 16); changing N reshuffles most targets
relabel_configs:
  - source_labels: [__address__]
    modulus: 2
    target_label: __tmp_hash
    action: hashmod
  - source_labels: [__tmp_hash]
    regex: "1"            # this server is shard 1 of 2
    action: keep

With the Operator this is one field, shards: 2 on the Prometheus resource, which adds those two rules to every job. Run by hand, you must add them to every job yourself.

Federation

A higher-level Prometheus can scrape /federate?match[]=… on lower ones. It needs honor_labels: true so incoming labels aren’t overwritten, and distinct external labels per source so you can tell them apart.

The book’s verdictFederate only small, preferably aggregated subsets: if a series has an instance label, don’t federate it. Federating everything recreates the oversized server you sharded to escape. In the author’s experience it is a stop-gap nine times out of ten; go to Thanos or remote storage instead.

High availability

Prometheus has no built-in HA, so you run identical copies that scrape the same targets and evaluate the same rules, and differ only in one external label, for example prometheus_replica. Put them in different availability zones and have them monitor each other; for the last few percent, a SaaS check that watches the watchers.

Two consequences. Alerts from the two replicas differ in the replica label, so Alertmanager would page twice; alert_relabel_configs with labeldrop on the replica label fixes that (the Operator adds it). And users now have two endpoints. The options for one view are federation with max or min over the replica label, a load balancer with sticky sessions (which shows different gaps after rolling restarts), remote storage, or the author’s favourite, Thanos Sidecar plus Thanos Query, which deduplicates on the replica label and fills one replica’s gaps from the other.

Say it in an interview

One Prometheus runs out of road on cardinality and on long-term storage. I shard scrape jobs by service when ownership is clear, or with hashmod relabeling when I need balance, and I run every shard as two identical replicas in different zones that differ only in a replica external label. Alertmanager drops that label to deduplicate alerts, and Thanos Query or remote storage gives users one deduplicated view. Federation I keep for small aggregated subsets.

On AWSMost AWS teams skip hand-built sharding and HA queries by remote-writing every replica to Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus: AMP deduplicates HA pairs that share a cluster label and differ in __replica__, scales storage and queries itself, and gives Grafana a single endpoint. Keep replicas in different AZs, or use the AMP managed collector, which runs scraping for you. POC 25 has the kube-prometheus-stack values and Terraform.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Design Prometheus for 40 EKS clusters with one place to query and alert. What do you build?

Show a model answer

I’d separate collection from storage. In each cluster, collection stays local and simple: a Prometheus in agent mode (or the ADOT collector, or the AMP managed collector) scraping that cluster, with an external label cluster and, if I run two replicas, a replica label.

Storage and querying are central. On AWS I’d remote-write every cluster to Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, one workspace per environment or per tenant boundary, with IRSA roles that allow only aps:RemoteWrite. AMP deduplicates HA pairs and serves PromQL, and Amazon Managed Grafana gets one data source per workspace.

If I couldn’t use a managed service, I’d choose between Thanos (sidecars uploading blocks to S3, with Query, Store and Compactor centrally) when I want clusters to keep working if the centre fails, and Mimir when I want central ingestion and multi-tenancy.

Rules and alerts: cluster-local alerts evaluate centrally on the cluster label, and SLO rules live in AMP rule groups. Alertmanager is AMP’s, routing by cluster and team to SNS.

Guard rails: per-cluster sample_limit and write-relabel drops, cardinality dashboards per cluster, and a meta-monitoring alert when a cluster stops sending, since agents have no local query to tell you.

Quick check: What does sharding with hashmod actually split?
Each server keeps only targets whose hashed address modulo N equals its shard number.
Quick check: What must you do so two HA replicas don’t page twice?
Identical alerts then share a label set and Alertmanager deduplicates them.
Your turnIn POC 22 run test_small_target_counts_are_uneven_and_resharding_moves_most_targets, then change the shard count from 2 to 4 and measure how many targets move. In POC 25 read dedup_thanos() and dedup_mimir() and explain the difference to someone in two sentences.
Key takeaways
  • Cardinality and long-term storage are what break a single server.
  • Shard by service for predictability or hashmod for balance; federate only aggregates.
  • HA is identical replicas plus a replica label, deduplicated by Alertmanager and by Thanos or remote storage.
Prometheus · ScalingChapter 7 · POC 21 · 7 min read

Keeping Prometheus fast: cardinality, recording rules, jitter, profiling and GC

You will learn
  • Reading /tsdb-status and finding the label that causes the damage
  • Dropping series safely and setting scrape limits
  • Recording rule naming and the cost of too many rules
  • Scrape jitter, pprof and promtool debug, query logs and limits
  • GOGC and GOMEMLIMIT

Finding cardinality

Status → TSDB Status lists the top ten in four tables. Label names by value count is the important one; ignore __name__, which is always first. Series count by metric name shows which metrics are expensive to query (the book’s top metric was four times slower than up). Label names with high memory use factors in value length. Series count by label pair mostly finds labels that are the same everywhere, such as env="production", which belong in external labels.

# which metrics carry the high-cardinality "name" label, and how many values each
sort_desc(count by (__name__) ({name!=""}))

Fixing it

Drop what you don’t need in metric_relabel_configs (or metricRelabelings on a ServiceMonitor): whole metrics with action: drop on __name__, or individual histogram buckets by matching __name__ and le together, as the chart already does for API server latency buckets. labeldrop works too, but the remaining series must still be unique or the scrape is rejected.

Then prevent the next one with limits, set globally or per job: sample_limit, label_limit, label_value_length_limit and label_name_length_limit. They are checked after metric relabeling, and any breach fails the whole scrape, so pair them with an alert on up == 0. Limits are what let you give teams self-service onboarding without fearing one bad deploy.

Recording rules

A recording rule evaluates PromQL on a schedule and stores the result as a new series, so dashboards read one cheap series instead of recomputing an expensive query on every refresh.

ConventionExample
level:metric:operationsjob:http_requests:rate5m
Operations newest first:sum_rate5m is a sum of a 5-minute rate
Drop _total after ratehttp_requests_total → http_requests:rate5m
With without, list only the key labels in the levelnode_namespace_pod_container:…

The cost is constant background querying: the author has seen the rule manager use a quarter of a server’s memory. Rules in a group run in order, so a rule that reads another rule’s output must come after it; better still, don’t chain them.

Scrape jitter

Delta-of-delta encoding only costs one bit when scrapes are exactly evenly spaced. If they are off by a few milliseconds, every timestamp costs 16 bits or more, and the book calls this the most common cause of oversized blocks. Prometheus snaps timestamps within 2 ms by default; --scrape.timestamp-tolerance raises that, up to 1% of the scrape interval.

  1. Measureoy-scrape-jitter reported 2 aligned and 22 unaligned targets, worst 30 ms
  2. Tuneset scrape.timestamp-tolerance to 30ms (allowed: up to 300 ms for a 30 s interval)
  3. Check23 aligned, 1 unaligned. Don’t chase the last one; recheck when disk usage grows
Going deeper profiling, query control and garbage collection

pprof and promtool debug

Prometheus exposes Go’s profiler at /debug/pprof. go tool pprof http://…/debug/pprof/heap then top or web shows what holds memory; in the book it was label building and the scrape cache. Heap isn’t total memory, so don’t expect the numbers to match the process size.

Without Go installed, promtool debug pprof collects every profile into a tarball and promtool debug all adds the server’s own metrics. The author’s team runs debug all before restarting a misbehaving server, so the evidence survives the restart.

Query logs and limits

query_log_file writes every completed query as JSON with its source (for example, which rule file) and timings. In-flight queries are always tracked in queries.active in the data directory and logged after a crash. --query.max-concurrency (default 20, low for big setups) and --query.max-samples (default 50 million samples loaded, not returned) stop runaway queries.

GOGC and GOMEMLIMIT

SettingEffectBook’s advice
GOGC=100 (default)Collect when the heap has grown 100% over the live heap after the last collectionFine for small servers
GOGC=50Collect at 50% growth: less memory, more CPUStart here above a few million head series
GOMEMLIMITA soft absolute limit; the collector works harder as memory approaches itAbout 90% of the memory Prometheus has, e.g. 28 GiB on 32 GiB

The failure GOMEMLIMIT prevents: a WAL compaction and a few heavy queries spike memory, the next GC target lands above physical memory, and the kernel’s OOM killer gets there first.

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that Observability with Grafana also covers, from the knowledge map:
  • Series and cardinality: A metric name plus one label set; every new value is a new series in memory and index. See Grafana ch 5.
  • Scrape limits: sample_limit and label limits fail a scrape that would explode cardinality. See Grafana ch 15.
  • Observability cost: Plan what you need, drop at collection, isolate noisy environments. See Grafana ch 15.
Say it in an interview

I find cardinality on the TSDB status page, look for label names with the most values, drop what nobody uses with metric relabeling, and put sample and label limits on scrape jobs so a bad deploy fails one scrape instead of the server. I precompute dashboard queries with recording rules named level:metric:operations, check scrape jitter when disk usage grows, and on big servers set GOGC to 50 and GOMEMLIMIT to about 90% of memory.

On AWSOn AMP you don’t tune GC or TSDB flags, but cardinality still matters because you pay per sample ingested and per active series: drop at the scraper (Prometheus agent, ADOT, or the AMP managed collector all accept relabeling) and watch AMP’s CloudWatch usage metrics against your quotas. Recording rules run in AMP rule groups namespaces. If you self-manage on EKS, set memory requests from head-series counts, set GOMEMLIMIT through an environment variable, and keep promtool debug all output in S3 before restarts.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Prometheus memory doubled overnight and it was OOM-killed twice. Walk me through your investigation.

Show a model answer

First stabilise: raise the memory limit or move it to a bigger node so it stays up long enough to investigate, and capture promtool debug all before any further restart.

Then find what changed. prometheus_tsdb_head_series over the last two days tells me whether series count jumped; if it did, cardinality is the cause. TSDB Status shows the top metrics and label names by value count, and comparing with yesterday points at the new one. count by (__name__) over a new label, and the scrape job’s scrape_samples_scraped, find the target.

If series didn’t change, look at queries: the query log or queries.active for a new dashboard or rule hitting tens of millions of samples, and prometheus_rule_group_last_duration_seconds for a slow recording rule.

Fix: drop the offending label or metric with metric relabeling, add sample_limit to that job, and talk to the owning team about putting that dimension in logs or traces. If it was a query, add a recording rule or tighten --query.max-samples.

Prevent: an alert on head-series growth rate, GOMEMLIMIT at about 90% of the limit so GC works harder before the OOM killer acts, and scrape limits on every job by default.

Quick check: What happens when a scrape exceeds sample_limit?
Limits apply after metric relabeling, and a breach fails the entire scrape; up becomes 0.
Quick check: What is the most likely cause of unexpectedly large TSDB blocks, according to the book?
Irregular intervals make each timestamp cost 16 bits or more instead of one.
Your turnRun POC 21’s cardinality_report() on the /metrics of three exporters you run. Write the metric_relabel_configs that would drop the worst label, then set limits that would have caught it, and check with apply_limits().
Key takeaways
  • TSDB Status finds the label; metric relabeling removes it; limits stop it returning.
  • Recording rules make dashboards cheap but cost the server constantly.
  • Jitter inflates disk; GOMEMLIMIT prevents GC-driven OOMs.
Prometheus · ScalingChapter 8 · POC 21 · 5 min read

The Node Exporter, and what any exporter is made of

You will learn
  • The parts of an exporter: descriptors, collector, registry, handler
  • The collectors that matter most and the queries that go with them
  • Why load average misleads and pressure stall information doesn’t
  • The textfile collector and how to keep it honest
  • Troubleshooting slow scrapes per collector

What an exporter is

An exporter is a separate program that reads some other system and exposes what it finds as Prometheus metrics. Its anatomy is small: metric descriptors (name, help, labels), a collector with Describe and Collect methods, a registry, and an HTTP handler on /metrics that runs every collector on each scrape. The client library adds Go runtime and HTTP metrics for free.

The Node Exporter is one of the few exporters maintained by the Prometheus project itself, alongside the Blackbox and SNMP exporters. Its motto in the book: if it is in /proc, the Node Exporter can get it. It has 49 collectors on by default on Linux, each running in its own goroutine, so turning collectors off doesn’t make scrapes faster. On Windows, use windows_exporter.

The collectors you will query

CollectorKey metricsUse
cpunode_cpu_seconds_total{mode}Utilisation is the rate of non-idle seconds
meminfoMemTotal, MemAvailable, MemFreeUse Available (free plus reclaimable cache), not Free
filesystemnode_filesystem_size_bytes, _free_bytesDisk full forecasts with predict_linear
diskstatsnode_disk_io_time_seconds_total, read and written bytesI/O saturation
netdevtransmit and receive bytes and dropsThroughput and drops
conntracknode_nf_conntrack_entries vs _limitA full table silently drops connections
pressurenode_pressure_{memory,io}_stalled_seconds_totalReal contention (kernel 4.20+)
timexnode_timex_offset_secondsClock drift
# CPU used, in cores, and normalised by a recording rule that counts cores
sum without (cpu, mode) (rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode!="idle"}[5m]))
/ count without (cpu, mode) (node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"})

Pressure, not load average

The author begs you not to alert on load average; the kernel source itself calls it a silly number. Pressure stall information measures time lost waiting for CPU, memory or I/O. For memory and I/O it has two levels: waiting (some tasks blocked but the CPU found other work) and stalled (everything blocked, CPU cycles wasted). CPU has only waiting. Alert on memory and I/O stalled time; it can replace naïve “95% memory used” alerts, which fire on healthy caches.

Going deeper the textfile collector and troubleshooting

The textfile collector

Point --collector.textfile.directory at a directory (globs allowed) and the Node Exporter includes every *.prom file in it, in the text exposition format. It is the right tool for facts about the machine produced by short-lived jobs: when the last backup ran, whether the last configuration-management run succeeded.

# HELP backup_last_success_timestamp_seconds Last successful nightly backup.
# TYPE backup_last_success_timestamp_seconds gauge
backup_last_success_timestamp_seconds 1714052400

The trap is silent staleness: if the job stops running, the file keeps saying all is well. Alert on time() - node_textfile_mtime_seconds exceeding the expected interval. Service-level batch metrics belong in the Pushgateway, not here. The community keeps a collection of ready-made textfile scripts.

When scrapes get slow

node_scrape_collector_duration_seconds per collector usually shows one culprit. In the author’s story it was the non-default processes collector, contending for a kernel lock with the application and intermittently exceeding the scrape timeout, which left gaps in every node graph. Don’t alert on node_scrape_collector_success == 0 blindly: some default collectors (InfiniBand, Fibre Channel) always fail on hosts without that hardware.

Say it in an interview

An exporter is a small program with descriptors, a collector and a registry behind a /metrics handler. From the Node Exporter I rely on cpu, meminfo with MemAvailable, filesystem, diskstats, netdev, conntrack and especially pressure stall information, which shows real contention where load average misleads. For machine facts from batch jobs I use the textfile collector with an alert on file age so it can’t go stale silently.

On AWSOn EC2, run node_exporter as a systemd service from the AMI or install it with SSM Run Command, and discover it with ec2_sd_configs. On EKS, it runs as a DaemonSet from kube-prometheus-stack, or use the ADOT collector’s hostmetrics receiver instead. The CloudWatch agent covers similar host metrics for CloudWatch-native setups, but doesn’t expose pressure stall information by default. For Windows instances, windows_exporter.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

How would you alert on memory problems on Linux hosts without paging on healthy page cache?

Show a model answer

Linux uses spare memory for cache, so “memory used above 90%” fires on perfectly healthy machines. The first improvement is to use node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes, which counts reclaimable cache as available, rather than MemFree.

The better signal is the cost of the shortage, not the level. Pressure stall information gives node_pressure_memory_stalled_seconds_total: the share of time every task was blocked on memory. A rate of that above a few percent for ten or fifteen minutes means the host is genuinely thrashing. Combining low MemAvailable and a high rate of major page faults is the book’s alternative for older kernels.

Then decide severity. A single host under pressure in an autoscaled group is a ticket or nothing at all if the service’s SLO is fine; it pages only through the service’s burn-rate alert. I’d also alert on OOM kills from node_vmstat_oom_kill as an event, with send_resolved off.

Quick check: Why does the book discourage alerting on load average?
Load average mixes runnable and uninterruptible tasks and doesn’t correlate well with impact.
Quick check: What protects against a stale textfile metric?
The file keeps its last values forever; its modification time tells you the writer stopped.
Your turnWrite a textfile-collector script for your own nightly job that writes a success timestamp, plus the alerting rule on file age and on the timestamp itself. Add it to POC 23’s config/rules.yml and run the linter.
Key takeaways
  • An exporter is descriptors, a collector, a registry and a handler.
  • Use MemAvailable and pressure stall information; avoid load average.
  • The textfile collector needs an age alert; per-collector durations find slow scrapes.
Prometheus · ScalingChapter 9 · POC 25 · 6 min read

Remote write and remote read: VictoriaMetrics and Mimir

You will learn
  • Remote read and remote write, and why write won
  • Agent mode: scraping with no local queries
  • Tuning remote write: relabeling, queues, shards, capacity, backoff
  • VictoriaMetrics against Mimir: storage, efficiency, compatibility, HA dedup

Two APIs

Prometheus keeps its storage local and unreplicated on purpose. To go further it offers two HTTP APIs using protocol buffers and Snappy compression. Remote read lets Prometheus query another store alongside its own; few people use it, partly because a broken remote store can break alert queries. Thanos uses it the other way round, to read from Prometheus. Remote write streams every sample to another system and is how you feed AMP, Mimir, Cortex or VictoriaMetrics. With --web.enable-remote-write-receiver, Prometheus can also accept writes, which is how Loki’s ruler sends metrics it derives from logs.

Agent mode

--enable-feature=agent (2.32) turns Prometheus into a scraper only: no queries, no rules, no local blocks. The WAL is kept just long enough to send, up to about two hours. You keep pull’s advantages, such as the up series, and gain push’s: stateless edge collectors and one central store. The book still called it experimental; it is how many teams run collection today.

Tuning remote write

Remote write sends everything unless you say otherwise, the opposite of federation. Start by sending less with write_relabel_configs, which run after ingestion and see all labels, for example only one team’s series or only production. Don’t micro-optimise; the config becomes unreadable.
