Then size the queue. Each destination gets an in-memory queue divided into shards that send in parallel. If a shard fills, Prometheus stops reading the WAL; nothing is lost unless the backlog outlives WAL truncation, which happens every two hours.

SettingDefaultAdvice
min_shards1About samples per second ÷ capacity, so startup doesn’t lag. Get the rate from rate(prometheus_tsdb_head_samples_appended_total[5m])
max_shards200Leave it; lower it if you raise the two below, to cap memory
capacity2500Samples each shard buffers; keep at least 3 × max_samples_per_send
max_samples_per_send500Batch size; raise for high throughput
batch_send_deadline5sSend a partial batch after this long
min_backoff / max_backoff30ms / 5sRetry delay doubles up to the max, then repeats

VictoriaMetrics or Mimir

VictoriaMetricsGrafana Mimir
StorageLocal or block storage (EBS)Object storage (S3); monolithic local disk only for evaluation
EfficiencyVery frugal: a 2020 benchmark claims ~0.3 vs 2.1 bytes per sample and ~5× less RAM than PrometheusAbout Prometheus-level; built for scale, not thrift
Query languageMetricsQL, a superset of PromQL; 72.78% on the compliance suite because some results differ on purposeFull PromQL
DeploymentSingle node scales a long way (1.5M+ samples/s per the docs); cluster for multi-tenancyMicroservices for production; Helm chart
HA pairsReplicas must have identical external labels; dedup per scrape intervalHA tracker elects a leader replica via Consul or etcd; fails over after 30 s, losing that gap
Licence and modelOpen-core: downsampling, full multi-tenancy, mTLS in enterpriseAGPLv3; Cortex is the Apache-licensed sibling
Multi-tenancyEnterpriseX-Scope-OrgID header on writes and on the Grafana data source
A detail interviewers likeMetricsQL’s rate() includes the last sample before the window, while PromQL uses only samples inside it, so the same query can return slightly different numbers on the two systems. Neither is a bug; they are different definitions.

The author’s summary: VictoriaMetrics if efficiency matters most and local disks are fine; Mimir if you want cheap object storage, long retention and native multi-tenancy, and accept higher resource use.

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that Observability with Grafana also covers, from the knowledge map:
  • Remote write: Sharded queues with backoff to long-term storage. See Grafana ch 5.
  • Thanos, Mimir, VictoriaMetrics: Object-storage blocks with a global query layer, central multi-tenant ingestion, or efficient local disks. See Grafana ch 5.
Say it in an interview

Remote write streams every sample to a central store; I filter with write_relabel_configs, size min_shards from the ingestion rate divided by capacity, and keep capacity at three times the batch size. For collection I like Prometheus in agent mode: pull semantics at the edge, no local state. Between backends, VictoriaMetrics wins on efficiency with local disks, Mimir on object storage, multi-tenancy and strict PromQL, and on AWS AMP gives me the Mimir-style model as a managed service.

On AWSAmazon Managed Service for Prometheus is the AWS answer to this chapter: a Cortex-based remote-write target on object storage with SigV4 auth, multi-AZ durability and HA-pair dedup on cluster and __replica__. Point any Prometheus, agent, ADOT collector or the AMP managed collector at its remote-write URL with an IRSA role that has aps:RemoteWrite. POC 25 has Terraform for the workspace and role, and kube-prometheus-stack values with tuned queues.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Remote write to your central store is falling behind during traffic peaks. How do you diagnose and fix it?

Show a model answer

I’d look at Prometheus’ own remote-write metrics. prometheus_remote_storage_highest_timestamp_in_seconds minus prometheus_remote_storage_queue_highest_sent_timestamp_seconds is the lag. prometheus_remote_storage_shards against shards_max shows whether it has scaled out fully, and failed or retried sample counters show whether the backend is rejecting or throttling.

If shards are at the max and the backend is healthy, the queue is too small for the rate: raise max_samples_per_send and capacity together (capacity at least three times the batch), set min_shards near the ingestion rate divided by capacity so it starts warm, and lower max_shards if memory is tight.

If the backend is throttling, retries back off to max_backoff; the fix is on the backend side, such as raising an AMP ingestion quota or scaling Mimir distributors and ingesters.

In every case I’d send less: write_relabel_configs dropping high-cardinality histograms nobody queries centrally. And I’d alert on the lag, because if it exceeds the two-hour WAL window, data is lost.

Quick check: Unlike federation, what does remote write send by default?
Remote write forwards everything unless write_relabel_configs filters it.
Quick check: How does Mimir deduplicate an HA Prometheus pair?
Leader election via Consul or etcd; failover after a configurable silence, with a small gap.
Your turnUse POC 25’s remote_write_plan() on your own ingestion rate (from rate(prometheus_tsdb_head_samples_appended_total[5m])) and turn the result into the queueConfig block in config/prometheus-remote-write.yml.
Key takeaways
  • Remote write won; agent mode makes collectors stateless.
  • Filter first, then size shards from samples per second ÷ capacity.
  • VictoriaMetrics for thrift on local disks, Mimir for object storage and tenants, AMP when you want it managed.
Prometheus · ScalingChapter 10 · POC 25 · 6 min read

Thanos: a global view and unlimited retention, one component at a time

You will learn
  • The three goals of Thanos and the StoreAPI that ties it together
  • Sidecar, Compactor, Query, Query Frontend, Store, Ruler and Receive
  • Vertical compaction and downsampling, and what each really buys
  • Scaling the read path: the distributed engine, splitting, sharding, caching, partitioning

The big picture

Thanos began at Improbable, written by Bartłomiej Płotka and Fabian Reinartz, and is a CNCF incubating project. Its goals are a global query view, unlimited retention and highly available components. Unlike Mimir or VictoriaMetrics it is not one system but a set of small components, all subcommands of one thanos binary, that you add as you need them. The author recommends it as the first step beyond plain Prometheus, and notes almost nobody runs every component.

The components

ComponentJobWorth knowing
SidecarServes Prometheus data over StoreAPI (via remote read) and uploads each 2h block to object storageNeeds local compaction off: min and max block duration both 2h (the Operator does this). Also reloads Prometheus on config or rule changes, with env-var substitution
QueryPromQL across every StoreAPI endpoint, deduplicating on the replica label100% PromQL compatible; can point at other Queries. Discovers endpoints statically, by dns+ or dnssrv+
Query FrontendSplits long range queries (24h by default), shards some by labels, caches resultsCache only for range queries; Memcached or Redis for more than one replica
StoreServes blocks from object storageQueried even when the sidecar has the same data: set --max-time=-7d to avoid overlap. Partition by time or by external labels; cache index and chunks
CompactorCompacts and downsamples blocks in the bucketOne per bucket. Optional vertical compaction merges replica blocks; risky
RulerEvaluates rules across many Prometheus servers through QueryAdditive only: local rules almost never fail, global ones depend on Query and every sidecar. Stateless mode writes results by remote write
ReceiveA remote-write receiver that keeps a local TSDB (15 days) and uploads blocksHashring with Ketama consistent hashing, replication factor with write quorum, multi-tenancy; no built-in dedup

Compaction and downsampling

The Compactor compacts as Prometheus would. Vertical compaction also merges overlapping blocks from HA replicas to save storage; it needs three flags precisely because a mistake can destroy history, and the book says not to turn it on after reading one chapter.

Downsampling is widely misunderstood. It doesn’t save space: it adds a 5-minute version of raw data older than 40 hours and a 1-hour version of 5-minute data older than 10 days, each storing count, sum, min, max and a counter value. Because the index barely shrinks, expect storage to double or triple. What you gain is fast queries over months. Keep the three per-resolution retentions equal, or old data becomes reachable only at a coarse step.

Going deeper scaling the read path

Making Query fast

The default engine is Prometheus’ own: single-threaded, and it pulls every matching series to the querier before aggregating. It can’t push an avg down to the leaves, because the average of averages isn’t the average. Thanos’ own engine (--query.promql-engine=thanos) is multi-threaded and can run distributed: a top querier delegates sum(x) to sub-queriers, each of which sums its own Prometheus servers, and only adds their results.

In front of that, Query Frontend splits a week into seven one-day queries spread over queriers, which also stops one huge query from OOM-ing a querier, and caches results so a dashboard opened by ten people runs once. In the book, a week-long p99 went from about 30 s to 20 s with the frontend, and to 15 s with a second querier.

Receive in more detail

Receive spreads incoming series over a hashring defined in JSON. Plain hashmod reshuffles most series when you add a node; the Ketama consistent hashing algorithm (--receive.hashrings-algorithm=ketama) moves far fewer, which POC 25 measures. With a replication factor of 3, a write succeeds when two receivers accept it.

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that Observability with Grafana also covers, from the knowledge map:
  • Thanos, Mimir, VictoriaMetrics: Object-storage blocks with a global query layer, central multi-tenant ingestion, or efficient local disks. See Grafana ch 5.
Say it in an interview

Thanos is a toolbox around Prometheus. Sidecars expose each server over the StoreAPI and upload two-hour blocks to S3; Query fans out across them and deduplicates HA replicas on the replica label; Store serves the bucket; the Compactor compacts and downsamples, which speeds long queries rather than saving space. I add Query Frontend for splitting and caching, Ruler only for global rules, and Receive when clusters must push rather than be queried.

On AWSOn AWS, Thanos uses S3 for blocks with an IRSA role per component, and S3 lifecycle rules move old blocks to Standard-IA. Query, Store, Compactor and Frontend run on EKS; ElastiCache for Memcached or Redis backs the frontend and store caches. The managed alternative is AMP, which gives the same global view and long retention without operating components, at the cost of central ingestion. POC 25 includes the S3 objstore config, the bucket Terraform and simulations of dedup, downsampling, splitting and hashrings.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

When would you choose Thanos over remote write to a central store such as Mimir or AMP?

Show a model answer

The core difference is where data lives. With Thanos sidecars, each Prometheus keeps recent data locally and uploads blocks; queries fan out at read time. With remote write, every sample is pushed to a central system that becomes the source of truth.

Thanos fits when clusters must stay independent: if the central query layer fails, every Prometheus still has its data and still alerts locally. It also fits when network egress or central ingestion cost is a concern, since only finished blocks are uploaded, and when you want to start small and add components.

Remote write to Mimir or AMP fits when you want one place where all data lands quickly, strong multi-tenancy, simpler query paths, and stateless collectors in agent mode, especially for many small or short-lived clusters.

On AWS I’d default to AMP for most teams because it removes the operational load, and pick Thanos where data residency, cost at very high volume, or independence from a central service is the deciding factor. Either way, the HA-pair and external-label design is the same.

Quick check: What does Thanos downsampling primarily improve?
It adds coarser blocks; storage grows because the index stays large, but long queries read far fewer samples.
Quick check: Why should Prometheus’ local compaction be disabled when the Sidecar uploads blocks?
It ignores blocks with compaction level above 1, so local compaction would stop uploads.
Your turnRun POC 25’s tests, then change test_ketama_moves_far_fewer_series_than_hashmod_when_adding_a_receiver to go from 4 to 6 receivers. Then sketch, for your own setup, which Thanos components you would run and which you would skip, and why.
Key takeaways
  • Every Thanos component speaks the StoreAPI; add them one at a time.
  • Sidecar + Query gives a global, deduplicated view; Store + Compactor give retention.
  • Downsampling speeds long queries and costs storage; the Thanos engine and Query Frontend scale reads.
Prometheus · ScalingChapter 11 · POC 29 · 5 min read

Jsonnet and monitoring mixins: configuration you can reuse and override

You will learn
  • Why templating YAML goes wrong and what Jsonnet does instead
  • The Jsonnet features you need: locals, hidden fields, self, super and $, imports and +:, comprehensions, functions, errors and asserts
  • Rendering YAML and multiple files
  • What a monitoring mixin is and how to consume one with jsonnet-bundler

The big picture

Prometheus configuration is YAML, and lots of it: thousands of lines of scrape config and rules files full of repeated label matchers and annotations. Templating YAML with Jinja or Go templates is fragile because whitespace is syntax. Jsonnet, released by Google in 2014 from its internal configuration language, is the Prometheus community’s answer. It is a superset of JSON (any JSON file is valid Jsonnet) with variables, functions, imports and inheritance, and it outputs JSON or YAML.

The language in one table

FeatureSyntaxWhy it matters
Variableslocal m = 'env="prod"';One label matcher, used in every rule
String formatting'%(m)s' % _config, ||| blocksReadable multi-line PromQL with substitutions
Hidden fields_config:: {...}Configuration that isn’t emitted; the heart of mixins
Referencesself, super, $This object, the object being extended, the outermost object
Inheritancebase + { ... }Extend an object, overriding fields
Merge overridefield+: [...], field+:: {...}Add to an inherited field instead of replacing it
Importsimport 'x.libsonnet'Libraries by convention end in .libsonnet
Comprehensions[r.name for r in rules if r.page]Generate lists and objects; computed keys in brackets
Functionslocal f(x) = ...;Python-style arguments and defaults
Errors and assertsname: error 'set me', assert std.length(self.rules) > 0 : '...'Force overrides; validate inputs
local rules = (import 'base-rules.libsonnet') {
  _config+:: { selector: 'job="checkout"' },          // override one config value
  groups+: [{ name: 'extra', rules: [] }],            // append, don't replace
};
std.manifestYamlDoc(rules)                              // render as YAML (use jsonnet -S)

Two quirks to remember: output keys come out in alphabetical order, and for must be quoted because it is a keyword. Render files with -o (and -c to create directories), YAML with std.manifestYamlDoc and -S, and many files at once by making the top-level object a map of file names and running with -m. Use jsonnetfmt and jsonnet-lint once a team shares code, and leave real validation to promtool: Jsonnet is not a validation language (look at CUE or Nickel if you need one).

Monitoring mixins

Started in 2018 by Tom Wilkie and Frederic Branczyk, the Monitoring Mixins project defines a minimal standard for packaging Prometheus alerts, recording rules and Grafana dashboards together, so that the people who write a piece of software can ship the monitoring for it.

FieldContents
prometheusAlertsAlerting rule groups
prometheusRulesRecording rule groups
grafanaDashboardsA map of file name to dashboard JSON
_configSelectors and thresholds you override

Most users already run one without knowing: kube-prometheus-stack ships the kubernetes-mixin. The author’s complaint is exactly that ignorance, because unknown mixins with wrong selectors give you dashboards and alerts that silently don’t work.

  1. jb initcreate jsonnetfile.json
  2. jb install github.com/thanos-io/thanos/mixin@mainvendor the mixin and its dependencies, with a lock file
  3. thanos.jsonnetimport mixin.libsonnet; override selectors; set unused components (store, receive, rule…) to null
  4. jsonnet -J vendor -Sm out thanos.jsonnetrender alerts, rules and one file per dashboard

The payoff: alerts such as Thanos Query’s gRPC error-rate alert, written by people who know which gRPC codes matter, without you becoming a gRPC expert. That removes some of the unknown unknowns of running other people’s software. Grafana’s jsonnet-libs repository is a good catalogue.

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that Observability with Grafana also covers, from the knowledge map:
  • Dashboards and rules as code: Team folders, Terraform, linting in CI. See Grafana ch 8, Grafana ch 10.
Say it in an interview

Jsonnet is JSON with variables, functions, imports and inheritance, which makes large Prometheus and Grafana configs DRY and reviewable. A monitoring mixin packages alerts, recording rules and dashboards with a hidden _config you override; I vendor mixins with jsonnet-bundler, override selectors and disable what I don’t run, render them myself, and validate the output with promtool in CI.

On AWSRendered mixin output goes wherever rules and dashboards go on AWS: alert and recording groups into AMP rule groups namespaces (aws_prometheus_rule_group_namespace), dashboards into Amazon Managed Grafana through the grafana Terraform provider. Run the render in CodeBuild or GitHub Actions and commit the output, so reviewers see the generated YAML diff. POC 29 shows the override pattern in Python and the Terraform that publishes dashboards.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Your team runs twenty services, each with hand-written, slightly different alert rules. How would you standardise them?

Show a model answer

I’d separate the pattern from the parameters. Most service alerts are the same handful: error-budget burn, latency SLO burn, saturation, and “is it scraping”. Those become one library, as a Jsonnet mixin or a generator, with a _config per service for selectors, SLO targets and owning team.

Each service’s repo or folder then holds only its overrides. Rendering produces plain YAML that goes through promtool check rules, unit tests and Pint in CI, then into the rules backend.

I’d keep an escape hatch: a service can add its own rules alongside the generated ones, but can’t edit the generated ones by hand. Changes to the shared library get reviewed once and roll out to everyone, which is the shift-down idea from the platform book applied to monitoring.

For third-party software I’d use upstream mixins (Kubernetes, Thanos, Redis…) rather than writing alerts from scratch, checking their selectors match how we label things.

Quick check: In a mixin, where do selectors and thresholds live?
Hidden fields (::) aren’t emitted; consumers override _config to adapt the mixin.
Quick check: What does field+: do in Jsonnet?
For a list it appends, for an object it merges.
Your turnIn POC 29, use merge() to override the latency SLO and add a team, then generate the dashboard and run the linter. If you have Jsonnet installed, vendor the kubernetes-mixin with jb and render only its alerts.
Key takeaways
  • Jsonnet makes config reusable; render it and validate with promtool.
  • A mixin is alerts, rules and dashboards plus a _config you override.
  • Know which mixins you already run, and check their selectors.
Prometheus · ScalingChapter 12 · POC 23 · 5 min read

CI for Prometheus: promtool, amtool and Pint

You will learn
  • GitHub Actions vocabulary and running workflows locally with act
  • Validating Prometheus config and rules, and running rule unit tests
  • Validating Alertmanager config and regression-testing routes
  • Linting rules against a live server with Pint, and Pint in pull requests

The big picture

Prometheus and Alertmanager configuration lives in Git, and code review alone misses things: a typo in a rule, a route added at the bottom that never matches, an alert on a metric that doesn’t exist. CI takes the human error out. The chapter uses GitHub Actions, run locally with act, but the commands are the same in any CI system.

TermMeaning
WorkflowJobs triggered by an event such as a pull request
JobSteps on one runner; jobs run in parallel unless one needs another
StepA shell command or a reusable action
RunnerThe machine (or container) that executes a job

Three layers of checks

CheckCommandCatches
Prometheus configpromtool check config prometheus.ymlInvalid YAML and settings
Rule syntaxpromtool check rules rules/*.yamlBad PromQL, missing fields
Rule behaviourpromtool test rules tests/*.yamlAlerts that fire at the wrong time or with the wrong labels
Alertmanager configamtool check-config alertmanager.ymlInvalid routing or receivers
Routingamtool config routes test --verify.receivers=pagerduty-devops team=devops environment=productionA new route that never matches because an earlier one catches the alert
Rules against realitypint lintMetrics that don’t exist, label mismatches, bad annotations, alerts that would have fired constantly

Run the Prometheus and Alertmanager checks inside the official container images so the tool versions match production. The author’s advice applies even if you are the only person changing the files: these steps have saved him repeatedly.

Pint

Pint comes from Cloudflare, which runs Prometheus at very large scale and didn’t want its monitoring team to be a bottleneck for every other team’s rules. Its key difference from promtool is that it queries live Prometheus servers while it lints, so it can say “this alert’s metric has had no series for a week”.

  • Required labels and annotations, with regexes (anchored, as in Prometheus)
  • A comparison operator in every alert
  • Would this new alert have fired too often recently?
  • External labels used in templates actually exist; no conflicts with alert labels
  • Template syntax in labels and annotations
  • Aggregations keep the labels routing needs
  • Links in annotations work
  • Range selectors longer than the server’s retention
rule {
  match { kind = "alerting" }
  label "severity" {
    severity = "bug"
    value    = "(critical|warning|info)"
    required = true
  }
  annotation "summary" {
    severity = "bug"
    required = true
    value    = "[A-Z][^{.]+.\\."       # one sentence, no templates
  }
}

Pint is configured in HCL (.pint.hcl), can be silenced per rule with comments such as # pint disable promql/series(probe_success), and in CI it checks only the files a pull request changes and comments on the exact lines. The mixin conventions it enforces are a severity of critical, warning or info, a one-sentence summary, and a description with templated detail.

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the SRE book, the platform book and Observability with Grafana also cover, from the knowledge map:
  • Configuration as code: Versioned, reviewed, tested and rolled out like a binary. See SRE ch 14, platform ch 15, Grafana ch 10.
Say it in an interview

I put Prometheus config in Git and gate every pull request on promtool check config, check rules and test rules, amtool check-config plus a set of amtool routes tests that pin which receiver each label set reaches, and Pint linting against a live server so rules on non-existent metrics or with missing annotations never merge. That lets teams who aren’t Prometheus experts change alerting safely.

On AWSRun the same commands in CodeBuild or GitHub Actions using the official Prometheus and Alertmanager images. For Pint against AMP, put a SigV4 proxy (such as aws-sigv4-proxy) in front of the workspace query endpoint. Deploy rules after the checks pass with aws amp put-rule-groups-namespace or Terraform, and the Alertmanager definition with aws amp put-alert-manager-definition. POC 23 contains the workflow, a Pint config, rules, unit tests and an Alertmanager config with SNS receivers.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

What would you put in a CI pipeline for alerting rules, and why each step?

Show a model answer

Syntax first: promtool check rules fails fast on invalid PromQL or YAML. It is cheap and catches typos.

Behaviour next: promtool test rules with input series that model the failure, a gap from a missed scrape, and recovery, asserting the alert fires at the right evaluation time with the right labels and annotations. That protects against someone “tidying” a for duration or a matcher later.

Reality: Pint against a live server, which catches metrics that don’t exist (renamed by an exporter upgrade), label mismatches in vector matching, alerts that would have fired dozens of times last week, and missing severity, summary or runbook_url.

Routing: amtool check-config and route tests that assert which receiver a given label set reaches, so a new route can’t silently swallow alerts meant for another team.

Finally deployment through the pipeline only, so production always matches Git. Each step catches a different class of mistake, and together they let any team contribute.

Quick check: What can Pint check that promtool can’t?
Pint queries real Prometheus servers while linting.
Quick check: What does amtool config routes test --verify.receivers catch?
It asserts which receiver a given label set reaches, a regression test for the routing tree.
Your turnCopy POC 23’s ci/observability-ci.yml into a repository of your own Prometheus config. Add two more amtool config routes test lines for your most important routes, and one promtool test for your most important alert that includes a missed scrape (_).
Key takeaways
  • promtool for config, rule syntax and rule behaviour; amtool for config and routes.
  • Pint lints against live data and comments on pull requests.
  • CI is what makes self-service alerting safe.
Prometheus · ScalingChapter 13 · POC 24 · 6 min read

SLOs with Prometheus: recording rules, burn-rate alerts, Sloth and Pyrra

You will learn
  • SLIs, SLOs, SLAs, error budgets, and who should set SLOs
  • Request-based and window-based SLOs, with PromQL for both
  • Recording rules for SLOs and the 30-day ratio
  • Multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerts
  • Sloth and Pyrra, and how their outputs differ

The big picture

An SLI is a measurement (good events over valid events), an SLO a target for it over a window, and an SLA an SLO with a contract and penalties. The error budget is one minus the objective, and the burn rate is how fast you are spending it. The SRE lessons covered the theory (SRE chapter 8); this chapter is the Prometheus implementation.

Two points of emphasis from the author. SLOs work best set bottom-up by the team that runs the service, signed off by leadership, because missing them must be allowed to redirect work to reliability. And they should be realistic, not aspirational: some teams even schedule outages when they over-achieve, so users don’t come to depend on more than was promised.

Two kinds of SLO

Request-basedWindow-based
MeasuresGood requests ÷ all requestsGood time windows ÷ all windows
SuitsSteady traffic; requests that are revenue (payments)Low traffic; “how long were we down” (Prometheus itself)
WeaknessTen requests a minute: one failure is 10%Resolution is the window size; a bad window counts the same however bad
Book’s exampleA 500 req/s spike in one window among 20 req/min windows needs almost 16 days of normal traffic to get back to 50%The same spike is one bad window: 15 good windows (3.75 h) restore 95%
# request-based latency SLI: share of requests answered within 100 ms
clamp_min(sum without (pod, instance) (increase(prometheus_http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.1"}[5m])), 1)
/ ignoring (le)
clamp_min(sum without (pod, instance) (increase(prometheus_http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="+Inf"}[5m])), 1)

# window-based: each 5-minute window is good (1) or bad (0), averaged over 30 days
avg_over_time((slo:sli_success:ratio5m >= bool 0.999)[30d:5m])

clamp_min(…, 1) stops endpoints with no traffic from producing missing results; the book admits the edge case where a single slow request still scores 100%. The window-based version leans on bool, which turns a comparison into 0 or 1, and a subquery.

Recording rules first

Use one series name per kind of value and labels to tell SLOs apart, for example slo:sli_error:ratio_rate5m{service="checkout", slo="availability"}. The 30-day value is sum_over_time(…5m[30d]) / count_over_time(…5m[30d]), deliberately the same formula Sloth and Pyrra use.

Alerting on burn rate

Alerting when the SLO is already broken is too late. Alert on burn rate instead, and require both a long and a short window to exceed it: the long window makes the alert significant, the short one makes it stop soon after the problem does.

A correction to the bookThe printed example compares slo:sli_success:ratio5m with 14.4 * 0.001. A success ratio sits around 0.999, so that alert would always fire. Burn-rate alerts compare the error ratio with burn × (1 − objective), which is what Sloth generates and what POC 24 emits and tests.
Going deeper Sloth and Pyrra

Generating it all

SlothPyrra
ModelCLI that writes rule files; the maintainer considers it finishedLong-running service beside each Prometheus with a web UI; also has generate
Specerror_query and total_query with {{.window}}; raw.error_ratio_query for window-basedKubernetes-style ServiceLevelObjective; native latency indicator with success and total metrics and a grouping
Output17 rules in 3 groups, including the objective as a series; windows 5m, 30m, 1h, 2h, 6h, 1d, 3d, 30dOver a dozen rules; only plain selectors allowed, so no clamp_min or without
GotchaPage vs ticket naming takes explainingBurn windows assume a 28-day period: 32m, 1h4m, 2h9m, 6h26m, 1d1h43m, 4d6h51m

The book counts more than 80% fewer lines with Pyrra than writing the rules by hand. Either tool is a good choice; the point is that every team gets the same reviewed rules.

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the SRE book and Observability with Grafana also cover, from the knowledge map:
  • SLI, SLO, SLA: Indicator (good events over valid events), objective (the target), agreement (what happens if it is missed). See SRE ch 8, Grafana ch 9.
  • Error budget: One minus the SLO: the failure you are allowed, to be spent on change. See SRE ch 2, SRE ch 8.
  • Burn rate: How fast the budget is being spent. Page on a fast burn confirmed by a short window. See SRE ch 8.
  • Low-traffic alerting: Page only when a confidence interval’s lower bound exceeds the threshold. See SRE ch 8, SRE ch 9.
  • Window-based SLO: Count good and bad time windows instead of requests; suits low traffic. See SRE ch 8.
Say it in an interview

I define SLIs as good over valid events in recording rules with consistent names and labels, compute the 30-day ratio from the 5-minute one, and alert on burn rate with paired windows: 14.4× over five minutes and an hour, and 6× over thirty minutes and six hours, page; 3× and 1× open tickets. Window-based SLOs, with bool and a subquery, suit low-traffic services. In practice I generate it all with Sloth or Pyrra so every team gets the same rules.

On AWSLoad generated SLO rules into an AMP rule groups namespace and route severity=page and ticket alerts to different SNS topics through the AMP Alertmanager; show budget remaining in Amazon Managed Grafana. For services instrumented with CloudWatch Application Signals, CloudWatch SLOs offer burn-rate alarms natively. POC 24 generates the rules, simulates outages and slow burns, and has Terraform for the AMP namespace and alert routing.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Why multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerts rather than “error rate above 0.1% for five minutes”?

Show a model answer

A fixed threshold on a short window has two problems. It pages on brief blips that barely touch the budget, so people learn to ignore it, and it can miss a slow, steady burn that exhausts the budget in a week without ever crossing the threshold for long.

Burn rate normalises errors against the budget. A 14.4× burn spends 2% of a 30-day budget in an hour, worth waking someone; a 1× burn spends it exactly over the month, worth a ticket.

Using two windows per condition solves the other half. The long window (one hour) says the problem is significant, the short one (five minutes) says it is still happening, so the page stops within minutes of recovery instead of an hour later.

Two page conditions catch fast and medium burns, two ticket conditions catch slow ones. In POC 24’s simulation, a full outage pages within a couple of minutes, three minutes of 10% errors pages nobody, and a steady 4× burn opens a ticket but never pages.

Quick check: In a 14.4× burn-rate alert with 5m and 1h windows, what is the short window for?
The long window gives significance; the short one confirms the burn is still happening, so it resets quickly.
Quick check: Which SLO type suits a service that gets ten requests a minute?
One failed request out of ten is a 10% error rate; windows weight time instead of requests.
Your turnAdd a third SLO to POC 24’s slo.yml for a low-traffic admin API, regenerate, and write a window-based rule for it with window_based_rule(). Then explain to yourself why the test test_a_brief_blip_pages_nobody passes.
Key takeaways
  • SLI in recording rules, 30-day ratio from the 5-minute one.
  • Page on fast burn confirmed by two windows; ticket on slow burn.
  • Generate rules with Sloth or Pyrra; compare error ratios, never success ratios.
Prometheus · ScalingChapters 14–15 · POC 27, 28 · 6 min read

OpenTelemetry, and the signals Prometheus doesn’t cover

You will learn
  • What OpenTelemetry is: specification, API, SDKs, semantic conventions and OTLP
  • The collector’s receivers, processors and exporters, core and contrib
  • Scraping Prometheus metrics with the collector, and pushing OTLP into Prometheus
  • Logs, traces and exemplars: where metrics stop being enough

OpenTelemetry in one picture

OpenTelemetry (OTel) is not a program you run; it is a specification. It came from a rare event: two competing projects, Google’s OpenCensus (2017) and the CNCF’s OpenTracing (2016), merged in 2019 instead of becoming the fifteenth competing standard in the xkcd strip the book reprints.

PartFor
APIPeople writing OTel SDKs
SDKsApplication developers instrumenting code
Semantic conventionsEveryone: standard names for metrics, spans and attributes, so http.server.request.duration means the same thing in every service. The author’s favourite part
OTLPA separate protocol spec for sending all three signals over gRPC (preferred) or HTTP

Many teams still use Prometheus client libraries for metrics, partly because OTel’s model differs: an OTel “counter” need not be monotonic. In the collector a Prometheus counter becomes a Sum, a gauge a Gauge, and labels become data point attributes.

The collector

Receiverspush (OTLP) or pull (prometheus receiver)
→
Processorsfilter, transform, enrich, batch; optional
→
ExportersPrometheus remote write, OTLP, vendors

One pipeline per signal. Core releases are minimal; contrib has dozens of components; the builder makes a custom binary with only what you need.

The prometheus receiver accepts a normal scrape_configs block, service discovery included. The collector exposes its own metrics on port 8888.

OTLP into Prometheus

From 2.47, Prometheus can receive OTLP with --enable-feature=otlp-write-receiver; the collector’s otlphttp exporter points at http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/otlp and adds /v1/metrics itself. The author’s caution: the up series you see then comes from the collector’s own scrape, not from Prometheus, so it says nothing about whether delivery works. Have Prometheus scrape the collector and watch otelcol_exporter_send_failed_metric_points_total, and ask whether mixing push and pull is worth it; Prometheus is still pull-first.

Going deeper chapter 15: beyond Prometheus

What metrics can’t do

Observability is about unknown unknowns. Metrics must be defined before you need them, so some questions will always lack a metric. Logs and traces fill the gap.

LogsThe oldest and most accessible signal and the worst signal-to-noise. Mostly unstructured; JSON is hard to read; logfmt (key=value, used by Prometheus itself) is the compromise. Don’t derive metrics by parsing logs: formats change and the parsing breaks silently. Emit the metric.
TracesThe newest core signal and the best signal-to-noise, once sampled: keep 1% of normal requests, half of slow ones and all errors. Because they are sampled they can’t replace metrics’ complete view; they add the detail.
ExemplarsWith --enable-feature=exemplar-storage, a sample can carry the trace ID of a request it counted, so Grafana can jump from a latency spike straight to an example trace.

The glue is consistent metadata: if metrics say app="servicex", logs must not say app="service-x". Grafana’s Loki (“like Prometheus, but for logs”: labels, a WAL, LogQL, object storage, a single-binary mode) and Tempo (TraceQL) were built to share Prometheus’ label model; with Mimir and Grafana they form the LGTM stack. The author runs Loki at several hundred thousand lines a second. The Grafana track of this course covers that stack in depth.

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that Observability with Grafana also covers, from the knowledge map:
  • Trace context: W3C traceparent and baggage carried across every hop; X-Ray and B3 at the edges. See Grafana ch 6.
  • Collector topology: Node agents, a single cluster agent and a gateway, with buffers sized for outages. See Grafana ch 10, Grafana ch 11.
Say it in an interview

OpenTelemetry is a vendor-neutral specification: APIs, SDKs, semantic conventions and the OTLP protocol, with a collector that receives, processes and exports all three signals. I scrape Prometheus metrics with the collector’s prometheus receiver or remote-write from it, and I’m careful with OTLP push into Prometheus because the up series no longer tells you delivery works. Metrics can’t answer every question, so I add logs and sampled traces with shared labels, and exemplars to jump from a metric to a trace.

On AWSAWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) is AWS’s supported collector and SDKs: OTLP in, Prometheus remote write with SigV4 to AMP, awsxray to X-Ray, awscloudwatchlogs to CloudWatch Logs, installed on EKS as an add-on. X-Ray propagates its own header, which ADOT’s SDKs handle alongside W3C. CloudWatch Application Signals builds service maps and SLOs on top. POC 28 is a full ADOT architecture for EKS with a validator; POC 27 covers propagation, sampling and TraceQL.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

An application team wants to switch from the Prometheus client library to the OpenTelemetry SDK for metrics. What would you tell them?

Show a model answer

It is a reasonable direction because the SDK gives one API for metrics, traces and logs, semantic-convention names, and exemplars linking metrics to traces. But I’d point out the practical differences before they start.

Collection changes from pull to push unless they keep a Prometheus exporter in the SDK. With OTLP push they lose the free up series, so we need another way to know a service stopped reporting: alert on the absence of its metrics, and monitor the collector’s send failures.

Names and types change. OTel names use dots and units (http.server.request.duration in seconds); converted to Prometheus they gain suffixes such as _seconds and _total. Every dashboard, recording rule and alert that uses the old names needs migrating, and histograms may become exponential histograms, which the backend must support.

So I’d suggest running both for a while, renaming in dashboards and rules through a mixin or generator, and agreeing semantic conventions across teams first, since consistency is the real win.

Quick check: Which part of OpenTelemetry standardises attribute and metric names?
Semantic conventions define names and meanings so every service reports the same way.
Quick check: When the collector pushes OTLP into Prometheus, why is the up series misleading?
It says the collector scraped; it doesn’t say the push to Prometheus succeeded.
Your turnRead POC 28’s gateway.yaml and trace one span from the node agent to X-Ray and the span metrics it produces to AMP. Then run POC 27 and convert a W3C traceparent into an X-Ray header with to_xray().
Key takeaways
  • OTel is a specification; semantic conventions and OTLP are its most useful parts.
  • The collector is receivers, processors and exporters; scraping Prometheus is a receiver like any other.
  • Logs and traces cover what metrics can’t; shared labels and exemplars connect them.
Observability with GrafanaRob Chapman and Peter Holmes · Packt, January 2024 · 15 chapters · 4 min read

Observability with Grafana: the fourth book on the map

You will learn
  • What this book adds to the Prometheus book
  • The five personas it uses, and why they matter in interviews
  • How the lessons are grouped and which POCs go with them

Where it fits

The Prometheus book goes deep on one signal. This book goes wide: logs in Loki, metrics in Mimir and Prometheus, traces in Tempo, profiles in Pyroscope, real user monitoring with Faro, load tests with k6, and Grafana itself for dashboards, alerting, on-call and incidents. It then turns to running all of that as a platform: infrastructure as code, architecture, access control, and observability across the DevOps life cycle.

It is written for a broad audience, so some chapters are walkthroughs of the Grafana Cloud UI. The lessons here keep the concepts and the decisions, and leave the click-by-click steps to the book’s repository.

Five personas

Every chapter frames its advice around five people. Using them in an interview answer (“for the on-call engineer this dashboard needs…, for the service manager…”) shows you design observability for users, not for tools.

PersonaRoleNeeds from observabilityPain
Diego DeveloperFrontend, backend, platformEasy instrumentation libraries; clear performance standardsToo much noise; being forced to change code when tooling changes
Ophelia OperatorSRE, DevOps, supportGood data fast; seeing that a deploy happened when trouble startedAlerts she can’t fix; burnout
Steven ServiceService delivery, incident coordinationComparisons across products; getting the right people on a call; a record for the post-mortemFinding who can fix it
Pelé ProductProduct managerHow customers actually use the product; a shared language with engineersNo view of usage; lost trust when stability slips
Masha ManagerLeadershipAggregated, trustworthy data on delivery and costApologising to customers; cloud overspend

Grafana · SignalsChapter 1 · 6 min read

Observability, the signals, and the Grafana stack

You will learn
  • Monitoring versus observability, from control theory and a steam engine
  • Metrics, logs, traces, and the other signals: profiles and events
  • What each part of the LGTM stack does, and what else Grafana Labs offers
  • The alternatives, and the SaaS versus self-hosted choice

The big picture

Modern systems have moved from complicated (an engine: clear cause and effect) to complex (city traffic: behaviour emerges from interactions). Downtime is expensive; the book quotes an estimate of about $9,000 a minute from a 2016 Ponemon study. Observability is how you manage that risk, and done badly it is a cost of its own.

The term comes from control theory. James Watt’s steam-engine governor illustrates both ideas. Its spinning weights measure one predefined quantity, shaft speed, and adjust the throttle: that is monitoring. But if the governor spins oddly fast or slow, you can infer that the sliding ring is sticking or the adjustment is wrong, without having defined “too fast” in advance and without knowing the whole engine: that is observability, inferring internal state from external outputs.

The Panama Canal example

Monitor and alert onObserve within normal limits
A gate stuck openA gate that is slowly taking longer to open: maintenance due
Water level dropping fast: a leakWater dropping only when the level is high: a small leak near the top of the wall
A ship taking too long to exitShips slower when the wind blows from one direction: compare hourly averages

The lesson: the same data that drives alerts also answers questions nobody thought to alert on.

The signals

SignalWhat it isStrengthWeakness
MetricsNumbers at points in time with labelsCheap, fast to search, ideal for “is something wrong?”Must be defined in advance
LogsText records of events, usually unstructuredRich detail about what happenedSlow to search; the same failure is worded many ways
TracesThe path of one request: a trace ID shared by spans, each with its own ID and parentShows where time and errors go across servicesVolume; needs propagation and sampling
ProfilesStack samples of CPU and memory useFinds the expensive function; cuts costLow level, needs domain knowledge
EventsA whole action, such as “deployed v1.4”Context that shortens incidentsOverloaded term

A trace across the canal locks: the ship gets a trace ID at the first lock, each lock creates a span (entry, exit, events such as gates opening, attributes such as the ship’s ID) and passes the trace ID and its span ID on to the next lock.

The Grafana stack

LokiLogs. Indexes only labels, stores lines compressed in object storage, scales queriers horizontally. GA November 2019.
GrafanaVisualisation since 2014: 150+ data source plugins and thousands of community dashboards. Began as a fork of Kibana for Graphite.
TempoTraces on object storage, aiming to keep 100% of the read path; 2M+ spans per second at 1.0. Can generate metrics from spans. GA June 2021.
MimirMetrics: a Prometheus-compatible TSDB on object storage, forked from Cortex, load-tested to a billion active series. GA March 2022.

Together, LGTM (a joke on “looks good to me”). Around them: Grafana Agent (collection, since succeeded by Grafana Alloy), Enterprise data-source plugins (GitLab, Snowflake, Databricks…), the incident response tools (Alerting, OnCall, Incident), Faro for real user monitoring, k6 for load testing (acquired 2021) and Pyroscope for continuous profiling (acquired 2023, merged with Phlare).

Going deeper alternatives and deployment choices

Alternatives and deployment

The book lists collectors (OpenTelemetry Collector, Fluent Bit, Vector, Beats, Telegraf, StatsD, collectd, rsyslog, Fluentd, Zipkin) and around fifty storage and visualisation products, from CloudWatch and Datadog to Elastic, Honeycomb, Jaeger, New Relic, Splunk, Thanos and VictoriaMetrics. Knowing the landscape matters more than memorising it.

Grafana Labs’ products are mostly open source and can run anywhere, packaged for Linux, Windows, containers, Helm and Tanka. The alternative is Grafana Cloud, which gives you the storage backends and Grafana with an SLA and none of the operational work. The book uses Cloud’s free tier for its examples.

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the SRE book and Mastering Prometheus also cover, from the knowledge map:
  • Observability: Someone without tribal knowledge can test and reject hypotheses quickly. See SRE ch 9, Prometheus ch 1.
Say it in an interview

Monitoring watches for conditions you defined in advance; observability lets you infer internal state from outputs and answer new questions. I use metrics to know something is wrong, traces to find where, logs and profiles to find why, and events like deployments for context. In the Grafana world that is Mimir or Prometheus, Tempo, Loki and Pyroscope, all on object storage, with Grafana on top.

On AWSThe AWS-native equivalents: CloudWatch metrics and Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus for metrics, CloudWatch Logs for logs, X-Ray (and Application Signals) for traces, CloudWatch RUM for the frontend, CloudWatch Synthetics for probes, and Amazon Managed Grafana to view them all. Many teams mix: AMP plus Amazon Managed Grafana for application metrics, CloudWatch for AWS service metrics, and Loki or CloudWatch Logs for logs.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

What is the difference between monitoring and observability, and does the distinction matter in practice?

Show a model answer

Monitoring is watching for conditions you defined in advance: CPU above a threshold, an endpoint returning errors, a queue too long. It answers known questions, and it is how you get alerted.

Observability is a property of the system: how well you can understand its internal state from what it emits, including for questions nobody anticipated. The book’s canal example makes it concrete: the same water-level data that alerts on a big leak can reveal a small leak near the top of the wall, if you can slice it by level and time.

In practice it matters in two ways. It changes what you collect: high-dimensional data you can slice later (traces with attributes, structured logs, labelled metrics) rather than only pre-aggregated checks. And it changes how incidents go: when the failure is novel, which in a complex system is most of the time, you need to ask new questions quickly, not wait for someone to add a dashboard.

I wouldn’t throw monitoring away; alerts on user-facing symptoms are still the entry point. Observability is what you need after the page.

Quick check: What does the L in LGTM stand for, and what does it store?
Loki stores logs, indexing only labels.
Quick check: Which signal is best for answering “is something wrong right now?” cheaply?
Metrics are small, fast to query and ideal for alerting.
Your turnPick a system you know and write the canal table for it: three things you would alert on, and three questions you could answer from the same data without new alerts.
Key takeaways
  • Monitoring answers known questions; observability lets you ask new ones.
  • Metrics, logs, traces, profiles and events each answer a different question.
  • LGTM: Loki, Grafana, Tempo, Mimir, all on object storage.
Grafana · SignalsChapters 2–3 · POC 27 · 6 min read

Instrumenting applications and infrastructure

You will learn
  • Structured, semi-structured and unstructured logs, and seven common formats
  • Counters, gauges, histograms and summaries, and how metric protocols differ
  • Spans, traces and tracing protocols, and best practice for each signal
  • Automatic versus manual instrumentation; infrastructure telemetry through syslog and SNMP
  • The book’s lab: Grafana Cloud plus the OpenTelemetry demo

Logs

StructureWhat it isTrade-off
StructuredA fixed shape, usually JSON or key=value; can be validated against a schemaEasy for machines; JSON is hard for people to scan
Semi-structuredHuman-readable with a known pattern, parsed by regular expressionsFragile parsing
UnstructuredFree text, colours, spacing for terminalsEvery consumer writes custom parsing; developers can’t change the log without breaking someone. Multi-line entries such as stack traces need encapsulation on the leading timestamp
FormatWhere you meet it
CEFSecurity tools (ArcSight, SIEMs): prefix, pipe-separated header, key=value body
NCSA Common Log FormatWeb servers; fixed fields, - for missing
W3C ExtendedIIS; configurable #Fields
Windows Event LogWindows; categorised, documented event IDs
JSONModern applications
SyslogNetwork devices, Linux; ports 514 and 6514 (TLS)
logfmtGo projects, Prometheus itself; key=value, human-readable

Metrics

A metric is a name, a value and dimensions. The four types behave differently, and protocols define them slightly differently: StatsD resets counters on every flush, Prometheus only when the process restarts. Know which one you are using.

CounterGaugeHistogramSummary
Goes downNo (resets only)YesNoNo
PercentilesNoNoEstimated at query timeComputed in the client
Aggregate across instancesYesYesYesNo
Typical queryrate()valuehistogram_quantile(rate(_bucket))read quantile
A correction to the book’s tableIt says only counters can be used with a rate function. In Prometheus, histogram _bucket, _sum and _count series are counters, and you always take their rate() before histogram_quantile. See the PromQL lesson.
ProtocolPush or pullTypes
StatsDPush (UDP 8125)Counters, gauges, timers, histograms, meters
DogStatsDPushStatsD plus tags, histograms, service checks, events
OTLPPush (gRPC 4317, HTTP 4318)Counters, gauges, histograms, legacy summaries
PrometheusPull (/metrics)Counters, gauges, cumulative histograms, summaries

Best practice from the book: decide what you want metrics for first (it feeds SLIs and SLOs), manage cardinality (labelling by server gives hundreds of series, by user millions, and you pay for each), and add context with exemplars so a data point links to a trace.

Traces

A trace is a directed acyclic graph of spans. The trace has an ID, a name and start and end times. Each span has the trace ID, its own span ID, its parent’s span ID, a name and timings. If a service receives no trace ID it starts a new one; otherwise it passes the one it received to every call it makes.

ProtocolNotes
OTLPAttributes, context propagation, span events, span links, span kind
ZipkinTags, annotations, kind; B3 headers
JaegerThrift and Proto formats; the Jaeger SDKs are retired in favour of OpenTelemetry
ConcernMitigation
Performance: latency, memory, startup cost, worse with auto-instrumentationSampling between 0% and 100%, decided at the root and passed down so traces stay whole
Cost: network and storageSample, filter, set retention
AccuracyValidate context propagation, or spans split into separate traces

Libraries

Automatic instrumentation is fast to adopt and gives visibility in minutes, by bytecode manipulation in Java or monkey patching in Python and JavaScript; without care it costs performance and money. Manual instrumentation gives exactly the telemetry you want but needs code and API knowledge. The industry is converging on OpenTelemetry SDKs; Spring Boot 3’s Micrometer exports OTLP by default.

Going deeper infrastructure telemetry and the lab

Infrastructure

ComponentTelemetryHow
Servers (bare metal or VMs)Temperature, CPU, disk, memory: capacity forecastingAn agent on the OS
Network and security devicesLatency, throughput, packet loss, bandwidthSNMP polling and traps; syslog from firewalls
Power and coolingSupply and backup state, voltage, wattageSNMP; Modbus registers on older kit

Syslog (from Sendmail in the 1980s) and SNMP (part of the original IETF suite, with traps for events) are still everywhere; most collectors, the OpenTelemetry Collector included, can receive them.

The lab

Chapter 3 builds the environment the rest of the book uses: a Grafana Cloud free stack (about 10,000 metric series, 50 GB each of logs, traces and profiles, three IRM users, 500 k6 virtual-user hours), a local k3d Kubernetes cluster, the OpenTelemetry Collector Helm chart with credentials in a separate values file, and the OpenTelemetry demo, a polyglot telescope shop with a load generator. The common mistake is endpoints: Loki needs /loki/api/v1/push, Prometheus /api/prom/push, and Tempo a host and port 443 with no scheme.

Say it in an interview

I prefer structured logs in JSON or logfmt so nobody depends on fragile parsing, histograms over summaries because they aggregate across instances, and OpenTelemetry SDKs for traces with context propagated on every call and sampling decided at the root. Before instrumenting I decide what questions the data must answer, because that drives which SLIs I need and keeps cardinality, and cost, under control.

On AWSThe ADOT SDKs and collector are AWS’s OpenTelemetry distribution; auto-instrumentation agents exist for Java, Python, .NET and Node.js and are injected by the ADOT operator on EKS. CloudWatch embedded metric format turns structured JSON logs into metrics for CloudWatch-native setups. For network gear, run an SNMP exporter or the collector’s SNMP receiver in a VPC that can reach devices, and syslog into CloudWatch Logs or Loki through Fluent Bit.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

A team asks whether to use auto-instrumentation or manual instrumentation for a new Java service. What do you recommend?

Show a model answer

Both, in that order. Auto-instrumentation with the OpenTelemetry Java agent gives server and client spans for HTTP, gRPC, database and messaging libraries, plus standard metrics, on day one with no code changes. That covers most of what an on-call engineer needs: where time goes and which dependency fails.

Then add manual instrumentation where the business logic lives: spans around important internal steps, attributes such as tenant or order type (on spans, not metric labels), and a few domain metrics such as orders placed. Auto-instrumentation can’t know those.

I’d watch three things. Overhead: measure startup time and latency with the agent, and turn off instrumentations you don’t need. Sampling: parent-based, decided at the edge, so traces stay complete. And naming: follow semantic conventions so dashboards work across services.

On AWS I’d use the ADOT Java agent, injected by the operator via a pod annotation, exporting OTLP to the node collector.

Quick check: Why can’t summaries from several pods be combined into one percentile?
That is why the book marks summaries as not aggregatable across series.
Quick check: What happens if a service drops the incoming trace context?
Broken propagation splits one request into several traces.
Your turnTake one service you know and list: its log format (and whether anyone parses it), its three most important metrics and their types, and where trace context could be dropped (queues, thread pools, third-party calls). Then run POC 27 and check a traceparent header from your own logs with parse_traceparent().
Key takeaways
  • Prefer structured logs; know which format each source uses.
  • Know your metric types and your protocol’s definitions of them.
  • Traces depend on propagation; sample at the root.
Grafana · SignalsChapter 4 · POC 26 · 5 min read

Logs with Loki and LogQL

You will learn
  • How Loki stores logs: streams, labels and chunks
  • LogQL’s two halves: stream selectors and the pipeline
  • Parsers, typed label filters, line and label formatting
  • Metric queries over logs, including unwrap
  • Loki’s architecture and the label rules that keep it cheap

The big picture

Loki was built to be the Prometheus of logs: simple ingestion with no parsing at write time, an index of labels only, and everything in object storage. Each entry has a nanosecond timestamp, a label set and the raw line. Every unique label set is a stream; a stream’s lines are batched, compressed and stored as chunks. Labels are the index and the only thing you can use to find chunks.

LogQL

A query is a stream selector followed by an optional pipeline. The selector uses Prometheus matchers and must include at least one that doesn’t match empty ({app=~".+"} is fine, {app=~".*"} isn’t). The pipeline runs line by line, left to right, dropping lines as it goes.

{component=~".+service"}
  |= "emailservice"                                  # line filter: cheap, do it first
  | json                                              # parse JSON into labels
  | resources_k8s_container_restart_count > 0        # typed label filter
  | line_format "{{.body}}"                           # rewrite the line
  | __error__=""                                       # drop lines that failed to parse
StageSyntaxNotes
Line filters|= != |~ !~A distributed grep, case-sensitive. |= ip("10.0.0.0/8") matches addresses and ranges. | decolorize strips terminal colour codes
Parsersjson, logfmt, pattern, regexp, unpackjson flattens nested keys with _ and skips arrays; pattern is <ip> - <_> … for unstructured lines
Label filtersstatus >= 500, latency > 250ms, size > 2MBThe value’s form sets the type: string, number, duration or bytes. Failed conversions set __error__. Chain with and, or, commas or spaces
Formattingline_format, label_format, dropGo templates with .label, __line__, __timestamp__; new=old renames, new="{{.old}}" copies

Metrics from logs

KindFunctionsExample
Log range aggregationsrate, count_over_time, bytes_rate, bytes_over_time, absent_over_timesum by (component) (rate({component=~".+service"} |= "error" [1m]))
Unwrapped range aggregationssum_over_time, avg_over_time, quantile_over_time, rate_counter…quantile_over_time(0.99, {container="web"} | json | unwrap duration_seconds(request_time) [1m]) by (path)
Aggregation operatorssum, avg, topk, sort_desc…topk(10, sum(rate({region="us-west1"}[10m])) by (name))

Architecture

Loki runs as one binary, as a simple scalable deployment (read, write and backend targets) or as full microservices. Reads and writes scale independently. The ruler turns LogQL into recording rules and alerts; the compactor applies retention and deduplicates.

Going deeper the rules that keep Loki cheap

Labels are locators, not content

Good labels: few values, used to find streamsBad labels: unbounded values
namespace, cluster, job, app, instance, filenameuser ID, trace ID, path, status code, date

A bad label multiplies streams and chunks: twenty namespaces, sixty apps and three clusters is 3,600 streams; add a user ID with fifty thousand values and it is 180 million. Leave those values in the line and extract them at query time with a parser. And filter first: line filters before parsers, because parsing is the expensive step.

The LogQL Analyzer on Grafana’s site explains each step of a query on sample lines, in far more detail than Explain query in the editor. LogCLI runs queries from a terminal, including instant metric queries and label statistics.

Say it in an interview

Loki indexes only labels, so a query is a cheap stream selector plus a pipeline that greps, parses and filters lines at read time. I keep labels to low-cardinality locators like namespace, app and cluster, put IDs and paths in the line, filter with |= before parsing, and use unwrap with quantile_over_time when the latency I need only exists in logs.

On AWSSelf-managed Loki on AWS runs in simple scalable mode on EKS with chunks and the TSDB index in S3 and an IRSA role per component. Ship logs with Fluent Bit (the AWS for Fluent Bit image has a Loki output) or the OpenTelemetry collector’s filelog receiver. CloudWatch Logs with Logs Insights is the AWS-native alternative; POC 26 maps three LogQL queries to their Insights equivalents. Grafana Cloud’s AWS integration can forward CloudWatch Logs into Loki with a Lambda or Firehose.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Your Loki queries are slow and ingestion costs are rising. What would you look at?

Show a model answer

Streams first. The number of active streams per tenant tells me whether a label with too many values has crept in. Typical culprits are request IDs, pod names on very short-lived pods, status codes and paths as labels. I’d move those into the log line and extract them with a parser at query time.

Then query shape. Queries that start with a broad selector and a parser, with no line filter, decompress and parse everything. Adding a |= "error" or |~ before | json often makes them an order of magnitude faster. Narrowing the selector with another label (namespace, app) reduces the chunks fetched.

Then the read path: query frontend splitting and caching, enough queriers, and results cache for dashboards that refresh often.

For cost, I’d look at volume by app with sum by (app) (bytes_over_time({…}[1h])), drop debug logs at the collector, and set retention by stream. Where people derive metrics from logs, I’d move that to emitting the metric directly, which the Prometheus book also recommends.

Quick check: What does Loki index?
Lines are stored compressed and searched at query time; the index holds labels.
Quick check: Which is a good Loki label?
Labels should be low-cardinality locators.
Your turnRun POC 26 and write a pipeline that finds 5xx lines from the access logs with the pattern parser and returns only the URI and status with line_format. Then use label_design() on your own log labels.
Key takeaways
  • Streams are label sets; labels are the only index.
  • Selector, then line filters, then parsers, then typed label filters.
  • Labels are locators: keep IDs, paths and codes in the line.
Grafana · SignalsChapter 5 · POC 20, 21 · 6 min read

Metrics in Grafana: PromQL in practice, protocols, storage and exemplars

You will learn
  • How PromQL looks from Grafana’s Explore: builder, code, table view, query types
  • Two PromQL queries every engineer writes: success rate and p95 latency
  • Push and pull protocols: StatsD, OTLP, Prometheus, SNMP
  • Graphite, Prometheus and Mimir storage compared
  • Exemplars: from a metric point to a trace

PromQL from Grafana

The PromQL itself is covered in depth in the Prometheus track. This chapter adds how it feels in Grafana. Explore has a builder and a code editor; switching the result to a table shows every series and label, and clicking a value adds it as a filter. A query of type Range draws a graph; Instant returns the latest value; a range vector like x[5m] on its own only works as an instant query.

Use $__rate_interval in every rate(): Grafana picks a window at least four scrape intervals long for the current zoom. Explain walks through a query step by step, Kick start your query offers templates, and the Query inspector shows timings and raw data.

Two queries to know by heart

# success rate per instance, so one failing pod isn’t hidden by healthy ones
sum by (instance) (rate(app_frontend_requests_total{status=~"2.."}[5m]))
/
sum by (instance) (rate(app_frontend_requests_total[5m]))

# p95 latency
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(http_server_duration_milliseconds_bucket[$__rate_interval])))
Two slips in the chapterThe printed success-rate query divides by app_frontend_requests without the _total suffix, which would return nothing; and its first vector-matching example says 31 + 8 = 29 (it is 39). Small, but in an interview “the denominator returns nothing” is exactly the bug you should spot.

Prefer percentiles to averages: a p95 of 300 ms means 95% of requests were at least that fast, while an average hides the slow tail that users notice.

Push and pull

ProtocolModelWorth knowing
StatsD / DogStatsDPush, UDP 8125Fast, no delivery guarantee, no authentication; expose it on localhost. The Prometheus statsd_exporter is a stepping stone to migrate
OTLPPush, gRPC 4317 / HTTP 4318Authentication, acknowledgements, server-side throttling, gzip. The collector accepts almost any input, so it suits a mixed estate
PrometheusPull, /metricsThe app needs no knowledge of who reads it; matches Kubernetes’ liveness and readiness pattern; rich service discovery
SNMPPull, plus traps that pushSince 1988, universal on network hardware; a large attack surface if misconfigured

Where metrics are stored

Graphite (Whisper)PrometheusMimir
LayoutOne fixed-size file per seriesTwo-hour immutable blocks: chunks, index, meta.json; a head block with a WALThe same blocks, in object storage
ScaleSearching reads every file: heavy disk I/OOne node reads and writes; no replicationPer-tenant TSDBs on many ingesters; queries split by time across queriers
DurabilityNo built-in redundancyLocal diskReplicated writes; the compactor merges duplicates

Grafana Cloud still accepts Graphite data for teams that use it. The rest of the detail on blocks is in the TSDB lesson.

Exemplars

An exemplar is a sample trace attached to a metric point. Configure exemplars at collection, turn on the Exemplars toggle in a panel’s options, and stars appear on the graph. Hovering one shows the trace’s span ID and attributes; Query with Tempo opens the trace. It is the quickest route from “p99 jumped” to “this request, in this service”.

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that Mastering Prometheus also covers, from the knowledge map:
  • Series and cardinality: A metric name plus one label set; every new value is a new series in memory and index. See Prometheus ch 3, Prometheus ch 7.
  • Head block, WAL and blocks: Two hours in memory with a write-ahead log, then immutable blocks compacted up to 31 days. See Prometheus ch 3.
  • rate, increase and irate: Reset-aware, extrapolated over the window; irate uses the last two samples. See Prometheus ch 3.
  • Remote write: Sharded queues with backoff to long-term storage. See Prometheus ch 9.
  • Thanos, Mimir, VictoriaMetrics: Object-storage blocks with a global query layer, central multi-tenant ingestion, or efficient local disks. See Prometheus ch 9, Prometheus ch 10.
Say it in an interview

In Grafana I write PromQL with $__rate_interval, check series in the table view, and choose range or instant query types deliberately. I compute success rates per instance so one bad pod isn’t averaged away, and latency as a histogram percentile. Prometheus pulls, StatsD and OTLP push; Mimir keeps Prometheus’ block format but in object storage with replicated ingestion. Exemplars link a metric point to the trace behind it.

On AWSAmazon Managed Grafana with an AMP data source gives the same Explore experience; enable SigV4. AMP stores exemplars sent by remote write, so exemplar stars work when your collector forwards them and the trace backend (X-Ray or Tempo) is configured as the exemplar link. CloudWatch metrics are queried at read time through the CloudWatch data source. POC 20 computes these queries by hand; POC 21 shows the block internals.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Your error-rate panel shows 0.1% but users report many failures. What could be hiding the errors?

Show a model answer

First, aggregation. If the panel sums across all instances, one failing pod among fifty is diluted to 2% of traffic, and if that pod only takes some routes, even less. Splitting by instance, route and status class usually reveals it, which is why the book’s success-rate query groups by instance.

Second, what the metric counts. If errors are measured at the server and the failures happen before it (DNS, load balancer, TLS, timeouts at the client), the server never sees them. Load balancer metrics, client-side metrics or RUM catch those.

Third, the query itself: a status regex that misses some codes, a missing _total so the denominator is wrong, or a rate() window shorter than two scrapes giving gaps. And retries: a client retrying until success makes the server count several attempts, hiding user-visible slowness.

Then I’d align the SLI with the user journey: measure at the edge or the client where possible, and alert on burn rate per journey, not one global average.

Quick check: Why use $__rate_interval in Grafana rather than a fixed [1m]?
A fixed window can contain fewer than two samples at some resolutions, producing gaps.
Quick check: What distinguishes Mimir’s storage from a single Prometheus?
Mimir keeps the TSDB format and scales it horizontally.
Your turnIn Grafana (any instance), build the success-rate and p95 queries above for a service you have, switch the panel to table view and filter by clicking a label value. If your stack sends exemplars, turn them on and follow one to its trace.
Key takeaways
  • Use the table view, the right query type and $__rate_interval.
  • Success rate by instance; latency by histogram percentile.
  • Exemplars connect metrics to traces.
Grafana · SignalsChapter 6 · POC 27 · 5 min read

Traces with Tempo and TraceQL, and how context propagates

You will learn
  • Tempo’s view of a trace, its search modes and the service graph
  • TraceQL: intrinsic and attribute fields, selection, structural operators, aggregates
  • Pivoting between traces, logs and metrics
  • OTLP, Zipkin and Jaeger; W3C traceparent, B3, Jaeger headers and baggage
  • Tempo’s architecture and the metrics generator

The big picture

Tempo stores traces in object storage and searches them with TraceQL, modelled like LogQL on PromQL. At the version the book covers (2.3), TraceQL selects spans and traces well but analysis is limited; that is changing fast.

Search modeUse
TraceQLThe default: precise queries
Search (basic)Drop-downs; deprecated from Grafana 10.3
Loki searchFind log lines carrying trace IDs, then open the trace
JSON fileImport an exported trace, good for sharing and learning the data model
Service graphServices as nodes, calls as edges with rates and latency, errors in red, with RED panels above

TraceQL

Field kindExamples
Intrinsicstatus (error, ok, unset), statusMessage, duration, name, kind (server, client, producer, consumer, internal), traceDuration, rootName, rootServiceName
Span attributesspan.http.method, set by the application
Resource attributesresource.k8s.node.name, describing what produced the span
Either.http.method: works, but say span. or resource. for efficiency
{ resource.service.name = "checkout" && status = error }          # spans
{ .service.name = "frontend" } > { .service.name = "productcatalogservice" }   # direct child
{ .service.name = "frontend" } >> { .service.name = "cartservice" }   # any descendant
{ .service.name = "frontend" } ~ { .service.name = "frontend" }     # siblings
{ status = error } | count() > 10                                   # aggregate per trace
{ span.http.method = "GET" } | avg(duration) > 20ms

Pivoting

From a span, Logs for this span opens Loki filtered by the span’s service name and namespace. In the other direction, services that write trace and span IDs into their logs let Loki link back to Tempo. From a metric, exemplars open a trace. That three-way movement is what makes the stack worth more than its parts.

Context propagation

Spans reach the collector separately from each service; what ties them together is the context each service passes in request headers.

FormatHeaderStatus
W3C Trace Contexttraceparent: 00-{32 hex trace}-{16 hex parent}-{flags} and tracestateStandard since November 2021; flags currently only “sampled”
W3C Baggagebaggage: k=v,…, percent-encoded, at most 64 members and 8,192 bytesCarries context such as a tenant ID downstream; visible on the wire, so no secrets
Zipkin B3X-B3-TraceId, -SpanId, -ParentSpanId, -Sampled, -Flags, or single b3Still common; OTel supports it
Jaegeruber-trace-id: trace:span:parent:flags, uberctx-*Deprecated with the Jaeger SDKs

OTel SDKs speak W3C, B3 and Jaeger. AWS X-Ray’s header isn’t in the mainline distribution, which is why AWS ships its own distribution, ADOT. Baggage is the elegant part: a top-level service can pass tenantId so a downstream service can record it in telemetry without adding it to its own data model.

Going deeper architecture

Tempo’s architecture

Distributorroutes spans to ingesters by trace ID
→
Ingestergroups spans into traces, batches into blocks, writes bloom filters and indexes, flushes
→
Object storageS3, GCS, Azure

Optional metrics generator: receives spans from the distributor and writes service-graph and span metrics to any Prometheus remote-write backend.

Reads go through a query frontend that shards queries by block, and queriers that read flushed blocks from storage or recent ones from ingesters. A compactor optimises storage. Like Loki and Mimir, everything scales horizontally.

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that Mastering Prometheus also covers, from the knowledge map:
  • Trace context: W3C traceparent and baggage carried across every hop; X-Ray and B3 at the edges. See Prometheus ch 14.
Say it in an interview

Tempo stores traces in object storage and I search them with TraceQL: intrinsic fields like status and duration, span and resource attributes, and structural operators for parent, descendant and sibling relationships. Traces only work if context propagates, so I standardise on W3C traceparent, use baggage for things like tenant IDs, and link spans to logs and metrics to traces through exemplars. Tempo’s metrics generator turns spans into RED metrics and service graphs.

On AWSX-Ray is AWS’s trace store, with Application Signals building service maps and SLOs on it; Tempo on EKS with S3 is the self-managed option, and Amazon Managed Grafana can query both. ADOT handles X-Ray’s X-Amzn-Trace-Id alongside W3C so traces survive ALB, API Gateway and Lambda hops; use an X-Ray-compatible trace ID generator when exporting to X-Ray. POC 27 converts headers, enforces baggage limits, evaluates TraceQL structural operators and builds span metrics and a service graph.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Traces from your checkout flow show up as several disconnected traces. How do you find and fix the break?

Show a model answer

Disconnected traces mean some hop isn’t passing context. I’d look at where the split happens: the first span of each fragment tells me which service started a new trace instead of continuing one.

The usual causes: a service whose HTTP or gRPC client isn’t instrumented, so outgoing calls carry no traceparent; a message queue where context must be put into message attributes and extracted by the consumer; a thread pool or async boundary where the current context isn’t carried over; and mixed formats, such as one service expecting B3 and another sending W3C, or an AWS hop expecting X-Ray headers.

Fixes: instrument the client or add the propagator explicitly; configure composite propagators (W3C plus B3, plus X-Ray on AWS) during a migration; for queues, inject and extract context per message, or use span links when one consumer processes many messages.

Then I’d prevent regressions: a synthetic request in CI that asserts one trace ID across all expected services, and a TraceQL query on root spans from unexpected services as a dashboard panel.

Quick check: What does the TraceQL operator >> mean?
> is direct child, >> any descendant, ~ sibling.
Quick check: Why must baggage never carry secrets?
Anyone who can see the traffic, and every downstream service, can read it.
Your turnRun POC 27 and write the TraceQL for “payment spans with errors under a checkout server span” using structural(). Then generate a traceparent, convert it to B3 and X-Ray, and decide which of your services would need each.
Key takeaways
  • TraceQL: intrinsics, span and resource attributes, structural operators, aggregates.
  • Traces exist only through propagation: standardise on W3C, use baggage carefully.
  • Pivot freely: spans to logs, logs to traces, metrics to traces.
Grafana · SignalsChapter 7 · POC 28 · 5 min read

Collecting from Kubernetes, AWS, GCP and Azure

You will learn
  • The OpenTelemetry components for Kubernetes and where each must run
  • Kubernetes attributes and how pod association works
  • The two ways to see AWS telemetry in Grafana: query in place or ingest
  • The GCP and Azure data sources and their query languages
  • Performance, cost, limits and security when integrating clouds

Kubernetes

ComponentCollectsRun as
