Kubernetes attributes processorAdds namespace, pod name and UID, start time, deployment and node to every signalAnywhere
Kubeletstats receiverNode, pod, container (and volume) metrics from the kubelet on port 10250DaemonSet
Filelog receiverContainer logs from /var/log/pods, with parsers for JSON, regex, CSV, key-value, URIs and syslogDaemonSet
Kubernetes cluster receiverCluster metrics: pod phases, node conditions, allocatable resourcesExactly one instance
Kubernetes objects receiverAny API object, by periodic pull or a watch stream (typically events)Exactly one instance
Prometheus receiverAnything with a scrape configCareful: replicas scrape everything twice
Host metrics receiverCPU, disk, load, filesystem, memory, network; paging and processes off by defaultDaemonSet; preset scrapes every 10 s, consider 60 s

The Helm chart has presets that wire these up with RBAC: kubernetesAttributes, logsCollection, kubernetesEvents, clusterMetrics, kubeletMetrics, hostMetrics. The attributes processor associates incoming data with a pod by trying sources in order: a k8s.pod.ip resource attribute, then k8s.pod.uid, then the connection’s source IP. It can also copy pod and namespace labels and annotations into attributes, such as an owning team.

AWS: query in place or ingest

CloudWatch data sourceAWS integration
Data livesIn AWS; Grafana queries at read timeCopied into Grafana Cloud: metrics in Mimir, logs in Loki
Query withThe CloudWatch metrics builder (namespace, metric, statistic) and Logs Insights query languagePromQL and LogQL
SetupIAM permissions and credentials on the data source; X-Ray trace links; pre-built dashboardsGuided: CloudWatch metric scrape jobs (only resources with tags are discovered), logs through a Lambda or Firehose
Trade-offNo duplication, but every query is a remote API call (latency and cost)Fast queries and one language; you pay to store a copy

GCP and Azure

CloudData sourceQuery options
Google CloudGoogle Cloud Monitoring (JWT key or GCE default service account)Metrics builder, Monitoring Query Language, SLO queries
AzureAzure Monitor (client secret)Metrics, Logs with KQL, Traces from Application Insights, Azure Resource Graph across subscriptions
Going deeper choosing well

Four considerations

ConcernWhat to weigh
PerformanceRemote data sources add latency at query time; data in Loki, Mimir or Tempo is closer. Some data sources cache
CostShipping and storing a copy, versus API charges per query on the provider’s side
ConstraintsAPI rate limits and quotas, soft or hard; check your expected query volume against them
SecuritySeparate data sources and credentials per concern; Private Data Source Connect for data behind a private network
Say it in an interview

On Kubernetes I run node-scoped receivers (kubelet stats, host metrics, container logs) as a DaemonSet, cluster-scoped ones (cluster metrics, events) as a single instance, and add Kubernetes attributes to everything so signals correlate. For clouds I choose per data set between querying in place, which avoids copies but costs latency and API calls, and ingesting into the same stores as everything else for speed and one query language.

On AWSOn EKS the ADOT collector add-on or the OpenTelemetry Helm chart provides exactly these receivers; give the cluster-level collector a single replica and the node collector a DaemonSet with IRSA. For AWS services, Amazon Managed Grafana’s CloudWatch data source queries in place; when you want AWS service metrics alongside application metrics in AMP, scrape them with the CloudWatch exporter (YACE) or stream them out with CloudWatch metric streams. Container Insights (the CloudWatch Observability add-on) is AWS’s packaged version. POC 28 is the full architecture with a validator.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

You run the cluster receiver in the node DaemonSet and Kubernetes events appear five times each. Why, and what is the right layout?

Show a model answer

The cluster receiver and the objects receiver read cluster-wide state from the API server. Every copy of them sees everything, so a DaemonSet on five nodes produces five copies of every event and cluster metric.

The right layout splits collectors by scope. A DaemonSet for node-scoped data: kubelet stats, host metrics, container log files and OTLP from pods on that node. A single-replica Deployment for cluster-scoped data: the cluster and objects receivers. And usually a gateway Deployment behind a Service for processing, sampling and export, so credentials and fan-out live in one place.

Two refinements. The single cluster collector is a single point of failure for events; Kubernetes restarts it, and a short gap is acceptable, but alert if it stops sending. And if the Prometheus receiver runs in a multi-replica collector, it has the same duplication problem, so shard it or use the operator’s target allocator.

Quick check: Where should the kubeletstats receiver run?
It reads the kubelet of the node it runs on.
Quick check: What is the main trade-off of the CloudWatch data source compared with ingesting AWS data?
Querying in place avoids storing a copy but pays at read time.
Your turnRun POC 28 and break the configs on purpose: move k8s_cluster into the node agent, remove the filelog exclude, drop SigV4 from the AMP exporter. Read each error, then decide which AWS data you would query in place and which you would ingest, and why.
Key takeaways
  • Node-scoped receivers in a DaemonSet; cluster-scoped receivers in one instance.
  • Kubernetes attributes on every signal make correlation possible.
  • Query in place or ingest: weigh latency, cost, limits and security per data set.
Grafana · Running itChapter 8 · POC 29 · 6 min read

Dashboards with a purpose

You will learn
  • Building and improving a first panel: rate, legend, title, description, query type
  • What every panel can configure: units, thresholds, overrides, value mappings
  • Three questions that give a dashboard its purpose, per persona
  • Layout and technical techniques that reduce cognitive load
  • Folders, tags and permissions; the Steven case study

From a query to a useful panel

The chapter’s first dashboard shows why the defaults aren’t enough. Adding app_frontend_requests_total{target="/api/cart"} from Explore gives an ever-rising line with an unreadable legend and a meaningless title. Four edits make it useful: wrap it in rate(…[$__rate_interval]) (Grafana even suggests it), set the legend to {{method}}, give it a title that says it is a rate and a description that says what to look for, and set the query type to Range only so instant points don’t appear on a time series.

What a panel can configure

OptionUse
Title and descriptionSay what it shows and what to do about it; the description appears behind an i icon
LegendReadable series names, and click to filter
Standard optionsUnit, min and max, decimals, display name, colour scheme
ThresholdsColour by value: green, orange, red
OverridesPer-series formatting
Value mappingsTurn values, ranges or regex matches into text or colours: 0 → Down
VisualisationTime series, Stat, Gauge, Bar chart, Table, Logs… play.grafana.org shows them all with real data

Give the dashboard a purpose

Three questions: who is the audience, what do they need, and where will they view it (a wall screen, a laptop, a phone, an emailed PDF)? The personas answer differently.

PersonaNeedsWhere
Diego DeveloperTraffic through his services; deep detail on errors and bugsLaptop
Ophelia OperatorProblems as they happen, clear colours, readable at a glanceWall screen, and laptop when investigating
Steven ServiceThe whole system, and who can fix a problemLaptop
Pelé ProductUsage by feature and device, exportable to a spreadsheetLaptop
Masha ManagerAggregated trends, recovery rates, capacityLaptop, plus scheduled PDF reports

Layout

  • A short top title, and a description saying how to use the dashboard and who it is for.
  • Key indicators first, top left, as Stats with sparklines.
  • A grid that leads the eye; similar visualisations grouped together.
  • Don’t cram: link to other dashboards instead. Transparent panels for breathing space.
  • Rows to group related panels; collapsed rows don’t run their queries until opened, which also makes the dashboard faster.

Technical habits

  • Save often, export JSON, and write meaningful change messages; versions can be compared when something breaks.
  • Use variables instead of hard-coded values, so the dashboard keeps working as systems are added.
  • Default to a relative time range such as now-15m.
  • Transformations reshape data for display; annotations mark deployments and other events on every graph.
Going deeper organising dashboards, and the case study

Folders, tags and permissions

Folders group dashboards and are the boundary for permissions. Tags make related dashboards easy to find. Permissions can be given to users or teams, view-only for people who don’t need to edit, and folders can be hidden on a need-to-know basis.

Case study: a dashboard for Steven

  1. Requirement“An overall view that helps me see the wider picture, and who can solve a problem. On my computer.”
  2. Break it downA top-level view, problem indicators, more detail on demand, help identifying who to call
  3. ResearchThe OpenTelemetry demo’s architecture diagram, conversations with Diego, and a scrapbook dashboard of interesting panels
  4. Choose metricsThe four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation (RED and USE are in the next lesson)
  5. First rowStats with timelines, most important on the left; gauges for saturation; thresholds, overrides and mappings to draw the eye
  6. DetailA collapsed row per team that starts with a text panel of contacts and how to engage them; tables with colour coding; links to support pages

It takes several iterations, and more than telemetry goes into it. That is the point: a dashboard is built for a person and a question.

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the SRE book, the platform book and Mastering Prometheus also cover, from the knowledge map:
  • Four golden signals: Latency, traffic, errors, saturation, with the same names everywhere. See SRE ch 9, platform ch 16.
  • Dashboards and rules as code: Team folders, Terraform, linting in CI. See Prometheus ch 11.
Say it in an interview

Before building a dashboard I ask who it’s for, what question it answers and where they’ll look at it. Then key indicators go first as Stats with sparklines, detail sits in collapsed rows, every panel has a unit and a description, values come from variables, rates use $__rate_interval, and deployments show as annotations. Dashboards live in team folders, as code.

On AWSIn Amazon Managed Grafana, sign-in comes from IAM Identity Center or SAML, and Grafana teams can be mapped from groups, so folder permissions follow your organisation. Manage dashboards as JSON in Git and publish them with the grafana Terraform provider. CloudWatch dashboards are the AWS-native alternative for AWS service metrics. POC 29 generates a golden-signals dashboard with collapsed team rows, lints it against this chapter’s rules, and publishes it to AMG with Terraform.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

A director asks for one dashboard that shows everything about the platform. How do you respond?

Show a model answer

I’d start by asking what decisions it should support, because “everything” on one screen helps nobody. Usually the director wants to know whether customers are affected, whether things are getting better or worse, and where to invest.

That suggests a top-level dashboard with a handful of indicators: SLO compliance and error budget remaining per critical user journey, incident count and time to restore over the quarter, and maybe cost per request. Each is a Stat with a trend, coloured by thresholds agreed with the teams.

Behind it, links rather than more panels: each SLO tile links to the service’s own dashboard, which the owning team maintains; incident tiles link to the incident tool. Collapsed rows can hold a little more detail without loading by default.

I’d also ask where it will be viewed. If it is a weekly review, a scheduled PDF report may serve better than a live screen. And I’d iterate: show a first version, ask which tiles they actually used, and remove the rest.

Quick check: Why put detail panels in collapsed rows?
Collapsed rows defer their queries as well as reducing clutter.
Quick check: What are the three questions that give a dashboard a purpose?
Audience, requirements and viewing context.
Your turnPick one of your dashboards and run it through POC 29’s lint_dashboard() (export its JSON). Fix the findings, then rewrite its description to say who it is for and what question it answers.
Key takeaways
  • Who, what and where come before any panel.
  • Indicators first, detail in collapsed rows, links instead of cramming.
  • Units, descriptions, variables, $__rate_interval and annotations everywhere.
Grafana · Running itChapter 9 · POC 23, 24 · 9 min read

Incident management with Grafana Alerting, OnCall and Incident

You will learn
  • Roles before an incident, and the gold–silver–bronze command structure
  • Cutting noise in telemetry and in communication
  • RED, USE, golden signals, Web Vitals, and white- versus black-box monitoring
  • Escalation, communication and blameless post-incident reviews
  • Grafana Alerting, OnCall and Incident in practice

Being alerted versus being alarmed

Bad incident management is genuinely harmful: stress, burnout, worse. The chapter organises good practice into before, during and after an incident, and draws on the UK government’s emergency response guidance, Atlassian’s incident handbook, ServiceNow’s guide and Google’s SRE books. Frameworks to borrow from include ITIL, Google SRE, NIST and SANS.

Before: roles and structure

CommanderHas authority, calls people in, signs off customer and leadership communication. Every other role reports to them.
CommunicationsInternal, third-party and customer communication, on a cadence.
Technical leadDirects the investigators and knows who is looking at what.
LevelWhoResponsible for
Gold · strategicSenior leadersStrategy, resources and specialists, media, legal, shareholders, approving silver’s plans, leading the debrief
Silver · tacticalDepartment managersThe tactical plan, documented procedures, customer-communication approach, tools, resourcing, keeping gold informed
Bronze · operationalRespondersRunning the incident, informing silver, finding the cause, fixing it, communicating within the plan, post-incident reports

The gold–silver–bronze structure comes from UK emergency services. Most incident frameworks describe only bronze; agreeing silver and gold responsibilities in advance is what lets a serious incident escalate cleanly.

Cutting noise

  • In telemetry: document each service’s critical SLIs, trace calls so service graphs exist, write clear log messages, and don’t flood logs when something fails. AIOps anomaly detection helps but doesn’t replace domain knowledge.
  • In communication: a named group declares incidents and severities; declaring automatically updates a status page and an incident channel; protected channels between bronze, silver and gold; pre-written status messages.

During: knowing something is wrong

MethodSignalsFits
REDRate, Errors, DurationRequest-driven services such as web servers
USEUtilisation, Saturation, Errors (of resources: CPU, memory, I/O, threads)Things that provide resources: storage, a Kubernetes cluster
Golden signalsLatency, traffic, errors, saturation; latency distinguishes slow successes from fast errorsEither
Core Web VitalsLCP, FID (now INP), CLS from real browsersThe user’s experience of a web app

That is white-box monitoring, from inside. Black-box monitoring checks from outside as a user would: synthetic probes (the Prometheus blackbox exporter for HTTP, DNS, TCP, ICMP and gRPC; a third-party service to prove SLA compliance) and real user monitoring. Black-box checks also cover things you don’t control, such as ISPs and DNS, so expect some false positives. Runbooks and a strong post-incident process move an organisation away from a hero culture, where a few people hold everything together at the expense of their health.

Escalation and communication

An escalation policy answers: who is paged first (in hours, out of hours, by severity)? Who is next if they don’t answer? Who takes over, and when (duration, severity, time of day)? How is it handed over? What if two incidents run at once? Leadership must make sure juniors know it is fine to escalate, and audit rotas for overload.

Communication has three strands: the incident team (one paging channel, the bridge link in every alert, an expected response time, and a recorded timeline); internal stakeholders (a regular cadence, even “still investigating” beats silence); and customers (status page, email, social, SMS, the support portal, with pre-approved messages, including one for “we’re investigating a possible issue”).

After: blameless reviews

Blame leads to heavy process, less innovation and people hiding mistakes. A blameless review assumes good intent and keeps accountability without fear of reprimand: open communication, honesty about failure, a detailed timeline from chat and system records, and decisions on improvements.

SLIs, SLOs and SLAs

Three to five SLIs per service; RED, USE, golden signals and Web Vitals are good candidates. With an agreed SLI (“errors in a 15-minute period”) and SLO (“no more than 3% of requests in 10 minutes”), writing an alert is just translating the sentence into PromQL or LogQL. SLAs are contractual and built from SLIs and SLOs; keep the SLOs tighter so the SLA is rarely at risk. The Prometheus track covers burn-rate alerting properly.

Going deeper Grafana Alerting, OnCall and Incident

Grafana Alerting

An alert rule is a query, a reduce step (last, max…), and a threshold. The book’s rule is the percentage of 5xx responses over ten minutes with a threshold of 3, the SLO. States are normal, pending and firing; an evaluation group runs its rules in sequence every minute here, with a five-minute pending period.

Don’t evaluate every 10 secondsEvery minute is 1,440 queries a day per rule; every 10 seconds is 8,640, six times the load for little benefit. And keep the query window at least as long as the evaluation interval, or minutes go unchecked and intermittent errors hide.

Annotations carry a readable summary, a description, a runbook URL and a dashboard link. Labels drive routing. Contact points are named sets of integrations (chat, email, webhooks, Kafka…) with optional notification templates. Notification policies are a tree, like Alertmanager’s, that can match on labels straight from the telemetry, such as service_name, continue to a central team, and apply mute timings. Silences cover maintenance. The admin page exports the Alertmanager configuration as JSON.

Grafana OnCall

OnCall adds alert ingestion from 20+ systems and any webhook, alert groups (firing, acknowledged, silenced, resolved) that responders can merge or escalate, Jinja2 templates that parse each source’s payload (grouping ID, auto-resolve), routes to escalation chains, schedules with overrides, a mobile app, and outbound ChatOps and webhooks to ServiceNow, Jira or Zendesk.

Escalation stepEffect
WaitPause before the next step
Notify users / from on-call schedule / round robinPage people according to their personal notification rules
Notify Slack channel or user groupBroadcast
Trigger outgoing webhookAutomation
Continue if time in range / if more than X alerts in Y minutesConditional escalation
Resolve automatically; repeat (up to 5 times)Finish or loop

Grafana Incident

Declare an incident from Slack and Incident opens a video bridge, updates a status page, records GitHub and Jira context, assigns a commander and investigators, tracks tasks, and builds a timeline of chat, queries, alerts and panels for the review. Its Insights page summarises 90 days of incidents and is meant for silver to review with gold. The machine-learning features include Suggestbot (suggests dashboards from the conversation), OpenAI-written summaries, forecasting, outlier detection, and Sift, which looks for error-log patterns, crashing pods, noisy nodes, throttled containers, recent deployments and slow traces.

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the SRE book, the platform book and Mastering Prometheus also cover, from the knowledge map:
  • SLI, SLO, SLA: Indicator (good events over valid events), objective (the target), agreement (what happens if it is missed). See SRE ch 8, Prometheus ch 13.
  • Four golden signals: Latency, traffic, errors, saturation, with the same names everywhere. See SRE ch 9, platform ch 16.
  • Incident roles: Commander directs, operations acts, communications informs. See SRE ch 10.
  • Blameless postmortem: Why the action made sense at the time; several contributing factors. See SRE ch 4, SRE ch 11.
  • Sustainable on-call: Limits on on-call share, rotation size and incidents per shift. See SRE ch 6, SRE ch 10.
  • Alertmanager routing: A tree of matchers with grouping, inhibition, silences and timers. See Prometheus ch 5.
  • RED and USE: Rate, errors, duration for requests; utilisation, saturation, errors for resources. See SRE ch 9.
  • Gold, silver, bronze: Strategic, tactical and operational levels of incident command. See SRE ch 10.
Say it in an interview

I prepare for incidents before they happen: clear roles (commander, communications, technical lead), an escalation policy, protected channels and pre-written status messages, with gold, silver and bronze levels agreed for serious incidents. I detect with RED for request-driven services, USE for resources, and black-box probes for the user’s view, alert on a few SLIs per service, and finish with a blameless review built from a recorded timeline.

On AWSOn AWS, AWS Systems Manager Incident Manager provides on-call schedules, escalation plans, engagement by SMS, voice and chat, response plans with runbooks, and a timeline; it is triggered from CloudWatch alarms or EventBridge. AMP’s Alertmanager pages through SNS. Amazon Managed Grafana includes Grafana alerting with contact points such as SNS. CloudWatch Synthetics canaries are the black-box probes, CloudWatch RUM the user’s view. Grafana OnCall and Incident are available in Grafana Cloud.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

How would you run the first 30 minutes of a major customer-facing incident?

Show a model answer

First minutes: acknowledge the page, confirm user impact from SLO dashboards or synthetic checks, and declare an incident with a severity. Declaring early is cheap; it starts the machinery: an incident channel, a bridge, a status-page entry.

Assign roles straight away: a commander who coordinates and decides but doesn’t debug, a technical lead who directs investigators, and a communications lead who owns updates to stakeholders and customers on a fixed cadence. In a small team one person may hold two roles, but say so.

Mitigate before diagnosing: the commander asks “what changed?” (deployment annotations, recent config pushes) and pushes for generic mitigations such as rollback, failover or shedding load, while the technical lead runs parallel hypotheses.

Escalate by policy, not by heroics: if it isn’t mitigated within the agreed time, page the next level and inform silver leadership. Customer communication goes out from pre-approved templates, even if it only says we are investigating.

Throughout, the timeline is recorded automatically from the channel, so the blameless review afterwards has facts rather than memories.

Quick check: Which method suits a storage system or a Kubernetes cluster best?
USE describes resources: utilisation, saturation and errors.
Quick check: In the gold–silver–bronze structure, who leads the post-incident debrief?
The book gives the debrief to the strategic, gold level; bronze completes the post-incident reports.
Your turnWrite a one-page incident policy for your team: the three roles, your escalation steps with times, the channels and the three pre-written customer messages. Then compare your paging route with POC 23’s Alertmanager config and POC 24’s page/ticket split.
Key takeaways
  • Roles, escalation and communication are decided before the incident.
  • RED for requests, USE for resources, black-box for the user’s view.
  • Blameless reviews from a recorded timeline; Grafana Alerting, OnCall and Incident cover detection to review.
Grafana · Running itChapter 10 · POC 28, 29 · 6 min read

Automating the observability platform with Helm, Ansible and Terraform

You will learn
  • Why automate, and the four systems of an observability platform
  • The OpenTelemetry Collector Helm chart: modes, presets, pipelines, connectors, values files
  • The OpenTelemetry and Grafana Agent operators, and Ansible on VMs
  • The Grafana Cloud API and the Grafana API, through Terraform and Ansible
  • Dashboards and alert rules as code

Why automate

  • Fewer risks from manual steps.
  • Domain experts encode the data architecture, the system architecture and visualisation practice once, and developers use them correctly without becoming experts.
  • Self-service frees the experts for harder work; a golden path makes adoption quick.
  • Practices scale as the organisation grows, and costs stay attributable.
SystemOwned byAutomated with
Data productionEach application teamThe app’s own tests; schemas validated with JSON Schema
Data collectionPlatform, observability or SRE teamIaC and static analysis
Data storageA vendor, or the collection teamIaC for self-hosted; IaC configuration for SaaS
Data visualisationShared: platform runs Grafana, teams own their dashboardsIaC, with tooling given to teams

The collector’s Helm chart

ModeRunsPresets that belong here
daemonsetOne per nodelogsCollection (with includeCollectorLogs: false to avoid reading its own output), kubeletMetrics, hostMetrics
deploymentA fixed number of replicaskubernetesEvents, clusterMetrics (single replica)
statefulsetStable identitiesThe same, when you need them
anykubernetesAttributes

The config block holds receivers, processors, exporters and connectors, which act as an exporter for one pipeline and a receiver for another. The book’s pipeline uses spanmetrics (RED metrics from spans, with dimensions such as HTTP method and status) and servicegraph (metrics describing calls between services) to feed the metrics pipeline from the traces pipeline. Extensions like health_check sit outside pipelines.

metrics:
  receivers: [otlp, spanmetrics, servicegraph]
  processors: [memory_limiter, filter/ottl, transform, batch]   # name/instance for a second copy
  exporters: [prometheusremotewrite, logging]

A useful Helm habit: split values across files, such as one for the pipeline and one for credentials, and pass several --values flags. The last file wins on conflicts and lists are replaced rather than merged, so arrange them carefully.

Operators and VMs

Running helm upgrade for every change means a central system with credentials for every cluster. The OpenTelemetry Operator instead defines collectors as Kubernetes resources, which CI can validate and GitOps can pull from Git into each cluster, handles some upgrades, and above all injects auto-instrumentation into pods through an annotation. Grafana has an Agent chart and an Agent Operator with resources for metrics and logs. On VMs, the collector ships as .deb, .rpm and .apk packages with its config at /etc/otelcol/config.yaml; Grafana maintains an Ansible collection with a grafana_agent role.

Going deeper the APIs, Terraform and Ansible

Two APIs

APIManagesKey resources
Grafana Cloud APIThe SaaS accountAccess policies and tokens (keys are deprecated), stacks, plugins, regions
Grafana APIAny Grafana, cloud or self-hostedDashboards and folders (UIDs are global, IDs local), permissions (1 view, 2 edit, 4 admin), search, teams, the whole alerting model

Applications should use service accounts. The Terraform provider covers both APIs: a cloud stack data source, an access policy scoped to a stack with logs:write, metrics:write and traces:write, a token for collectors (best written straight into a secrets manager), and in the instance, folders, dashboards and rule groups.

resource "grafana_dashboard" "team" {
  for_each    = fileset("${path.module}/dashboards", "*.json")
  config_json = file("${path.module}/dashboards/${each.value}")
  overwrite   = true
}

Ansible’s Grafana collection manages stacks and dashboards (iterate with with_fileglob), but at the time of writing it didn’t support the new alerting model; Terraform’s grafana_rule_group does. Keep dashboard deployment, owned by teams, separate from infrastructure tooling, owned by the platform team.

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the SRE book, the platform book and Mastering Prometheus also cover, from the knowledge map:
  • Configuration as code: Versioned, reviewed, tested and rolled out like a binary. See SRE ch 14, platform ch 15, Prometheus ch 12.
  • Golden path: The supported, documented, easiest way to do a common task. See SRE ch 18, platform ch 18, platform ch 19.
  • Collector topology: Node agents, a single cluster agent and a gateway, with buffers sized for outages. See Prometheus ch 14.
  • Dashboards and rules as code: Team folders, Terraform, linting in CI. See Prometheus ch 11.
Say it in an interview

I treat the observability platform as four systems: production owned by app teams, collection and storage by the platform team, visualisation shared. Collectors deploy through Helm or the OpenTelemetry Operator with node-scoped presets in a DaemonSet and cluster-scoped ones in a single replica; connectors like spanmetrics and servicegraph derive metrics from traces. Grafana itself, access policies, folders, dashboards and alert rules are all Terraform, with dashboards owned by teams in their own folders.

On AWSTerraform manages the AWS side (AMP workspaces, rule groups namespaces, Alertmanager definitions, the Amazon Managed Grafana workspace and its IAM role) and the grafana provider manages what is inside the workspace. On EKS, the ADOT add-on installs the OpenTelemetry Operator, which can inject auto-instrumentation into pods by annotation. Store collector tokens and Grafana service-account tokens in AWS Secrets Manager. POC 28 has the collector configs; POC 29 has the AMG Terraform with dashboards, folder permissions and an alert rule group.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

How would you let 30 product teams manage their own dashboards and alerts without the platform team becoming a bottleneck or the instance becoming a mess?

Show a model answer

Give each team a folder they own, with edit rights there and view rights everywhere else, managed in Terraform and synced from identity groups. That bounds what they can break.

Give them a paved road: a repository template with dashboards as JSON (or generated from a small library), alert rules as code, and a pipeline that lints dashboards (units, descriptions, variables, rate windows), checks rules with promtool or Pint, and applies with Terraform using a team-scoped service account.

Provide building blocks rather than reviews: a golden-signals dashboard generator, SLO rule generators, and mixins for shared infrastructure, so most teams only fill in parameters.

The platform team owns the Grafana instance, data sources, access policies, contact points and the default notification policy tree, and watches usage dashboards to spot problems. Changes to shared pieces go through the platform repo; changes inside a team folder don’t need us at all.

Quick check: What is a collector connector?
spanmetrics and servicegraph turn trace pipelines into metric pipelines this way.
Quick check: Why run logsCollection only in daemonset mode?
The filelog receiver reads files on the local node.
Your turnIn POC 29, add a second team folder and dashboard to terraform/amg.tf, generate its JSON with golden_signals_dashboard(), and run the tests. Then sketch the CI pipeline a team would use to change it.
Key takeaways
  • Four systems, different owners: automate each where it lives.
  • Collector modes and presets must match scope; connectors derive metrics from traces.
  • Grafana Cloud and Grafana APIs through Terraform; teams own dashboards in their folders.
Grafana · Running itChapter 11 · POC 28 · 7 min read

Architecting an observability platform

You will learn
  • Starting from the problem, and agreeing a data architecture with the organisation
  • Which signal suits which data, and testing organisation-specific fields
  • Data production standards and collection patterns: agentless, agent, gateway, Kubernetes
  • Deployment modes for Loki, Mimir and Tempo, and planning for failure
  • Proofs of concept, RBAC, and sharing telemetry with SIEM and BI

Start with the problem

The most undervalued step is articulating what the organisation is trying to solve, with leadership: customer-affecting incidents (a compliance, operational and reputational risk), visibility of KPIs, how customers use the product, and the cost to serve them (COGS and OPEX). The answers decide what data you need.

Data architecture

Observability systems are data systems, and their data is most valuable when it joins up with the rest of the organisation. Find whoever owns the organisation’s data model. The author’s cautionary tale: months spent arguing whether tenantID and customerID were the same thing, then months of rework in two systems and the logging platform, all avoidable with an owner and early requirements.

Translate external requirements into an observability requirements document, in MoSCoW form (must, should, could, won’t). Finance needing cost centres, for example, could be met by putting it on every signal, by requiring an organization.costcenter label on every service, or by a service-to-cost-centre lookup table. Pick one and write it down.

StoreBest for
Loki log fieldsString state (error, warn), business fields (service, customer, user), low- to medium-cardinality indexed fields and high-cardinality unindexed ones; links to traces
Prometheus / MimirNumeric state (records processed), service and host labels, low- to medium-cardinality dimensions such as HTTP method
Tempo spansSystem state, high-cardinality fields, business attributes such as customer ID, cross-system context
Kubernetes labels and cloud tagsOwnership and cost allocation, attached to every signal at collection

Libraries are well tested; your organisation-specific fields, like customer ID, are not, and executives may make decisions on them. Test them like any other output; the book recommends Martin Fowler’s article on domain-oriented observability.

System architecture

The standard the book proposes for applications: OpenTelemetry SDK; logs to stdout and stderr; metrics both on a Prometheus endpoint and over OTLP; traces over OTLP to localhost:4317 or 4318. The Prometheus endpoint is there so the Kubernetes HPA, through the Prometheus adapter, can scale on request rate rather than only CPU, which is the steam-engine governor again: a system that corrects itself.

For Kubernetes the book combines them: a node agent on every node (OTLP, kubelet, host metrics), a gateway for processing, and a single cluster agent for the Kubernetes API, because any more would duplicate data. State which protocols are preferred and which accepted, set end-of-life dates for the ones you want gone, and keep default ports.

Storage and visualisation

The first question is who is responsible: an internal team, or a vendor with a contract (helpful when something goes wrong). If you run it yourself, Loki, Mimir and Tempo each have modes:

ModeShapeProduction?
MonolithicEverything in one process, scaled by adding copies; read and write can’t scale independentlyNo
MicroservicesEach component deployed and scaled separatelyYes, for Mimir and Tempo
Simple scalable (Loki only)Separate write, read and backend targetsYes, for Loki

Failure

An agent that fails can only be restarted. A pipeline that fails can buffer: in memory with the batch processor, on disk with the file storage extension. Size the buffer from how long an outage you must tolerate and your throughput, and publish that tolerance as an SLI of the collection layer.

Going deeper proofs of concept, access and other consumers

Proving a design

Production is the real test, so build the path to production early. Before that, use local clusters (k3d, KinD, MicroK8s, minikube; the authors like KinD), Vagrant for VMs, demo applications (the OpenTelemetry demo, AWS’s One Observability Workshop, the simpler mythical-creatures app), and replayed data with k6, Locust, Postman, Insomnia or ghz for gRPC, recorded with Wireshark or Fiddler.

Access

Grafana Cloud has organisation roles for billing, stacks, members and support. Inside a Grafana instance there are basic roles (Admin, Editor, Viewer, None for service accounts, and a server-wide Grafana Admin), fixed roles that add specific permissions, and custom roles created through the API or Terraform. Permissions also apply per data source, team, dashboard and folder. In Grafana Cloud, separate parts of the organisation with stacks rather than organisations.

PersonaAccess
DiegoRead everything; edit dashboards and alerts only in his service’s folder
StevenView dashboards; manage on-call schedules and silences
PeléView dashboards and incident history, plus a limited service account to feed business metrics to BI

Audit powerful provisioning service accounts; let a senior team member manage their own team’s limited account.

Other consumers

Logs often feed a SIEM and aggregates a BI platform. Either fork data in the collection pipeline (agree needs to avoid paying to store everything twice) or query Grafana on a schedule, ideally from recording rules that precompute the business metric, such as daily unique logins.

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that Mastering Prometheus also covers, from the knowledge map:
  • Collector topology: Node agents, a single cluster agent and a gateway, with buffers sized for outages. See Prometheus ch 14.
Say it in an interview

I start an observability platform from the business problems and the organisation’s data model, decide which signal carries which field, and publish a production standard: OpenTelemetry SDKs, logs to stdout, metrics on a Prometheus endpoint and OTLP, traces over OTLP. Collection uses node agents, a gateway and a single cluster agent on Kubernetes, with buffers sized from the outage I need to survive; storage runs in microservices or simple scalable mode, or with a vendor; access is least privilege by folder and team.

On AWSA typical AWS reference: ADOT node agents and a gateway on EKS; metrics to AMP, traces to X-Ray or Tempo, logs to CloudWatch Logs or Loki on S3; Amazon Managed Grafana with IAM Identity Center groups mapped to Grafana teams and folders; cost allocation through EKS pod labels and AWS cost allocation tags; security logs forked to Security Lake or a SIEM in the collector; business aggregates exported from recording rules to S3 for Athena or QuickSight. Separate AMP workspaces or AMG data sources for load-test and CI environments.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Design the observability architecture for a company moving 200 services onto EKS.

Show a model answer

I’d start with the questions it must answer: customer-impacting incidents, SLOs per user journey, cost per team. That gives the data requirements: every signal carries service, namespace, team and cost centre, from Kubernetes labels at collection, and the organisation’s customer ID on spans and logs, not on metrics.

Production standard for the 200 services: OpenTelemetry SDKs or auto-instrumentation via the operator, logs as JSON to stdout, metrics on a Prometheus endpoint (for HPA) and OTLP, traces over OTLP with W3C propagation and parent-based sampling.

Collection per cluster: ADOT node agents as a DaemonSet (OTLP, kubelet, host, container logs with Kubernetes attributes), one cluster agent for events and cluster metrics, and an autoscaled gateway for tail sampling, span metrics, filtering and export with IRSA credentials, routing spans by trace ID so tail sampling sees whole traces. Disk buffers sized for 30 minutes of backend outage.

Storage: AMP for metrics, X-Ray or Tempo on S3 for traces, CloudWatch Logs or Loki on S3 for logs; Amazon Managed Grafana on top with folder-per-team permissions. Load-test and CI telemetry go to separate workspaces.

Operating it: everything in Terraform and Helm through GitOps; SLO rules generated per service; a platform SLO for the collection layer itself; and usage and cardinality dashboards so we see cost growth before the bill does.

Quick check: Why does the book run exactly one cluster agent on Kubernetes?
Cluster-scoped receivers would duplicate every event and metric in each copy.
Quick check: Which deployment mode does the book recommend for Loki in production?
Simple scalable separates write, read and backend targets; microservices is recommended for Mimir and Tempo.
Your turnWrite a one-page MoSCoW requirements document for your organisation’s observability data: which fields must appear on every signal, which should, and where each type of field lives. Then check POC 28’s configs against it.
Key takeaways
  • Start from the business problem and the organisation’s data model.
  • Put each field in the signal that suits it; test your organisation-specific fields.
  • Agent, gateway and a single cluster agent; buffers sized for failure; least-privilege access.
Grafana · Running itChapters 12–13 · POC 30 · 7 min read

Real user monitoring, continuous profiling and load testing

You will learn
  • What Faro collects and how Frontend Observability is set up
  • Web Vitals and their targets
  • Pivoting from a user session to backend traces and logs
  • Continuous profiling with Pyroscope: top table, flame graphs, eBPF versus SDKs
  • The six kinds of load test, and k6 checks, thresholds, options and life cycle

Real user monitoring

RUM measures what real users experience in their browsers, all the way through to the backend. Grafana’s version is the open-source Faro Web SDK in your web app, a hosted collector (or your own agent), and a Frontend Observability app with Overview, Errors and Sessions tabs. By default Faro sends Web Vitals, unhandled exceptions, browser details, page URL changes, a session ID and activity traces; it uses opentelemetry-js for tracing. Logs go to Loki and traces to Tempo; the metrics are generated from logs with LogQL.

Setting up an app asks for a name, the allowed CORS origins, extra Loki labels and an acknowledgement of the cost, then offers NPM, CDN-with-tracing or CDN-without-tracing snippets.

Web VitalMeasuresGood
LCP · Largest Contentful PaintWhen the largest visible element has rendered≤ 2.5 s
FID · First Input DelayFrom first interaction to the browser handling it≤ 100 ms (replaced by INP, March 2024)
CLS · Cumulative Layout ShiftHow much visible content moves≤ 0.1
TTFB · Time to First ByteRequest to first response byte≤ 0.8 s
FCP · First Contentful PaintPage start to anything visible≤ 1.8 s
INP · Interaction to Next PaintWorst interaction latency over the visit, ignoring outliers≤ 200 ms

From the Sessions tab, a session ID opens its own vitals, exceptions and, if the backend is traced, links into the traces and on to backend logs: one user’s experience reconstructed end to end. A session starts when Faro initialises and ends when the visitor leaves (the end event isn’t sent by default). Enhancements, each with configuration effort and some browser overhead: frontend tracing, custom errors, measurements, logs, and events (stored in Loki with kind=event).

Continuous profiling

Profiles are the fourth signal: which functions use CPU and memory, sampled continuously (every 15 seconds by default in Pyroscope, with a few percent overhead), so code behaviour can be tied to what users were doing. Pyroscope (founded 2020, acquired 2023, merged with Grafana’s Phlare) uses the same horizontally scalable, object-storage architecture as Loki, Mimir and Tempo. Its query is selection only: a profile type and tags.

Top tableSelf: time spent in the function itself. Total: time including everything it calls. High self time is a hot function; high total, low self is a hot path.
Flame graphDepth is the call stack; width is the share of samples. The x-axis is not time. Wide boxes are candidates, but only domain knowledge says whether they are a problem.
ClientStrengthsWeaknesses
eBPFWhole-node profiles, any language, Kubernetes metadata for freeLinux kernel constraints, weak tagging of user code, memory profiles expensive, awkward locally
Language SDKs (Go, Java, .NET, Python, Ruby, Rust, Node.js)Flexible tags, detailed, memory profiles, easy locallyHard across many languages; infrastructure tags by hand. Only Go supports pull
AWS Lambda extensionProfiles inside functions: why is it slow, costly or failing?Lambda only
Going deeper load testing with k6

Load testing

TestLoadDurationAnswers
SmokeMinimalMinutesDoes it work at all? Run after every deploy
Average loadTypicalShortHow does it behave normally?
StressAbove-average peakUnder a dayCan it sustain a peak?
SpikeSudden, hugeShortWhat does a surge or attack do?
BreakpointRamping upLongWhere does it break?
SoakAverageLong, e.g. 48 hLeaks and slow degradation

Keep load-test telemetry away from production stacks: it is high volume and low value. Running your own storage in the test environment, with the same dashboards, is an advantage of open-source tooling.

k6 came from Grafana’s acquisition of LoadImpact. Tests are JavaScript (without Node modules) run from a CLI that can pause, resume and scale tests, locally, on Kubernetes through an operator, or in Grafana Cloud. A browser module tests real pages.

import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
export const options = {
  vus: 100, duration: '30m',
  thresholds: { http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'], http_req_duration: ['p(95)<200'] },
};
export default function () {
  const res = http.get('http://www.acme.com');
  check(res, { 'is status 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}

Checks record pass or fail without failing the test; thresholds fail the run, and the book suggests deriving them from your SLOs. The life cycle is init code (once per virtual user), setup() once, the default function per iteration, and teardown() once, skipped if setup failed. From the CLI: k6 run -u 10 -i 20 test.js, or stages such as -s 20s:50 -s 60s:50 -s 10s:0; replace run with cloud to use cloud runners.

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the SRE book and the platform book also cover, from the knowledge map:
  • Client-side telemetry: What servers can’t see: DNS, certificates, crashes, retries hiding errors. See SRE ch 9.
  • Fleet-wide profiling: One profiler everywhere shows which shared component costs the most. See platform ch 14.
  • Continuous profiling: Self time and total time; flame graph width is share of samples. See platform ch 14.
  • Load test types: Smoke, average, stress, spike, breakpoint, soak; thresholds from SLOs. See SRE ch 15.
Say it in an interview

I measure the user’s side with RUM, judging Web Vitals such as LCP, INP and CLS at the 75th percentile and following a bad session into backend traces. I use continuous profiling to explain why code is slow or expensive: self time for hot functions, total time for hot paths. And I load test with thresholds taken from our SLOs, using smoke tests after every deploy and stress, spike, breakpoint and soak tests before big events, with their telemetry kept out of production.

On AWSCloudWatch RUM collects Web Vitals, JavaScript errors and sessions and links to X-Ray traces; CloudWatch Synthetics runs scripted canaries. For load tests, k6 on EKS with the k6 operator, Grafana Cloud k6, or the Distributed Load Testing on AWS solution; send their telemetry to a separate AMP workspace. For profiling, run Pyroscope on EKS with the eBPF DaemonSet or language SDKs. POC 30 turns SLOs into k6 thresholds, scores Web Vitals at p75 and computes a top table and flame-graph widths.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Checkout conversion dropped 5% after a release, but every backend metric looks normal. How do you investigate?

Show a model answer

Normal backend metrics with a drop in conversion points at the client side, so I’d go to real user monitoring first. Compare Web Vitals before and after the release by page and browser: a rise in LCP or INP on the checkout page, or in CLS (a button moving as users tap it), would explain lost conversions without any server error.

Then errors: Faro or CloudWatch RUM shows unhandled JavaScript exceptions by page, browser and version. A new exception in a payment widget on one browser is a classic cause, and invisible to backend metrics because the request is never sent.

Then sessions: follow a few sessions that reached checkout and didn’t complete. Where tracing is on, the session links to backend traces, so I can see whether calls were slow, retried or never made.

If I find a regression, I roll back or fix forward, and add a guard: a Web Vitals threshold in the release pipeline’s synthetic test, and a RUM-based SLO for the checkout journey, so the next one pages instead of showing up in a business report.

Quick check: In a flame graph, what does the width of a box represent?
Width is proportion of samples; the x-axis is not time.
Quick check: What is the difference between a k6 check and a threshold?
Thresholds turn SLO-style criteria into a pass or fail result.
Your turnRun POC 30. Feed rate_vital() the LCP and INP values from your own site’s RUM (or from a Lighthouse run), and generate a k6 script for a spike test with k6_script(kind="spike"). Which threshold would fail first?
Key takeaways
  • RUM measures the user’s experience; Web Vitals are judged at p75.
  • Profiles explain cost and slowness: self time versus total time.
  • Six load test shapes; thresholds from SLOs; keep test telemetry separate.
Grafana · Running itChapters 14–15 · POC 30 · 8 min read

Observability across the DevOps life cycle, troubleshooting, and what’s next

You will learn
  • From Agile to DevOps to platform engineering, and why the life cycle is only a tool
  • What Grafana contributes at each phase: code, test, release, deploy, operate, monitor, plan
  • Monitoring third-party platforms: observability, CI, CD, resource and security platforms
  • Preparing data collection and the Grafana stack, and a checklist for debugging each
  • Pitfalls to avoid, and the trends to watch

The life cycle, with a caution

Iterative methods (RAD, Scrum, XP, FDD) predate the 2001 Agile Manifesto, which values individuals and interactions, working software, customer collaboration and responding to change. DevOps (the first DevOps Days was 2009) brought developers, testers and operators together; Werner Vogels’ 2006 “you build it, you run it” became its slogan. Team Topologies warns of the anti-patterns and cognitive load that follow when that is applied badly. The DevOps life cycle is a useful frame, but it is a tool: don’t value it above the people.

PhaseWhat Grafana and observability contribute
CodeInstrument (libraries, SDKs, injection at deploy; decide who owns it), plan custom fields so they can be tested, and run a local Grafana stack for instant feedback
TestMonitor the CI platform; k6 end-to-end tests that can rerun at deploy time. Beware Rube Goldberg pipelines of custom CI metrics
ReleaseShow the new version meets its SLOs, ideally under k6 load; release dashboards linking test reports and tickets
DeployWatch the rollout on dashboards; black-box checks through OnCall; deployment annotations via the API; let the CD job query Loki, Mimir and Tempo and roll back automatically; deploy dashboard changes with Terraform in the same window
OperateSLOs, errors, incidents (integrated with ServiceNow and the like); support teams reconstruct sessions from RUM and traces
MonitorUnderstand to improve: RUM for usage, metrics plus logs plus traces for slow functions, profiles for why, SLOs for behaviour, infrastructure data for scaling, metrics for long-term trends
PlanHow many customers does this affect? How much capacity headroom is left? (k6 spike, stress and breakpoint tests)

The difference between operate and monitor is the aim: operate keeps the system working for customers now; monitor documents how it works so the next plan improves it.

Automated deployment verification

Watching a dashboard during a deploy works when deploys are rare. When they are frequent, write it into the pipeline: query the error ratio from logs, confirm logins succeed (tied to a smoke test), check calls to downstream services, and roll back automatically if any check fails. That cuts the time to recover from bad releases and frees engineers during deploys. POC 30 implements the gate.

Monitoring platforms you didn’t build

PlatformWhat to do
Observability platformEat your own dog food: SLIs, SLOs, dashboards, incident process. Use the community OpenTelemetry Collector dashboards. Plan for the SaaS being down: be able to spin up Prometheus or a full stack per cluster (the authors learned this painfully). Control noisy sources: compartmentalise, revoke keys, filter, switch off
CI (GitHub Actions, GitLab, Jenkins, Azure DevOps…)“Why did my build fail?”: runner failures and noisy neighbours need platform data. Logs and metrics, no traces needed. DORA metrics need agreed definitions. A separate Grafana stack for CI
CD: push (Jenkins, Actions) and pull (Argo CD, Flux)Annotate every deployment. Pull tools expose Prometheus metrics and events. Push tools that both consume third-party code and hold production credentials are a supply-chain risk worth monitoring closely
Resource platforms (databases, caches, queues, web servers)OpenTelemetry contrib receivers or Prometheus exporters, plus public dashboards. Monitoring a database is not the same as using it as a Grafana data source
Security tools (Falco, OPA, kube-bench, Trivy)Many expose metrics. Share one log pipeline with the security team, and watch it closely
Going deeper chapter 15: troubleshooting and the future

Prepare before you collect

The authors repeatedly find agents deployed without thought, sending everything: undefined telemetry and big bills. Plan for what is, not what might be; adding later is easier than removing. Questions first: who the customers are, which log formats exist, where data comes from, which metrics serve SLOs, whether tracing helps, what dashboards need.

SignalDecisions
LogsAn extensible format; Loki labels chosen for cardinality (extract the rest at query time); which metrics come from logs
MetricsDrop what you don’t need, or just its worst labels; read each protocol’s definitions; protect verbose protocols (limit histogram buckets); add exemplars
TracesValidate span accuracy; sampling, filtering and retention
Libraries and collectorMaintained libraries; prove the collector works in your environment, including permissions on the path to production; know its support model

Debugging checklists

Telemetry missingGrafana misbehaving
Collector logs for errorsSend test data with curl or Postman straight to the API
Rejections: sample too old, trace too large, rate limitedBreak big queries down: short ranges, strong filters
Credentials: expiry and scopesFunction order matters, as in maths
Ports and protocols on ingestCount data points; cap max data points; raise the minimum interval; group to shrink results
Sampling or redaction changing dataUsage Insights: top dashboards, data sources and users with errors
Exporters and the next hopBilling/Usage dashboard for limit rejections; cardinality dashboards
Network: firewalls, network policiesQuery history to compare attempts

Pitfalls and trends

  • Treat the platform as a product that evolves; requirements from many customers; a 6- and 12-month roadmap.
  • Watch cost at collection, where it is cheapest to fix; fix cardinality early with standards and governance.
  • Isolate high-load, low-value environments such as performance tests in cheaper, short-lived stacks.
  • Monitor your platform’s usage and your collector estate.

The trends the authors point to: cost reduction (usage dashboards, Adaptive Metrics, Log Volume Explorer), AI (generated panel titles, incident summaries, root-cause analysis after Grafana’s acquisition of Asserts.ai), better developer tooling (a VS Code extension for dashboards), OpenTelemetry maturing into the standard, fleet management for collectors (OpAMP; Grafana Agent Flow, now Grafana Alloy), and platform engineering making observability the default.

Across the booksIdeas in this lesson that the SRE book, the platform book and Mastering Prometheus also cover, from the knowledge map:
  • Progressive rollout: Small exposure first, growing in stages with bake time. See SRE ch 14, SRE ch 17, platform ch 16.
  • Automatic rollback: A regression halts and reverts the rollout without a human. See SRE ch 17, platform ch 16.
  • Platform SLOs: The platform is everyone’s single point of failure and needs stricter objectives. See platform ch 16.
  • Platform as a product: Customers, a value proposition, a lifecycle; jobs to be done. See platform ch 19.
  • Scrape limits: sample_limit and label limits fail a scrape that would explode cardinality. See Prometheus ch 7.
  • Deployment verification: Query telemetry after a deploy and roll back automatically. See SRE ch 14, platform ch 16.
  • Observability cost: Plan what you need, drop at collection, isolate noisy environments. See Prometheus ch 7.
Say it in an interview

I use observability at every phase: a local stack while coding, SLO evidence under load at release, deployment annotations and automated verification with rollback at deploy, SLOs and incidents in operate, and usage, profiles and trends in monitor to feed planning. I treat the observability platform itself as a product with SLOs and a disaster plan, and I control cost at collection: plan what you need, drop what you don’t, fix cardinality early, and isolate noisy environments.

On AWSAutomated verification on AWS: CodeDeploy deployment groups with CloudWatch alarms for automatic rollback, or Argo Rollouts analysis runs querying AMP. Post Grafana annotations from CodePipeline or GitHub Actions. Monitor the observability platform itself: AMP and AMG publish usage metrics to CloudWatch, and collectors expose their own metrics. For a SaaS outage, keep a minimal in-cluster Prometheus or a CloudWatch fallback dashboard. Track cost with AMP and CloudWatch usage metrics and cost allocation tags per team.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Your observability bill doubled in six months while traffic grew 20%. What do you do?

Show a model answer

Find where the growth is before cutting anything. Usage dashboards (Grafana Cloud’s Billing/Usage, or AMP and CloudWatch usage metrics) split it by signal; then by team or service using the labels and cost-allocation tags we require on every signal.

Metrics growth is almost always cardinality: a new label with unbounded values, more histogram buckets, or a new exporter scraping everything. Cardinality dashboards and TSDB status find the label; drop it at the collector, set limits, and fix the instrumentation with the team.

Logs growth is usually debug logs left on, a chatty dependency, or a noisy environment such as load tests sharing the production stack. Log volume by app finds it; drop at the collector and move load tests to their own cheap stack.

Traces: check sampling. Moving from head sampling of everything to tail sampling that keeps errors and slow traces plus a small baseline cuts volume a lot without losing the useful traces.

Then prevent recurrence: governance at collection (limits, required labels, end-of-life for old protocols), cost per team visible on a dashboard, and a review in the platform roadmap. Plan for what is, not what might be.

Quick check: What is the main difference between the operate and monitor phases in the book?
Same tools, different aim.
Quick check: What should the observability platform team have for a SaaS outage?
The authors advise a simple, tested disaster plan, learned the hard way.
Your turnUse POC 30’s verify_deployment() with three checks that matter for one of your services. Then write the disaster plan for your observability backend being down for four hours: what still alerts, who notices, and what you spin up.
Key takeaways
  • Observability helps at every phase, not just operate.
  • Automate deployment verification; annotate every deploy.
  • Treat the observability platform as a product: SLOs, a disaster plan, and cost control at collection.
Hands-on · SLO journeyLesson 1 of 5 · SRE ch 8 “Critical User Journeys”, ch 9 · POC 31 · 4 min read

One SLO for a journey: measure it where the customer is

You will learn
  • What a critical user journey (CUJ) is, and why it gets one SLO
  • Why the journey SLI is measured at the edge, not by averaging services
  • How to define valid and good events in writing

Press Place order in an online shop and a chain starts: checkout checks the basket, reserves stock, charges the card through a payment provider and saves the order. Five teams own those pieces. The customer sees one thing: did my order go through, quickly? Your SRE book calls this a critical user journey, a series of steps a user takes to do something that matters to them, and it gets one SLO.

Measure where every attempt passes

The SLI is the share of events that were good. For checkout an event is one attempt to place an order, and a good one ends with a confirmed order in under two seconds. Count them at the load balancer, gateway or ingress: every attempt passes there, including the ones that fail before any service runs. Add client-side measurement later (it needs a looser target, because phones and patchy networks add noise) and a synthetic probe that places a real test order. The book warns that probing only the home page tests a fraction of what matters.

Why not average the services’ own numbers?

  • Unseen failures. A crashed checkout pod never records the requests it dropped; the load balancer records the 502 it sent back.
  • Absorbed failures. A payment call that failed and was retried successfully looks bad on payment’s dashboard and was fine for the customer.
  • Accidental weighting. Inventory might answer ten calls per order and payment one, so an average of success rates weights them by accident.

Service numbers still matter: they show where a problem is, and each team uses them for its internal SLO (lesson 2).

Write down what counts

EventValid?Good?
Order confirmed (200) in 0.4 sYesYes
Card declined, answered 200 “declined” in 0.3 sYesYes: a correct answer
Order confirmed, but in 3.4 sYesNo: slow
502 from the load balancer: no checkout pod readyYesNo
429 from your own rate limiter during a saleYesNo: your system turned them away
400 malformed formNo: the customer sent something broken
Health checks and load testsNo: not customers
Recommendations panel failed, order confirmed in 1.1 sYesYes: soft dependency
Say it in an interview

I set one SLO per critical user journey and measure it where every attempt passes, the load balancer or gateway, as confirmed outcomes within a latency threshold over valid attempts. I don’t average service success rates: a crashed service can’t count what it dropped, retried failures never reached the customer, and the average weights services by call volume. Service metrics are for diagnosis and internal SLOs.

On AWSOn EKS, measure at the ingress controller or gateway (route and status labels) and scrape it with ADOT or the AMP managed collector. An ALB’s CloudWatch metrics have no per-route detail, so they can’t give a per-journey SLI by themselves. Add CloudWatch RUM for the client view and a CloudWatch Synthetics canary that places a test order.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Checkout calls five services and each has a good dashboard. Why not average their success rates to get checkout’s SLI?

Show a model answer

Because the customer experiences one thing: did my order go through, quickly? I’d measure that where every attempt passes, at the load balancer or gateway, as confirmed orders under two seconds divided by valid attempts.

Averaging service numbers goes wrong three ways. A service can’t count requests that never reached it, like the 502s while its pods were crashing. A failure one service records may have been retried and never reached the customer. And services handle different numbers of calls per order, so an average weights them by accident.

I still use the service metrics, to find where a problem is and as each team’s internal SLO, just not as the journey’s SLI.

Quick check: Checkout’s pods were OOM-killed for 20 minutes; the load balancer returned 502 to 4% of attempts. Does checkout’s own success metric show it?
Only the load balancer saw those attempts. POC 31 exercise 2 shows it live.
Quick check: Which event should be left out of valid events?
Valid events are real customer attempts; your own 429s and timeouts are bad events, not excluded ones.
Your turnClone the repo and start POC 31 (make prometheus && make up). After three minutes run python lab.py status, then do exercise 1 in EXERCISES.md: compute the journey SLI by hand from edge_request_duration_seconds_count and compare it with the recording rule.
Key takeaways
  • One SLO per critical user journey, measured where every attempt passes.
  • Never average service SLIs into a journey SLI.
  • Write down valid and good events before you write any query.
Hands-on · SLO journeyLesson 2 of 5 · SRE ch 8, Appendix E · POC 31 · 4 min read

What target can the design actually meet?

You will learn
  • Who agrees the target, and what data to bring
  • Serial dependencies multiply; parallel ones multiply failures
  • The rule of the extra nine, and splitting the budget into internal SLOs
  • Why latency percentiles don’t add

Who sets the number

Your SRE book is clear that engineering doesn’t pick the target alone: business, product, engineering and operations agree it together, because missing it has business consequences. Its example is three nines for everything except checkout at four, and it finds fewer than five top-level SLOs enough for most services. Bring two things to that meeting: what the edge has measured over recent months, and the design’s ceiling, the best availability the way it’s built allows even if every team does its job.

Hard dependencies multiply

A hard dependency is one every order needs. With independent failures, multiply success rates: five at 99.9% give about 99.5%. For small numbers, add the failure rates instead. Appendix E’s example: a service calling an 80% and a 90% dependency in turn can reach 72% at most; calling both in parallel and taking the first answer (hedging), it fails only when both fail, so it can reach 98%. A soft dependency, one with a fallback, leaves the product entirely.

Checkout’s ceiling: change the design

Set each piece’s availability and whether an order needs it. The bar shows how much of the error budget the hard pieces use between them.

The rule of the extra nine

Each critical dependency should be about one nine better than the service relying on it: 99.99% for a 99.9% checkout. Each then uses about a tenth of the budget. With five, half the budget is gone before checkout’s own bugs, which is why removing a hard dependency is often the cheapest reliability win.

Split the budget into internal SLOs

At 99.9% over 30 days the budget is about 43 minutes of total outage. Turn each share into a number: 99.99% by default; if the card provider’s record is 99.97%, give payment a deliberate third (0.1% ÷ 3 ≈ 0.033%, an internal SLO of about 99.967%) and squeeze the rest. Measure each internal SLO as the success rate of checkout’s calls to that dependency. The book describes internal SLOs as covering smaller pieces of a journey with no money changing hands: a team that misses one puts engineering time into the fix. With many dependencies, set the journey and core-component SLOs first and negotiate the middle.

Latency doesn’t add up

The 99th percentile is the time 99% of requests beat. If cart’s p99 is 300 ms and payment’s 800 ms, checkout’s p99 can be above or below 1.1 s, depending on whether slow calls land on the same orders. In POC 31, with 2% slow calls on two dependencies, each p99 read about 1.5 s and the journey’s 1.74 s, nowhere near their 3-second sum. Budget time per step, measure the journey end to end.

Say it in an interview

Before agreeing a target I check the design’s ceiling: hard dependencies multiply, so five at 99.9% cap the journey near 99.5%. I give each critical dependency an internal SLO about one nine tighter, measured from the caller’s side, make dependencies soft where a fallback exists, and never add latency percentiles; I measure journey latency at the edge.

On AWSOn AWS the same arithmetic applies to managed services: check each service’s published availability (and your own measured record) before promising a journey SLO. Multi-AZ and multi-provider designs are the hedged case, but only if the copies share nothing that fails together.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

The payment team asks what internal SLO they should hold so checkout can meet 99.9%. What do you tell them?

Show a model answer

Payment is a hard dependency: no payment, no order. Checkout’s 99.9% lets 0.1% of checkouts fail, about 43 minutes’ worth a month, and that has to cover checkout’s own deploys and every other dependency too.

By the extra-nine rule payment should hold 99.99%, which uses about a tenth of the budget. If the provider’s record makes that impossible, we give payment a bigger share on purpose, say a third (about 99.967%), and squeeze the others.

It’s measured as the success rate of checkout’s calls to payment. If even that isn’t realistic, we make payment softer, for example by accepting the order and confirming payment shortly after, or we lower checkout’s target.

Quick check: Four hard dependencies, each 99.95%, independent failures. Best the journey can do?
0.9995⁴ ≈ 0.998.
Quick check: Two independent replicas at 99% each, hedged (first answer wins). Availability?
It fails only when both fail: 0.01 × 0.01.
Your turnIn the ceiling widget, start from the defaults (below target). Make the fewest changes that reach 99.9%, then do POC 31 exercise 6 (recommendations soft, then hard) and watch the same effect in live traffic.
Key takeaways
  • Hard dependencies multiply; fallbacks and hedging raise the ceiling.
  • Dependencies need internal SLOs about one nine tighter, measured from the caller.
  • Percentiles don’t add: measure journey latency end to end.
Hands-on · SLO journeyLesson 3 of 5 · SRE ch 8; Appendix E assumptions · POC 31 · 4 min read

What breaks the simple maths

You will learn
  • When retries help and when they don’t
  • Shared parts that break independence
  • Async work, third parties, and who owns the journey SLO

The multiplication rules assume each failure is independent of the others. Real systems break that assumption in predictable ways, and interviewers ask about all of them.

Retries help only when failures are independent

If the card provider drops 0.5% of calls at random, one retry means a payment fails only when both attempts fail: 0.005 × 0.005 = 0.0025%. If the same 0.5% comes as outages, the retry lands in the same outage and fails too. Retries also add load just when a dependency struggles and add time to the journey: cap them, back off, and use an idempotency key so a repeated charge is ignored. In POC 31, 2% random payment failures burned budget at about 20×; one retry brought the journey down to 0.4× while payment, seen from checkout, still showed about 98%.

Check that “independent” is true

Two inventory replicas that read one database, run on one network or ship through one pipeline fail together. Treat them as one dependency no better than the part they share, not as a 99.9999% pair.

Async work gets its own SLI

The confirmation email goes through a queue after the order is saved. The order succeeded even if the email is late, so email isn’t in the checkout SLI. Give it a freshness SLI: 99% of confirmation emails sent within five minutes of the order.

Third parties count against you

The card provider’s failures are your customers’ failures, so they stay in the SLI. You can’t fix the provider, so you design around it (careful retries, a second provider, confirm-payment-later) and set the target from its measured record, not its contract.

One team owns the journey SLO

Usually the team that owns checkout, with SRE support, owns the journey SLO and its error budget policy. Dependency teams own their internal SLOs. Policies often carve out exceptions: Google’s example lets a team keep releasing when another team’s outage spent the budget and that team has frozen its own releases. Your SRE book adds that a policy usually applies only to committed SLOs, and that a monthly reset keeps one bad January from freezing releases all year.

Say it in an interview

Retries rescue scattered failures, not outages, and they hide failures from the journey, not from the dependency’s own SLI. Shared databases or networks break the independence that multiplication assumes. Async work gets its own freshness SLI, third-party failures stay in mine, and the journey’s owner holds the error budget policy while dependencies hold internal SLOs.

On AWSRetries with exponential backoff and jitter are built into the AWS SDKs; check the defaults before adding your own on top, or retries multiply. For multi-AZ “redundancy”, look for shared parts: one RDS primary, one NAT gateway, one deploy pipeline.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

A dependency fails 1% of calls. A teammate proposes three retries to make it disappear. What do you say?

Show a model answer

It depends on how the failures arrive. If they’re scattered and independent, one retry already cuts the dependency’s impact to about 0.01% of orders; three is overkill and adds load and latency.

If the 1% comes as outages, retries a few hundred milliseconds apart all land inside the same outage, so they barely help and they pile load onto a struggling service.

So I’d look at the failure pattern first, cap retries at one or two with backoff and jitter and an idempotency key, and for outages invest in a fallback or a second provider instead.

Quick check: Two replicas at 99.9% each, hedged, both reading one 99.95% database. Best availability?
The shared database fails both at once, so it sets the limit.
Quick check: Emails are delayed two hours by the mail provider. Effect on the checkout SLO?
The orders succeeded on time; async work has its own SLI.
Your turnDo POC 31 exercises 3–5: 2% random payment failures, then one retry, then the same rate as outages. Note the burn rate and payment’s own success rate each time.
Key takeaways
  • Retries multiply away independent failures only.
  • Look for shared parts before you trust a parallel design.
  • Async work, third parties and ownership each need an explicit decision.
Hands-on · SLO journeyLesson 4 of 5 · SRE ch 8 “Automatic Alert Configurations”; Mastering Prometheus ch 13 · POC 31 · 4 min read

The journey SLI and burn-rate alerts in PromQL

You will learn
  • Recording rules for good, valid and error ratio
  • The histogram bucket trap in Prometheus 3
  • Multiwindow burn-rate pages and tickets
  • Rolling several SLIs into one: the bad-minute rule

An SLI is a ratio of two rates: good events per second over valid events per second. Latency comes from a histogram: each _bucket series with label le counts requests at or under that boundary, and _count counts all of them. These are the rules POC 31 runs:

rules/checkout-slo.yml
- record: journey:checkout_good:rate5m
  expr: sum(rate(edge_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route="POST /checkout", code=~"2..", le=~"2(\\.0)?"}[5m]))
- record: journey:checkout_valid:rate5m
  expr: sum(rate(edge_request_duration_seconds_count{route="POST /checkout", code!="400"}[5m]))
- record: journey:checkout_error_ratio:rate5m
  expr: 1 - journey:checkout_good:rate5m / journey:checkout_valid:rate5m
# repeated for 30m, 1h, 6h, 3d and 30d
The le trap

A bucket only exists where the histogram has a boundary (defaults: 1, 2.5, 5 s), and Prometheus 3 stores bucket labels in float form, le="2.0", even when a client sends 2. An exact le="2" then matches nothing: the good rate is empty, the error ratio is empty and no alert can ever fire. We found this while building POC 31; the rules match le=~"2(\\.0)?".

Burn-rate alerts

Burn rate is the error ratio divided by the budget ratio (0.1% for 99.9%). A burn of 14.4 spends 2% of a 30-day budget in an hour. The fast page needs both the last hour and the last five minutes above it: the hour proves it matters, the five minutes stops the page soon after a fix. A second page at 6× over 6 hours and 30 minutes, and a ticket at 1× over 3 days and 6 hours, catch slower leaks. Your SRE book says Google now generates these from each SLO definition, and uses a Wilson score test instead of fixed thresholds for services under about 100 requests an hour.

rules/checkout-slo.yml
- alert: CheckoutBudgetBurnFast
  expr: |
    journey:checkout_error_ratio:rate1h > (14.4 * 0.001)
    and
    journey:checkout_error_ratio:rate5m > (14.4 * 0.001)
  for: 2m
  labels: {severity: page, journey: checkout}
RuleLong windowShort windowBurnBudget usedAction
Fast1 h5 min14.4×2% in an hourPage
Slow6 h30 min6×5% in six hoursPage
Leak3 d6 h1×10% in three daysTicket

Test the rules like code

POC 31 pins each behaviour with promtool unit tests: healthy traffic stays quiet, a 15-minute outage pages and clears five minutes after the fix, a two-minute blip pages nobody, slow successes burn budget, 400s aren’t valid, and a missing 2-second bucket leaves the SLI empty.

terminal
cd rules && promtool test rules checkout-slo.test.yml

Several requests, no single edge

When a journey is several requests with no single one covering it, multiply each step’s ratio, or use the rule from your SRE book’s chapter 9: judge the journey minute by minute and count a minute as bad if any step’s SLI was bad. That is a window-based SLO, the kind Mastering Prometheus builds with bool and a subquery:

solutions/bad-minute.yml
- record: journey:checkout_bad_minute:bool
  expr: max(dep:checkout_dependency_error_ratio:rate1m{dep!="recommendations"} > bool 0.001)
- record: journey:checkout_good_minutes:ratio_1h
  expr: 1 - avg_over_time(journey:checkout_bad_minute:bool[1h])
Say it in an interview

I record good and valid rates at the edge for every alert window, page when the 1-hour and 5-minute burn rates both exceed 14.4×, page again at 6× over 6 hours, ticket at 1× over 3 days, and test the rules with promtool, including a check that the SLI returns data at all, because on Prometheus 3 an exact le="2" matcher silently matches nothing.
