On AWSLoad the same rule files into Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus as rule group namespaces and route severity=page and severity=ticket through the AMP alert manager to SNS and Incident Manager. POC 31’s terraform/amp.tf does exactly this.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Your burn-rate alert didn’t fire during a real outage. What do you check?

Show a model answer

First whether the SLI returns data at all: run the good and valid recording rules on their own. A matcher that finds nothing, such as le="2" when Prometheus 3 stores le="2.0", or a renamed route label, makes the error ratio empty, and an empty comparison never fires.

Then the windows and thresholds: was the outage long enough for the 1-hour window to cross 14.4× with the for duration? A 10-minute outage at 100% does; a 10-minute outage at 5% doesn’t, by design.

Finally the pipeline: did Prometheus evaluate the rules (rule evaluation failures), was the alert routed (Alertmanager receivers, silences, inhibition)? Then I’d add a promtool test that reproduces the outage so it can’t regress.

Quick check: SLO 99.9%, last-hour error ratio 1.8%, last 5 minutes 0.2% after a fix. Does the fast page fire?
Both windows must be above 14.4 × 0.1% = 1.44%.
Quick check: Why match le=~"2(\.0)?" instead of le="2"?
Label matching is exact text; POC 31 exercise 9 shows the empty result.
Your turnRun make rules-test in POC 31. Then break one rule on purpose (change the matcher to le="2"), rerun, and read which test catches it.
Key takeaways
  • An SLI is good rate ÷ valid rate, recorded for every alert window.
  • Fast page: 1 h and 5 min above 14.4×; test the rules with promtool.
  • Check that every SLI series returns data.
Hands-on · SLO journeyLesson 5 of 5 · About 90 minutes · verified end to end with Prometheus 3.5 · POC 31 · 5 min read

Lab: run the shop, break it, watch the SLO react

You will learn
  • Start the shop, load and Prometheus on your laptop
  • Predict, break, observe: eight exercises
  • Write an internal SLO and the bad-minute rule yourself

POC 31 runs this track’s checkout for real: an edge (the load balancer), checkout and five dependencies, about ten orders a second, and Prometheus running the rules from lesson 4. You change things from the terminal with lab.py. With Docker you also get a Grafana dashboard. For each exercise, write your prediction down before you run it.

terminal
git clone https://github.com/phaniuk111/sre && cd sre/poc-31-checkout-journey-slo-lab
pip install prometheus_client
make prometheus        # one time: prometheus + promtool into ./bin
make up                # shop + load + Prometheus on :9090   (or: make compose-up, adds Grafana on :3000)
python lab.py status   # after about 3 minutes
Windows are real

A page needs its condition to hold for 2 minutes and stops about 5 minutes after the fix. Wait, and reset each change before the next exercise (python lab.py chaos <service> --reset).

1 · Kill checkout: who notices?

terminal
python lab.py stop checkout
sleep 150; python lab.py status
python lab.py start checkout
What you should see

The journey SLI falls and the edge answers 502, but checkout’s own metric still reads 100%: it isn’t being scraped and never received those requests. The fast page fires after 2 minutes and stops about 5 minutes after the restart, while the 1-hour burn rate is still huge.

2 · Payment fails 2% of calls, then one retry

terminal
python lab.py chaos payment --error-rate 0.02 --mode random
sleep 180; python lab.py status
python lab.py config --retries payment=1
sleep 330; python lab.py status
What you should see

Without the retry the burn rate is about 20× and it pages. With one retry the journey drops to about 0.4× (we measured 0.036% errors), but payment, as checkout sees it, still shows about 98%.

3 · The same rate as outages

terminal
python lab.py chaos payment --error-rate 0.1 --mode outage --period-s 300
sleep 330; python lab.py status
What you should see

A block of 503s every five minutes; with the retry still on, we lost about 9% of orders over a five-minute window. The retry lands in the same outage.

4 · Recommendations: soft, then hard

terminal
python lab.py chaos recommendations --error-rate 0.05
sleep 120; python lab.py status
python lab.py config --recommendations hard
sleep 330; python lab.py status
What you should see

While soft, recommendations show about 95% and the journey is untouched. Once hard, the journey loses about 5% of orders and pages.

5 · Slow successes and a long tail

terminal
python lab.py chaos payment --latency-ms 2300               # (a)
python lab.py chaos payment --reset
python lab.py chaos cart --slow-rate 0.02 --slow-ms 1500    # (b)
python lab.py chaos payment --slow-rate 0.02 --slow-ms 1500
What you should see

(a) Every order is a 200, yet the SLI collapses: a slow success is a bad event. (b) We measured cart p99 1.47 s, payment 1.52 s and the journey 1.74 s, nowhere near the 3-second sum.

6 · Write payment’s internal SLO

Write recording rules and a fast-burn alert for payment at 99.99% (budget ratio 0.0001) from checkout_dependency_attempts_total{dep, outcome}, routed as a ticket to the payment team. Load it and repeat exercise 2 with the retry on.

What you should see

The journey stays healthy and its page stays quiet, but PaymentInternalSLOBurnFast fires with owner=payment-team. Compare with solutions/internal-slos.yml.

7 · The le trap

terminal
python lab.py promql 'count by (le) (edge_request_duration_seconds_bucket)'
python lab.py promql 'sum(rate(edge_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="2"}[5m]))'
What you should see

The bucket is stored as le="2.0", and le="2" returns nothing.

8 · The bad-minute rule

Write a 0/1 bad-minute rule from the per-dependency error ratios (ignore recommendations) and the share of good minutes in the last hour, then run python lab.py chaos inventory --error-rate 0.005.

What you should see

The request-based SLI barely moves (0.5% of orders fail), but most minutes turn bad, because at ten orders a second almost every minute contains a failure. Compare with solutions/bad-minute.yml.

EXERCISES.md in the repo has all eleven, including reading the SLI by hand and deploying the same rules to Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus with Terraform.

Say it in an interview

I’ve built this end to end: a shop with five dependencies, a journey SLI at the edge, multiwindow burn-rate alerts tested with promtool, and chaos experiments showing that retries fix scattered failures but not outages, that soft dependencies raise the ceiling, and that slow successes burn budget too.

On AWSterraform/amp.tf in POC 31 creates an AMP workspace, loads the journey and internal SLO rules as rule group namespaces, and routes pages and tickets to two SNS topics. Point a local Prometheus at it with remote_write and SigV4, then terraform destroy when you finish.

Interview practice

Answer aloud for two minutes before you open the model answer.

Tell me about a time you tested your alerting.

Show a model answer

In my SLO lab I wrote the journey SLI and burn-rate alerts as recording and alerting rules, then pinned their behaviour with promtool unit tests: an outage pages and clears five minutes after the fix, a two-minute blip pages nobody, slow successes burn budget.

Then I ran the real system and injected faults: I killed checkout and watched the edge SLI drop while checkout’s own metric stayed at 100%, and I compared random failures with outages to show that retries only help the first.

The most useful finding was a silent failure: on Prometheus 3 an exact le="2" matcher returns nothing, so the alert could never fire. Now every SLI rule has a test that it returns data.

Quick check: In exercise 2, after adding one retry, what does payment’s own success rate (seen from checkout) show?
Retries hide failures from the journey, not from the dependency’s internal SLO.
Quick check: In exercise 3, why doesn’t the retry help?
Retries rescue independent failures only.
Your turnDo all eight exercises, writing your prediction before each one. Then explain exercise 2’s result out loud in under a minute, as if to an interviewer.
Key takeaways
  • Measure, break, observe: the numbers you can quote come from your own runs.
  • Retries, soft dependencies and slow tails each move the SLO differently.
  • Test that every SLI returns data.

Study notes written in my own words from Site Reliability Engineering, 2nd Edition (Beyer, Jones, Leng, Huska, Petoff, Murphy; O’Reilly). from the early release of Platform Engineering at Google (O’Reilly; 10 of 31 planned chapters), from Mastering Prometheus (William Hegedus; Packt, 2024) and from Observability with Grafana (Rob Chapman and Peter Holmes; Packt, 2024). They don’t replace the books. Code and Terraform: github.com/phaniuk111/sre.

SynthesisAll four books on one page

Executive summary

The short version of all four books, and where they meet. S8 means SRE chapter 8; P15 means platform book chapter 15 in its final numbering; M3 means Mastering Prometheus chapter 3; G9 means Observability with Grafana chapter 9. The references are links.

The books in one paragraph each

Site Reliability Engineering, 2nd Edition describes how to run software so that it is as reliable as its users need and no more. It treats operations as an engineering problem, makes reliability measurable through service level objectives and error budgets, and organises everything else as a pyramid, the hierarchy of production health: culture at the base, then awareness, preparedness, infrastructure design, resilient products and, at the top, platforms that make services reliable by default.

Platform Engineering at Google starts where that pyramid ends. Its claim is that security, reliability and efficiency can’t be delivered by asking every developer to be careful. They have to be moved down into the languages, libraries, pipelines and infrastructure that all code is built on, so that experts solve each problem once and every team inherits the result. Only ten of its thirty-one planned chapters are published.

Mastering Prometheus (Hegedus, 2024) goes underneath the query language. It explains how the time series database stores samples, how discovery and relabeling decide what is scraped, how Alertmanager routes and groups, and then how to scale: sharding, high availability, remote storage, Thanos, mixins, CI for rules, SLOs and OpenTelemetry. Its theme is that Prometheus is simple until it isn’t, and that most trouble is cardinality.

Observability with Grafana (Chapman and Holmes, 2024) is the wider view: logs with Loki, metrics with Mimir and Prometheus, traces with Tempo, collected by OpenTelemetry and joined up in Grafana. Its second half is about running observability for an organisation: dashboards built for a person and a question, incident management, automation, platform architecture, real user monitoring, profiling, load testing and the DevOps life cycle.

What the SRE book argues

  • 100% is the wrong target. Pick a target from what users need, and treat the gap as a budget to spend on change. (S2, S8)
  • Culture comes first. Blameless learning, psychological safety and sustainable on-call are the base of the pyramid, not a soft extra. (S1, S4)
  • Measure from the user’s side. SLOs belong to user journeys, alerts fire on how fast the budget burns, and low-traffic services need statistics, not thresholds. (S8, S9)
  • Mitigate before you understand. Clear roles, generic mitigations and practised emergency modes shorten incidents more than better diagnosis does. (S10, S17)
  • Accidents are control problems. STPA and CAST replace the hunt for a root cause with the question of why the system allowed the unsafe action. (S11, S12)
  • Changes cause most outages. So test configuration like code, roll out progressively, compare a canary with a control, and roll back automatically. (S14, S17)
  • Shift down. The durable fix for a class of failure is a platform that makes it impossible or handles it by default. (S18, S23)
  • AI cuts both ways. AI systems need quality as a reliability signal, and AI operators need autonomy that is earned, bounded and reversible. (S19–S21)

What the platform book argues

  • Shift down, not only left. Shifting left finds a problem earlier and leaves it with the developer. Shifting down makes the platform responsible. (P15, P16)
  • Conformity buys leverage. The more an ecosystem limits choice, the more liability it can carry for its users. Make that trade explicit with resources, rights and responsibilities. (P12)
  • Coupling is a decision. It buys efficiency, performance, atomicity and traceability and costs reuse, extensibility, robustness and choice. The danger is coupling nobody chose. (P9)
  • Layers move at different speeds. Experiments and products are fast; infrastructure, directives, culture and law are slow. Fast layers propose and slow layers decide. (P10)
  • If it isn’t secure, it shouldn’t compile. Wrap each risky operation in a safe abstraction so the vulnerable program can’t be written, then carry the same idea into builds and deployment. (P15)
  • SRE is the blueprint; the platform is the machinery. Put into the platform whatever has a wide blast radius, needs rare expertise or fails catastrophically. (P16)
  • One optimisation, every team. Shared foundations let you see the whole fleet and fix the biggest consumer once, on by default. (P14)
  • A platform nobody uses is worth nothing. Design the experience, run the platform as a product, and measure adopters against non-adopters. (P18, P19)
  • AI amplifies what is already there. Good platforms and current documentation make assistants useful; poor ones make the mess arrive faster. (P22, P24)

What the two observability books add

  • Cardinality is the cost. Every label value is a new series in memory, in the index and on the bill. Limit it at the scrape, review it in CI, and keep IDs out of labels. (M3, M7, G4, G15)
  • Know what rate() really does. It is reset-aware and extrapolates to the window edges; use $__rate_interval and at least four scrape intervals. (M3, G5)
  • Alerting needs routing, not just rules. Group, inhibit and silence in Alertmanager; send every Prometheus to every Alertmanager; add a dead man’s switch. (M5, M6, G9)
  • Scale by federation of storage, not of servers. HA pairs with a replica label, then remote write or Thanos for global queries and retention. (M6, M9, M10)
  • Treat monitoring as code. Mixins, unit-tested rules, Pint in pull requests, dashboards and alert rules in Terraform. (M11, M12, G10)
  • Burn-rate SLO alerts are generated, not hand-written. Request-based for steady traffic, window-based for low traffic. (M13, S8)
  • Each signal stores different things. Numbers in metrics, events in logs with few labels, high-cardinality context in traces; link them with exemplars and trace IDs. (G4, G5, G6, G11)
  • Collect with a topology. Node agents, one cluster agent and a gateway that does tail sampling and span metrics, with buffers sized for outages. (G10, G11, M14)
  • Observability runs through the life cycle. Local stacks while coding, SLO thresholds in load tests, annotations and automatic verification at deploy, RUM and profiles in operation. (G12, G13, G14)
IdeaIn SRE or platform bookIn the observability books

Where the two books meet

IdeaIn the SRE bookIn the platform book
Reliable by defaultEmergent reliability, the top of the pyramid (S1, S18)The whole thesis: quality attributes as properties of the platform (P12, P15, P16)
Budget for riskError budgets and a policy with three zones (S8)Risk profiles: the budget sets the deployment policy automatically (P16)
Design for human errorBlameless postmortems, STPA and CAST (S11, S12)Safe abstractions and guardrails that make the mistake impossible (P15)
Make the right way the easy wayGolden paths over mandates; the effectiveness zone (S18)Path of least resistance; “friction is a directive” (P12, P18)
Hyrum’s lawUsers depend on the reliability you actually deliver (S8)Hidden dependencies block change; randomise what you don’t promise (P9, P14)
Safe changeCanaries, progressive rollout, config testing (S14, S17)Canary analysis as a platform gate; signed artifacts; blueprints (P15, P16)
Break the rules safelyEmergency modes with independent fallbacks (S17)Break-glass: permitted, logged, alerted, reviewed (P16)
Sublinear scalingCost grows more slowly than the service (S2)Cost of each capability paid once and amortised (P14, P16)
AIEarned, reversible autonomy for agents (S21)Guardrails as a containment field for generated code (P12, P15)

The difference is the point of view. The SRE book is written from the seat of the people operating services. The platform book is written from the seat of the people building what those services stand on. In an interview, the strongest answers use both: name the principle, then say which platform mechanism makes it the default.

How to turn this into interview answers

  1. Principle. One sentence, in your own words.
  2. Mechanism. The concrete thing that enforces or measures it.
  3. AWS. Which services you would use.
  4. Evidence. One number or one story from the books or from your own work.

Example: “We shouldn’t rely on reviewers to catch SQL injection. I’d wrap the database driver in a typed query API and fail the build on raw queries. On AWS that is a wrapper over the RDS Data API and a CodeBuild check. Google reports no SQL injection in protected applications for over ten years with this approach.”

What this summary does not cover

  • Twenty-one chapters of the platform book are not published yet, including the ones that define ecosystem types, shifting down and golden paths.
  • SRE appendices E and F were read once, not twice. Citation-only footnotes in the platform book were skipped.
  • These are study notes in my own words. They don’t replace either book.
  • The two Packt observability books were read in full once, figures included; corrections to their examples are noted in the lessons and POCs.
